# The OSF/1 calls, from the OSF/1 1.0 manual

This is the second half of the specification our server is tested
against. `docs/osf1-interface.md` holds what cuts across calls: boot,
the system-call path, threads and signals, the Mach seam. This file
holds each call on its own: its arguments, flags, defaults, side
effects, return values and every error, as the OSF/1 manual states
them. Each item is one behaviour a test can check.

Begun 23 October 2026.

## The source

The OSF/1 1.0 manual as DEC shipped it for MIPS ("OSF/1 1.0 (TIN)
MIPS"), kept at `https://typewritten.org/Manual/DEC/OSF:1/1.0/mips/`.
It is the earliest OSF/1 manual that is public. Each page is headed
either "OSF", a reference page OSF supplied with OSF/1, or "Digital", a
page DEC wrote. Most pages also have an "ENVIRONMENT NOTES" section,
which the manual describes as "system features that are not generic to
OSF/1 but that are provided in this OSF/1 implementation".

Our baseline is OSF/1 R1.2 (`docs/osf1-interface.md`, "The baseline").
No R1.2 manual is public. Where 1.0 and R1.2 differ, VSX and VSE decide.

The pages used: all of section 2, and the parts of sections 3, 4, 5, 7
and 8 that bear on the system interface — signals, terminals, timers,
scheduling, threads, `sysconf` and `pathconf`, the IPC structures,
`signal.h`, `termios.h`, `limits.h`, `inittab`, `fstab`, the special
files, and `init`, `getty`, `mount`, `swapon`, `kloadsrv` and the boot
and shutdown commands. That is 332 manual names whose text makes 265
distinct pages, written up as 4,431 items: 919 errors, and
2,655 behaviours tagged [OSF/1], 684 [DEC], 118 [Compat] and
55 [Fortran]. Each page's SHA-256, as fetched on 23 October 2026, is
in `docs/reference/osf1-1.0-man.sha256`. The pages are DEC's and OSF's
copyright, and are cited, not carried. This file restates the interface
they describe, which is functional fact; it quotes only short phrases
where the exact words decide a test.

## How this was made

Each page was converted to text, then written up by one agent into
items, under fixed instructions: every behaviour and every error is an
item; nothing is added from general knowledge; "may", "unspecified" and
"implementation-defined" are kept as written. A second agent then
checked every item against its page, fixed what was wrong and added
what was missing. A script checked that every error number a page names
appears in its items. Nothing was taken from source code.

## How to read it

Each page is a section headed with all the names that share its text.
Under the heading:

- `Page:` the page it comes from, and the names that share it.
- `Origin:` whether OSF or Digital wrote the page.
- Items, `**name-N**` for behaviour and `**name-EN**` for errors. Pages
  from sections other than 2 add the section to the name, so
  `mount.8-3` is the third item of `mount(8)`; a Fortran page adds
  `.3f`.
- `Test:` lines say how a program checks an item. Error items have
  none: produce the condition, expect −1 and that `errno`, unless the
  page says otherwise.
- `Note:` lines record where the page itself is wrong, unclear or
  damaged. They say what the page says; they do not correct it.
- `Related:` the page's own list of related pages.

Scope tags:

- `[OSF/1]` stated by an OSF page as the interface. A conforming server
  must do this.
- `[DEC]` from an ENVIRONMENT NOTES section, said by the page to be DEC,
  ULTRIX or MIPS specific, or from any page DEC wrote. A guide, not a
  requirement.
- `[Compat]` said by the page to exist for compatibility — with BSD,
  System V, or "older" or "old" UNIX systems — or to be had only
  through the compatibility libraries `libbsd` or `libsys5`.
- `[Fortran]` from a page that documents the Fortran library
  `libU77.a` under a C name. Out of scope.

Where this file and `docs/osf1-interface.md` meet, the two should
agree; where they do not, the disagreement is recorded there as an ERR
entry.

## Section 2 — system calls

### exit(2), atexit(2), _exit(2)

Page: `man2/_exit.html`; same text as `atexit(2)`, `exit(2)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**exit-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`) for `atexit()` and `_exit()`.
  Test: link a program calling `atexit` and `_exit` with only libc.
Note: The page's LIBRARY line names only `atexit()` and `_exit()`, not `exit()`.

**exit-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `void exit(int status)`, `void _exit(int status)`, `int atexit(void (*function)(void))`, with `<stdlib.h>` included.
  Test: compile calls to all three against `<stdlib.h>`.

**exit-3** [OSF/1] `status` indicates the status of the process.
  Test: covered by exit-15.

**exit-4** [OSF/1] `atexit()` registers functions to be called at normal process termination for cleanup processing.
  Test: register a function that writes a marker to a pipe; after `exit(0)` the parent reads the marker.

**exit-5** [OSF/1] Registered functions form a push-down stack: the last function registered is the first called.
  Test: register A then B, each writing its letter; child calls `exit(0)`; parent reads "BA".

**exit-6** [OSF/1] A function registered more than once is called again for each registration.
  Test: register A twice; on exit the output is "AA".

**exit-7** [OSF/1] Up to 32 functions can be registered with `atexit()`.
  Test: 32 calls to `atexit` all return 0.

**exit-8** [OSF/1] `atexit()` returns 0 on success, and a nonzero value if there is an attempt to register more functions than the `atexit()` array can hold.
  Test: register 32 functions (each returns 0), then a 33rd; check whether it returns nonzero.
Note: The page says "up to 32" but does not state that the 33rd call must fail; the array may hold more.

**exit-9** [OSF/1] `exit()` first calls the Standard I/O Library `_cleanup()` function to flush buffered output, then calls the functions registered with `atexit()` in reverse order of registration.
  Test: `printf("x")` without newline to a pipe then `exit(0)`; the parent reads "x".
Note: The page says `_cleanup()` is called before the `atexit` functions, and then says again that `exit()` flushes all output streams; the order relative to the handlers is not fully clear.

**exit-10** [OSF/1] `exit()` also flushes all open output streams, closes all open streams, and removes all files created by `tmpfile()`.
  Test: child writes buffered data to an `fopen`ed file and calls `exit(0)`; parent sees the data in the file. Removal of `tmpfile()` files: compare free inodes (`statfs`) of the temp file system before and after the child exits.

**exit-11** [OSF/1] Finally `exit()` calls `_exit()`, which completes process termination and does not return.
  Test: code after `exit(0)` is never reached (child writes nothing after the call).

**exit-12** [OSF/1] `_exit()` closes all file descriptors, directory streams and message catalog descriptors open in the calling process. Errors in these close operations go unreported.
  Test: child holds the write end of a pipe and calls `_exit(0)`; the parent's read returns 0 (EOF).

**exit-13** [OSF/1] Exiting does not terminate the process's children. The parent process ID of all its children and zombie children is set to the process ID of `init`, which inherits them, catches their `SIGCHLD` signals and calls `wait()` for each.
  Test: child forks a grandchild and `_exit`s; the grandchild keeps running and `getppid()` returns 1.
Note: The page says "the process ID of init" without giving the number; 1 is the usual value but the page does not state it.

**exit-14** [OSF/1] If the parent is in `wait()` or `waitpid()`, it is notified of the termination and the low-order 8 bits (0377 or 0xFF) of `status` are made available to it.
  Test: child `_exit(0x1234)`; parent's `waitpid` gives `WEXITSTATUS` = 0x34.

**exit-15** [OSF/1] If the parent is not waiting when the child terminates, it may wait later and get the child's status then. Meanwhile the child becomes a zombie, and the parent is sent `SIGCHLD`.
  Test: child `_exit(7)`; parent sleeps 1 s then `waitpid`; gets status 7.

**exit-16** [OSF/1] A zombie occupies a process table slot but has no other space in user or kernel space. The slot is partly overlaid with time accounting information used by `times()` (see `sys/proc.h`). A zombie remains until its parent issues one of the wait functions; then its process table entry is released.
  Test: child `_exit(5)`; parent sleeps 1 s, then `waitpid` still returns the child's PID with status 5 (the zombie persisted until waited for).

**exit-17** [OSF/1] The parent is sent `SIGCHLD` when a child terminates; since the default action for this signal is to ignore it, it usually is not seen.
  Test: parent installs a `SIGCHLD` handler; child exits; the handler runs. With default action, the parent is not killed.

**exit-18** [OSF/1] If the exiting child's parent is ignoring `SIGCHLD`, the child's parent process ID is changed to that of `init`, which catches `SIGCHLD` and calls `wait()`.
  Test: parent sets `SIGCHLD` to `SIG_IGN`, child exits; Not directly observable from user space except that no zombie remains (`kill(pid,0)` fails with `ESRCH` soon after).

**exit-19** [OSF/1] If the process is a controlling process, `SIGHUP` is sent to each process in the foreground process group of its controlling terminal, and the controlling terminal is disassociated from the session so that a new controlling process can acquire it.
  Test: on a pseudo-terminal, a session leader with a foreground child catching `SIGHUP` exits; the child gets `SIGHUP`.

**exit-20** [OSF/1] If the exit causes a process group to become orphaned and any member of that group is stopped, `SIGHUP` is sent to each process in the newly orphaned group.
  Test: child in its own process group stops itself (`SIGSTOP`) with a `SIGHUP` handler; its parent (the only link outside) exits; the child receives `SIGHUP`.
Note: The page does not mention `SIGCONT` here; tests should not require it.

**exit-21** [OSF/1] Each attached shared memory segment is detached and `shm_nattach` in its data structure is decremented by 1.
  Test: child attaches a segment and exits; `shmctl(IPC_STAT)` shows the attach count back to its earlier value.
Note: The page spells the field `shm_nattach`.

**exit-22** [OSF/1] For each semaphore for which the process set a `semadj` value, that value is added to the semaphore's `semval`.
  Test: child does `semop` with `SEM_UNDO` adding 1 and exits; the semaphore value returns to its earlier value.

**exit-23** [OSF/1] If the process has a process, text or data lock, an unlock is performed (see `plock()`).
  Test: as root, child calls `plock(PROCLOCK)` and exits; parent can then `plock` without error.

**exit-24** [OSF/1] If system accounting is enabled, an accounting record is written to the accounting file (see `acct()`).
  Test: as root with accounting on, a child's exit grows the accounting file.

**exit-25** [OSF/1] Locks set by `fcntl()`, `flock()` and `lockf()` are removed.
  Test: child takes an `fcntl` write lock and exits; parent's `F_SETLK` on the same range then succeeds.

**exit-26** [OSF/1] If a thread calls `_exit()`, the entire process exits and all threads in the process are terminated.
  Test: create a second thread that loops forever; main thread calls `_exit(3)`; parent's `waitpid` returns status 3 promptly.

**exit-27** [OSF/1] NOTES: the system `init` process assists cleanup of terminating processes. A replacement `init` program must accept `SIGCHLD` signals and issue a `wait()` for each.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires replacing `init`).

**exit-28** [OSF/1] `exit()` and `_exit()` do not return.
  Test: as exit-11.

Related: Functions: acct(2), sigaction(2), times(3), wait(2), sigvec(2)

### accept(2)

Page: `man2/accept.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**accept-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int accept(int socket, struct sockaddr *address, int *address_len)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**accept-2** [OSF/1] `socket` must have been created with `socket()`, bound with `bind()`, and have had a successful `listen()`.
  Test: `accept` on a bound socket without `listen`; expect `EINVAL`.

**accept-3** [OSF/1] `address` points to a `sockaddr` whose format is determined by the domain and requested behaviour, overlaying `sockaddr_in`, `sockaddr_un` or `sockaddr_ns`. With `_SOCKADDR_LEN` defined before `sys/socket.h`, it takes 4.4BSD form with a length field and the 4.3BSD form is named `osockaddr`; otherwise the 4.3BSD form is used, with the address length assumed 14 bytes or less.
  Test: compile with and without `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN` and check layouts.

**accept-4** [OSF/1] `address_len` specifies the length of the `sockaddr` structure pointed to by `address`.
  Test: see accept-8.

**accept-5** [OSF/1] `accept()` extracts the first connection on the queue of pending connections, creates a new socket with the same properties as `socket`, and allocates a new file descriptor for it.
  Test: connect a client; `accept` returns a new fd different from the listener; data from the client is read on it.

**accept-6** [OSF/1] If the listen queue is empty, `accept()` blocks for a blocking socket until a connection is present, or returns `EWOULDBLOCK` for a nonblocking socket.
  Test: blocking `accept` returns only after a client connects 1 s later; nonblocking gives `EWOULDBLOCK`.

**accept-7** [OSF/1] The accepted socket cannot itself accept more connections; the original socket remains open and can accept more connections.
  Test: accept two clients in turn on the listener; `accept` on the accepted socket fails.

**accept-8** [OSF/1] On success returns the nonnegative descriptor of the accepted socket, stores the peer's address in `*address`, and sets `*address_len` to the address length; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: TCP client from 127.0.0.1; `address` holds 127.0.0.1 and the client's port; `*address_len` is `sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**accept-E1** `EINVAL`: The socket is not accepting connections.

**accept-E2** `EBADF`: The `socket` parameter is not valid.

**accept-E3** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**accept-E4** `EOPNOTSUPP`: The referenced socket cannot accept connections.

**accept-E5** `EFAULT`: `address` is not in a writable part of the user address space.

**accept-E6** `EWOULDBLOCK`: The socket is marked nonblocking, and no connections are present to be accepted.

**accept-E7** `EMFILE`: There are too many open file descriptors.

**accept-E8** [DEC] `ENOMEM`: The system was unable to allocate kernel memory to increase the process descriptor table. (ENVIRONMENT NOTES, under "ULTRIX Compatibility"; features not generic to OSF/1.)

Related: Functions: bind(2), connect(2), listen(2), socket(2)

### access(2)

Page: `man2/access.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**access-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <unistd.h>`; `int access(const char *path, int access_mode)`.
  Test: Compile the call.

**access-2** [OSF/1] `access()` checks whether the file named by `path` is accessible.
  Test: `access` on an existing readable file with `R_OK` returns 0.

**access-3** [OSF/1] If `path` is a symbolic link, `access()` reports on the file the link points to.
  Test: A symlink to a nonexistent target with `F_OK` gives −1 and `ENOENT`. A symlink to an existing file gives 0.

**access-4** [OSF/1] Permission for every component of `path` is checked with the real user ID instead of the effective one, and with a group access list (including the real group ID) instead of the effective group ID.
  Test: In a setuid-root program run by an ordinary user, `access` on a root-only file with `R_OK` gives `EACCES`.

**access-5** [OSF/1] `access_mode` is the bitwise OR of these values: `R_OK` checks read permission, `W_OK` write permission, `X_OK` execute (search) permission, and `F_OK` whether the file exists.
  Test: On a mode-0400 file owned by the caller, `R_OK` gives 0, `W_OK` gives `EACCES`, and `R_OK|W_OK` gives `EACCES`.

**access-6** [OSF/1] Only the access bits are checked. A directory may be reported writable, yet opening it for writing fails (though files can be created in it). A file's bits may say it is executable, yet `execve()` can fail if the file is not in the proper format.
  Test: `access(dir, W_OK)` returns 0 while `open(dir, O_WRONLY)` fails. A mode-0755 text file without the proper format passes `X_OK`.

**access-7** [OSF/1] On success, `access()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`, and access to the file is denied.
  Test: Check the return values.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**access-E1** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

**access-E2** `EINVAL`: the pathname contains a character with the high-order bit set.

**access-E3** `ENAMETOOLONG`: a component of the pathname exceeded `PATH_MAX` characters, or the whole pathname exceeded `NAME_MAX` characters.
Note: The page appears to have `PATH_MAX` and `NAME_MAX` swapped compared with the other pages, which apply `PATH_MAX` to the whole path and `NAME_MAX` to a component.

**access-E4** `ENOENT`: the named file does not exist, or the path is an empty string.

**access-E5** `EACCES`: the file's permission bits do not allow the requested access, or search permission is denied on a component of the path prefix. The owner is checked against the "owner" read, write and execute bits. Members of the file's group, other than the owner, are checked against the "group" bits. Everyone else is checked against the "other" bits.

**access-E6** `ELOOP`: too many symbolic links were met while translating the pathname.

**access-E7** `EROFS`: write access is requested for a file on a read-only file system.

**access-E8** `ETXTBSY`: write access is requested for a pure-procedure (shared text) file that is being executed.

**access-E9** `EFAULT`: `path` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**access-E10** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while reading from or writing to the file system.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), stat(2)

### acct(2)

Page: `man2/acct.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**acct-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int acct(char *path)`.
  Test: compile a call with a `char *` argument.

**acct-2** [OSF/1] `path` points to the pathname of the accounting file, or is a null pointer.
  Test: covered by acct-4 and acct-5.

**acct-3** [OSF/1] `acct()` enables and disables process accounting; when enabled, an accounting record is produced for each terminating process.
  Test: as superuser, `acct("/tmp/acctf")` on an existing empty regular file; fork a child that exits; the file grows.

**acct-4** [OSF/1] `path` names the file to which accounting records are written.
  Test: as acct-3; records appear in the named file.

**acct-5** [OSF/1] When `path` is 0 or null, `acct()` disables accounting.
  Test: after enabling, `acct(NULL)`; a child that exits afterwards does not grow the file.

**acct-6** [OSF/1] If `path` refers to a symbolic link, records are written to the file the link points to.
  Test: enable accounting through a symlink to a regular file; the target file grows when a child exits.

**acct-7** [OSF/1] If Network File System is installed, the accounting file can reside on another node. To ensure accurate accounting, each node must have its own accounting file, which can be on any node in the network.
  Test: Not testable without an NFS setup.

**acct-8** [OSF/1] The calling process must have superuser privilege to enable or disable accounting.
  Test: as non-root, `acct(path)` returns −1 with `EPERM`.

**acct-9** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise −1 with `errno` set.
  Test: as root with a valid file, returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**acct-E1** `EPERM`: the calling process does not have appropriate system privilege.

**acct-E2** `ENOENT`: the file named by `path` does not exist.

**acct-E3** `EACCES`: the file named by `path` is not an ordinary file.

**acct-E4** `EACCES`: write permission is denied for the named accounting file.

**acct-E5** `EROFS`: the named file resides on a read-only file system.

Related: Functions: exit(2), sigaction(2), sigvec(2), expacct(3), raise(3)

### adjtime(2)

Page: `man2/adjtime.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**adjtime-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/time.h>`; `int adjtime(struct timeval *delta, struct timeval *old_delta)`.
  Test: Compile the call.

**adjtime-2** [OSF/1] `delta` points to the amount by which to change the time. `old_delta` receives the correction still outstanding from an earlier call.
  Test: Covered below.
Note: The page says `old_delta` holds "the number of nanoseconds still to be corrected", but its type is `struct timeval`, which holds microseconds (see adjtime-8).

**adjtime-3** [OSF/1] `adjtime()` makes small changes to the system time (as returned by `gettimer()`), moving it forward or back by `delta`.
  Test: As root, `adjtime` +1 s. Over time, the clock gains about 1 s against a reference.

**adjtime-4** [OSF/1] With a negative `delta`, the clock is slowed by advancing it more slowly than normal until the correction is complete. With a positive `delta`, a larger increment than normal is used until the correction is complete. The skew is "generally a fraction of one percent". So time always increases monotonically.
  Test: Apply −1 s, then sample `gettimeofday` in a tight loop. It never goes backwards.

**adjtime-5** [OSF/1] A correction from an earlier call "may not be finished" when `adjtime()` is called again. In that case, the remaining delta from the earlier call is replaced by the new call's delta.
  Test: Call +10 s, then immediately call +0. `old_delta` from the second call is close to 10 s, and no further skew follows.

**adjtime-6** [OSF/1] If `old_delta` is non-zero, then on return the structure it points to holds the time remaining from the earlier call.
  Test: As in adjtime-5. Passing NULL is also accepted.

**adjtime-7** [OSF/1] Only users with superuser privilege may call `adjtime()`.
  Test: As non-root, expect −1 and `EPERM`.

**adjtime-8** [Compat] (Notes.) BSD defines system time in seconds and microseconds, and the POSIX real-time extensions in seconds and nanoseconds. Because POSIX does not specify `adjtime()`, the existing BSD interface is kept.
  Test: The `delta` argument is a `struct timeval` (`tv_sec`, `tv_usec`), and compiling with it works.

**adjtime-9** [OSF/1] On success, `adjtime()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: As root, `adjtime({0,0}, NULL)` returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**adjtime-E1** `EFAULT`: an argument address refers to invalid memory.

**adjtime-E2** `EPERM`: the process's effective user ID lacks the needed system privilege.

Related: Functions: gettimeofday(2), gettimer(3)

### async_daemon(2)

Page: `man2/async_daemon.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**async_daemon-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `async_daemon(void)`; no return type is shown.
  Test: compile a call.

**async_daemon-2** [OSF/1] `async_daemon()` starts an NFS compatible asynchronous I/O server.
  Test: as root in a child process, call; the child stays in the call.

**async_daemon-3** [OSF/1] Normally the function does not return unless the server is terminated by a signal.
  Test: kill the child from async_daemon-2 with `SIGTERM`; it ends.
  Note: The page does not say what the call returns, or whether it returns at all, when the signal is caught rather than fatal.

**async_daemon-4** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: start daemons until failure; expect −1 with `EBUSY`.
  Note: The page does not say whether privilege is needed.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**async_daemon-E1** `EBUSY`: The system limit on asynchronous daemons has been exceeded.

Related: Functions: nfssvc(2)

### atomic_op(2)

Page: `man2/atomic_op.html`.
Note: The page is marked "Digital" rather than "OSF", so all items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**atomic_op-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int atomic_op(int op, int *addr)` (old-style declaration), with `#include <sys/lock.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including `<sys/lock.h>`.

**atomic_op-2** [DEC] `atomic_op()` provides a test-and-set operation on a user address; `addr` is the target address.
  Test: on an `int` that is 0, `atomic_op(ATOMIC_SET, &x)` returns 0.

**atomic_op-3** [DEC] `op` = `ATOMIC_SET`: test-and-set on the location `addr`.
  Test: `atomic_op(ATOMIC_SET, &x)` twice; the first returns 0, the second returns −1 with `EBUSY`.

**atomic_op-4** [DEC] `op` = `ATOMIC_CLEAR`: clear operation on the location `addr`.
  Test: after a set, `atomic_op(ATOMIC_CLEAR, &x)` returns 0 and a following `ATOMIC_SET` returns 0.

**atomic_op-5** [DEC] Whether `atomic_op()` runs as a system call is hardware-dependent.
  Test: Not testable from user space in a portable way; informational.

**atomic_op-6** [DEC] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and a more specific error code is stored in `errno`.
  Test: as atomic_op-2.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**atomic_op-E1** `EBUSY`: the location `addr` is already set.

**atomic_op-E2** `EINVAL`: `op` is not a valid operation type, or `addr` is not aligned on an integer boundary.

**atomic_op-E3** `EACCES`: the address in `addr` is not write accessible.

**atomic_op-E4** `EFAULT`: an error occurred while reading or writing the location `addr`.

### bind(2)

Page: `man2/bind.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**bind-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int bind(int socket, struct sockaddr *address, int address_len)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**bind-2** [OSF/1] `socket` is the descriptor of the socket to be bound.
  Test: as bind-5.

**bind-3** [OSF/1] `address` points to a `sockaddr` whose format is determined by the domain and the behaviour requested; it overlays `sockaddr_in`, `sockaddr_un` or `sockaddr_ns` depending on the active address family. With `_SOCKADDR_LEN` defined before `sys/socket.h`, it takes 4.4BSD form with a length field and the 4.3BSD form is named `osockaddr`; otherwise the default 4.3BSD form is used, with the address length assumed 14 bytes or less.
  Test: compile with and without `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN` and check the structure layouts.

**bind-4** [OSF/1] `address_len` specifies the length of the structure pointed to by `address`.
  Test: pass `sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)`; succeeds.

**bind-5** [OSF/1] `bind()` assigns an address to an unnamed socket; sockets created by `socket()` are unnamed and identified only by their address family.
  Test: `bind` an `AF_INET` socket to 127.0.0.1 port P; `getsockname` returns port P.

**bind-6** [OSF/1] The assigned name can be retrieved with `getsockname()`.
  Test: as bind-5.

**bind-7** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as above.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**bind-E1** `EBADF`: The `socket` parameter is not valid.

**bind-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**bind-E3** `EADDRNOTAVAIL`: The specified address is not available from the local machine.

**bind-E4** `EADDRINUSE`: The specified address is already in use.

**bind-E5** `EINVAL`: The socket is already bound to an address.

**bind-E6** `EACCES`: The requested address is protected and the current user does not have permission to access it.

**bind-E7** `EFAULT`: `address` is not in a readable part of the user address space.

Related: Functions: connect(2), listen(2), socket(2), getsockname(2)

### brk(2), sbrk(2)

Page: `man2/brk.html`; same text as `sbrk(2)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**brk-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int brk(char *addr)` and `int sbrk(int incr)`; in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile and link calls to both.
  Note: The page gives `sbrk` a return type of `int` though it says `sbrk` returns a pointer and the old break value.

**brk-2** [OSF/1] `brk()` sets the break (the lowest data segment location not used by the program) to `addr`, rounded up to the next multiple of the system's page size.
  Test: `brk(sbrk(0) + 1)` returns 0; then `sbrk(0)` is above the old break.
  Note: The page does not say whether `sbrk(0)` reports the rounded or the requested value.

**brk-3** [OSF/1] `sbrk()` adds `incr` bytes to the program's data space and returns a pointer to the start of the new area; `incr` may be positive or negative.
  Test: `p = sbrk(4096)`; `p` equals the old `sbrk(0)`; writing to `p[0..4095]` works; `sbrk(-4096)` succeeds.

**brk-4** [OSF/1] When a program begins execution through `execve()`, the break is set at the highest location defined by the program and data storage areas; so only programs with growing data areas should need `sbrk()`.
  Test: at start of `main`, `sbrk(0)` is ≥ the address of every static data object of the program.

**brk-5** [OSF/1] `sbrk(0)` reliably returns the current value of the program break.
  Test: `sbrk(0)` twice without allocation gives the same value; after `sbrk(n)` it grows by n.

**brk-6** [OSF/1] `getrlimit()` may be used to find the maximum permissible size of the data segment; the break cannot be set beyond the value returned by `getrlimit()`.
  Test: set `RLIMIT_DATA` low, then `sbrk` past it; expect −1 with `ENOMEM`.

**brk-7** [OSF/1] If the data segment was locked when `brk()` is called, memory added to the data segment by `brk()` is also locked.
  Test: `plock(DATLOCK)` as root, then grow with `brk`; new pages are locked (Not readily testable from user space beyond `plock` success).

**brk-8** [OSF/1] The current break is a historical remnant; OSF/1 allows discontiguous memory areas (e.g. via `mmap()`), so references above the break may be legitimate and not cause memory violations.
  Test: `mmap` a page above the break and touch it; no fault.

**brk-9** [OSF/1] On success `brk()` returns 0 and `sbrk()` returns the old break value; on failure either returns −1 and sets `errno`. On failure no additional memory is allocated.
  Test: after a failed `sbrk`, `sbrk(0)` is unchanged.

**brk-10** [OSF/1] If `brk()` cannot allocate the requested memory, the message `cmd: could not sbrk, return = n` is printed, where `cmd` is the name of the executing command and `n` is the internal kernel error code from `vm_allocate()`.
  Test: force failure; check stderr/console for the message.
  Note: The page does not say where the message is printed.

**brk-11** [OSF/1] Failure may occur if the requested break would make the data segment collide with previously allocated memory (e.g. memory from `mmap()` or `vm_allocate()`).
  Test: `mmap` with `MAP_FIXED` just above the break, then `sbrk` across it; expect −1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**brk-E1** `ENOMEM`: The requested change would allocate more space than allowed by the limit returned by `getrlimit()`.

Related: Functions: exec(2), getrlimit(2), malloc(3), plock(2), mmap(2)

### chdir(2), fchdir(2)

Page: `man2/chdir.html`; same text as `fchdir(2)`. AES: Full use chdir() only.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**chdir-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int chdir(const char *path)` and `int fchdir(int filedes)`; the page names no header.
  Test: compile calls to both.

**chdir-2** [OSF/1] `chdir()` changes the current directory to the directory named by `path`.
  Test: `chdir("/tmp")`, then `getcwd()` or `stat(".")` matches `/tmp`.

**chdir-3** [OSF/1] `fchdir()` changes the current directory to the directory referred to by the open descriptor `filedes`.
  Test: `open("/tmp", O_RDONLY)`, `fchdir(fd)`, compare `stat(".")` with `stat("/tmp")`.

**chdir-4** [OSF/1] If `path` refers to a symbolic link, `chdir()` sets the current directory to the directory the link points to.
  Test: `symlink("/tmp", "l")`, `chdir("l")`, compare `stat(".")` with `stat("/tmp")`.

**chdir-5** [OSF/1] The current directory is the starting point of searches for pathnames that do not begin with `/`.
  Test: `chdir(dir)`, create `"f"`, check `dir/f` exists.

**chdir-6** [OSF/1] The calling process must have search access to a directory for it to become the current directory.
  Test: as non-root, `chdir` into a directory with mode 0600 fails with `EACCES`.

**chdir-7** [OSF/1] The current working directory is shared by all threads in a process; a `chdir()` or `fchdir()` by one thread affects every other thread.
  Test: thread A calls `chdir`, thread B then opens a relative path and finds it in the new directory.

**chdir-8** [OSF/1] `chdir()` returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set. The page states return values for `chdir()` only.
  Test: successful call returns exactly 0.

**chdir-9** [OSF/1] If `chdir()` or `fchdir()` fails, the current directory remains unchanged.
  Test: `chdir("/nonexistent")` fails, `stat(".")` is unchanged.

Errors for `chdir()` (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**chdir-E1** `EACCES`: search access is denied for any component of the pathname.

**chdir-E2** `ELOOP`: too many symbolic links were encountered in translating the pathname.

**chdir-E3** `EFAULT`: `path` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**chdir-E4** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while reading from or writing to the file system.

**chdir-E5** `ENOENT`: the named directory does not exist, or is an empty string.

**chdir-E6** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

**chdir-E7** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

Errors for `fchdir()`:

**chdir-E8** `ENOTDIR`: the file descriptor does not reference a directory.

**chdir-E9** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not a valid open file descriptor.

Related: Functions: chroot(2); Commands: cd(1)

### chmod(2), fchmod(2)

Page: `man2/chmod.html`; same text as `fchmod(2)`. AES: Full use (chmod()) Trial use (fchmod()).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**chmod-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int chmod(const char *path, mode_t mode)` and `int fchmod(int filedes, mode_t mode)`, declared via `<sys/mode.h>`, `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/stat.h>`.
  Test: compile calls to both including the three headers.

**chmod-2** [OSF/1] `chmod()` sets the access permissions of the file named by `path` to the bit pattern `mode`.
  Test: `chmod(f, 0640)`; `stat` gives `st_mode & 07777` == 0640.

**chmod-3** [OSF/1] If `path` refers to a symbolic link, `chmod()` changes the permissions of the file the link refers to.
  Test: `chmod("l", 0600)` where `l` -> `f`; `stat("f")` shows 0600.

**chmod-4** [OSF/1] `fchmod()` sets the access permissions of the open file `filedes` to `mode`.
  Test: `fchmod(fd, 0600)`; `fstat` shows 0600.

**chmod-5** [OSF/1] The caller must have the same effective user ID as the file's owner, or superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, `chmod` a file owned by another user fails with `EPERM`.

**chmod-6** [OSF/1] On success, `chmod()` and `fchmod()` mark `st_ctime` of the file for update.
  Test: record `st_ctime`, sleep 1s, `chmod`, check it advanced.

**chmod-7** [OSF/1] `mode` is formed by ORing one or more values defined in `<sys/mode.h>`: `S_ISUID` (set effective user ID to the file's owner on execution), `S_ISGID` (set effective group ID to the file's group on execution), `S_ISVTX` (save text image after execution).
  Test: check the constants are defined in `<sys/mode.h>`; `chmod(f, S_ISUID|0755)` as owner and `stat` shows `S_ISUID`.

**chmod-8** [OSF/1] Owner bits: `S_IRWXU` (owner may read, write and execute, or search a directory), `S_IRUSR` (read), `S_IWUSR` (write), `S_IXUSR` (execute, or search a directory).
  Test: check `S_IRWXU == (S_IRUSR|S_IWUSR|S_IXUSR)` and `chmod` with each is reflected by `stat`.

**chmod-9** [OSF/1] Group bits: `S_IRWXG` (group may read, write and execute, or search a directory), `S_IRGRP` (read), `S_IWGRP` (write), `S_IXGRP` (execute, or search a directory).
  Test: check `S_IRWXG == (S_IRGRP|S_IWGRP|S_IXGRP)` and `chmod` with each is reflected by `stat`.

**chmod-10** [OSF/1] Other bits: `S_IRWXO` (others may read, write and execute, or search a directory), `S_IROTH` (read), `S_IWOTH` (write), `S_IXOTH` (execute, or search a directory).
  Test: as above for the other bits.

**chmod-11** [OSF/1] Other mode values exist that can be set with `mknod()` but not with `chmod()`.
  Test: `chmod(f, S_IFIFO|0644)` does not change the file type reported by `stat`.

**chmod-12** [OSF/1] If `S_ISGID` is set and `S_IXGRP` is not set, mandatory file record locking exists on a regular file; this "may affect" later calls on the file, including `open()`, `creat()`, `read()`, `write()` and `truncate()`.
  Test: informational; `chmod(f, 02644)` succeeds and `stat` shows `S_ISGID` set and `S_IXGRP` clear; effects on later calls are only "may".

**chmod-13** [OSF/1] The file's `S_ISGID` bit is cleared if: the file is a regular file; the caller's effective user ID lacks appropriate system privilege; and the effective group ID or one of the IDs in the process's group access list "does not match" the file's existing group ID.
  Test: as non-root owner not in the file's group, `chmod(f, 02755)`; `stat` shows `S_ISGID` clear.
  Note: The page lists the three conditions as bullets without saying whether all or any must hold, and the third bullet's wording ("or one of the IDs ... does not match") is ambiguous; the item keeps the page's wording.

**chmod-14** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; on failure returns -1, sets `errno`, and the file permissions remain unchanged.
  Test: a failing `chmod` (e.g. `EPERM`) leaves `st_mode` unchanged.

Errors for `chmod()` (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**chmod-E1** `ENOTDIR`: a component of `path` is not a directory.

**chmod-E2** `ENOENT`: the named file does not exist, or `path` is an empty string.

**chmod-E3** `ENOENT`: a symbolic link was named, but the file it refers to does not exist.

**chmod-E4** `EACCES`: search permission is denied on a component of `path`.

**chmod-E5** `EPERM`: the effective user ID does not match the owner of the file, or the owner does not have appropriate system privilege.
  Note: The page says "the owner does not have appropriate system privilege"; the `fchmod()` entry says "the calling process does not have superuser privilege", which is probably what is meant.

**chmod-E6** `EROFS`: the named file resides on a read-only file system.

**chmod-E7** `EFAULT`: `path` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**chmod-E8** `ESTALE`: the process's root or current directory is in a virtual file system that has been unmounted.

**chmod-E9** `ELOOP`: too many symbolic links were encountered in translating `path`.

**chmod-E10** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**chmod-E11** `EINTR`: a signal was caught during the system call.

Errors for `fchmod()`:

**chmod-E12** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not valid.

**chmod-E13** `EROFS`: the file referred to by `filedes` resides on a read-only file system.

**chmod-E14** `EPERM`: the effective user ID does not match the owner of the file, and the caller does not have superuser privilege.

**chmod-E15** `ESTALE`: the process's root or current directory is in a virtual file system that has been unmounted.

**chmod-E16** `EINTR`: a signal was caught during the system call.

Related: Functions: chown(2), fcntl(2), getgroups(2), mknod(2), open(2), read(2) setgroups(2) truncate(2) write(2); Commands: chmod(1)

### chown(2), fchown(2)

Page: `man2/chown.html`; same text as `fchown(2)`. AES: Full use (`chown()`), Trial use (`fchown()`).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**chown-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int chown(const char *path, uid_t owner, gid_t group)`; no header is listed.
  Test: compile and call.

**chown-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int fchown(int filedes, uid_t owner, gid_t group)`.
  Test: compile and call.

**chown-3** [OSF/1] If `path` refers to a symbolic link, `chown()` changes the ownership of the file the link points to.
  Test: as root, chown a symlink; the target's `st_uid` changes; `lstat()` of the link is unchanged.

**chown-4** [OSF/1] `filedes` is a valid open descriptor; `owner` and `group` are numeric owner and group IDs; the functions change the owner and group of the file.
  Test: as root, `fchown(fd, 123, 456)`; `fstat()` shows 123/456.

**chown-5** [OSF/1] A process can change the owner ID of a file only if it has superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root owner, `chown(path, other_uid, -1)`; expect −1 and the owner unchanged.
Note: The page's `EPERM` entries cover only an effective user ID that does not match the owner; it names no errno for this case.

**chown-6** [OSF/1] A process can change the group ID of a file if its effective user ID matches the file owner, or if it has superuser privilege.
  Test: non-root non-owner `chown(path, -1, mygid)`; expect −1 `EPERM`; as owner, succeeds.

**chown-7** [OSF/1] A process without superuser privilege can change the group ID only to its effective group ID or a group in its supplementary group list.
  Test: as owner, change group to a group not in the list; expect −1 (the page names no errno for this case); to a supplementary group, succeeds.

**chown-8** [OSF/1] If the owner ID is changed and the process lacks superuser privilege, the `S_ISUID` bit of a regular file is cleared.
  Test: Not testable as stated (a non-superuser cannot change the owner, chown-5).

**chown-9** [OSF/1] On successful return, `S_ISUID` is cleared if the file is a regular file and the process lacks superuser privilege.
  Test: as owner, chmod 04755, `chown(path, -1, mygid)`; `S_ISUID` clear.

**chown-10** [OSF/1] On successful return, `S_ISGID` is cleared if the file is a regular file and the process lacks superuser privilege.
  Test: as owner, chmod 02755, `chown(path, -1, mygid)`; `S_ISGID` clear.

**chown-11** [OSF/1] If `owner` is `(uid_t)-1` or `group` is `(gid_t)-1`, the corresponding ID of the file is unchanged.
  Test: as root, `chown(path, (uid_t)-1, 456)`; `st_uid` unchanged, `st_gid` 456.
Note: The page text is damaged here: it reads "(gid_t)-t"; `(gid_t)-1` is the evident reading.

**chown-12** [OSF/1] On success the functions mark `st_ctime` for update.
  Test: stat, sleep 1 s, chown, stat; `st_ctime` increased.

**chown-13** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 is returned, the owner and group are unchanged, and `errno` is set.
  Test: failing call (`EPERM`) leaves `st_uid`/`st_gid` unchanged.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**chown-E1** `EACCES` (`chown()`): search permission is denied on a component of `path`.

**chown-E2** `EFAULT` (`chown()`): `path` is an invalid address.

**chown-E3** `ELOOP` (`chown()`): too many links were encountered in translating `path`.

**chown-E4** `ENAMETOOLONG` (`chown()`): the length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX` or a component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**chown-E5** `ENOTDIR` (`chown()`): a component of `path` is not a directory.

**chown-E6** `ENOENT` (`chown()`): `path` does not exist or is an empty string.

**chown-E7** `EPERM` (`chown()`): the effective user ID does not match the file owner, and the process lacks appropriate privilege.

**chown-E8** `EROFS` (`chown()`): the named file is on a read-only file system.

**chown-E9** `EBADF` (`fchown()`): `filedes` is not valid.

**chown-E10** `EROFS` (`fchown()`): the file referred to by `filedes` is on a read-only file system.

**chown-E11** `EPERM` (`fchown()`): the effective user ID does not match the file owner, and the process lacks appropriate privilege.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), chmod(2); Commands: chown(1)
Note: The page lists chmod(2) twice.

### chroot(2)

Page: `man2/chroot.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**chroot-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int chroot(const char *path)`.
  Test: compile a call with this type.

**chroot-2** [OSF/1] `chroot()` makes the directory named by `path` the effective root directory.
  Test: as root, create `/tmp/r/marker`, `chroot("/tmp/r")`; `access("/marker", F_OK) == 0`.

**chroot-3** [OSF/1] If `path` is a symbolic link, the effective root becomes the directory it points to.
  Test: `symlink("/tmp/r", "/tmp/rl")`; `chroot("/tmp/rl")` gives the same result as chroot-2.

**chroot-4** [OSF/1] The effective root directory is the starting point for pathname searches beginning with `/`.
  Test: see chroot-2.

**chroot-5** [OSF/1] The current working directory is not affected by `chroot()`.
  Test: `chdir("/tmp/x")`, `chroot("/tmp/r")`; a relative `open("f")` still opens `/tmp/x/f`.

**chroot-6** [OSF/1] The caller must have superuser privilege, and must also have search access to the new root directory.
  Test: as non-root, `chroot("/tmp")` fails with `EPERM`.

**chroot-7** [OSF/1] `..` in the effective root directory means the effective root itself, so `..` cannot reach files outside the subtree.
  Test: after `chroot("/tmp/r")`, `chdir("/")`, `stat("/..")` and `stat("/")` give the same `st_ino` and `st_dev`.

**chroot-8** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; on failure -1, `errno` is set, and the effective root directory is unchanged.
  Test: as non-root, after failure `/` still refers to the original root.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**chroot-E1** `EACCES`: search permission is denied for any component of the pathname.

**chroot-E2** `EPERM`: the process does not have appropriate privilege.

**chroot-E3** `EFAULT`: `path` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**chroot-E4** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while reading from or writing to the file system.

**chroot-E5** `ENOENT`: `path` does not exist or points to an empty string.

**chroot-E6** `ENAMETOOLONG`: `path` is longer than `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**chroot-E7** `ENOTDIR`: a component of `path` is not a directory.

**chroot-E8** `ELOOP`: more than `MAXSYMLINKS` symbolic links are encountered while resolving `path`.

Related: Functions: chdir(2). Commands: chdir(1)

### close(2)

Page: `man2/close.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**close-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int close(int filedes)`. The page lists no header.
  Test: Compile the call.

**close-2** [OSF/1] `close()` closes the file associated with `filedes`, which must be a valid open descriptor.
  Test: After `close(fd)`, `fcntl(fd, F_GETFD)` fails with `EBADF`.

**close-3** [OSF/1] Every region of the file that this process locked with `lockf()` is unlocked, even if the process still has the file open through another descriptor.
  Test: Lock with `lockf` via fd A, open the file again as fd B, and close B. A child can now lock the region.

**close-4** [OSF/1] When every descriptor of a pipe or FIFO has been closed, any data left in it is discarded.
  Test: Write to a FIFO, close all ends, reopen it, and a nonblocking read finds no data.

**close-5** [OSF/1] When every descriptor associated with an open file descriptor is closed, the open file descriptor is freed.
  Not testable from user space directly: this is kernel bookkeeping.

**close-6** [OSF/1] If the file's link count is 0 when every descriptor for it has been closed, its space is freed and the file can no longer be reached.
  Test: Unlink an open file and close it. `statfs` free blocks go up.

**close-7** [OSF/1] When `close()` must block, only the calling thread is suspended, not every thread in the process.
  Test: Thread A blocks in `close` on a stream that is draining. Thread B keeps making progress.

**close-8** [OSF/1] The last `close()` of a stream dismantles the stream. This pops any modules and closes the driver.
  Test: Push a module, then close the last descriptor. Reopen the stream, and `I_LOOK` shows no module.

**close-9** [OSF/1] If `O_NDELAY` and `O_NONBLOCK` are clear and no signals are posted for the stream, `close()` waits up to 15 seconds for each module to drain and up to 15 seconds for each driver to drain.
  Test: Close a stream whose output cannot drain, with no module pushed. `close` returns after no more than about 15 s.

**close-10** [OSF/1] If `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` is set, or if any signals are pending, `close()` does not wait for output to drain and dismantles the stream at once.
  Test: Repeat close-9 with `O_NONBLOCK` set. `close` returns at once.

**close-11** [OSF/1] When a STREAMS file is closed and the caller had registered to receive `SIGPOLL` for events on it (via `I_SETSIG`), the caller is unregistered for that file's events.
  Test: Register `I_SETSIG`, close, and cause an event from the peer. No `SIGPOLL` arrives.

**close-12** [OSF/1] On success, `close()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: Check the return values.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**close-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not a valid open file descriptor.

**close-E2** `EINTR`: `close()` was interrupted by a caught signal.

**close-E3** `ENOLINK`: the descriptor is on a remote machine and the link to that machine is no longer active.

Related: Functions: exec(2), fcntl(2), lockf(3), open(2), open(2), pipe(2), socket(2), streamio(7)

### connect(2)

Page: `man2/connect.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**connect-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int connect(int socket, struct sockaddr *address, int address_len)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>` and `#include <sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including both headers.

**connect-2** [OSF/1] `address` points to a `sockaddr` whose format depends on the domain and the behaviour requested; it overlays a `sockaddr_in`, `sockaddr_un` or `sockaddr_ns`, depending on the active address family. `address_len` is its length.
  Test: `connect` a `AF_UNIX` stream socket to a listening path with a `sockaddr_un`; returns 0.

**connect-3** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined before `sys/socket.h` is included, `sockaddr` has 4.4BSD layout with a field for the address length. Otherwise the default 4.3BSD `sockaddr` is used, and the address length is assumed to be 14 bytes or less.
  Test: compile code using `struct sockaddr` both with and without `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN`; with it, the structure contains an extra length field (name not given by the page).
  Note: The page does not name the length field.

**connect-4** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined, the 4.3BSD `sockaddr` is available under the name `osockaddr`.
  Test: with `_SOCKADDR_LEN`, code declaring `struct osockaddr` compiles.

**connect-5** [OSF/1] `connect()` requests a connection between two sockets; the kernel sets up the links, and both sockets must use the same address format and protocol.
  Test: connect a TCP socket to a listener; `accept` on the listener returns a new socket.

**connect-6** [OSF/1] For a `SOCK_DGRAM` socket, `connect()` sets the peer address, to which all datagrams are sent on later `send()` calls; no connection is made.
  Test: `connect` a UDP socket to a peer, then `send` without address; the peer receives the datagram.

**connect-7** [OSF/1] For a `SOCK_STREAM` socket, `connect()` attempts a connection to the socket named by `address`; each communication space interprets `address` differently.
  Test: as connect-5.

**connect-8** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: as connect-5.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**connect-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**connect-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**connect-E3** `EADDRNOTAVAIL`: the address is not available from the local machine.

**connect-E4** `EAFNOSUPPORT`: addresses in the given address family cannot be used with this socket.

**connect-E5** `EISCONN`: the socket is already connected.

**connect-E6** `ETIMEDOUT`: establishing the connection timed out.

**connect-E7** `ECONNREFUSED`: the connection attempt was rejected.

**connect-E8** `ENETUNREACH`: no route to the network or host is present.

**connect-E9** `EADDRINUSE`: the address is already in use.

**connect-E10** `EFAULT`: `address` is not in a readable part of the user address space.

**connect-E11** `EWOULDBLOCK`: the socket is nonblocking and the connection cannot be completed immediately. The program can select the socket for writing during the connection process.

Related: Functions: accept(2), bind(2), socket(2), getsockname(2), select(2), send(2)

### open(2), creat(2)

Page: `man2/creat.html`; same text as `open(2)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**open-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int open(const char *path, int oflag [, mode_t mode])`, with headers `<fcntl.h>`, `<sys/stat.h>`, `<sys/types.h>`; the `mode` argument is optional.
  Test: compile a call `open(path, O_RDONLY)` and `open(path, O_CREAT|O_WRONLY, 0644)` with those headers; both must compile and return an `int`.

**open-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int creat(const char *path, mode_t mode)`, same headers.
  Test: compile and call `creat(path, 0644)`; expect a nonnegative `int`.

**open-3** [OSF/1] If `path` refers to a symbolic link, `open()` opens the file the link points to.
  Test: create file F and symlink L to F; open L, write data, and check F contains the data.

**open-4** [OSF/1] `mode` gives the read, write and execute permissions of a file created via `O_CREAT`; it is built by ORing values from `sys/mode.h`; if the file already exists, `mode` is ignored.
  Test: create a file with mode 0600 and umask 0, stat it (expect 0600); reopen with `O_CREAT` and mode 0777, stat again (still 0600).

**open-5** [OSF/1] `open()` and `creat()` connect the file named by `path` to a file descriptor, which later I/O functions such as `read()` and `write()` use to access the file.
  Test: open a file, write through the descriptor, read back through another open of the same file.

**open-6** [OSF/1] The returned descriptor is the lowest descriptor not previously open for the process.
  Test: close descriptor 0 (or 3 after opening 3 and 4), open a file, expect 0 (or 3).

**open-7** [OSF/1] No process can have more than `OPEN_MAX` file descriptors open at once.
  Test: open files in a loop until failure; the count of open descriptors never exceeds `OPEN_MAX`.

**open-8** [OSF/1] When `open()` or `creat()` blocks until the request completes, only the calling thread is suspended, not the whole process.
  Test: in a threaded program, one thread opens a FIFO `O_RDONLY` (blocks); another thread keeps running and then opens it for writing, releasing the first.

**open-9** [OSF/1] The file offset of the new descriptor is set to the beginning of the file.
  Test: open an existing non-empty file; `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR)` returns 0.

**open-10** [OSF/1] The new descriptor is set to remain open across `exec` functions (see `fcntl()`).
  Test: after `open()`, `fcntl(fd, F_GETFD)` shows `FD_CLOEXEC` clear; exec a child that writes to that descriptor number successfully.

**open-11** [OSF/1] `oflag` is formed by bitwise-inclusive ORing exactly one file access flag (`O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY`, `O_RDWR`) with one or more file status flags, defined in `fcntl.h`.
  Test: open with `O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC`; succeeds.

**open-12** [OSF/1] `O_RDONLY`: the file is open for reading only.
  Test: open `O_RDONLY`; `read()` succeeds, `write()` fails.

**open-13** [OSF/1] `O_WRONLY`: the file is open for writing only.
  Test: open `O_WRONLY`; `write()` succeeds, `read()` fails.

**open-14** [OSF/1] `O_RDWR`: the file is open for reading and writing.
  Test: open `O_RDWR`; both `read()` and `write()` succeed.

**open-15** [OSF/1] Exactly one of `O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY`, `O_RDWR` must be specified; if none is set, `O_RDONLY` is assumed.
  Test: open with only status flags (e.g. `O_APPEND` alone); `fcntl(fd, F_GETFL) & O_ACCMODE` equals `O_RDONLY`, and `write()` fails.
Note: The page does not say what happens when more than one access flag is set.

**open-16** [OSF/1] `O_CREAT`: if the file exists, the flag has no effect except as described for `O_EXCL`.
  Test: open an existing file with `O_CREAT|O_RDWR`; contents and mode are unchanged.

**open-17** [OSF/1] `O_CREAT` on a nonexistent file creates a regular file whose owner ID is the effective user ID of the process.
  Test: create a file; `stat()` shows `st_uid == geteuid()` and `S_ISREG`.

**open-18** [OSF/1] The group ID of a newly created file is set to the group ID of its parent directory.
  Test: create a file in a directory whose group differs from the process's effective group; `st_gid` equals the directory's group.

**open-19** [OSF/1] The permission and attribute bits of a new file are `mode` with all bits set in the process file mode creation mask cleared.
  Test: `umask(022)`, create with 0666; `st_mode & 07777` is 0644.

**open-20** [OSF/1] For a new file, the set-user-ID bit (`S_ISUID`) is cleared.
  Test: create with mode `S_ISUID|0755`; `st_mode` lacks `S_ISUID`.

**open-21** [OSF/1] For a new file, the set-group-ID bit (`S_ISGID`) is cleared.
  Test: create with mode `S_ISGID|0755`; `st_mode` lacks `S_ISGID`.

**open-22** [OSF/1] For a new file, the `S_ISVTX` bit is cleared.
  Test: create with mode `S_ISVTX|0755`; `st_mode` lacks `S_ISVTX`.

**open-23** [OSF/1] To create a new file, the process must have write permission on the parent directory "with respect to all access control policies".
  Test: as non-root, try to create a file in a directory with mode 0555; expect −1 with `EACCES`.

**open-24** [OSF/1] `O_EXCL`: if `O_EXCL` and `O_CREAT` are both set, the open fails if the file exists.
  Test: `open(existing, O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_WRONLY, 0644)` returns −1 with `EEXIST`.

**open-25** [OSF/1] `O_NOCTTY`: if `path` identifies a terminal device, the terminal does not become the controlling terminal of the process.
  Test: in a new session without a controlling terminal, open a pty slave with `O_NOCTTY`; opening `/dev/tty` afterwards fails.

**open-26** [OSF/1] `O_TRUNC`: if the file does not exist, the flag has no effect.
  Test: `open(newfile, O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_WRONLY, 0644)` succeeds and creates an empty file.

**open-27** [OSF/1] `O_TRUNC`: if the file exists, is a regular file, and is successfully opened `O_RDWR` or `O_WRONLY`, its length is truncated to 0.
  Test: open a non-empty file with `O_TRUNC|O_WRONLY`; `fstat()` shows `st_size == 0`.

**open-28** [OSF/1] On such an `O_TRUNC` truncation, the owner and group of the file are unchanged.
  Test: compare `st_uid`/`st_gid` before and after an `O_TRUNC` open; equal.

**open-29** [OSF/1] On such an `O_TRUNC` truncation, the set-user-ID attribute of the file mode is cleared.
  Test: as owner (non-root), chmod a file to `04755`, open with `O_TRUNC|O_WRONLY`; `S_ISUID` is clear afterwards.
Note: The page lists "set-user ID attribute ... is cleared" twice; the second bullet probably means the set-group-ID attribute, but the page does not say so.

**open-30** [OSF/1] The `O_TRUNC` open fails if the file supports enforced record locks and another process has locked a portion of the file.
  Test: see open-E12.

**open-31** [OSF/1] The `O_TRUNC` open fails if the file does not allow write access.
  Test: as non-root, open a 0444 file with `O_TRUNC|O_WRONLY`; expect −1 (`EACCES`).

**open-32** [OSF/1] If `oflag` also specifies `O_SYNC`, the `O_TRUNC` truncation is a synchronous update.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires observing permanent storage); check only that `O_SYNC|O_TRUNC|O_WRONLY` succeeds and truncates.

**open-33** [OSF/1] `O_SYNC`: if set, updates and writes to regular files and block devices are synchronous updates; file updates are performed by `fclear()`, `ftruncate()`, `open()` with `O_TRUNC`, and `write()`.
  Test: open with `O_SYNC|O_WRONLY`; `fcntl(fd, F_GETFL)` includes `O_SYNC`; `write()` succeeds.

**open-34** [OSF/1] On return from a synchronous update (one of the calls above with `O_SYNC` set), all data for the file has been written to permanent storage, even if the file is also open for deferred update.
  Test: Not testable from user space (needs inspection of the storage device after a crash).

**open-35** [OSF/1] `O_APPEND`: if set, the file pointer is set to the end of the file before each write.
  Test: open with `O_APPEND|O_WRONLY`, `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_SET)`, write; data appears at the end of the file.

**open-36** [OSF/1] `O_NONBLOCK`, `O_NDELAY`: if set, `open()` does not block, and later `read()` or `write()` operations on the file are nonblocking.
  Test: open a FIFO with `O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK` and no writer; it returns at once; `read()` does not block.

**open-37** [OSF/1] The effect of `O_CREAT` is immediate.
  Test: after a successful `open(..., O_CREAT ...)` and before any write or close, `stat()` of the path succeeds.

**open-38** [OSF/1] Opening a FIFO with `O_RDONLY` and neither `O_NDELAY` nor `O_NONBLOCK` blocks until another process opens the file for writing; if the file is already open for writing (even by the calling process), `open()` returns without delay.
  Test: child opens FIFO for reading and blocks until the parent opens it for writing; separately, open for writing with `O_NONBLOCK` after a reader, then open `O_RDONLY` returns at once.

**open-39** [OSF/1] Opening a FIFO with `O_RDONLY` and `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` set returns immediately.
  Test: open a FIFO without writers `O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK`; returns a descriptor at once.

**open-40** [OSF/1] Opening a FIFO with `O_WRONLY` and neither `O_NDELAY` nor `O_NONBLOCK` blocks until another process opens it for reading; if it is already open for reading (even by the calling process), `open()` returns without delay.
  Test: open the FIFO `O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK`, then `O_WRONLY` in the same process; returns at once.

**open-41** [OSF/1] Opening a FIFO with `O_WRONLY` and `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` set returns an error if no process has the file open for reading.
  Test: see open-E9.

**open-42** [OSF/1] Opening a block or character special file that supports nonblocking opens (such as a terminal) with neither `O_NDELAY` nor `O_NONBLOCK` blocks until the device is ready or available.
  Test: Not reliably testable from user space (needs a device that is not ready, e.g. a modem line without carrier).

**open-43** [OSF/1] With `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` set, such an open returns without waiting for the device; later behaviour of the device is device-specific.
  Test: open a terminal line with `O_NONBLOCK`; it returns without blocking.

**open-44** [OSF/1] When opening a STREAMS file, `oflag` may be built from `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` ORed with `O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY` or `O_RDWR`; other flag values do not apply to STREAMS devices and have no effect on them. The value of `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` affects STREAMS drivers and some calls (`read()`, `getmsg()`, `putmsg()`, `write()`); for drivers its implementation is device-specific, and each STREAMS driver may treat it differently.
  Test: open a STREAMS device with `O_RDWR|O_NONBLOCK`; succeeds.
Note: The page writes "NON_BLOCK" in two places, apparently meaning `O_NONBLOCK`.

**open-45** [OSF/1] On success `open()` and `creat()` return the file descriptor, a nonnegative integer; otherwise −1 and `errno` set.
  Test: successful open returns a value `>= 0`; open of a missing file returns −1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**open-E1** `ENOENT`: `O_CREAT` is not set and the named file does not exist; or `O_CREAT` is set and the path prefix does not exist; or `path` points to the empty string.

**open-E2** `EACCES`: search permission is denied on a component of the path prefix; or the access type in `oflag` is denied for the file; or the file does not exist and write permission is denied for the parent directory; or `O_TRUNC` is given and write permission is denied.

**open-E3** `EISDIR`: the named file is a directory and write access is requested.

**open-E4** `EMFILE`: the per-process limit of open descriptors has already reached `OPEN_MAX`.

**open-E5** `EFAULT`: `path` is an invalid address.

**open-E6** `ENFILE`: the system file table is full.

**open-E7** `ENXIO`: the named file is a character or block special file and its associated device does not exist.

**open-E8** `ENXIO`: the named file is a multiplexed special file and either the channel number is out of the valid range or no more channels are available.

**open-E9** `ENXIO`: `O_NONBLOCK` is set, the named file is a FIFO, `O_WRONLY` is set, and no process has the file open for reading.

**open-E10** `ENXIO`: a STREAMS module or driver open routine failed.

**open-E11** `EEXIST`: `O_CREAT` and `O_EXCL` are set and the named file exists.

**open-E12** `EAGAIN`: `O_TRUNC` is set, the named file exists with enforced record locking enabled, and there are record locks on the file.

**open-E13** `EINTR`: a signal was caught during `open()`.

**open-E14** `EROFS`: the named file is on a read-only file system and write access is required.

**open-E15** `ENOSPC`: the directory that would contain the new file cannot be extended, the file does not exist, and `O_CREAT` is requested.

**open-E16** `EDQUOT`: the directory receiving the new entry cannot be extended because the user's quota of disk blocks or i-nodes on that file system is exhausted.

**open-E17** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

**open-E18** `ELOOP`: too many links were encountered in translating `path`.

**open-E19** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of the path string exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**open-E20** `ETXTBSY`: the file is being executed and `oflag` is `O_WRONLY` or `O_RDWR`.

**open-E21** `EIO`: a hangup or error occurred during a STREAMS `open()`.

**open-E22** `EMULTIHOP`: components of `path` require hopping to multiple remote machines.

**open-E23** `ENOLINK`: `path` points to a remote machine and the link to it is no longer active.

**open-E24** `ENOMEM`: the system is unable to allocate a send descriptor.

**open-E25** `ENOSR`: unable to allocate a stream.

**open-46** [DEC] (Environment notes, Digital extensions) The returned descriptor is the lowest one not previously open; processes have a fixed limit on simultaneously open descriptors, and `getdtablesize(2)` returns this system-defined limit.
  Test: open descriptors until failure; the number reached equals `getdtablesize()`.

**open-E26** [DEC] `EMFILE`: the system limit for open file descriptors has already been reached.

**open-E27** [DEC] `ENOMEM`: the system was unable to allocate kernel memory for more file descriptors.

**open-47** [OSF/1] A program can request some control over when updates are made permanent for a regular file opened for write access (via `O_SYNC`).
  Test: covered by open-33.

Related (Environment notes): Functions: getdtablesize(2)

Related: Functions: chmod(2), close(2), fcntl(2), lockf(3), lseek(2), read(2), stat(2), truncate(2), umask(2), write(2), getmsg(2), utmsg(2)
Note: The page lists "utmsg(2)", probably meaning putmsg(2).

### dup(2), dup2(2), fcntl(2)

Page: `man2/dup.html`; same text as `dup2(2)` and `fcntl(2)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

Note: The page's NAME line lists the names in the order "fcntl, dup, dup2". Identifiers use `dup` after the page file name.

**dup-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <fcntl.h>`, `#include <sys/types.h>`, `#include <unistd.h>`; `int fcntl(int filedes, int request [, int argument | struct flock *argument])`; `int dup(int filedes)`; `int dup2(int old, int new)`.
  Test: Compile calls to all three.

**dup-2** [OSF/1] `filedes` is an open file descriptor obtained from a successful `open()`, `fcntl()` or `pipe()`. `request` is the operation. `argument` depends on `request`. For `dup2`, `old` is an open descriptor and `new` is the descriptor that `dup2()` returns.
  Test: Covered by the items below.

**dup-3** [OSF/1] `fcntl()` performs controlling operations on the open file `filedes`.
  Test: Covered by the requests below.

**dup-4** [OSF/1] When `fcntl()`, `dup()` or `dup2()` must block, only the calling thread is suspended, not every thread in the process.
  Test: Thread A blocks in `fcntl(F_SETLKW)` on a region another process holds. Thread B keeps running and finishes work during that time.

**dup-5** [OSF/1] `F_DUPFD` returns a new descriptor that has these properties:
- It is the lowest-numbered available descriptor that is at least `argument` (taken as an `int`).
- It refers to the same object as the original.
- It shares the file pointer with the original (when the object is a file).
- It has the same access mode (read, write or read-write).
- It shares the same file status flags.
- Its close-on-exec flag (`FD_CLOEXEC`) is cleared, so it stays open across exec.
  Test: `fcntl(fd, F_DUPFD, 10)` returns 10 when 10 is free, and 11 when 10 is in use. `lseek` on one moves the other. `O_APPEND` set via one shows via the other. `F_GETFD` on the new descriptor is 0 even when the original has `FD_CLOEXEC`.

**dup-6** [OSF/1] `F_GETFD` gets the close-on-exec flag of `filedes`. Descriptor flags belong to one descriptor and do not affect others that refer to the same file. `argument` is ignored.
  Test: Set `FD_CLOEXEC` on fd A and dup it to B. `F_GETFD` is `FD_CLOEXEC` on A and 0 on B.

**dup-7** [OSF/1] `F_SETFD` sets the close-on-exec flag of `filedes` to `argument` (taken as an `int`). With 0, the file stays open across exec. With `FD_CLOEXEC`, the file is closed when the next exec succeeds.
  Test: Set `FD_CLOEXEC`, then exec a helper that checks the fd: it is closed. With 0 it is open.

**dup-8** [OSF/1] `F_GETFL` gets the file status flags and access modes of the file. The access mode can be extracted with the mask `O_ACCMODE`. Status flags and access modes belong to the open file description: they do not affect descriptors that refer to the same file through a different open file description. `argument` is ignored.
  Test: Open with `O_RDWR|O_APPEND`. `F_GETFL & O_ACCMODE` is `O_RDWR`, and `O_APPEND` is set. A second independent `open` of the file does not show `O_APPEND`.

**dup-9** [OSF/1] `F_SETFL` sets the file status flags to `argument` (taken as an `int`). The access mode is not changed.
  Test: On an `O_RDONLY` fd, set `O_NONBLOCK|O_WRONLY`. `F_GETFL` shows `O_NONBLOCK`, and the access mode is still `O_RDONLY`.

**dup-10** [OSF/1] `F_GETOWN` gets the process ID or process group that currently receives `SIGIO` and `SIGURG`. Process groups are returned as negative values.
  Test: After `F_SETOWN` with `-pgid`, `F_GETOWN` returns `-pgid`.

**dup-11** [OSF/1] `F_SETOWN` sets the process or process group that receives `SIGIO` and `SIGURG`. A negative `argument` names a process group. Otherwise `argument` (taken as an `int`) is a process ID.
  Test: On a socket, `F_SETOWN` `getpid()`, then `F_GETOWN` equals `getpid()`.

**dup-12** [OSF/1] `F_GETLK` gets the first lock that blocks the lock description in the `struct flock` that `argument` points to. The result overwrites the structure. If no lock would prevent this one, the structure is unchanged except that `l_type` is set to `F_UNLCK`.
  Test: With no locks held, `F_GETLK` with `F_WRLCK` returns `l_type` = `F_UNLCK` and the other fields unchanged. When another process holds the region, the returned fields describe its lock.

**dup-13** [OSF/1] `F_SETLK` sets or clears a file segment lock as described by the `struct flock` at `argument`. It sets shared locks (`F_RDLCK`) and exclusive locks (`F_WRLCK`) and removes either kind (`F_UNLCK`). If a shared or exclusive lock cannot be set, `fcntl()` returns −1 at once.
  Test: A child holds a write lock. The parent's `F_SETLK` with `F_WRLCK` returns −1 at once.

**dup-14** [OSF/1] `F_SETLKW` is like `F_SETLK`, except that if the lock is blocked by other locks the process waits until it is unblocked. If a signal arrives while it waits, the call is interrupted, returns −1 and sets `errno` to `EINTR`.
  Test: Block on a held region, raise an alarm with a handler installed, and expect −1 and `EINTR`.

**dup-15** [OSF/1] The `O_NDELAY` and `O_NONBLOCK` requests affect only operations on descriptors that come from the same `open()`.
  Test: Open a FIFO twice. Set `O_NONBLOCK` via one; the other's `F_GETFL` does not show it.

**dup-16** [OSF/1] The page notes that in BSD, `O_NDELAY` and `O_NONBLOCK` apply to every descriptor that refers to the object.
  Not testable from user space as an OSF/1 requirement: this states BSD behaviour for contrast.

**dup-17** [OSF/1] When a shared lock is set on a segment, other processes can set shared locks on that segment or part of it. A shared lock prevents any other process from setting an exclusive lock on any part of the protected area.
  Test: A child holds a read lock. The parent's read lock succeeds, and its write lock gets `EAGAIN` or `EACCES`.

**dup-18** [OSF/1] A request for a shared lock fails if the descriptor was not opened with read access.
  Test: On an `O_WRONLY` fd, `F_SETLK` with `F_RDLCK` gives −1 and `EBADF`.

**dup-19** [OSF/1] An exclusive lock prevents any other process from setting a shared or exclusive lock on any part of the protected area. A request for an exclusive lock fails if the descriptor was not opened with write access.
  Test: On an `O_RDONLY` fd, `F_WRLCK` gives −1 and `EBADF`. While a child holds an exclusive lock, the parent's read lock fails.

**dup-20** [OSF/1] `struct flock` describes the segment to lock: `l_type` is the type, `l_whence` the starting offset, `l_start` the relative offset, `l_len` the size and `l_pid` the process ID.
  Test: Compile code that uses all five fields.

**dup-21** [OSF/1] `l_whence` is `SEEK_SET`, `SEEK_CUR` or `SEEK_END`: `l_start` is measured from the start of the file, the current position, or the end of the file.
  Test: Lock with `SEEK_END` and `l_start` −10, `l_len` 10. `F_GETLK` from another process reports the region at the last 10 bytes.

**dup-22** [OSF/1] `l_len` is the number of consecutive bytes to lock. It "may be negative" where the definition of `off_t` permits negative values.
  Test: See dup-25.

**dup-23** [OSF/1] `l_pid` is used only with `F_GETLK`, to return the process ID of the process that holds a blocking lock.
  Test: `F_GETLK` returns `l_pid` equal to the PID of the child that holds the lock.

**dup-24** [OSF/1] After a successful `F_GETLK`, `l_whence` is `SEEK_SET`.
  Test: Call `F_GETLK` with `l_whence` = `SEEK_CUR` against a held lock. The result has `l_whence` == `SEEK_SET`.

**dup-25** [OSF/1] For positive `l_len`, the area runs from `l_start` to `l_start + l_len - 1`. For negative `l_len`, it runs from `l_start + l_len` to `l_start - 1`.
  Test: Lock `l_start` 100 with `l_len` −10. Another process can lock 100 but not 90 to 99.

**dup-26** [OSF/1] Locks may start and extend beyond the current end of the file, but may not be negative relative to the start of the file.
  Test: Locking at offset 1000 on an empty file succeeds. A region that resolves to a negative offset fails.

**dup-27** [OSF/1] With `l_len` = 0, a lock "may be set to always extend" to the largest possible file offset. If such a lock also has `l_start` = 0 and `l_whence` = `SEEK_SET`, the whole file is locked.
  Test: Lock with 0/0/`SEEK_SET`. Another process cannot lock any offset, including one past EOF.

**dup-28** [OSF/1] Changing or unlocking a part in the middle of a larger locked segment leaves a smaller segment at each end.
  Test: Lock 0–99 and unlock 40–59. Another process can lock 40–59 but not 0–39 or 60–99.

**dup-29** [OSF/1] Locking a segment the caller already holds replaces the old lock type with the new one.
  Test: Hold a read lock, set a write lock on the same range, and `F_GETLK` from another process reports `F_WRLCK`.

**dup-30** [OSF/1] All of a process's locks on a file are removed when the process closes any descriptor for that file, or when the process that holds the descriptor ends.
  Test: Lock via fd A, open the file again as fd B, and close B. Another process can now lock the region.

**dup-31** [OSF/1] A child does not inherit locks across `fork()`.
  Test: The parent holds a write lock. In the child, `F_GETLK` reports the parent's lock, and the child's `F_SETLK` fails.

**dup-32** [OSF/1] If a regular file has enforced record locking enabled, record locks affect other calls, including `creat()`, `open()`, `read()`, `write()`, `truncate()` and `ftruncate()`.
  Test: Enable mandatory locking on a file (method not given on this page). While another process holds a write lock, `read` blocks or fails.
Note: The page does not say how enforced locking is enabled or what the affected calls do.

**dup-33** [OSF/1] If the system detects that sleeping until a locked region is unlocked would cause a deadlock, `fcntl()` fails with `EDEADLK`.
  Test: Processes P1 and P2 each hold a region and then each `F_SETLKW` the other's. One gets `EDEADLK`.

**dup-34** [OSF/1] (Notes.) `dup(filedes)` is equivalent to `fcntl(filedes, F_DUPFD, 0)`.
  Test: `dup` returns the lowest free descriptor, which shares the file offset and has `FD_CLOEXEC` clear.
Note: The page spells the function "fnctl" here.

**dup-35** [OSF/1] (Notes.) `dup2(oldfiledes, newfiledes)` is similar to `close(newfiledes)` followed by `fcntl(oldfiledes, F_DUPFD, newfiledes)`.
  Test: `dup2(a, 7)` with 7 open on another file returns 7, and 7 now refers to `a`'s file.

**dup-36** [OSF/1] (Notes.) Locks set by `fcntl()` and `lockf()` do not interact with locks set by `flock()`. An exclusive lock set with `fcntl()` or `lockf()` does not affect a process that sets or clears locks on the same file with `flock()`, so the two can disagree. `fcntl()` and `lockf()` share the same record-locking mechanism.
  Test: A child holds an `fcntl` write lock on a file. The parent's `flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB)` still succeeds. A `lockf` lock conflicts with an `fcntl` lock.

**dup-37** [OSF/1] Return values on success: `F_DUPFD` returns a new descriptor. `F_GETFD` returns `FD_CLOEXEC` or 0. `F_SETFD`, `F_SETFL`, `F_GETLK`, `F_SETLK` and `F_SETLKW` return a value other than −1. `F_GETFL` returns the status flags and access modes, which are never negative. `F_GETOWN` returns the descriptor owner. On failure, `fcntl()` returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: Check each request's return as stated.
Note: The page gives no return values for `F_SETOWN`, `dup()` or `dup2()`.

Errors for `fcntl()` (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**dup-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not a valid open file descriptor.

**dup-E2** `EBADF`: `request` is `F_SETLK` or `F_SETLKW`, `l_type` is a shared lock (`F_RDLCK`), and `filedes` is not a valid descriptor open for reading.

**dup-E3** `EBADF`: `l_type` is an exclusive lock (`F_WRLCK`) and `filedes` is not a valid descriptor open for writing.
