### getitimer(2), setitimer(2)

Page: `man2/getitimer.html`; same text as `setitimer(2)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getitimer-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int setitimer(int which, struct itimerval *value, struct itimerval *ovalue)` and `int getitimer(int which, struct itimerval *value)`, declared in `<sys/time.h>`.
  Test: compile calls; check return types `int`.

**getitimer-2** [OSF/1] `<sys/time.h>` defines `ITIMER_REAL` 0, `ITIMER_VIRTUAL` 1, `ITIMER_PROF` 2; `which` is one of these.
  Test: check the three constant values.

**getitimer-3** [OSF/1] `value` points to an `itimerval` giving a timer interval and the time left to the end of the interval; `ovalue` points to an `itimerval` giving the current interval and time left.
  Test: see below.

**getitimer-4** [OSF/1] `getitimer()` stores the current value of timer `which` in `*value`.
  Test: `setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, {0,0},{10,0})`, then `getitimer`; `it_value.tv_sec` is ≤ 10 and > 0.

**getitimer-5** [OSF/1] `setitimer()` sets the timer to `*value`, and returns the previous value in `*ovalue` if `ovalue` is nonzero.
  Test: set 10 s, then set 5 s with `ovalue`; `ovalue->it_value` is close to 10 s. Passing `ovalue = NULL` succeeds.

**getitimer-6** [OSF/1] Field `struct timeval it_interval`: if nonzero, the value used to reload `it_value` when the timer expires.
  Test: set `it_interval` 0.1 s; expect repeated `SIGALRM`s.

**getitimer-7** [OSF/1] Field `struct timeval it_value`: if nonzero, the time to the next timer expiration.
  Test: set `it_value` 0.2 s; `SIGALRM` arrives after about 0.2 s.

**getitimer-8** [OSF/1] Setting `it_value` to 0 disables a timer.
  Test: set a timer then set `it_value` to 0; no signal arrives; `getitimer` shows 0.

**getitimer-9** [OSF/1] Setting `it_interval` to 0 makes the timer disabled after its next expiration (if `it_value` is nonzero).
  Test: `it_value` 0.1 s, `it_interval` 0; exactly one `SIGALRM` in 1 s.

**getitimer-10** [OSF/1] Time values smaller than the resolution of the system clock are rounded up to that resolution.
  Test: set `it_value` 1 µs; `getitimer` immediately shows a value ≥ 1 µs or the timer fires; it is not treated as 0 (disabled).

**getitimer-11** [OSF/1] Each process has three interval timers, defined in `sys/time.h`.
  Test: all three `which` values are accepted.

**getitimer-12** [OSF/1] `ITIMER_REAL` decrements in real time; `SIGALRM` is delivered on expiry.
  Test: set 0.2 s while sleeping in `pause()`; `SIGALRM` arrives.

**getitimer-13** [OSF/1] `ITIMER_VIRTUAL` decrements in process virtual time, running only while the process is executing; `SIGVTALRM` is delivered on expiry.
  Test: set 0.2 s and sleep 1 s; no signal; then spin; `SIGVTALRM` arrives.

**getitimer-14** [OSF/1] `ITIMER_PROF` decrements both in process virtual time and when the system runs on behalf of the process; it is meant for interpreters' statistical profiling; `SIGPROF` is delivered each time it expires.
  Test: set 0.1 s interval and spin; `SIGPROF` arrives repeatedly.

**getitimer-15** [OSF/1] Because `SIGPROF` may interrupt in-progress system calls, programs using `ITIMER_PROF` must be prepared to restart interrupted system calls.
  Test: none required; advice.

**getitimer-16** [OSF/1] `sys/time.h` defines three macros: `timerclear()` sets a time value to zero, `timerisset()` tests whether a time value is nonzero, `timercmp()` compares two time values; the comparisons `>=` and `<=` do not work with `timercmp()`.
  Test: `timerclear(&t)` then `!timerisset(&t)`; `timercmp(&a,&b,<)` is right for a < b.

**getitimer-17** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as above.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**getitimer-E1** `EFAULT`: `value` specified a bad address.

**getitimer-E2** `EINVAL`: `value` specified a time that was too large to be handled.

Note: The page lists no error for an invalid `which`.

Related: Functions: gettimeofday(2)

### getlogin(2), getlogin_r(2), setlogin(2)

Page: `man2/getlogin.html`; same text as `getlogin_r(2)`, `setlogin(2)`. AES: Full use (`getlogin()`).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getlogin-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `char *getlogin(void)`; `int getlogin_r(char *name, int len)`; `setlogin(char *name)`.
  Test: compile calls of all three with these types.
  Note: The page gives no return type for `setlogin()`; RETURN VALUES implies an integer.

**getlogin-2** [OSF/1] `name` points to the login name; `len` is the length of the buffer pointed to by `name`.
  Test: see getlogin-7.

**getlogin-3** [OSF/1] `getlogin()` returns the login name of the user associated with the current session, as previously set by `setlogin()`.
  Test: as root, `setsid()`, `setlogin("tuser")`; `getlogin()` returns "tuser".

**getlogin-4** [OSF/1] The name is normally associated with a login shell when a session is created, and is inherited by all processes descended from it, even ones that assume another user ID (for example via `su`).
  Test: after getlogin-3, `fork()`, child `setuid(other)`; child's `getlogin()` is still "tuser".

**getlogin-5** [OSF/1] `setlogin()` sets the login name of the current session's user to `name`; it is restricted to the superuser.
  Test: as non-root, `setlogin("x")` returns -1 with `EPERM`.

**getlogin-6** [OSF/1] `setlogin()` is normally used only when creating a new session for the named user (for example at login, or when a remote shell is invoked).
  Test: Not testable (usage advice).

**getlogin-7** [OSF/1] `getlogin_r()` is the reentrant version of `getlogin()`; on success the login name is stored in `name`.
  Test: after getlogin-3, `getlogin_r(b, sizeof b)` returns 0 and `b` is "tuser".

**getlogin-8** [OSF/1] On success `getlogin()` returns a pointer to a null-terminated string in a static buffer; if the name has not been set, it returns null.
  Test: two calls return the same pointer; in a fresh session with no name set, the result is `NULL`.

**getlogin-9** [OSF/1] `setlogin()` returns 0 on success, otherwise -1 with an error code in `errno`.
  Test: see getlogin-3 and getlogin-5.

**getlogin-10** [OSF/1] `getlogin_r()` returns 0 on success, otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: see getlogin-7.

**getlogin-11** [OSF/1] Login names are limited to `MAXLOGNAME` characters, defined in `sys/param.h`.
  Test: as root, `setlogin()` with a string of `MAXLOGNAME + 1` characters fails with `EINVAL`.

Errors (for `getlogin()`, `getlogin_r()` or `setlogin()`; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**getlogin-E1** `EFAULT`: `name` gave an invalid address.

**getlogin-E2** `EINVAL`: `name` pointed to a string that was too long.

**getlogin-E3** `EPERM`: the caller tried to set the login name and was not the superuser.

Related: Functions: setsid(2). Command: su(1)

### getmsg(2)

Page: `man2/getmsg.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**getmsg-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int getmsg(int fd, struct strbuf *ctlptr, struct strbuf *dataptr, int *flags)`, declared in `<stropts.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.
  Note: The page's synopsis omits the commas between parameters; the page header reads "Digital" rather than "OSF".

**getmsg-2** [DEC] `fd` specifies a file descriptor referencing an open stream.
  Test: call on a STREAMS device descriptor; succeeds.

**getmsg-3** [DEC] `struct strbuf` has member `int maxlen`: the maximum number of bytes the buffer `buf` can hold.
  Test: send a message larger than `maxlen`; expect only `maxlen` bytes retrieved.

**getmsg-4** [DEC] `struct strbuf` has member `int len`: on return, the number of bytes of data or control information actually received; 0 if there is a zero-length control or data part; −1 if no data or control information is present in the message.
  Test: send a data-only message; expect `ctlptr->len == -1` and `dataptr->len` equal to the bytes sent.

**getmsg-5** [DEC] `struct strbuf` has member `char *buf`: points to the buffer in which data or control information is placed.
  Test: check received bytes appear in `buf`.

**getmsg-6** [DEC] `ctlptr` holds the control part of the message and `dataptr` holds the data part.
  Test: `putmsg` with distinct control and data; `getmsg` returns each in the matching buffer.

**getmsg-7** [DEC] If `ctlptr` (or `dataptr`) is NULL or its `maxlen` is −1, that part is not processed, is left on the stream head read queue, and `len` is set to −1.
  Test: call with `dataptr->maxlen = -1`; expect `len == -1` and a second call retrieves the data.
  Note: The page says `len` is set to −1 even when the pointer is NULL, where there is no `len` to set.

**getmsg-8** [DEC] If `maxlen` is 0 and the part is zero-length, that zero-length part is removed from the read queue and `len` is set to 0.
  Test: send a zero-length data part; call with `maxlen = 0`; expect `len == 0` and the part gone.

**getmsg-9** [DEC] If `maxlen` is 0 and the part has more than zero bytes, that information is left on the read queue and `len` is set to 0.
  Test: send 10 data bytes; call with `maxlen = 0`; expect `len == 0`, then a later call gets the 10 bytes.

**getmsg-10** [DEC] If `maxlen` is less than the control or data part, `maxlen` bytes are retrieved, the remainder stays on the stream head read queue, and a non-zero return value is given.
  Test: send 100 data bytes, read with `maxlen = 10`; expect 10 bytes and return `MOREDATA`.

**getmsg-11** [DEC] `flags` may be set to 0 or `RS_HIPRI`; if information is retrieved from a priority message, `*flags` is set to `RS_HIPRI` on return.
  Test: send a priority message; call with `*flags = 0`; expect `*flags == RS_HIPRI` afterwards.
  Note: The page names the flag `RS_HIPRI` in PARAMETERS but `S_HIPRI` in DESCRIPTION; the page is inconsistent.

**getmsg-12** [DEC] `getmsg` retrieves the contents of a message at the stream head read queue of a STREAMS file into user buffer(s); the message must contain a data part, a control part, or both, and the parts go into separate buffers.
  Test: `putmsg` then `getmsg`; contents match.

**getmsg-13** [DEC] The semantics of each part is defined by the STREAMS module that generated the message.
  Test: Not testable generically; module-defined.

**getmsg-14** [DEC] By default `getmsg` processes the first priority or non-priority message available on the stream head read queue.
  Test: queue a normal message; call with `*flags = 0`; it is returned.

**getmsg-15** [DEC] If `flags` is set to the high-priority value, `getmsg` processes the next message only if it is a priority message.
  Test: queue only a normal message; call with `*flags = RS_HIPRI` and `O_NONBLOCK`; expect `EAGAIN` and the message still queued.

**getmsg-16** [DEC] If `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` is clear, `getmsg` blocks until a message of the type(s) specified by `flags` is available on the stream head read queue.
  Test: blocking `getmsg` on an empty stream; send a message from another process after 1 s; call returns then.

**getmsg-17** [DEC] The page states: if neither `O_NDELAY` nor `O_NONBLOCK` has been set and no message of the specified type(s) is present, `getmsg` fails with `EAGAIN`.
  Test: see getmsg-E1.
  Note: The page says "neither ... has been set" here, which contradicts getmsg-16 and the `EAGAIN` entry (flag set); it almost certainly means one of them is set.

**getmsg-18** [DEC] If a hangup occurs on the stream, `getmsg` continues to operate normally until the stream head read queue is empty; thereafter it returns 0 in the `len` fields of `ctlptr` and `dataptr`.
  Test: queue messages, hang up the stream, read them all; next call gives `len == 0` in both.

**getmsg-19** [DEC] `getmsg` can also fail if a STREAMS error message had been received at the stream head before the call; the error returned is the value contained in the STREAMS error message.
  Test: have a module send an M_ERROR with a known errno; expect `getmsg` to fail with that errno.

**getmsg-20** [DEC] On success a non-negative value is returned: 0 means a full message was read; `MORECTL` means more control information is waiting; `MOREDATA` means more data is waiting; `MORECTL|MOREDATA` means both remain. Subsequent `getmsg` calls retrieve the remainder of the message.
  Test: send control and data both larger than buffers; expect `MORECTL|MOREDATA`, then further calls drain it and finally return 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**getmsg-E1** `EAGAIN`: The `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` flag is set, and no messages are available.

**getmsg-E2** `EBADF`: `fd` is not a valid file descriptor open for reading.

**getmsg-E3** `EBADMSG`: The queued message to be read is not valid for `getmsg`.

**getmsg-E4** `EFAULT`: `ctlptr`, `dataptr`, or `flags` points to a location outside the allocated address space.

**getmsg-E5** `EINTR`: A signal was caught during the `getmsg` system call.

**getmsg-E6** `EINVAL`: An illegal value was specified in `flags`, or the stream referenced by `fd` is linked under a multiplexor.

**getmsg-E7** `ENOSTR`: A stream is not associated with `fd`.

Related: poll(2), putmsg(2), read(2), write(2)

### getpeername(2)

Page: `man2/getpeername.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getpeername-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int getpeername(int socket, struct sockaddr *address, int *address_len)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**getpeername-2** [OSF/1] `socket` is the descriptor of a connected socket; `getpeername()` operates only on connected sockets.
  Test: call on an unconnected `SOCK_STREAM` socket; expect `ENOTCONN`.

**getpeername-3** [OSF/1] `address` points to a `sockaddr` structure whose format is determined by the domain and the behaviour requested for the socket; `sockaddr` is an overlay for `sockaddr_in`, `sockaddr_un` or `sockaddr_ns`, depending on the active address family.
  Test: on a connected `AF_INET` socket, the result's family is `AF_INET`.

**getpeername-4** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined before `sys/socket.h` is included, `sockaddr` takes 4.4BSD behaviour, with a field for the length of the socket address, and the 4.3BSD structure is named `osockaddr`.
  Test: compile with `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN`; `struct sockaddr` has a length field and `struct osockaddr` exists.

**getpeername-5** [OSF/1] Otherwise the default 4.3BSD `sockaddr` structure is used, with the socket address length assumed to be 14 bytes or less.
  Test: compile without the option; `struct sockaddr` has no length field and `sizeof(struct sockaddr)` leaves at most 14 bytes for the address.

**getpeername-6** [OSF/1] `address_len` specifies the length of the `sockaddr` structure pointed to by `address`.
  Test: pass `sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)`; call succeeds.
  Note: The page does not say whether `*address_len` is updated on return.

**getpeername-7** [OSF/1] `getpeername()` retrieves the name (address) of the peer socket at the remote end of the connection; this lets a process that inherited open sockets identify their addresses.
  Test: connect to a listening TCP socket on a known port; the peer address returned has that port.

**getpeername-8** [OSF/1] A process can use `getsockname()` to retrieve the local address of a socket.
  Test: none here; see getsockname(2).

**getpeername-9** [OSF/1] On success returns 0 and `address` holds the peer's address; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as getpeername-7.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**getpeername-E1** `EBADF`: The `socket` parameter is not valid.

**getpeername-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**getpeername-E3** `ENOTCONN`: The socket is not connected.

**getpeername-E4** `ENOBUFS`: Insufficient resources were available in the system to complete the call.

**getpeername-E5** `EFAULT`: `address` or `address_len` is not in a writable part of the user address space.

Related: Functions: accept(2), bind(2), getsockname(2), socket(2)

### getpgrp(2), getpid(2), getppid(2)

Page: `man2/getpgrp.html`; same text as `getpid(2)`, `getppid(2)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getpgrp-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `pid_t getpid(void)`, `pid_t getpgrp(void)`, `pid_t getppid(void)`, declared via `<unistd.h>` and `<sys/types.h>`.
  Test: compile calls; check return type `pid_t`.

**getpgrp-2** [OSF/1] `getpid()` returns the process ID of the calling process.
  Test: fork; the value `fork` returned to the parent equals the child's `getpid()`.

**getpgrp-3** [OSF/1] `getpgrp()` returns the process group ID of the calling process.
  Test: `setpgid(0,0)`; `getpgrp() == getpid()`.

**getpgrp-4** [OSF/1] `getppid()` returns the parent process ID of the calling process; when a process is created its parent process ID is the process ID of its parent.
  Test: fork; child's `getppid()` equals parent's `getpid()`.

**getpgrp-5** [OSF/1] If a parent process exits, the parent process IDs of its child processes are changed to the process ID of `init`.
  Test: fork a child that forks a grandchild and exits; grandchild's `getppid()` becomes 1 (init's ID per intro(2)).

**getpgrp-6** [OSF/1] The page gives no error returns for these functions.
  Test: none.

Related: System calls: fork(2), kill(2), setpgid(2), setsid(2), wait(2)

### getpriority(2), setpriority(2)

Page: `man2/getpriority.html`; same text as `setpriority(2)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getpriority-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int getpriority(int which, int who)`, with `#include <sys/resource.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including `<sys/resource.h>`.

**getpriority-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int setpriority(int which, int who, int priority)`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types.

**getpriority-3** [OSF/1] `which` is one of `PRIO_PROCESS`, `PRIO_PGRP` or `PRIO_USER`; `who` is then read as a process ID, process group ID or user ID respectively.
  Test: `getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, getpid())`, `getpriority(PRIO_PGRP, getpgrp())` and `getpriority(PRIO_USER, getuid())` all succeed.

**getpriority-4** [OSF/1] A `who` value of 0 means the current process, process group or user.
  Test: `getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0)` equals `getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, getpid())`.

**getpriority-5** [OSF/1] `priority` is a value in the range −20 to 20. The default priority is 0. Negative priorities give more favorable scheduling.
  Test: a freshly started process (with no inherited change) has `getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0)` equal to 0.

**getpriority-6** [OSF/1] `setpriority()` sets the scheduling priority of every specified process to the given value.
  Test: `setpriority(PRIO_PGRP, 0, 5)` in a group of two processes; both then report priority 5.

**getpriority-7** [OSF/1] `getpriority()` returns the highest priority (lowest numerical value) of any of the specified processes.
  Test: in a process group, set one member to 3 and another to 7; `getpriority(PRIO_PGRP, pgid)` returns 3.

**getpriority-8** [OSF/1] In `setpriority()`, a value less than −20 is treated as −20, and a value greater than 20 is treated as 20.
  Test: `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, 50)` then `getpriority` returns 20; as superuser, `setpriority(..., -50)` gives −20.

**getpriority-9** [OSF/1] On success `getpriority()` returns an integer from −20 to 20; otherwise it returns −1.
  Test: `getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0)` lies in [−20, 20].
  Note: The page does not say how a caller tells a priority of −1 apart from failure.

**getpriority-10** [OSF/1] On success `setpriority()` returns 0; otherwise −1.
  Test: `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0))` returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**getpriority-E1** `ESRCH`: no process was found using the given `which` and `who` values.

**getpriority-E2** `EINVAL`: `which` was not recognized.

Note: The page then says `setpriority()` "can fail with errno set to one of the following values" but lists none (the original HTML is the same), so its extra errors are unknown.

Related: Functions: exec(2), nice(3)

### getrlimit(2), setrlimit(2)

Page: `man2/getrlimit.html`; same text as `setrlimit(2)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getrlimit-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/time.h>` and `<sys/resource.h>`): `int setrlimit(int resource1, struct rlimit *rlp)`; `int getrlimit(int resource1, struct rlimit *rlp)`.
  Test: compile calls of both with these types.

**getrlimit-2** [OSF/1] `RLIMIT_CPU`: the maximum CPU time, in seconds, used by each process.
  Test: set soft `RLIMIT_CPU` to 1, spin; the process gets `SIGXCPU`.

**getrlimit-3** [OSF/1] `RLIMIT_FSIZE`: the largest size, in bytes, of any single file that can be created.
  Test: set to 1024, ignore `SIGXFSZ`, write 2048 bytes; the file does not exceed 1024 bytes.

**getrlimit-4** [OSF/1] `RLIMIT_DATA`: the maximum size, in bytes, of a process's data segment; it bounds how far the break can be extended with `sbrk()`.
  Test: set low, call `sbrk()` beyond it; the call fails.

**getrlimit-5** [OSF/1] `RLIMIT_STACK`: the maximum size, in bytes, of the stack segment; the system extends the stack automatically.
  Test: set low and recurse deeply; the process gets `SIGSEGV`.

**getrlimit-6** [OSF/1] `RLIMIT_CORE`: the largest size, in bytes, of a core file that can be created.
  Test: set to 0 and `abort()`; no core file is created.

**getrlimit-7** [OSF/1] `RLIMIT_RSS`: the maximum size, in bytes, to which the resident set size can grow; it limits physical memory given to a process, and when memory is tight the system prefers to take memory from processes exceeding their declared resident set size.
  Test: `setrlimit(RLIMIT_RSS, ...)` and `getrlimit()` round-trip the value; enforcement is not testable from user space (depends on memory pressure).

**getrlimit-8** [OSF/1] `rlp` points to an `rlimit` structure holding the current soft and hard limits; `getrlimit()` returns the requested limits in it and `setrlimit()` takes the new limits from it.
  Test: `setrlimit()` a lower soft limit, then `getrlimit()` returns that value.

**getrlimit-9** [OSF/1] `getrlimit()` obtains the limits on resource consumption by the current process and each process it creates; `setrlimit()` sets them.
  Test: set a limit, `fork()`; the child's `getrlimit()` shows the same limit.

**getrlimit-10** [OSF/1] Each limit has a soft and a hard value; when a soft limit is exceeded (for example CPU time) a process "can receive a signal" until it reaches the hard limit or modifies its limit. The `rlimit` structure is defined in `sys/resource.h`.
  Test: soft CPU 1 s, hard 3 s, catch `SIGXCPU`; at least one `SIGXCPU` arrives before the hard limit.

**getrlimit-11** [OSF/1] Superuser privilege is required to raise the maximum (hard) limits.
  Test: as non-root, raising `rlim_max` fails with `EPERM`.

**getrlimit-12** [OSF/1] An unprivileged process can set `rlim_cur` anywhere from 0 to `rlim_max`, or can lower `rlim_max`, irreversibly.
  Test: as non-root, lower `rlim_max`; raising it back fails with `EPERM`.

**getrlimit-13** [OSF/1] An infinite limit is represented by `RLIM_INFINITY`.
  Test: `RLIM_INFINITY` is defined; setting a soft limit to it when the hard limit is `RLIM_INFINITY` succeeds.

**getrlimit-14** [OSF/1] Limits are per-process information, so `setrlimit()` must be run directly by the shell to affect all future processes it creates; `limit` is therefore a shell built-in.
  Test: limit set in a parent is seen by later children (see getrlimit-9).

**getrlimit-15** [OSF/1] A `brk()` call fails if the data space limit is reached.
  Test: lower `RLIMIT_DATA`; `brk()` past it returns failure.

**getrlimit-16** [OSF/1] When the stack limit is reached the process receives `SIGSEGV`; if the signal is not caught by a handler running on the signal stack, it kills the process.
  Test: see getrlimit-5; the child is killed by `SIGSEGV` unless it handles it on an alternate signal stack.

**getrlimit-17** [OSF/1] A file I/O operation that would create a file that is too large generates `SIGXFSZ`; this normally terminates the process but can be caught.
  Test: set `RLIMIT_FSIZE` small and write past it; with default action the child dies of `SIGXFSZ`; with a handler, the handler runs.

**getrlimit-18** [OSF/1] When the soft CPU time limit is exceeded, `SIGXCPU` is sent to the process.
  Test: see getrlimit-2.

**getrlimit-19** [OSF/1] `ulimit()` is implemented in terms of `setrlimit()`; the two should not be used in the same program, and the result of doing so is undefined.
  Test: Not testable (undefined behaviour).

**getrlimit-20** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: `getrlimit(RLIMIT_CPU, &r) == 0`.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**getrlimit-E1** `EFAULT`: the address given for `rlp` is invalid.

**getrlimit-E2** `EINVAL`: `resource1` is not a valid resource.

**getrlimit-E3** `EPERM`: the limit given to `setrlimit()` would raise the maximum limit value and the caller lacks appropriate privilege.

Related: Functions: quota(2), setquota(2), sigaction(2), sigstack(2), sigvec(2), ulimit(3)

### getrusage(2), vtimes(2)

Page: `man2/getrusage.html`; same text as `vtimes(2)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getrusage-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int getrusage(int who, struct rusage *r_usage)`, declared via `<sys/time.h>` and `<sys/resource.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with these headers and types; check it returns `int`.

**getrusage-2** [Compat] Synopsis: `vtimes(struct vtimes *par_vm, struct vtimes ch_vm)` declared via `<sys/vtimes.h>`, with no stated return type; `vtimes()` only is in the Berkeley Compatibility Library (`libbsd.a`).
  Test: link a program calling `vtimes()` against `libbsd.a`; it links.
  Note: The page gives the second parameter as `struct vtimes ch_vm` (not a pointer), yet the notes speak of both parameters as pointers that may be zero; the synopsis looks wrong.

**getrusage-3** [OSF/1] `getrusage()` returns information describing the resources utilized by the current process or by its terminated child processes.
  Test: burn CPU, call `getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF, &ru)`; expect 0 and nonzero `ru_utime`.

**getrusage-4** [OSF/1] `who` = `RUSAGE_SELF` retrieves information about resources used by the current process.
  Test: `getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF, &ru)` returns 0 and user time grows after a CPU loop.

**getrusage-5** [OSF/1] `who` = `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` retrieves information about resources used by child processes of the current process (the description says terminated children).
  Test: fork a child that burns CPU, `wait()` for it, then `getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN, &ru)`; expect nonzero `ru_utime`.

**getrusage-6** [OSF/1] `r_usage` points to a buffer that is filled in as described in the `sys/resource.h` header file.
  Test: fill the buffer with a pattern, call, check fields have been overwritten.

**getrusage-7** [OSF/1] The numbers in the `ru_inblock` and `ru_outblock` fields account only for real I/O; data supplied by the caching mechanism is charged only to the first process to read or write the data.
  Test: process A reads a file (counts rise); process B then reads the cached file; expect B's `ru_inblock` not to rise.

**getrusage-8** [Compat] `vtimes()` is supported to provide compatibility with older programs and is superseded by `getrusage()`.
  Test: Not testable as behaviour; documentary.

**getrusage-9** [Compat] `vtimes()` returns accounting information for the current process and for the terminated child processes of the current process.
  Test: call `vtimes(&p, &c)` after a terminated child; expect both buffers filled.
  Note: The page does not say which buffer receives which information; the parameter names suggest `par_vm` for the current process and `ch_vm` for the children.

**getrusage-10** [Compat] Either `par_vm` or `ch_vm` or both may be zero; then information is returned only for the nonzero pointers.
  Test: `vtimes(&p, 0)` succeeds and fills `p`; `vtimes(0, 0)` does not fault.

**getrusage-11** [Compat] After the `vtimes()` call, each buffer contains information as defined by the `sys/vtimes.h` include file.
  Test: check the fields defined in `sys/vtimes.h` are set.

**getrusage-12** [OSF/1] On success `getrusage()` returns 0; otherwise it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: valid call returns 0; invalid `who` returns −1.

**getrusage-13** [Compat] The page gives no return value or errors for `vtimes()`.
  Test: none.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**getrusage-E1** `EINVAL`: The `who` parameter is not a valid value.

**getrusage-E2** `EFAULT`: The address specified for `r_usage` is not valid.

Related: Functions: gettimer(3), time(3), times(3), wait(2)

### getsockname(2)

Page: `man2/getsockname.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getsockname-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`): `int getsockname(int socket, struct sockaddr *address, int *address_len)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**getsockname-2** [OSF/1] `socket` is the socket whose local address is wanted.
  Test: bind a UDP socket to 127.0.0.1 port P; `getsockname()` returns that address and port.

**getsockname-3** [OSF/1] `address` points to a `sockaddr` structure whose format is determined by the domain and the behaviour requested for the socket; it is an overlay for a `sockaddr_in`, `sockaddr_un` or `sockaddr_ns`, depending on the active address family.
  Test: for an `AF_INET` socket, cast the result to `struct sockaddr_in` and read `sin_port`.

**getsockname-4** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined before `sys/socket.h` is included, `sockaddr` has 4.4BSD behaviour, with a field giving the length of the socket address; in that case the 4.3BSD structure is named `osockaddr`.
  Test: compile with `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN`; code using `sa_len` and `struct osockaddr` compiles.
  Note: The page does not name the length field; `sa_len` in the test is an assumption to be confirmed from `sys/socket.h`.

**getsockname-5** [OSF/1] Otherwise the default 4.3BSD `sockaddr` is used, and the socket address length is assumed to be 14 bytes or less.
  Test: without `_SOCKADDR_LEN`, `sizeof(((struct sockaddr *)0)->sa_data) == 14` compiles and holds.
  Note: The page states only "14 bytes or less"; the `sa_data` name in the test is an assumption.

**getsockname-6** [OSF/1] `address_len` gives the length of the `sockaddr` structure pointed to by `address`.
  Test: pass `len = sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)`; the call succeeds.

**getsockname-7** [OSF/1] `getsockname()` retrieves the locally bound address of the socket, including for sockets inherited from a creating process.
  Test: parent binds a socket, forks; child calls `getsockname()` on the inherited descriptor and gets the same address.

**getsockname-8** [OSF/1] A process can use `getpeername()` to find the address of the destination socket of a connection.
  Test: see getpeername(2).

**getsockname-9** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned and `address_len` points to the size of the socket address; otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: for an `AF_INET` socket, after the call `len == sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)`.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**getsockname-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**getsockname-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**getsockname-E3** `ENOBUFS`: insufficient system resources are available to complete the call.

**getsockname-E4** `EFAULT`: `address` or `address_len` is not in a writable part of the user address space.

Related: Functions: accept(2), bind(2), getpeername(2), socket(2)

### getsockopt(2)

Page: `man2/getsockopt.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getsockopt-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int getsockopt(int socket, int level, int option_nam, char *option_value, int *option_len)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types including both headers.

**getsockopt-2** [OSF/1] `getsockopt()` lets a program query socket options: the caller names the socket, the option, and a place to store the information, and the system returns the option information from its internal data structures.
  Test: `getsockopt(s, SOL_SOCKET, SO_TYPE, ...)` on a `SOCK_STREAM` socket returns 0 and the value `SOCK_STREAM`.

**getsockopt-3** [OSF/1] `level` is the protocol level of the option: `SOL_SOCKET` for socket-level options; for other levels, the protocol number of the controlling protocol (for example TCP's number as defined in `<netinet/in.h>` or found with `getprotobyname()`).
  Test: on a TCP socket, query an option TCP supports with `level` = `getprotobyname("tcp")->p_proto`; the call returns 0.

**getsockopt-4** [OSF/1] Options may exist at multiple protocol levels and are always present at the uppermost socket level; the caller specifies both the level and the option name.
  Test: informational; covered by getsockopt-3.

**getsockopt-5** [OSF/1] `option_nam` names a single option to retrieve; socket-level options are enabled or disabled with `setsockopt()`.
  Test: `setsockopt(SO_REUSEADDR, 1)`, then `getsockopt` reports nonzero.

**getsockopt-6** [OSF/1] `SO_DEBUG`: reports whether debugging information is being recorded; returns an `int`.
  Test: `getsockopt(SO_DEBUG)` succeeds and sets `option_len` to `sizeof(int)`.

**getsockopt-7** [OSF/1] `SO_ACCEPTCONN`: reports whether socket listening is enabled; returns an `int`.
  Test: value is 0 before `listen()` and nonzero after.

**getsockopt-8** [OSF/1] `SO_BROADCAST`: reports whether transmission of broadcast messages is supported; returns an `int`.
  Test: set it on a UDP socket with `setsockopt`, read back nonzero.

**getsockopt-9** [OSF/1] `SO_REUSEADDR`: reports whether the address validation rules used by `bind()` should allow reuse of local addresses; returns an `int`.
  Test: see getsockopt-5.

**getsockopt-10** [OSF/1] `SO_KEEPALIVE`: reports whether connections are kept active by periodic transmission of messages; if the connected socket fails to respond, the connection is broken and processes using the socket are notified with `SIGPIPE`. Returns an `int`.
  Test: set and read back nonzero; the `SIGPIPE` behaviour needs an unresponsive peer and is hard to test.

**getsockopt-11** [OSF/1] `SO_DONTROUTE`: reports whether outgoing messages should bypass the standard routing facilities ("Not recommended, for debugging purposes only"); returns an `int`.
  Test: set and read back nonzero.

**getsockopt-12** [OSF/1] `SO_USELOOPBACK`: only valid for routing sockets; reports whether the sender receives a copy of each message; returns an `int`.
  Test: on a routing socket, `getsockopt(SO_USELOOPBACK)` returns 0 with an `int` value.

**getsockopt-13** [OSF/1] `SO_LINGER`: reports whether the socket lingers on `close()` if data is present; returns a `struct linger`.
  Test: set `l_onoff`=1, `l_linger`=5 with `setsockopt`, read back the same `struct linger`.

**getsockopt-14** [OSF/1] If `SO_LINGER` is set, the system blocks the process during `close()` until it can transmit the data or until the time expires; if it is not specified, `close()` is handled so the process can continue as quickly as possible.
  Test: with linger set and unsent data to a non-reading peer, measure that `close()` blocks up to the linger time.

**getsockopt-15** [OSF/1] `SO_OOBINLINE`: reports whether received out-of-band (urgent) data is left in line; returns an `int`.
  Test: set and read back nonzero.

**getsockopt-16** [OSF/1] `SO_SNDBUF` and `SO_RCVBUF`: report send and receive buffer size information; each returns an `int`.
  Test: read both on a TCP socket; `option_len` is `sizeof(int)` for each.

**getsockopt-17** [OSF/1] `SO_SNDLOWAT` and `SO_RCVLOWAT`: report send and receive low-water mark information; each returns an `int`.
  Test: read both; `option_len` is `sizeof(int)`.

**getsockopt-18** [OSF/1] `SO_SNDTIMEO` and `SO_RCVTIMEO`: report send and receive time-out information; each returns a `struct timeval`.
  Test: read both; `option_len` is `sizeof(struct timeval)`.

**getsockopt-19** [OSF/1] `SO_ERROR`: reports the error status and clears it; returns an `int`.
  Test: after a failed non-blocking `connect`, `SO_ERROR` gives a nonzero error value and a second read gives 0.

**getsockopt-20** [OSF/1] `SO_TYPE`: reports the socket type; returns an `int`.
  Test: see getsockopt-2.

**getsockopt-21** [OSF/1] Options at other protocol levels vary in format and name.
  Test: informational.

**getsockopt-22** [OSF/1] `option_value` points to a buffer; `option_len` initially holds the buffer size and on return is set to the actual size of the value returned. If no option value is supplied or returned, `option_value` can be 0.
  Test: pass `option_len` = 64 for `SO_TYPE`; on return it is `sizeof(int)`.

**getsockopt-23** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: successful call returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**getsockopt-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**getsockopt-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**getsockopt-E3** `ENOPROTOOPT`: the option is unknown.

**getsockopt-E4** `EFAULT`: `option_value` is not in a valid (writable) part of the process space, or `option_len` is not in a valid part of the process address space.

Related: Functions: bind(2), close(2), endprotoent(3), getprotobynumber(3), getprotoent(3), setprotoent(3), setsockopt(2), socket(2)

### intro(2)

Page: `man2/intro.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**intro-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <errno.h>`.
  Test: compile a file including `<errno.h>` that refers to `errno`.

**intro-2** [DEC] Section 2 describes the DEC OSF/1 system calls, the entries into the operating system kernel.
  Test: none; documentary.

**intro-3** [DEC] Section 2 pages come from an OSF-supplied component (title line labelled "OSF") and a Digital-supplied component (labelled "Digital").
  Test: none; documentary.

**intro-4** [DEC] If OSF-supplied code operates differently on Digital platforms or has Digital extensions, an Environment Notes section is added to the OSF page, and such pages carry an "Environment_Note_Added" label on the title line. Technical corrections have been made to OSF pages where needed.
  Test: none; documentary.

**intro-5** [DEC] Suffixes on some Digital-supplied pages (one to four letters) exist only to allow pages with the same base name to coexist; see man(1).
  Test: none; documentary.

**intro-6** [DEC] Descriptor: an integer assigned by the system when a file is referenced by `open`, `dup` or `pipe`, or a socket by `socket` or `socketpair`; it uniquely identifies an access path to that file or socket from a given process or any of its children.
  Test: `open` returns a non-negative integer that a forked child can `read` from.

**intro-7** [DEC] Directory: a special file holding references to other files (links); by convention it contains at least the links dot (`.`, the directory itself) and dot-dot (`..`, its parent).
  Test: `mkdir` a directory; `stat("d/.")` matches `d`, `stat("d/..")` matches the parent.

**intro-8** [DEC] Access to system resources is governed by the effective user ID, the effective group ID, and the group access list.
  Test: see the File Access Permissions items.

**intro-9** [DEC] The effective user ID and effective group ID are initially the process's real user ID and real group ID; either can be changed by executing a set-user-ID or set-group-ID file, "or possibly by one of its ancestors" (see execve(2)).
  Test: a fresh non-setuid process has `geteuid() == getuid()`; exec a setuid file owned by another user and check `geteuid()`.

**intro-10** [DEC] The group access list is an extra set of group IDs used only in determining resource accessibility.
  Test: add a supplementary group; file readable only by that group can be opened.

**intro-11** [DEC] Every file has access permissions, established when the file is created and changeable with `chmod`; they decide whether a process may perform an operation such as opening for writing.
  Test: create 0400 file; `open` for writing fails as non-root; after `chmod 0600` it succeeds.

**intro-12** [DEC] File access is of three types: read, write and execute; for directories, execute permission controls whether the directory can be searched.
  Test: directory mode 0600 (no x); as non-root, `stat("dir/file")` fails (this page gives no errno).

**intro-13** [DEC] Permissions apply to three classes: the owner, users in the file's group, and anyone else, each with an independent set; the check uses the information applicable to the caller.
  Test: see intro-14 to intro-17.

**intro-14** [DEC] Read, write and execute/search are granted if the effective user ID is that of the superuser.
  Test: as root, open a mode 0000 file for reading; succeeds.

**intro-15** [DEC] Access is granted if the effective user ID matches the file owner's user ID and the owner permissions allow the access.
  Test: owner opens a 0600 file for read/write; succeeds.

**intro-16** [DEC] Access is granted if the effective user ID is not the owner's, but the effective group ID matches the file's group or the file's group is in the group access list, and the group permissions allow the access.
  Test: non-owner in the file's group opens a 0060 file; succeeds.

**intro-17** [DEC] Access is granted if neither the effective user ID nor the effective group ID and group access list match the file's, but the "other" permissions allow access.
  Test: unrelated user opens a 0006 file; succeeds.
  Note: The page does not state that an owner is denied when owner bits deny but group/other bits allow; it only lists when access is granted.

**intro-18** [DEC] Execute permission is denied when trying to execute an image on a file system mounted no-execute.
  Test: as root mount noexec, `execve` a 0755 binary there; expect failure (errno not given by this page).

**intro-19** [DEC] If the effective UID is not root and the process accesses a character or block special device on a file system mounted `nodev`, access is denied.
  Test: as non-root, open a device node on a nodev mount; expect failure.

**intro-20** [DEC] If the effective UID is not root and the process tries to execute an image with the setuid or setgid bit set on a file system mounted `nosuid`, execute permission is denied.
  Test: as non-root, exec a setuid binary on a nosuid mount; expect failure.

**intro-21** [DEC] File names of up to `{FILENAME_MAX}` characters can name an ordinary file, special file or directory.
  Test: create a file whose name is `FILENAME_MAX` characters long; succeeds.
  Note: The page uses `{FILENAME_MAX}`; other pages use `NAME_MAX` for this limit.

**intro-22** [DEC] File name characters can be any ASCII character except null (0) and the ASCII code for backslash (`\`); the parity bit (bit 8) must be 0.
  Test: creating a name with a high-bit character fails (cf. `EINVAL` on other pages).
  Note: The page excludes backslash rather than slash; this looks wrong, since slash is the path separator.

**intro-23** [DEC] Users should avoid `*`, `?` and `[ ]` in file names because of their special meaning to the shell.
  Test: none; advice only.

**intro-24** [DEC] The parent process ID of a process is the process ID of its creator (see fork(2)).
  Test: fork; child's `getppid()` equals parent's `getpid()`.

**intro-25** [DEC] A pathname is a null-terminated string: an optional slash, then zero or more directory names separated by slashes, optionally followed by another slash and a file name; its total length must be less than `{PATHNAME_MAX}` characters.
  Test: a path of length ≥ the limit is rejected (this page gives no errno).
  Note: The page uses `{PATHNAME_MAX}`; other pages use `PATH_MAX`.

**intro-26** [DEC] A pathname beginning with a slash is searched from the root directory; otherwise from the current working directory. A slash alone names the root directory.
  Test: `stat("/")` equals the root; relative `stat` resolves against `chdir` target.

**intro-27** [DEC] A null pathname refers to the current directory.
  Test: `stat("")`; see Note.
  Note: The page says a null pathname refers to the current directory, but other pages (e.g. mknod) give `ENOENT` for an empty string; the pages conflict.

**intro-28** [DEC] Each active process is uniquely identified by a positive integer process ID, in the range 0 to `{PROC_MAX}`.
  Test: `getpid()` is positive and unique among live processes.
  Note: The page says "positive" yet the range starts at 0 (process 0 is the scheduler).

**intro-29** [DEC] Each active process belongs to a process group identified by a positive integer process group ID, which is the process ID of the group leader; this permits signalling related processes (see csh(1)).
  Test: after `setpgid(0,0)`, `getpgrp() == getpid()`; `kill(-pgrp, sig)` reaches group members.

**intro-30** [DEC] Each user is identified by a positive integer real user ID, and belongs to one or more groups; one distinguished group, used for accounting, gives the real group ID.
  Test: `getuid()`, `getgid()` return the login IDs.

**intro-31** [DEC] All processes have a real user ID and real group ID, initialized from the parent process.
  Test: fork; child's `getuid()`/`getgid()` equal the parent's.

**intro-32** [DEC] Each process has a root directory and a current working directory for resolving pathnames; the process's root directory need not be the root of the root file system.
  Test: as root, `chroot("/tmp/x")`; `stat("/")` now gives `/tmp/x`.

**intro-33** [DEC] Each process group is a member of a session; a process belongs to the session of its process group; typically there is one session per login.
  Test: after `setsid()`, a child's `getpgrp()` is in the new session.

**intro-34** [DEC] A socket is an endpoint for communication between processes, with queues for sending and receiving data.
  Test: `socketpair`; data written to one end is read on the other.

**intro-35** [DEC] Sockets are typed by their communications properties: whether messages need the partner's name, whether communication is reliable, and the format used for naming recipients. Each system supports some collection of socket types (see socket(2)).
  Test: none; documentary.

**intro-36** [DEC] Each system supports some sets of communications protocols, each with an address format; an Address Family is the set of addresses for a group of protocols; each socket has an address from the family in which it was created.
  Test: `bind` an `AF_INET` socket to an `AF_UNIX` address; expect failure.

**intro-37** [DEC] Processes with IDs 0, 1 and 2 are special: 0 is the scheduler; 1 is `init`, the ancestor of every other process, which controls the process structure; 2 is the paging daemon.
  Test: `kill(1, 0)` succeeds or fails with `EPERM` (process 1 exists).

**intro-38** [DEC] A process is a superuser process, with special privileges, if its effective user ID is 0.
  Test: process with euid 0 can call `setgroups`; euid ≠ 0 gets `EPERM`.

**intro-39** [DEC] Each active process can belong to a terminal group identified by a positive integer tty group ID, used to arbitrate between jobs contending for the same terminal (see csh(1), tty(7)).
  Test: background process reading the terminal is stopped (needs a terminal).

**intro-40** [DEC] Most system calls have return values; an error is indicated by an otherwise impossible value, usually −1, and the error number is stored in the external variable `errno`.
  Test: `close(-1)` returns −1 and sets `errno`.

**intro-41** [DEC] `errno` is not cleared on successful calls; test it only after an error.
  Test: set `errno = 12345`, call `getpid()`; `errno` is still 12345.

**intro-42** [DEC] All return codes and values from functions are of type `int` unless otherwise noted.
  Test: none; applies to synopses.

**intro-43** [DEC] The list of errors and their names in `<errno.h>` is given on the errno(2) page.
  Test: none; documentary.

Related: cc(1), csh(1), tty(7), intro(3), perror(3)

### ioctl(2)

Page: `man2/ioctl.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**ioctl-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `ioctl(int d, unsigned long request, char *argp)`, declared in `<sys/ioctl.h>`; no return type is shown.
  Test: compile a call.
  Note: the page text is damaged here: the line `char *argp );` appears twice in the synopsis.

**ioctl-2** [OSF/1] `d` is the file descriptor of the device; `request` is the ioctl command; `argp` points to a parameter array for the request.
  Test: `ioctl(tty_fd, TIOCGWINSZ, &ws)` on a terminal returns non-negative.

**ioctl-3** [OSF/1] `ioctl()` performs a variety of operations on open descriptors; in particular many operating characteristics of character special files (for example, terminals) can be controlled with it.
  Test: as ioctl-2.

**ioctl-4** [OSF/1] A request encodes whether the parameter is "in" or "out", and the size of the `argp` parameter in bytes; the macros and defines for specifying requests are in `sys/ioctl.h`.
  Test: Not testable from this page alone: it does not name the encoding macros; check only that `<sys/ioctl.h>` compiles and defines the request constants.
  Note: The page does not name the macros.

**ioctl-5** [OSF/1] For non-STREAMS files, the functions are device-specific: `request` and the argument are passed to the file and interpreted by the device driver. Such control is infrequently used on non-STREAMS devices, basic I/O being done by `read()` and `write()`.
  Test: none generic; device-specific.
  Note: The page says "arg" and "fildes" here, where the synopsis uses `argp` and `d`.

**ioctl-6** [OSF/1] For STREAMS files, the functions performed, and STREAMS errors, are as described in streamio(7).
  Test: see streamio(7).

**ioctl-7** [OSF/1] If an error occurs, −1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: `ioctl` on a regular file with `TIOCGWINSZ`; expect −1 with `ENOTTY`.
  Note: The page does not state the return value on success.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**ioctl-E1** `EBADF`: `d` is not a valid descriptor.

**ioctl-E2** `ENOTTY`: `d` is not associated with a character special device.

**ioctl-E3** `ENOTTY`: The request does not apply to the kind of object that `d` references.

**ioctl-E4** `EINVAL`: `request` or `argp` is not valid.

Related: Functions: exec(2), fcntl(2), streamio(7); Files: tty(7), lvm(7)

### kill(2)

Page: `man2/kill.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**kill-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>`, `#include <signal.h>`; `int kill(pid_t process, int signal)`. The page's library section names the Berkeley Compatibility Library (`libbsd.a`).
  Test: Compile and link the call.
Note: The page separates the parameters with ";" instead of ",". It also lists a parameter `process_grp` ("Specifies the process group") that is not in the synopsis.

**kill-2** [OSF/1] `kill()` sends `signal` to the process or group of processes given by `process`.
  Test: The child installs a `SIGUSR1` handler, the parent calls `kill(child, SIGUSR1)`, and the handler runs.

**kill-3** [OSF/1] If `signal` is 0 (the null signal), error checking is done but no signal is sent. This can be used to check whether `process` is valid.
  Test: `kill(getpid(), 0)` returns 0. `kill` on a PID that is not in use, with 0, gives −1 and `ESRCH`.

**kill-4** [OSF/1] To signal another process, at least one of these must hold: the sender's real or effective user ID matches the receiver's real or effective user ID; the signal is `SIGCONT` sent to a process in the sender's session; or the caller has superuser privilege.
  Test: As non-root, signalling a process owned by another uid gives `EPERM`. `SIGCONT` to a different-uid process in the same session succeeds.

**kill-5** [OSF/1] A process can send signals to itself.
  Test: `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)` runs the handler.

**kill-6** [OSF/1] (Notes.) Sending a signal "does not imply that the operation is successful". Every signal operation must pass the access checks of each access-control policy enforced on the system.
  Not testable from user space in general: it depends on which access-control policies are configured.

**kill-7** [OSF/1] (Notes.) If `process` is greater than 0, the signal goes to the process whose ID equals `process`.
  Test: As kill-2.

**kill-8** [OSF/1] (Notes.) If `process` is 0, the signal goes to every process, other than system processes, whose process group ID equals the sender's.
  Test: Put two children in the parent's group and ignore the signal in the parent. `kill(0, SIGUSR1)` reaches both children.

**kill-9** [OSF/1] (Notes.) If `process` is −1 and the sender's effective user ID has root privileges, the signal goes to every process other than system processes.
  Not testable from user space safely: it signals every process on the system.
Note: The page does not say what happens when `process` is −1 and the sender is not root.

**kill-10** [OSF/1] (Notes.) If `process` is negative but not −1, the signal goes to every process whose process group ID equals the absolute value of `process`.
  Test: Make a child a group leader with `setpgid`, add a grandchild, and `kill(-pgid, SIGUSR1)` reaches both.

**kill-11** [Compat] (Notes.) `killpg()` is provided "for binary compatibility only".
  Test: Check that `killpg()` is provided. The page states no other behaviour for it.

**kill-12** [OSF/1] On success, `kill()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1, sets `errno`, and sends no signal.
  Test: After a failing call, no handler runs.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**kill-E1** `EINVAL`: `signal` is not a valid signal number.

**kill-E2** `EINVAL`: `signal` is `SIGKILL`, `SIGSTOP`, `SIGTSTP` or `SIGCONT`, and `process` is 1 (proc1).

**kill-E3** `ESRCH`: no process matches `process`.

**kill-E4** `EPERM`: the real or saved user ID does not match the receiver's real or effective user ID, the caller lacks the needed privilege, and the signal is not `SIGCONT` sent to a process in the caller's session.
Note: This condition speaks of the sender's "real or saved" user ID, while kill-4 speaks of the "real or the effective" user ID.

**kill-E5** `EACCES`: the caller does not have the needed privilege.

Related: Functions: getpid(2), kill(2), setpgid(2), sigaction(2), sigvec(2)

### link(2)

Page: `man2/link.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**link-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int link(const char *path1, const char *path2)`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types.

**link-2** [OSF/1] `path1` names an existing file; `path2` names the directory entry to create.
  Test: `link("a", "b")` returns 0 and `b` then exists.

**link-3** [OSF/1] If `path2` names a symbolic link, an error is returned.
  Test: create a symlink `s`, then `link("a", "s")` returns −1.
  Note: The page does not name the errno for this case.

**link-4** [OSF/1] `link()` creates an additional hard link (directory entry) for an existing file; old and new links have equal access rights to the object.
  Test: write through `b`; the data is visible through `a`, and both have the same `st_ino`.

**link-5** [OSF/1] `link()` atomically creates the new link and increments the file's link count by one.
  Test: `st_nlink` of `a` goes from 1 to 2.

**link-6** [OSF/1] `path1` and `path2` must be on the same file system.
  Test: see link-E5.

**link-7** [OSF/1] A process must have superuser privilege to make a hard link to a directory.
  Test: as non-root, `link("dir", "dir2")` fails with `EPERM`.

**link-8** [OSF/1] On success, `link()` marks the file's `st_ctime` for update, and marks `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the directory holding the new entry for update.
  Test: sleep 1 s, `link`; the file's `st_ctime` and the directory's `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` have increased.

**link-9** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned. On failure −1 is returned, no link is created and `errno` is set.
  Test: after a failed `link` (e.g. `EEXIST`), `st_nlink` of `path1` is unchanged.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**link-E1** `ENOENT`: the file `path1` does not exist, or `path1` or `path2` is an empty string.

**link-E2** `EFAULT`: `path1` or `path2` is an invalid address.

**link-E3** `EEXIST`: the link named by `path2` already exists.

**link-E4** `EPERM`: `path1` is a directory and the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

**link-E5** `EXDEV`: `path2` and `path1` are on different file systems.

**link-E6** `EACCES`: the link requires writing in a directory whose mode denies write permission, or a component of `path1` or `path2` denies search permission.

**link-E7** `EMLINK`: the number of links to `path1` would exceed `LINK_MAX`.

**link-E8** `EROFS`: the link requires writing in a directory on a read-only file system.

**link-E9** `ENOSPC`: the directory for the new entry cannot be extended because no space is left on its file system.

**link-E10** `ELOOP`: too many links were met in translating `path1` or `path2`.

**link-E11** `ENAMETOOLONG`: `path1` or `path2` is longer than `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**link-E12** `ENOTDIR`: a component of either path prefix is not a directory.

**link-E13** `EDQUOT`: the directory for the new entry cannot be extended because the user's quota of disk blocks on its file system is exhausted.

Related: Functions: unlink(2); Commands: link(1)

### listen(2)

Page: `man2/listen.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**listen-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int listen(int socket, int backlog)`. The page lists no header.
  Test: Compile the call.

**listen-2** [OSF/1] `socket` names the socket. `backlog` is the largest number of outstanding connection requests.
  Test: Covered below.

**listen-3** [OSF/1] `listen()` identifies the socket that receives connections, marks it as accepting connections, and limits the number (`backlog`) of outstanding connection requests in the system queue.
  Test: After `bind` and `listen`, `connect` from another socket succeeds and `accept` returns it.

**listen-4** [OSF/1] `backlog` can specify a queue length of at most five. The maximum is given by `SOMAXCONN` in `sys/socket.h`.
  Test: `SOMAXCONN` == 5. With `listen(s, 100)` and no `accept`, the number of connections that complete is bounded by about 5.

**listen-5** [OSF/1] On success, `listen()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: Check the return values.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**listen-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**listen-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**listen-E3** `EOPNOTSUPP`: the socket is of a type that does not support `listen()`.

Related: Functions: accept(2), connect(2), socket(2)

### lseek(2)

Page: `man2/lseek.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**lseek-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `off_t lseek(int filedes, off_t offset, int whence)`, with headers `<sys/types.h>` and `<unistd.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with those headers.

**lseek-2** [OSF/1] `filedes` is a descriptor obtained from a successful `open()` or `fcntl()`.
  Test: `lseek()` on a descriptor from `fcntl(fd, F_DUPFD, 0)` succeeds.

**lseek-3** [OSF/1] A negative `offset` seeks in the reverse direction; the resulting file position may also be negative.
  Test: at position 10, `lseek(fd, -4, SEEK_CUR)` returns 6.
Note: The page says the resulting position "may also be negative" but also lists `EINVAL` when "the resulting file offset would be invalid"; it does not say whether a negative result is accepted.

**lseek-4** [OSF/1] `SEEK_SET` sets the file pointer to `offset`.
  Test: `lseek(fd, 5, SEEK_SET)` returns 5; next `read()` starts at byte 5.

**lseek-5** [OSF/1] `SEEK_CUR` sets the file pointer to its current location plus `offset`.
  Test: after `lseek(fd,5,SEEK_SET)`, `lseek(fd,3,SEEK_CUR)` returns 8.

**lseek-6** [OSF/1] `SEEK_END` sets the file pointer to the file size plus `offset`.
  Test: on a 100-byte file, `lseek(fd, -10, SEEK_END)` returns 90.

**lseek-7** [OSF/1] `lseek()` sets the file offset of the open file `filedes`, interpreted according to `whence`.
  Test: covered by lseek-4 to lseek-6.

**lseek-8** [OSF/1] The offset may be set beyond the end of existing data; if data is later written there, reading the gap returns bytes of value 0 until data is written into the gap.
  Test: on an empty file, seek to 100, write 1 byte, read bytes 0–99; all 0.

**lseek-9** [OSF/1] `lseek()` does not by itself extend the size of the file.
  Test: seek to 1000 on a 10-byte file, `fstat()`; `st_size` still 10.

**lseek-10** [OSF/1] On success the resulting pointer location, in bytes from the beginning of the file, is returned.
  Test: `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END)` returns `st_size`.

**lseek-11** [OSF/1] On failure the file offset remains unchanged, `(off_t)-1` is returned, and `errno` is set.
  Test: seek to 7, then call with an invalid `whence`; returns −1; `lseek(fd,0,SEEK_CUR)` still 7.

Errors (the call returns `(off_t)-1` and sets `errno`; the offset is unchanged; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**lseek-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not an open file descriptor.

**lseek-E2** `ESPIPE`: `filedes` is associated with a pipe (FIFO), a socket, or a multiplexed special file.

**lseek-E3** `EINVAL`: `whence` is invalid, or the resulting file offset would be invalid.

Related: Functions: fcntl(2), fseek(3), open(2), read(2), write(2)

### madvise(2)

Page: `man2/madvise.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**madvise-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int madvise(caddr_t addr, size_t len, int behav)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/mman.h>`.
  Test: compile a call including both headers.

**madvise-2** [OSF/1] `madvise()` lets a process advise the system of its expected future references to a mapped file or shared memory region; `addr` and `len` give the region's address and length in bytes.
  Test: `madvise` on a mapped page with `MADV_NORMAL` returns 0.

**madvise-3** [OSF/1] `behav` values, defined in `<sys/mman.h>`: `MADV_NORMAL` (no further special treatment), `MADV_RANDOM` (expect random page references), `MADV_SEQUENTIAL` (expect sequential references), `MADV_WILLNEED` (will need these pages), `MADV_DONTNEED` (do not need these pages), `MADV_SPACEAVAIL` (ensure that resources are reserved).
  Test: check all six constants are defined and each call returns 0 (or `ENOSPC` for `MADV_SPACEAVAIL`).

**madvise-4** [Compat] `madvise()` has no functionality in OSF/1 and is supported for compatibility only.
  Test: after `MADV_DONTNEED` on a written page, data is still readable (no effect).

**madvise-5** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: successful call returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**madvise-E1** `EINVAL`: `behav` is invalid.

**madvise-E2** `ENOSPC`: `behav` is `MADV_SPACEAVAIL` and resources cannot be reserved.

Related: Functions: mmap(2)

### mkdir(2)

Page: `man2/mkdir.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mkdir-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int mkdir(const char *path, mode_t mode)`, with `<sys/stat.h>` and `<sys/types.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types against the headers.

**mkdir-2** [OSF/1] `path` names the new directory. If NFS is installed, the path can cross into another node, and the directory is then created at that node.
  Test: with an NFS mount, `mkdir` a path under it; the directory appears on the server. Not testable without an NFS setup.

**mkdir-3** [OSF/1] If the final component of `path` refers to a symbolic link, the link is traversed and pathname resolution continues.
  Test: create symlink `L` -> `target` (nonexistent) in a writable directory; call `mkdir("L", 0777)` and record whether `target` is created.
Note: The page does not say whether a dangling symlink as the final component makes the call create the link's target or fail with `EEXIST`; the test should record the behaviour only as "the link is traversed".

**mkdir-4** [OSF/1] `mode` gives the read, write and execute flags for owner, group and others; it is built by ORing values described in `sys/stat.h`.
  Test: `mkdir(p, S_IRWXU|S_IRGRP)` with umask 0; `stat` shows exactly those permission bits.

**mkdir-5** [OSF/1] The new directory's owner ID is set to the process's effective user ID.
  Test: as a process with distinct real and effective UIDs, create a directory; `st_uid` equals the effective UID.

**mkdir-6** [OSF/1] The new directory's group ID is set to the group ID of its parent directory.
  Test: create a directory inside a parent whose group differs from the process's effective GID; `st_gid` equals the parent's group.

**mkdir-7** [OSF/1] Permission and attribute bits are set from `mode` modified by the process's file creation mask (see `umask()`).
  Test: set `umask(022)`, `mkdir(p, 0777)`; `stat` shows mode `0755`.

**mkdir-8** [OSF/1] The new directory is empty except for `.` and `..`.
  Test: `opendir`/`readdir` on the new directory lists only `.` and `..`.

**mkdir-9** [OSF/1] The process must have search permission to reach the parent directory of `path` and write permission in that parent directory, with respect to all the system's configured access control policies.
  Test: as a non-root user, `mkdir` in a directory of mode 0555 fails (`EACCES`); in mode 0755 owned by the user it succeeds.

**mkdir-10** [OSF/1] On success, `st_atime`, `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the new directory are marked for update, and `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the parent directory are marked for update.
  Test: record the parent's times, sleep 2 s, `mkdir`; the parent's `st_mtime`/`st_ctime` increase and the new directory's three times are at least the call time.

**mkdir-11** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: `mkdir` of a new name returns 0; repeating it returns −1.

**mkdir-12** [OSF/1] If `mkdir()` fails, the directory is not created.
  Test: `mkdir` under a read-only or unwritable parent fails and `stat` of the path then gives `ENOENT`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**mkdir-E1** `EACCES`: creating the directory requires writing in a directory whose mode denies write permission, or search permission is denied on the parent directory of the directory to be created.

**mkdir-E2** `EEXIST`: the named file already exists.

**mkdir-E3** `EMLINK`: the link count of the parent directory would exceed `LINK_MAX`.

**mkdir-E4** `ELOOP`: too many links were encountered in translating `path`.

**mkdir-E5** `EFAULT`: the `path` parameter is an invalid address.

**mkdir-E6** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**mkdir-E7** `ENOENT`: a component of `path` does not exist or points to an empty string.

**mkdir-E8** `EROFS`: the named file resides on a read-only file system.

**mkdir-E9** `ENOSPC`: the file system does not have enough space to hold the contents of the new directory or to extend the parent directory of the new directory.

**mkdir-E10** `EDQUOT`: the directory in which the entry for the new link is being placed cannot be extended because the user's quota of disk blocks or i-nodes on that file system is exhausted.

**mkdir-E11** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), mknod(2), rmdir(2), umask(2); Commands: chmod(1), mkdir(1), mknod(8)

### mknod(2)

Page: `man2/mknod.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mknod-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int mknod(const char *path, int mode, dev_t device)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/stat.h>`; in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile and link a call.

**mknod-2** [OSF/1] `mknod()` creates a special file or FIFO.
  Test: `mknod("f", S_IFIFO|0644, 0)` returns 0 and `stat` shows a FIFO.

**mknod-3** [OSF/1] If the final component of `path` names a symbolic link, the link is traversed and pathname resolution continues.
  Test: create symlink `l` to nonexistent `t`; `mknod("l", S_IFIFO|0644, 0)`; check what is created at `t`.
  Note: The page does not say what happens when the link's target already exists or is dangling.

**mknod-4** [OSF/1] `mode` specifies the file type, attributes and access permissions, built by ORing values described in `sys/mode.h`.
  Test: create a FIFO with mode 0640 and umask 0; `stat` shows FIFO type and 0640.

**mknod-5** [OSF/1] `device` depends on the configuration and is used only if `mode` specifies a block or character special file.
  Test: as root create a character special file with a given `device`; `st_rdev` equals it. For a FIFO, `device` is ignored.

**mknod-6** [OSF/1] If the file is a remote file, `device` must be meaningful on the node where the file resides.
  Test: Not readily testable; needs a remote file system.

**mknod-7** [OSF/1] Creating file types other than FIFO special requires superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, create a character special file; expect `EPERM`.

**mknod-8** [OSF/1] The process must have search and write permission in the parent directory of `path`.
  Test: as non-root, create a FIFO in a directory mode 0555; expect `EACCES`.

**mknod-9** [OSF/1] The new file's type is as specified by `mode`.
  Test: `stat` the new file; check `S_ISFIFO`.

**mknod-10** [OSF/1] The new file's owner ID is the process effective user ID.
  Test: `st_uid == geteuid()`.

**mknod-11** [OSF/1] The new file's group ID is the group ID of its parent directory.
  Test: create in a directory owned by another group the caller belongs to; `st_gid` equals the directory's group.

**mknod-12** [OSF/1] Permission and attribute bits are set from `mode`, with all bits set in the process file mode creation mask cleared.
  Test: umask 022, mode 0666; expect permissions 0644.

**mknod-13** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`. On failure the new file is not created.
  Test: failing call leaves no file at `path`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**mknod-E1** `EACCES`: A component of the path prefix denies search permission, or write permission is denied on the parent directory of the FIFO to be created.

**mknod-E2** `EPERM`: `mode` specifies a file type other than FIFO and the caller does not have sufficient privilege.

**mknod-E3** `EEXIST`: The named file exists.

**mknod-E4** `EROFS`: The directory in which the file is to be created is on a read-only file system.

**mknod-E5** `ENOSPC`: The directory that would contain the new file cannot be extended, or the file system is out of file allocation resources.

**mknod-E6** `EDQUOT`: The directory in which the entry for the new link is being placed cannot be extended because the user's quota of disk blocks or inodes on the file system is exhausted.

**mknod-E7** `ENAMETOOLONG`: The length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**mknod-E8** `ENOENT`: A component of the path prefix does not exist, or `path` points to an empty string.

**mknod-E9** `ENOTDIR`: A component of the path prefix is not a directory.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), mkdir(2), open(2), umask(2), stat(2); Commands: chmod(1), mkdir(1)

### mmap(2)

Page: `man2/mmap.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mmap-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `caddr_t mmap(caddr_t addr, size_t len, int prot, int flags, int filedes, off_t off)`, with headers `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/mman.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with those headers.

**mmap-2** [OSF/1] `mmap()` creates a new mapped file region or shared memory region.
  Test: map a file and read its first byte through the returned address.

**mmap-3** [OSF/1] `addr` and `len` give the requested start address and length in bytes; the address is a multiple of the page size returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`.
  Test: the returned address modulo `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)` is 0.

**mmap-4** [OSF/1] If `len` is not a multiple of the page size, the result of any reference between the end of the region and the end of the page containing it is undefined.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (undefined); only check that mapping a non-page-multiple `len` succeeds.

**mmap-5** [OSF/1] `flags` is a bitwise-inclusive OR of symbolic names defined in `sys/mman.h`.
  Test: compile using `MAP_FILE`, `MAP_ANONYMOUS`, `MAP_VARIABLE`, `MAP_FIXED`, `MAP_SHARED`, `MAP_PRIVATE` from `<sys/mman.h>`.

**mmap-6** [OSF/1] `MAP_FILE`: create a mapped file region.
  Test: see mmap-8.

**mmap-7** [OSF/1] `MAP_ANONYMOUS`: create an unnamed memory region. `MAP_FILE` and `MAP_ANONYMOUS` choose between a mapped file region and an anonymous shared memory region, and exactly one of them must be selected.
  Test: map with `MAP_ANONYMOUS|MAP_VARIABLE|MAP_PRIVATE` and `filedes` −1; succeeds.
Note: The page does not say what happens when neither or both are given, beyond `EINVAL` for invalid `flags`.

**mmap-8** [OSF/1] With `MAP_FILE`, a new mapped file region maps the file associated with `filedes`.
  Test: map a file with known contents; bytes at the returned address match the file.

**mmap-9** [OSF/1] With `MAP_FILE`, `off` is the file byte offset at which the mapping starts and must be a multiple of the page size returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`.
  Test: map at `off` = one page; the first byte equals the file byte at that offset; `off` = 1 fails with `EINVAL`.

**mmap-10** [OSF/1] With `MAP_FILE`, if the region extends beyond end of file, the result of referencing addresses corresponding to offsets beyond end of file is unspecified.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (unspecified).

**mmap-11** [OSF/1] With `MAP_ANONYMOUS`, a new memory region is created and initialized to all zeros; it can be shared only with descendants of the current process.
  Test: map anonymous `MAP_SHARED`, check all bytes 0; fork, child writes, parent sees the write.

**mmap-12** [OSF/1] With `MAP_ANONYMOUS`, `mmap()` fails if `filedes` is not −1.
  Test: see mmap-E7.

**mmap-13** [OSF/1] The region is placed at the requested address if that address is not null and the region can be placed there.
  Test: map once to learn a free address, unmap, map again with that `addr` and `MAP_VARIABLE`; returned address equals `addr`.

**mmap-14** [OSF/1] `MAP_VARIABLE` and `MAP_FIXED` control placement when the requested address is null or unusable; exactly one of them must be selected.
  Test: see mmap-15 and mmap-16.

**mmap-15** [OSF/1] A region is never placed at address zero or where it would overlap an existing region.
  Test: map with `addr` null and `MAP_VARIABLE`; result is non-zero and does not overlap a previous mapping.

**mmap-16** [OSF/1] `MAP_VARIABLE`: place the region at the computed address; if the requested address is null or the system cannot place the region there, the system selects the address.
  Test: map with `MAP_VARIABLE` and an `addr` that overlaps an existing mapping; succeeds at a different address.

**mmap-17** [OSF/1] `MAP_FIXED`: place the region at a fixed address; if the requested address is not null and the region cannot be placed there, `mmap()` fails.
  Test: `MAP_FIXED` with `addr` inside an existing mapping; expect (caddr_t)−1 (`ENOMEM`).

**mmap-18** [OSF/1] `MAP_FIXED` with a null address: the region is placed at its default exact mapping address; if it has none, the system selects an address, which becomes the default exact mapping address for later attempts to map the same region until all mappings of the region are unmapped.
  Test: map a file at offset 0 with `MAP_FIXED` and null `addr`, record address A; while that mapping exists, map the same file and offset the same way in another process that has no mapping there; expect address A.
Note: The page does not say whether the default exact mapping address applies across processes (see mmap-20).

**mmap-19** [OSF/1] With `MAP_FIXED` and a null address, if the region cannot be placed at its default exact mapping address, `mmap()` fails.
  Test: map the region `MAP_FIXED` with null `addr` (address A); while it stays mapped, map the same region the same way again in the same process (A is occupied, mmap-15); expect failure.

**mmap-20** [OSF/1] For default exact mapping, two mapped file regions are the same region if they map the same file starting at the same file offset.
  Test: map file F at offset 0 `MAP_FIXED` null twice in different processes while one mapping stays; addresses equal; at a different offset, addresses may differ.
Note: The page does not say whether the default exact address is per process or system-wide.

**mmap-21** [OSF/1] `MAP_SHARED`: share changes. `MAP_PRIVATE`: changes are private. Exactly one of `MAP_PRIVATE` and `MAP_SHARED` must be selected.
  Test: each flag alone works; see mmap-22 to mmap-24.

**mmap-22** [OSF/1] With `MAP_SHARED` on a mapped file region, modifications are visible to other processes that mapped the same region with `MAP_SHARED`, and are written to the file.
  Test: two processes map a file `MAP_SHARED`; one writes; the other sees it; after `munmap`/`msync`, `read()` of the file shows it.

**mmap-23** [OSF/1] With `MAP_PRIVATE`, the calling process's modifications are not visible to other processes that mapped the same region with `MAP_PRIVATE` or `MAP_SHARED`.
  Test: process A maps `MAP_PRIVATE` and writes; process B's `MAP_SHARED` mapping still shows the old byte.

**mmap-24** [OSF/1] With `MAP_PRIVATE`, the calling process's modifications are not written to the file.
  Test: write through a `MAP_PRIVATE` mapping, `munmap`, `read()` the file; unchanged.

**mmap-25** [OSF/1] It is unspecified whether modifications by `MAP_SHARED` mappers are visible to processes that mapped the same region with `MAP_PRIVATE`.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (unspecified).

**mmap-26** [OSF/1] `prot` access options from `sys/mman.h`: `PROT_READ` (the region can be read), `PROT_WRITE` (can be written), `PROT_EXEC` (can be executed), `PROT_NONE` (cannot be accessed).
  Test: map `PROT_NONE` and touch it; the access must not succeed (the page names no signal); map `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE` and read/write succeed.

**mmap-27** [OSF/1] `prot` is either `PROT_NONE` or any OR of `PROT_READ`, `PROT_WRITE`, `PROT_EXEC`; if `PROT_NONE` is not specified, access may be granted beyond what was requested, except that write access is not granted unless `PROT_WRITE` is specified.
  Test: map `PROT_READ` only; a write to the region must not succeed (the page names no signal).

**mmap-28** [OSF/1] For a mapped file mapped with `MAP_SHARED`, read or execute access is granted only if the descriptor is open for reading, and write access only if the descriptor is open for writing.
  Test: open `O_RDONLY`, map `MAP_SHARED` with `PROT_WRITE`; expect failure with `EACCES`.

**mmap-29** [OSF/1] For a mapped file mapped with `MAP_PRIVATE`, read, write or execute access is granted only if the descriptor is open for reading.
