  Test: open `O_RDONLY`, map `MAP_PRIVATE` with `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE`; succeeds and writes work.

**mmap-30** [OSF/1] For a shared memory region mapped with `MAP_ANONYMOUS`, all requested access permissions are granted.
  Test: anonymous map with `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC`; succeeds.

**mmap-31** [OSF/1] After `mmap()` succeeds, `filedes` may be closed without affecting the mapped region or the mapped file's contents.
  Test: map, close the descriptor, read through the mapping; data still correct.

**mmap-32** [OSF/1] Each mapped region creates a file reference, similar to an open descriptor, that prevents the file data from being deallocated.
  Test: map a file, close and unlink it; the mapping still reads the original data.

**mmap-33** [OSF/1] Whether `write()` changes are visible in mapped regions, and whether mapping changes are visible to `read()`, is undefined, except for the effect of `msync()`.
  Test: write through a `MAP_SHARED` mapping, call `msync()`, `read()` the file; data matches.

**mmap-34** [OSF/1] After `fork()`, the child inherits all mapped regions with the same sharing and protection attributes as the parent.
  Test: parent maps anonymous `MAP_SHARED` read/write; after fork, child writes; parent sees the write.

**mmap-35** [OSF/1] Every region created with `mmap()` is unmapped by a successful `exec`, unless the region was made inheritable across exec.
  Test: Not directly testable without a way to inspect the new image's address space; exec a program that probes the old address (expect a fault).

**mmap-36** [OSF/1] Memory acquired with `mmap()` is not locked, regardless of earlier use of `plock()`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (locking state not observable).

**mmap-37** [OSF/1] On success `mmap()` returns the address at which the mapping was placed; otherwise it returns `(caddr_t)-1` and sets `errno`.
  Test: failed call (bad descriptor) returns `(caddr_t)-1`.

Errors (the call returns `(caddr_t)-1` and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**mmap-E1** `EACCES`: the file referred to by `filedes` is not open for read access, or it is not open for write access and `PROT_WRITE` was set for a `MAP_SHARED` mapping.

**mmap-E2** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not a valid file descriptor.

**mmap-E3** `EINVAL`: `flags` or `prot` is invalid, or `addr` or `off` is not a multiple of the page size returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`.

**mmap-E4** `ENODEV`: `filedes` refers to an object that cannot be mapped, such as a terminal.

**mmap-E5** `ENOMEM`: there is not enough address space to map `len` bytes, or `MAP_FIXED` was set and part of the range [`addr`, `addr` + `len`) is already allocated.

**mmap-E6** `ENXIO`: the addresses in the range [`off`, `off` + `len`) are invalid for `filedes`.

**mmap-E7** `EINVAL`: `MAP_ANONYMOUS` was specified and `filedes` is not −1.

**mmap-E8** `EFAULT`: `addr` is an invalid address.

Related: Functions: fcntl(2), fork(2), madvise(2), mprotect(2), msync(2), munmap(2), plock(2), sysconf(3)

### mount(2), umount(2)

Page: `man2/mount.html`; same text as `umount(2)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mount-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/mount.h>`; `mount(int type, char *dir, int mnt_flag, caddr_t data)`; `umount(char *dir, int umnt_flag)`.
  Test: compile calls with these argument types.
  Note: The page's synopsis gives no return type for either function; RETURN VALUE implies an integer.

**mount-2** [OSF/1] `type` gives the file system type; the types defined in `sys/mount.h` are `MOUNT_NONE`, `MOUNT_UFS`, `MOUNT_NFS`, `MOUNT_MFS` and `MOUNT_S5FS`.
  Test: compile code referencing all five constants.

**mount-3** [OSF/1] `dir` points to a null-terminated string holding the pathname.
  Test: as root, mount a UFS device on a directory given by path; it succeeds.

**mount-4** [OSF/1] `mnt_flag` specifies which semantics to suppress when accessing the file system.
  Test: see mount-5 to mount-11.

**mount-5** [OSF/1] `M_RDONLY`: the file system is read-only; no writing is allowed, even by a privileged process. Physically write-protected and magnetic tape file systems must be mounted read-only, or errors occur when access times are updated, even without an explicit write.
  Test: mount with `M_RDONLY`; as root, `open(..., O_WRONLY|O_CREAT)` on it fails.

**mount-6** [OSF/1] `M_NOEXEC`: files on the file system may not be executed.
  Test: mount with `M_NOEXEC`; `execve()` of a program there fails.

**mount-7** [OSF/1] `M_NOSUID`: setuid and setgid bits on files are not honoured when executing them.
  Test: setuid-root program on such a mount, run as non-root, sees `geteuid() != 0`.

**mount-8** [OSF/1] `M_NODEV`: special files on the file system are not interpreted.
  Test: using a device node on such a mount does not access the device.

**mount-9** [OSF/1] `M_SYNCHRONOUS`: all I/O to the file system is done synchronously.
  Test: Not testable from user space (no observable difference without crash or timing).

**mount-10** [OSF/1] `M_FMOUNT`: mount forcibly even if the file system is unclean.
  Test: mount an unclean file system with `M_FMOUNT`; it succeeds where it fails with `EDIRTY` without it.
  Note: The page's error list says "`M_FORCE` is not set", while the flag list names `M_FMOUNT`; the two names presumably mean the same flag.

**mount-11** [OSF/1] `M_UPDATE`: the call applies to an already mounted file system, allowing its flags to change without unmounting and remounting.
  Test: mount read-write, then `M_UPDATE` with `M_NOEXEC`; exec on it then fails.

**mount-12** [OSF/1] Some file systems "may not allow all flags to be changed"; for example, most do not allow a change from read-write to read-only.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (file-system dependent).

**mount-13** [OSF/1] `data` points to a structure holding the type-specific mount parameters.
  Test: UFS mount passes a `ufs_args` whose `fspec` names the block device.

**mount-14** [OSF/1] `umnt_flag` `MNT_NOFORCE` or `MNT_WAIT`: the unmount fails if any files are active on the file system.
  Test: hold a file open on the file system; `umount(dir, MNT_NOFORCE)` fails with `EBUSY`.

**mount-15** [OSF/1] `umnt_flag` `MNT_FORCE` or `MNT_NOWAIT`: the file system is unmounted even if files are active; active special devices keep working, but further accesses to other active files give errors, even if the file system is later remounted. Support for forcible unmount is file-system dependent.
  Test: on a file system supporting it, hold a file open, `umount(dir, MNT_FORCE)` succeeds, then `read()` on the descriptor fails.

**mount-16** [OSF/1] `mount()` mounts a file system on directory `dir`; afterwards references to `dir` refer to the root directory of the mounted file system.
  Test: after mount, `stat(dir)` gives the root inode of the new file system (different `st_dev`).

**mount-17** [OSF/1] `dir` must point to an existing directory; its old contents are inaccessible while the file system is mounted.
  Test: create `dir/x`, mount over `dir`; `stat("dir/x")` fails with `ENOENT` (if not on the new file system).

**mount-18** [OSF/1] `umount()` unmounts the file system mounted at `dir`; the directory reverts to its ordinary interpretation.
  Test: after unmount, `dir/x` from mount-17 is visible again.

**mount-19** [OSF/1] Calling `mount()` or `umount()` requires superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, both fail with `EPERM`.

**mount-20** [OSF/1] Two `mount()` functions are supported: the BSD `mount()` (the default, documented here) and the System V `mount()`; to use the System V version, link with `libsys5` before `libc`.
  Test: link a program with `-lsys5` before `-lc` and confirm it resolves `mount` from `libsys5`.

**mount-21** [OSF/1] `mount()` returns 0 on success, otherwise -1. It can fail if `dir` does not exist or is not a directory.
  Test: `mount()` on a regular file fails with -1.

**mount-22** [OSF/1] For UFS or S5FS, the mount can fail if the special device in the `ufs_args` structure is inaccessible, is not an appropriate file, or is already mounted.
  Test: mount the same device twice; the second fails.

**mount-23** [OSF/1] A UFS, MFS or S5FS mount can also fail if too many file systems are already mounted.
  Test: Not practically testable (needs the mount table full).

**mount-24** [OSF/1] `umount()` returns 0 on success, otherwise -1; it fails if there are active files in the mounted file system.
  Test: see mount-14.

**mount-25** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/include/sys/mount.h`.
  Test: the header exists and compiles.

**mount-26** [DEC] (ULTRIX compatibility) An additional file system type, `MOUNT_CDFS`, is defined in `sys/mount.h`.
  Test: compile code referencing `MOUNT_CDFS`.

Errors (for `mount()`; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**mount-E1** `EPERM`: the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

**mount-E2** `ENAMETOOLONG`: a pathname component exceeded `NAME_MAX` characters, or a whole pathname exceeded `PATH_MAX` characters.

**mount-E3** `ELOOP`: too many symbolic links were encountered in translating a pathname.

**mount-E4** `ENOENT`: a component of `dir` does not exist.

**mount-E5** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the `name` parameter is not a directory, or a path prefix of the `special` parameter is not a directory.
Note: The page names parameters `name` and `special`, which do not appear in the synopsis.

**mount-E6** `EINVAL`: a pathname contains a character with the high-order bit set.

**mount-E7** `EBUSY`: another process currently holds a reference to `dir`.

**mount-E8** `EDIRTY`: the file system is not clean and `M_FORCE` is not set.

**mount-E9** `EFAULT`: `dir` points outside the process's allocated address space.

UFS or S5FS mount:

**mount-E10** `ENODEV`: a component of `ufs_args` `fspec` does not exist.

**mount-E11** `ENOTBLK`: `fspec` is not a block device.

**mount-E12** `ENXIO`: the major device number of `fspec` is out of range (no device driver exists for the hardware).

**mount-E13** `EBUSY`: the device named by `fspec` is already mounted.

**mount-E14** `EMFILE`: no space remains in the mount table.

**mount-E15** `EINVAL`: the file system's super block had a bad magic number or an out-of-range block size.

**mount-E16** `ENOMEM`: not enough memory was available to read the cylinder group information.

**mount-E17** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while reading the super block or cylinder group information.

**mount-E18** `EFAULT`: `fspec` points outside the process's allocated address space.

NFS-compatible mount:

**mount-E19** `ETIMEDOUT`: NFS timed out trying to contact the server.

**mount-E20** `EFAULT`: some part of the information described by `nfs_args` points outside the process's allocated address space.

MFS mount:

**mount-E21** `EMFILE`: no space remains in the mount table.

**mount-E22** `EINVAL`: the super block had a bad magic number or an out-of-range block size.

**mount-E23** `ENOMEM`: not enough memory was available to read the cylinder group information.

**mount-E24** `EIO`: a paging error occurred while reading the super block or cylinder group information.

**mount-E25** `EFAULT`: the `name` field points outside the process's allocated address space.

For `umount()`:

**mount-E26** `EPERM`: the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

**mount-E27** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path is not a directory.

**mount-E28** `EINVAL`: the pathname contains a character with the high-order bit set.

**mount-E29** `ENAMETOOLONG`: a pathname component exceeded `NAME_MAX` characters, or a whole pathname exceeded `PATH_MAX` characters.

**mount-E30** `ELOOP`: too many symbolic links were encountered in translating the pathname.

**mount-E31** `EINVAL`: the requested directory is not in the mount table.

**mount-E32** `EBUSY`: a process holds a reference to a file on the file system.

**mount-E33** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while writing cached file system information.

**mount-E34** `EFAULT`: `dir` points outside the process's allocated address space.

Related: Commands: mount(8)

### mprotect(2)

Page: `man2/mprotect.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mprotect-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int mprotect(caddr_t addr, size_t len, int prot)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/mman.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types including both headers.

**mprotect-2** [OSF/1] `mprotect()` modifies the access protection of a mapped file or shared memory region; `addr` and `len` give the address and the length in bytes of the region to modify.
  Test: `mmap` a page read/write, `mprotect` it to `PROT_READ`, write to it and expect `SIGSEGV`/`SIGBUS`.

**mprotect-3** [OSF/1] `len` must be a multiple of the page size as returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`; if it is not, the length of the region is rounded up to the next multiple of the page size.
  Test: `mprotect(addr, 1, PROT_READ)` on a read/write page, then write anywhere in that page and expect a fault.

**mprotect-4** [OSF/1] `prot` gives the new access protection: either `PROT_NONE`, or any combination of `PROT_READ`, `PROT_WRITE` and `PROT_EXEC` ORed together; these are defined in `<sys/mman.h>`.
  Test: check the four constants are defined in `<sys/mman.h>` and accepted.

**mprotect-5** [OSF/1] `PROT_READ`: the mapped region can be read.
  Test: after `mprotect(..., PROT_READ)`, reading the region succeeds.

**mprotect-6** [OSF/1] `PROT_WRITE`: the mapped region can be written.
  Test: after `mprotect(..., PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE)`, writing the region succeeds.

**mprotect-7** [OSF/1] `PROT_EXEC`: the mapped region can be executed.
  Test: copy machine code into an anonymous mapping, `mprotect` with `PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC`, call it.

**mprotect-8** [OSF/1] `PROT_NONE`: the mapped region cannot be accessed.
  Test: after `mprotect(..., PROT_NONE)`, a read of the region faults.

**mprotect-9** [OSF/1] If `PROT_NONE` is not specified, access permissions "may be granted" beyond those requested, except that write access is not granted unless `PROT_WRITE` is specified.
  Test: `mprotect(..., PROT_READ)` then write; expect a fault (extra read/exec access is permitted and not checked).

**mprotect-10** [OSF/1] For a file mapped with `MAP_SHARED`, read or execute access is granted only if the descriptor used to map the file is open for reading, and write access only if it is open for writing.
  Test: map a file `MAP_SHARED` with `PROT_READ` from an `O_RDONLY` descriptor; `mprotect` adding `PROT_WRITE` fails with `EACCES`.

**mprotect-11** [OSF/1] For a file mapped with `MAP_PRIVATE`, read, write or execute access is granted only if the descriptor used to map the file is open for reading.
  Test: map a file `MAP_PRIVATE` from an `O_RDONLY` descriptor; `mprotect(..., PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE)` succeeds.

**mprotect-12** [OSF/1] For a shared memory region mapped with `MAP_ANONYMOUS`, all requested access permissions are granted.
  Test: anonymous mapping, `mprotect` with `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC` returns 0.

**mprotect-13** [OSF/1] Protection of any region outside the specified region is not modified, except that the effect on addresses between the end of the region and the end of the page containing the end of the region is unspecified.
  Test: map three pages read/write, `mprotect` the middle one to `PROT_NONE`, check the first and third remain writable.

**mprotect-14** [OSF/1] If `mprotect()` fails for a reason other than `EINVAL`, the protection of some pages in [`addr`, `addr` + `len`) may have been changed; if the error occurs on a page at `addr2`, the protections of all whole pages in [`addr`, `addr2`) may have been modified.
  Test: not deterministically checkable; a test may only accept either outcome on the pages before the failing one.

**mprotect-15** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: successful call returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**mprotect-E1** `EACCES`: `prot` specifies a protection that conflicts with the access permission set for the underlying file.

**mprotect-E2** `EINVAL`: `prot` is invalid, or `addr` is not a multiple of the page size as returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`.

**mprotect-E3** `EFAULT`: the range [`addr`, `addr` + `len`) includes an invalid address.

Related: Functions: getpagesize(2), mmap(2), msync(2), sysconf(3)

### msgctl(2)

Page: `man2/msgctl.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msgctl-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int msgctl(int msqid, int cmd, struct msqid_ds *buf)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>`, `#include <sys/ipc.h>` and `#include <sys/msg.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including the three headers.

**msgctl-2** [OSF/1] `msgctl()` lets a process query or set the `msqid_ds` structure of the message queue `msqid`, or remove the queue ID and its `msqid_ds` structure; `cmd` selects the operation.
  Test: create a queue with `msgget`, run `IPC_STAT`, `IPC_SET` and `IPC_RMID` on it, each returning 0.

**msgctl-3** [OSF/1] `IPC_STAT` copies the queue's associated data structure into `buf`.
  Test: `IPC_SET` `msg_perm.mode` to 0600, then `IPC_STAT` into an allocated `buf` returns 0 and shows that mode.

**msgctl-4** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` copies values from `buf` into the corresponding fields of the queue's `msqid_ds` structure. It is restricted: the caller's effective user ID must be superuser or equal `msg_perm.uid` or `msg_perm.cuid`.
  Test: as the owner, `IPC_SET` a new mode; `IPC_STAT` shows it. As another non-root user, `IPC_SET` fails with `EPERM`.

**msgctl-5** [OSF/1] Only the superuser can raise `msg_qbytes`.
  Test: as the non-root owner, `IPC_SET` with `msg_qbytes` one larger than current fails with `EPERM`; a smaller value succeeds.

**msgctl-6** [OSF/1] `IPC_RMID` removes the queue ID and deallocates its `msqid_ds` structure. It is restricted in the same way as `IPC_SET` (superuser, or effective user ID equal to `msg_perm.uid` or `msg_perm.cuid`).
  Test: as owner, `IPC_RMID` returns 0; a following `IPC_STAT` fails with `EINVAL`.

**msgctl-7** [OSF/1] `buf` is used only with `IPC_STAT` and `IPC_SET`: with `IPC_STAT` the query results are copied into it; with `IPC_SET` its values set the queue's fields. The caller must allocate the structure before the call.
  Test: `IPC_RMID` with `buf` NULL returns 0.

**msgctl-8** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` sets `msg_perm.uid`, the owner's user ID.
  Test: as root, `IPC_SET` `msg_perm.uid` to 1234; `IPC_STAT` shows 1234.

**msgctl-9** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` sets `msg_perm.gid`, the owner's group ID.
  Test: as root, `IPC_SET` `msg_perm.gid` to 1234; `IPC_STAT` shows 1234.

**msgctl-10** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` sets `msg_perm.mode`, the queue's access modes; only the low-order nine bits are set.
  Test: `IPC_SET` mode 07777; `IPC_STAT` shows the low nine bits as 0777.

**msgctl-11** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` sets `msg_qbytes`, the maximum number of bytes on the queue.
  Test: `IPC_SET` a smaller `msg_qbytes`; `IPC_STAT` shows it.

**msgctl-12** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` sets `msg_ctime`, the time of the last `msgctl()` operation that changed the structure.
  Test: after `IPC_SET`, `IPC_STAT` shows `msg_ctime` at or after the time of the call.
  Note: The page lists `msg_ctime` among the members set from `buf`, but describes it as the time of the last change; it is unclear whether the value comes from `buf` or from the clock.

**msgctl-13** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` on a valid queue returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**msgctl-E1** `EINVAL`: `msqid` is not a valid message queue ID, or `cmd` is not a valid command.

**msgctl-E2** `EACCES`: `cmd` is `IPC_STAT` but the caller does not have read permission.

**msgctl-E3** `EPERM`: `cmd` is `IPC_RMID` or `IPC_SET` and the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

**msgctl-E4** `EPERM`: `cmd` is `IPC_SET` and the caller tries to increase `msg_qbytes` when its effective user ID does not have the `SET_OBJ_STAT` system privilege.
  Note: The page elsewhere says "Only superuser" can raise `msg_qbytes`; here it names the `SET_OBJ_STAT` privilege.

**msgctl-E5** `EFAULT`: `cmd` is `IPC_STAT` or `IPC_SET` and an error occurred in accessing `buf`.

Related: Functions: msgget(2), msgrcv(2), msgsnd(2); Data Structures: msqid_ds(4)

### msgget(2)

Page: `man2/msgget.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msgget-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int msgget(key_t key, int msgflg)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>`, `<sys/ipc.h>` and `<sys/msg.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**msgget-2** [OSF/1] `msgget()` returns (and possibly creates) the message queue ID for the queue identified by `key`.
  Test: create with a key, call again with the same key and 0 flags; same ID returned.

**msgget-3** [OSF/1] The `IPC_PRIVATE` key can be used to assure the return of a new, unused message queue ID; with `IPC_PRIVATE`, the ID returned is for a private (newly created) queue.
  Test: two calls `msgget(IPC_PRIVATE, 0600)` return two different IDs.

**msgget-4** [OSF/1] `msgflg` supplies creation options.
  Test: see following items.

**msgget-5** [OSF/1] `IPC_CREAT`: if the key does not exist, `msgget()` creates a new message queue for the key and returns the kernel-assigned ID.
  Test: with an unused key, `msgget(k, IPC_CREAT|0600)` returns an ID ≥ 0.

**msgget-6** [OSF/1] The PARAMETERS text says that with `IPC_CREAT`, "If the key does exist, it forces an error notification."
  Test: none recommended; see Note.
  Note: The page contradicts itself: the `EEXIST` entry says an error occurs only when both `IPC_CREAT` and `IPC_EXCL` are set for an existing key; this sentence of the page appears wrong.

**msgget-7** [OSF/1] `IPC_EXCL`: if the key already exists, `msgget()` fails and returns an error notification.
  Test: create key k, then `msgget(k, IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL|0600)`; expect `EEXIST`.

**msgget-8** [OSF/1] On creation, `msg_perm.cuid` and `msg_perm.uid` are set to the effective user ID of the caller.
  Test: create, `msgctl(IPC_STAT)`; both equal `geteuid()`.

**msgget-9** [OSF/1] On creation, `msg_perm.cgid` and `msg_perm.gid` are set to the effective group ID of the caller.
  Test: both equal `getegid()`.

**msgget-10** [OSF/1] On creation, the low-order nine bits of `msg_perm.mode` are set equal to the low-order nine bits of `msgflg`.
  Test: create with `IPC_CREAT|0640`; `msg_perm.mode & 0777 == 0640`.

**msgget-11** [OSF/1] On creation, `msg_qnum`, `msg_lspid`, `msg_lrpid`, `msg_stime` and `msg_rtime` are all set to zero.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` right after creation; all are 0.

**msgget-12** [OSF/1] On creation, `msg_ctime` is set to the current time.
  Test: `msg_ctime` within a second of `time(NULL)`.

**msgget-13** [OSF/1] On creation, `msg_qbytes` is set to the system limit.
  Test: `msg_qbytes` is positive and equal across newly created queues.

**msgget-14** [OSF/1] On success a message queue identifier is returned; on failure −1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: as above.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**msgget-E1** `EACCES`: A message queue identifier exists for `key` but operation permission, as specified by the low-order nine bits of `msgflg`, is not granted.

**msgget-E2** `ENOENT`: No message queue identifier exists for `key` and `IPC_CREAT` is not set.

**msgget-E3** `ENOSPC`: A message queue identifier can be created, but the system-imposed limit on the maximum number of message queue identifiers has been exceeded.

**msgget-E4** `EEXIST`: A message queue identifier exists for `key`, and both `IPC_CREAT` and `IPC_EXCL` are set.

Related: Functions: msgctl(2), msgrcv(2), msgsnd(2); Data Structures: msqid_ds(4)

### msgrcv(2)

Page: `man2/msgrcv.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msgrcv-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int msgrcv(int msqid, struct msgbuf *msgp, int msgsz, long msgtyp, int msgflg)`, with headers `<sys/types.h>`, `<sys/ipc.h>`, `<sys/msg.h>`.
  Test: compile and call.

**msgrcv-2** [OSF/1] `msqid` is the ID of the queue to receive from; `msgp` points to the `msgbuf` that receives the message; `msgsz` is the maximum number of bytes of received data; `msgtyp` is the message type to read; `msgflg` says what to do if there are no `msgtyp` messages.
  Test: send a message of type 1 with 5 bytes; `msgrcv(id, &buf, 100, 1, 0)` returns 5.

**msgrcv-3** [OSF/1] `msgrcv()` receives a message from the queue for `msqid` and returns the number of bytes in the received message; `msgp` points to a user-defined `msgbuf` that receives it.
  Test: covered by msgrcv-2.

**msgrcv-4** [OSF/1] If the message is longer than `msgsz` and `MSG_NOERROR` is not set, `E2BIG` is returned and the message stays on the queue.
  Test: send 10 bytes, receive with `msgsz` 5; −1 `E2BIG`; a second receive with 100 gets all 10 bytes.

**msgrcv-5** [OSF/1] If the message is longer than `msgsz` and `MSG_NOERROR` is set, the message is truncated to `msgsz`, and the truncated part is discarded without telling the caller.
  Test: send 10 bytes, receive with `msgsz` 5 and `MSG_NOERROR`; returns 5; queue is then empty.

**msgrcv-6** [OSF/1] `msgtyp` 0: the process receives the message at the head of the queue.
  Test: send types 3 then 1; receive with 0 gets type 3.

**msgrcv-7** [OSF/1] `msgtyp` > 0: the process receives the first message of that type.
  Test: send types 3, 1, 1; receive with 1 gets the first type-1 message.

**msgrcv-8** [OSF/1] `msgtyp` < 0: the process receives the first message of the lowest type on the queue; to qualify, the type must be less than or equal to the absolute value of `msgtyp`.
  Test: send types 5, 2, 3; receive with −4 gets type 2; receive with −1 on that queue blocks or gives `ENOMSG` with `IPC_NOWAIT`.
Note: The page says "the negative-integer type must be less than or equal to the absolute value"; the word "negative-integer" appears to be an error.

**msgrcv-9** [OSF/1] If no message of the requested type is on the queue and `IPC_NOWAIT` is set, the call returns immediately with −1 and `errno` `ENOMSG`.
  Test: empty queue, `IPC_NOWAIT`; −1 `ENOMSG`.

**msgrcv-10** [OSF/1] If `IPC_NOWAIT` is not set, the calling process is suspended until a message of the requested type appears (the process is then woken to receive it), the queue ID is removed, or the process catches a signal.
  Test: child blocks in `msgrcv`; parent sends a message; child returns with it.
Note: The page says "the kernel suspends the calling process"; it does not discuss threads.

**msgrcv-11** [OSF/1] If the queue ID is removed while the process waits, `errno` is set to `EIDRM` and −1 is returned.
  Test: child blocks; parent `msgctl(id, IPC_RMID)`; child gets −1 `EIDRM`.

**msgrcv-12** [OSF/1] If the waiting process catches a signal, it does not receive the message and resumes as directed by the `signal()` call.
  Test: child blocks with a `SIGALRM` handler and alarm; `msgrcv` returns −1 (`EINTR`, see msgrcv-E6) and the message, sent later, is still on the queue.

**msgrcv-13** [OSF/1] `msgbuf` field `mtype` (`mtyp_t`): set to the message type supplied by the sender.
  Test: send type 7; received `mtype` is 7.
Note: The page spells the field "mytpe" once.

**msgrcv-14** [OSF/1] `msgbuf` field `mtext` (`char []`): set to the message text; unless `MSG_NOERROR` is set, the message size is at most the `msgsz` given to `msgrcv()`.
  Test: received `mtext` bytes equal the bytes sent, and their count is at most `msgsz`.

**msgrcv-15** [OSF/1] On success the return value is the number of bytes actually stored in `mtext`.
  Test: covered by msgrcv-2 and msgrcv-5.

**msgrcv-16** [OSF/1] On success `msg_qnum` of the queue's `msqid_ds` is decremented by 1.
  Test: `msgctl(IPC_STAT)` before and after; `msg_qnum` drops by 1.

**msgrcv-17** [OSF/1] On success `msg_lrpid` is set to the caller's process ID.
  Test: `msgctl(IPC_STAT)`; `msg_lrpid == getpid()`.

**msgrcv-18** [OSF/1] On success `msg_rtime` is set to the current time.
  Test: `msg_rtime` is within a second of `time(NULL)`.

**msgrcv-19** [OSF/1] On success `msg_cbytes` is decremented by the message text size.
  Test: receive a 10-byte message; `msg_cbytes` drops by 10.

**msgrcv-20** [OSF/1] On failure −1 is returned and `errno` set.
  Test: covered by error items.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**msgrcv-E1** `EINVAL`: `msqid` is not a valid message queue ID, or `msgsz` is less than 0.

**msgrcv-E2** `EACCES`: the calling process does not have permission for the operation.

**msgrcv-E3** `EIDRM`: the queue ID (written "msgid") has been removed from the system.

**msgrcv-E4** `E2BIG`: the number of bytes to be received in `mtext` is greater than `msgsz` and `MSG_NOERROR` is not set.

**msgrcv-E5** `ENOMSG`: the queue has no message of the requested type and `IPC_NOWAIT` is set.

**msgrcv-E6** `EINTR`: the operation was interrupted by a signal.

Related: Functions: msgctl(2), msgget(2), msgsnd(2), sigaction(2); Data Structures: msqid_ds(4)

### msgsnd(2)

Page: `man2/msgsnd.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msgsnd-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int msgsnd(int msqid, struct msgbuf *msgp, int msgsz, int msgflg)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>`, `#include <sys/ipc.h>` and `#include <sys/msg.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including the three headers.

**msgsnd-2** [OSF/1] `msgsnd()` sends a message to the queue `msqid`, an ID typically returned by an earlier `msgget()`.
  Test: `msgsnd` a message to a new queue; `msgrcv` returns it.

**msgsnd-3** [OSF/1] `msgp` points to a user-defined `msgbuf` structure giving the message type and a data array with the message text.
  Test: send type 7 text "abc"; `msgrcv` with type 7 returns "abc".

**msgsnd-4** [OSF/1] `msgsz` is the size of the data array; it can be from zero to a system-defined maximum.
  Test: `msgsnd` with `msgsz` 0 returns 0.

**msgsnd-5** [OSF/1] `msgflg` sets the action taken if the number of bytes on the queue equals `msg_qbytes` (in `msqid_ds`), or the total number of messages on all queues equals the system-defined limit, or both.
  Test: covered by msgsnd-6 and msgsnd-7.

**msgsnd-6** [OSF/1] If `IPC_NOWAIT` is set in that situation, the message is not sent and the call returns to the caller immediately (with `EAGAIN`, per the errors).
  Test: set `msg_qbytes` to 10, send 10 bytes, then send 1 byte with `IPC_NOWAIT`: −1 with `EAGAIN`.

**msgsnd-7** [OSF/1] If `IPC_NOWAIT` is not set, the kernel suspends the calling process until the blocking condition is removed, in which case the message is sent.
  Test: fill the queue, send in a child without `IPC_NOWAIT`; it blocks until the parent `msgrcv`s, then returns 0.
  Note: The page says the "calling process" is suspended; it does not say whether only the calling thread is.

**msgsnd-8** [OSF/1] While suspended, if the queue ID is removed from the system, `errno` is set to `EIDRM` and −1 is returned.
  Test: block a child in `msgsnd`, then `IPC_RMID` the queue; the child gets −1/`EIDRM`.

**msgsnd-9** [OSF/1] While suspended, if the process catches a signal, the message is not sent and the process resumes execution "as directed by the signal() function".
  Test: block in `msgsnd`, deliver a caught signal; the call returns −1/`EINTR` and the queue's `msg_qnum` is unchanged.

**msgsnd-10** [OSF/1] On success the queue's `msqid_ds` is updated: `msg_qnum` is incremented by 1.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` before and after a send; `msg_qnum` rises by 1.

**msgsnd-11** [OSF/1] On success `msg_cbytes` is incremented by the message text size.
  Test: send 5 bytes; `msg_cbytes` rises by 5.

**msgsnd-12** [OSF/1] On success `msg_lspid` is set to the calling process's ID.
  Test: after a send, `msg_lspid` equals `getpid()`.

**msgsnd-13** [OSF/1] On success `msg_stime` is set to the current time.
  Test: after a send, `msg_stime` is within a second of `time(NULL)`.

**msgsnd-14** [OSF/1] NOTES: `struct msgbuf` member `mtype` (type `mtyp_t`) is a user-chosen positive integer; a receiver can use it to select messages (see `msgrcv()`).
  Test: send with types 1 and 2; `msgrcv` with type 2 returns only the second.
  Note: The page spells the field "mytpe" once.

**msgsnd-15** [OSF/1] NOTES: `struct msgbuf` member `mtext` (type `char[]`) is any text of length `msgsz`.
  Test: send 3 bytes containing a NUL; `msgrcv` returns all 3.

**msgsnd-16** [OSF/1] NOTES: to send, the kernel allocates space and copies the data from user space, then allocates a `msg` header structure, sets its fields and inserts it at the tail of the queue.
  Test: send messages "a" then "b"; `msgrcv` with type 0 gets "a" first.

**msgsnd-17** [OSF/1] NOTES: kernel `struct msg` member `msg_next` (`struct msg *`) points to the next message in the queue.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel structure).

**msgsnd-18** [OSF/1] NOTES: kernel `struct msg` member `msg_type` (`long`) is the type from the user's `msgbuf`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel structure).

**msgsnd-19** [OSF/1] NOTES: kernel `struct msg` member `msg_ts` (`long`) is the size of the message text.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel structure).

**msgsnd-20** [OSF/1] NOTES: kernel `struct msg` member `msg_addr` (`caddr_t`) is the address of the message text.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel structure).

**msgsnd-21** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: as msgsnd-2.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**msgsnd-E1** `EINVAL`: `msqid` is not a valid message queue ID; or `mtype` is less than 1; or `msgsz` is less than 0 or greater than the system-defined limit.

**msgsnd-E2** `EACCES`: the caller does not have permission for the operation.

**msgsnd-E3** `EAGAIN`: the maximum number of message headers has been allocated, or the message's bytes would exceed the maximum bytes on the queue, and `IPC_NOWAIT` is set; the message is not sent.

**msgsnd-E4** `EINTR`: the operation was interrupted by a signal.

**msgsnd-E5** `EIDRM`: `msqid` has been removed from the system.

Related: Functions: msgctl(2), msgget(2), msgrcv(2), sigaction(2); Data Structures: msqid_ds(4)

### msync(2)

Page: `man2/msync.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msync-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/mman.h>`): `int msync(caddr_t addr, size_t len, int flags)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**msync-2** [OSF/1] `addr` and `len` give the address and length in bytes of the region to synchronize.
  Test: `mmap()` a shared file page, modify it, `msync(addr, pagesize, MS_SYNC)` returns 0.

**msync-3** [OSF/1] `flags` is one of the constants defined in `sys/mman.h`: `MS_SYNC` (synchronous cache flush), `MS_ASYNC` (asynchronous cache flush), `MS_INVALIDATE` (invalidate cached pages).
  Test: compile code referencing all three.

**msync-4** [OSF/1] `msync()` controls caching of a mapped file region: it can ensure modified pages reach the file's underlying storage device, or control the visibility of modifications with respect to file system operations.
  Test: see msync-7 and msync-9.

**msync-5** [OSF/1] `len` must be a multiple of the page size returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`; if it is not, the region length is rounded up to the next multiple of the page size.
  Test: `msync(addr, 1, MS_SYNC)` on a mapped page succeeds and the whole page is flushed.
  Note: The page both says `len` "must be" a page multiple and says a non-multiple is rounded up; the second sentence governs what happens.

**msync-6** [OSF/1] With `MS_SYNC`, `msync()` does not return until the system completes all I/O operations.
  Test: Not testable from user space beyond success (completion of device I/O is not observable).

**msync-7** [OSF/1] With `MS_ASYNC`, `msync()` returns after the system schedules all I/O operations.
  Test: `msync(addr, len, MS_ASYNC)` on a shared mapping returns 0.

**msync-8** [OSF/1] With `MS_INVALIDATE`, all cached copies of the pages are invalidated; new copies must be obtained from the file system the next time they are referenced.
  Test: see msync-10.

**msync-9** [OSF/1] After a successful `MS_SYNC` call, all previous modifications to the mapped region are visible to processes using `read()`; previous modifications to the file made with `write()` "may be lost".
  Test: store "abc" through a shared mapping, `msync(MS_SYNC)`, then `read()` the file through a descriptor gets "abc".
  Note: The page says "using the read() parameter"; "function" is presumably meant.

**msync-10** [OSF/1] After a successful `MS_INVALIDATE` call, all previous modifications made to the file with `write()` are visible in the mapped region; previous direct modifications to the mapped region "may be lost".
  Test: map a file, `write()` "xyz" through a descriptor, `msync(MS_INVALIDATE)`; the mapping shows "xyz".

**msync-11** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: see msync-2.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**msync-E1** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while reading from or writing to the file system.

**msync-E2** `ENOMEM`: the range [`addr`, `addr` + `len`) is invalid for the process's address space, or includes one or more unmapped pages.

**msync-E3** `EINVAL`: `addr` is not a multiple of the page size returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`.

**msync-E4** `EINVAL`: `flags` is `MS_SYNC` or `MS_ASYNC` and the region was mapped with `MAP_PRIVATE`.

**msync-E5** `EFAULT`: the range [`addr`, `addr` + `len`) includes an invalid address.

Related: Functions: fsync(2), mmap(2), read(2), sysconf(3), write(2)

Page: `man2/munmap.html`. AES: Trial use.

**munmap-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int munmap(caddr_t addr, size_t len)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/mman.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types including both headers.

**munmap-2** [OSF/1] `munmap()` unmaps a mapped file or shared memory region; `addr` and `len` give the address and length in bytes of the region to unmap.
  Test: `mmap` a page, `munmap` it, check return is 0.

**munmap-3** [OSF/1] `len` must be a multiple of the page size as returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`; if it is not, the length is rounded up to the next multiple of the page size.

**munmap-5** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: successful call returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**munmap-E1** `EINVAL`: `addr` is not a multiple of the page size as returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`.

**munmap-E2** `EFAULT`: the range [`addr`, `addr` + `len`) includes an invalid address.

### mvalid(2)

Page: `man2/mvalid.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mvalid-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int mvalid(caddr_t addr, size_t len, int prot)`, with `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/mman.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types against the headers.

**mvalid-2** [OSF/1] `addr` is the address of the region to check; `len` is the region's length in bytes; `prot` is the desired access protection.
  Test: call on a page-aligned `mmap`ed region of one page with `PROT_READ`; returns 0.

**mvalid-3** [OSF/1] A region is valid if accesses of the requested type are allowed to all addresses in the region.
  Test: map two pages read-write, `mprotect` the second to `PROT_READ`; `mvalid(addr, 2*pagesize, PROT_WRITE)` returns −1, `mvalid(addr, pagesize, PROT_WRITE)` returns 0.

**mvalid-4** [OSF/1] `sys/mman.h` defines `PROT_READ` (region can be read), `PROT_WRITE` (region can be written) and `PROT_EXEC` (region can be executed).
  Test: check the three constants are defined in `<sys/mman.h>`.

**mvalid-5** [OSF/1] `prot` can be any combination of `PROT_READ`, `PROT_WRITE` and `PROT_EXEC` ORed together.
  Test: `mvalid` on a read-write mapping with `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE` returns 0.

**mvalid-6** [OSF/1] Returns 0 if accesses requiring the given protection are allowed to all addresses in the range; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: valid range returns 0; range over an unmapped page returns −1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**mvalid-E1** `EACCES`: the range [`addr`, `addr` + `len`) is invalid for the process's address space, or the range includes one or more unmapped pages, or one or more pages of the range disallow accesses of the given protection.

**mvalid-E2** `EINVAL`: the `prot` parameter is invalid, or `addr` is not a multiple of the page size as returned by `sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`.

Related: Functions: mmap(2), mprotect(2), sysconf(3)

### nfssvc(2)

Page: `man2/nfssvc.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**nfssvc-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `nfssvc(int sock, int mask, int match)`; no return type is shown.
  Test: compile a call.

**nfssvc-2** [OSF/1] `nfssvc()` starts an NFS daemon listening on socket `sock`, which must be in the `AF_INET` family and of type `SOCK_DGRAM`.
  Test: as root in a child, bind a UDP socket and call; the child stays in the call.
  Note: The page gives no error for a socket of the wrong family or type.

**nfssvc-3** [OSF/1] `mask` is applied to the client host address; `match` is compared with the client host address ANDed with `mask`; if equal, the daemon is started, otherwise the request is dropped by the server.
  Test: Not readily testable without an NFS client; with `mask` 0 and `match` 0 every client should be served.
  Note: The page says "the daemon is started" on a match per request, which is unclear; it presumably means the request is served.

**nfssvc-4** [OSF/1] Normally the function does not return unless the server is terminated by a signal, at which time it returns 0; otherwise it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: kill the child from nfssvc-2 with a signal; observe it ends.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**nfssvc-E1** `EBADF`: An invalid file descriptor was passed to `nfssvc()`.

**nfssvc-E2** `EPERM`: The caller is not the superuser.

### pipe(2)

Page: `man2/pipe.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**pipe-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int pipe(int filedes[2])`. The page lists no header.
  Test: Compile the call.

**pipe-2** [OSF/1] `pipe()` creates a one-way interprocess channel (a pipe) and returns two descriptors. `filedes[0]` is open for reading and `filedes[1]` for writing.
  Test: `F_GETFL & O_ACCMODE` is `O_RDONLY` on [0] and `O_WRONLY` on [1].

**pipe-3** [OSF/1] The two descriptors are the two lowest available when `pipe()` is called.
  Test: Close 3 and 5, with 4 in use. `pipe` returns {3,5}.

**pipe-4** [OSF/1] `O_NONBLOCK` is clear on both descriptors. `fcntl()` can be used to set it.
  Test: `F_GETFL` on both shows no `O_NONBLOCK`.

**pipe-5** [OSF/1] A process has the pipe open for reading if it has a descriptor open on the read end `filedes[0]`, and open for writing if it has one open on the write end `filedes[1]`.
  Test: Definitions only; exercised through pipe-2 and pipe-6.

**pipe-6** [OSF/1] Reading `filedes[0]` gets the data written to `filedes[1]` in first-in, first-out order.
  Test: Write "ab", then "cd". A read returns "abcd".

**pipe-7** [OSF/1] On success, `st_atime`, `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the pipe are marked for update.
  Test: `fstat` on [0] right after creation shows all three times at about the current time.

**pipe-8** [OSF/1] `FD_CLOEXEC` is clear on both descriptors.
  Test: `F_GETFD` on both returns 0.

**pipe-9** [OSF/1] On success, `pipe()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: Check the return values.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**pipe-E1** `EFAULT`: `filedes` is an invalid address.

**pipe-E2** `EMFILE`: more than `OPEN_MAX`−2 descriptors are already open in this process.

**pipe-E3** `ENFILE`: the system file table is full, or the device that holds pipes has no free i-nodes.

**pipe-10** [DEC] (Environment note, Digital extensions.) `EMFILE`: more than `getdtablesize()`−2 descriptors are already open in this process.
  Test: Open descriptors until `getdtablesize()`−1 are in use, then `pipe` gives −1 and `EMFILE`.

**pipe-11** [DEC] (Environment note, Digital extensions.) `ENOMEM`: the system could not allocate kernel memory for more descriptors.
  Not testable from user space reliably: it needs kernel memory exhaustion.

Environment note Related: Functions: getdtablesize(2)

Related: Functions: read(2), fcntl(2), select(2), write(2); Commands: sh(1)

### plock(2)

Page: `man2/plock.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**plock-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int plock(int opr)`, declared via `<sys/lock.h>`.
  Test: compile a call including `<sys/lock.h>`.

**plock-2** [OSF/1] `plock()` locks or unlocks a process's text segment, data segment, or both in physical memory; while locked, the physical pages holding the segment are not paged out.
  Test: as root, `plock(PROCLOCK)` returns 0 (paging behaviour itself is not observable from user space).

**plock-3** [OSF/1] `opr` is one of: `PROCLOCK` (lock text and data segments), `TXTLOCK` (lock text segment), `DATLOCK` (lock data segment), `UNLOCK` (remove locks).
  Test: as root, `plock(TXTLOCK)`, `plock(UNLOCK)`, `plock(DATLOCK)`, `plock(UNLOCK)` each return 0.

**plock-4** [OSF/1] It is an error to lock a segment that is already locked.
  Test: as root, `plock(TXTLOCK)` twice; the second fails with `EINVAL`.

**plock-5** [OSF/1] The caller must have superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, `plock(PROCLOCK)` fails with `EPERM`.

**plock-6** [OSF/1] Memory acquired after `plock()` "may or may not be locked", depending on how it is acquired: memory from `brk()` or `sbrk()` is locked if the data segment was locked; memory from `mmap()` or `vm_allocate()` is not locked.
  Test: Not testable from user space: residency of pages is not observable.

**plock-7** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: successful root call returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**plock-E1** `EPERM`: the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

**plock-E2** `EINVAL`: `opr` is `PROCLOCK`, but the text segment or the data segment is already locked.

**plock-E3** `EINVAL`: `opr` is `TXTLOCK`, but the text segment is already locked.

**plock-E4** `EINVAL`: `opr` is `DATLOCK`, but the data segment is already locked.

**plock-E5** `EINVAL`: `opr` is `UNLOCK`, but neither the text segment nor the data segment is locked.

Related: Functions: brk(2), mmap(2)

### poll(2)

Page: `man2/poll.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**poll-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/poll.h>`; `int poll(struct pollfd filedes[], unsigned int nfds, int timeout)`.
  Test: Compile a call with these argument types.

**poll-2** [OSF/1] `filedes` points to an array of `pollfd` structures, one for each descriptor of interest. `nfds` is the number of entries. `timeout` is the longest time to wait, in milliseconds, for at least one of the events.
  Test: Poll 3 entries with `nfds` = 3 and check that every `revents` is filled in.

**poll-3** [OSF/1] `poll()` reports I/O conditions on a set of descriptors and waits until one or more of them is true. The conditions include being able to read or write without blocking, and error conditions.
  Test: Poll a pipe read end. It blocks until data is written, then returns with `POLLIN` or `POLLNORM` set.

**poll-4** [OSF/1] `pollfd` field: `int fd` is the file descriptor. It names an open file descriptor.
  Test: Compile code that uses `.fd`.

**poll-5** [OSF/1] `pollfd` field: `short events` holds the requested conditions. `poll()` uses it to decide what to report for this descriptor.
  Test: Compile code that uses `.events`, and see poll-13.

**poll-6** [OSF/1] `pollfd` field: `short revents` holds the reported conditions. If one or more of the conditions is true, `poll()` sets this field.
  Test: Compile code that uses `.revents`, and see poll-14.

**poll-7** [OSF/1] `poll()` ignores any entry whose `fd` is less than 0.
  Test: Mix an entry with `fd` = −1 among valid ones. That entry's `revents` is not reported and is not counted.

**poll-8** [OSF/1] If every entry has `fd` less than 0, `poll()` returns 0 and does nothing else.
  Test: Poll two entries with `fd` = −1 and `timeout` 0. Expect 0.
Note: The page does not say whether `poll()` still waits for `timeout` in this case.

**poll-9** [OSF/1] `poll()` lets a program multiplex I/O over descriptors that refer to open streams. It shows on which streams messages can be sent or received, or on which certain events have happened. Messages can be received with `read()` or `getmsg()` and sent with `write()` or `putmsg()`. Some `ioctl()` calls, such as `I_RECVFD` and `I_SENDFD`, can also send and receive messages.
  Test: Poll a STREAMS descriptor for `POLLIN`. Send a message from the peer, and `poll` returns 1.

**poll-10** [OSF/1] Neither `O_NDELAY` nor `O_NONBLOCK` affects `poll()`. Its behaviour does not depend on whether `O_NONBLOCK` is set on any of the descriptors.
  Test: Repeat the same polls with `O_NONBLOCK` set and cleared. The results and blocking behaviour are the same.

**poll-11** [OSF/1] `events` and `revents` are bitmasks made of ORed condition flags. The caller sets `events` and `poll()` sets `revents`.
  Test: Request `POLLIN|POLLOUT` on a pipe end and check the bits that come back.

**poll-12** [OSF/1] The condition flags are these:
- `POLLERR`: an error has occurred on the descriptor. It is only valid in `revents` and is not used in `events`.
- `POLLHUP`: the device has been disconnected, or a hangup has occurred on the stream. It is mutually exclusive with `POLLOUT`: a stream can never be writable after a hangup.
- `POLLIN`: a non-priority or descriptor-passing message (see `I_RECVFD`) is on the stream head read queue. It is set even for a zero-length message. In `revents` it is mutually exclusive with `POLLPRI`.
- `POLLNORM`: data may be read without blocking.
- `POLLNVAL`: the value given for `fd` is invalid.
- `POLLOUT`: data may be written without blocking.
- `POLLPRI`: a priority message is on the stream head read queue. It is set even for a zero-length message. In `revents` it is mutually exclusive with `POLLIN`.
  Test: Check that each constant is defined. Poll a stream on which a hangup has occurred: expect `POLLHUP` and no `POLLOUT`. Poll a closed descriptor number: expect `POLLNVAL`. Send a zero-length normal message and a zero-length priority message on a stream: expect `POLLIN` alone and `POLLPRI` alone, never both.
Note: The page lists `POLLERR` and `POLLHUP` twice each, with different wording, which suggests two source descriptions were merged.

**poll-13** [OSF/1] `POLLNORM` and `POLLOUT` are true if and only if at least one byte can be read or written without blocking. The exception is regular files, which always poll true for `POLLNORM` and `POLLOUT`.
  Test: An empty pipe does not report `POLLNORM`. After one byte is written, it does. A regular file at EOF reports both `POLLNORM` and `POLLOUT`.

**poll-14** [OSF/1] `POLLERR`, `POLLHUP` and `POLLNVAL` are always set in `revents` when their condition is true, whether or not they are set in `events`.
  Test: With `events` = 0 on an invalid fd, `revents` contains `POLLNVAL`. With `events` = 0 on a stream with a hangup, `revents` contains `POLLHUP`.

**poll-15** [OSF/1] For each descriptor, the reportable conditions are the always-reported ones plus those requested in `events`. If any reportable condition is true for any descriptor, `poll()` returns with a bit set in `revents` for each true condition of that descriptor.
  Test: Request only `POLLIN` on a writable, readable pipe end. `POLLOUT` is not reported.

**poll-16** [OSF/1] If no reportable condition is true, `poll()` waits up to `timeout` milliseconds. If a condition becomes true in that time, it is reported in that descriptor's `revents` and `poll()` returns. If none becomes true, `poll()` returns without setting any `revents`.
  Test: Poll an empty pipe with `timeout` 200. It returns 0 after about 200 ms, and the `revents` values set beforehand are left unchanged.

**poll-17** [OSF/1] With `timeout` = −1, `poll()` does not return until at least one specified event has happened.
  Test: A child writes to a pipe after 1 s. `poll(..., -1)` returns at about 1 s with 1.

**poll-18** [OSF/1] With `timeout` = 0, `poll()` does not wait. It returns at once, even if no event has happened.
  Test: Poll an empty pipe with `timeout` 0. It returns 0 at once.

**poll-19** [Compat] `select()` is also supported, for compatibility with BSD systems.
  Test: Call `select()` on a pipe and check that it works.

**poll-20** [OSF/1] On success, `poll()` returns a nonnegative value. 0 means it timed out and set no `revents`. A positive value is the number of descriptors whose `revents` it set. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: Two readable pipes and one empty pipe give a return of 2.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**poll-E1** `EAGAIN`: internal data structures could not be allocated. A later call may succeed.

**poll-E2** `EINTR`: a signal was caught during `poll()`, and its handler was installed with an indication that functions are not to be restarted.

**poll-E3** `EINVAL`: `timeout` is a negative number other than −1.

**poll-E4** `EFAULT`: `filedes` together with `nfds` addresses a location outside the process's allocated address space.

Related: Functions: read(2), write(2), getmsg(2), putmsg(2), streamio(7)

### profil(2)

Page: `man2/profil.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**profil-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `void profil(short *short_buffer, unsigned int buffer_size, unsigned int offset, unsigned int scale)`; no header is listed.
  Test: compile and call; no return value.

**profil-2** [OSF/1] `profil()` controls execution profiling; `short_buffer` points to user memory whose length in bytes is `buffer_size`.
  Test: call with a zeroed buffer and a busy loop; some buffer entries become non-zero.

**profil-3** [OSF/1] `offset` is the delta between the program counter start and the buffer; an `offset` of 0 implies text begins at 0.
  Test: with `offset` equal to the address of a busy function and scale 0x10000, counts accumulate near the start of the buffer.

**profil-4** [OSF/1] After the call, the program counter is examined at regular intervals ("10 ms. in most implementations").
  Test: run a 1-second busy loop; total counts are roughly 100 (allow wide tolerance; interval not mandated).

**profil-5** [OSF/1] At each sample, `offset` is subtracted from the program counter and the result multiplied by `scale`; the matching location in `short_buffer` is incremented if the resulting number is less than `buffer_size`.
  Test: use a tiny `buffer_size` so the loop's PC maps beyond it; buffer stays zero.

**profil-6** [OSF/1] `scale` is an unsigned fixed-point fraction with 16 bits of mantissa: 0x10000 maps program counter values 1-to-1 to words of `short_buffer`; 0x8000 maps each pair of program counter values together.
  Test: profile the same loop with 0x10000 and 0x8000; the counts with 0x8000 fall at roughly half the buffer index.

**profil-7** [OSF/1] Profiling is turned off by a `scale` of 1.
  Test: start profiling, call with `scale` 1, run a loop; the buffer does not change.

**profil-8** [OSF/1] Profiling is turned off when an `execve()` is executed.
  Test: Not directly testable (new image cannot see the old buffer); check that the new image does not fault.

**profil-9** [OSF/1] Profiling remains on in both parent and child after a fork.
  Test: start profiling, fork; child runs a loop and checks its copy of the buffer changes.

**profil-10** [OSF/1] Profiling is turned off if an update of `short_buffer` would cause a memory fault.
  Test: profile into a buffer, then `munmap` it; process is not killed and keeps running.

**profil-11** [OSF/1] If the process contains multiple kernel threads, each is sampled independently and the counts are the sum of the samples of all threads.
  Test: two threads busy-loop for 1 s; total counts are about twice those of one thread.

Note: The page gives no RETURN VALUES or ERRORS section.

Related: Functions: exec(2), fork(2); Commands: prof(1), gprof(1)

### ptrace(2)

Page: `man2/ptrace.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**ptrace-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int ptrace(int request, int process, int *address, int data)`, with headers `<sys/signal.h>` and `<sys/ptrace.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with those headers.

**ptrace-2** [OSF/1] `ptrace()` lets a parent process control the execution of a child process; it is mainly used for breakpoint debugging.
  Test: child calls `ptrace(PT_TRACE_ME, 0, 0, 0)` and raises a signal; parent observes it stopped.

**ptrace-3** [OSF/1] A traced child behaves normally until it receives a signal; when a signal is delivered the child stops and `SIGCHLD` is sent to the parent, which can wait for the stop with `wait()`.
  Test: traced child does `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)`; parent receives `SIGCHLD` and `waitpid(..., WUNTRACED)` reports the child stopped with `SIGUSR1`.

**ptrace-4** [OSF/1] While the child is stopped, the parent may examine and modify the child's memory image, and terminate it or let it continue.
  Test: parent uses `PT_READ_D`/`PT_WRITE_D` on a known variable and then `PT_CONTINUE`; child sees the new value.

**ptrace-5** [OSF/1] As a security measure, `ptrace()` inhibits the set-user-ID facility when the child later calls any `exec` function.
  Test: traced child (non-root) execs a set-user-ID root program that prints `geteuid()`; it is not 0.

**ptrace-6** [OSF/1] When a traced process calls an `exec` function, it stops before executing the first instruction of the new image as if it had received `SIGTRAP`.
  Test: traced child execs a program; parent's `wait()` reports a stop with `SIGTRAP` before the program prints anything.

**ptrace-7** [OSF/1] Only `PT_TRACE_ME` may be issued by child processes; all other requests can only be used by the parent.
  Test: a process calls `PT_READ_D` on a process that is not its traced child; expect −1.
Note: The page does not name the errno for a request from a non-parent.

**ptrace-8** [OSF/1] For each parent request, `process` is the child's process ID, and the child must be stopped before the request is made.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (the page states a precondition only); issue requests only to a stopped child.
Note: The page does not say what happens when the child is not stopped.

**ptrace-9** [OSF/1] `PT_TRACE_ME` sets the child's trace flag; it must be issued by the child that is to be traced by its parent.
  Test: child issues `PT_TRACE_ME`; subsequent signal stops it (ptrace-10).

**ptrace-10** [OSF/1] When the trace flag is set, the child is left stopped on receipt of a signal, and the action set with `sigaction()` is ignored.
  Test: traced child installs a handler for `SIGUSR1` then raises it; it stops and the handler has not run when the parent sees the stop.

**ptrace-11** [OSF/1] For `PT_TRACE_ME`, `process`, `address` and `data` are ignored, and the return value is not defined.
  Test: call `PT_TRACE_ME` with arbitrary other arguments; tracing still takes effect.

**ptrace-12** [OSF/1] `PT_TRACE_ME` should not be issued when the parent does not expect to trace the child.
  Test: Not testable (advice to programmers).

**ptrace-13** [OSF/1] `PT_READ_I` and `PT_READ_D` return the data in the child's address space at the location `address` points to; the two give equal results; `data` is ignored.
  Test: parent reads a known word of the stopped child with both requests; both return the same known value.

**ptrace-14** [OSF/1] `PT_READ_I`/`PT_READ_D` fail when `address` is not in the child's address space, or on some machines when `address` is not properly aligned; they then return −1 and set the parent's `errno` to `EIO`.
  Test: read at an unmapped address; expect −1 and `EIO`.

**ptrace-15** [OSF/1] `PT_READ_U` returns the variable of the child's system per-process data area named by `address`; this area holds register values and other process information; on some machines `address` is subject to alignment constraints; `data` is ignored.
  Test: read offset 0 of the per-process area of a stopped child; call succeeds (value implementation-specific).

**ptrace-16** [OSF/1] `PT_READ_U` fails when `address` is outside the child's per-process data area; it returns −1 and sets the parent's `errno` to `EIO`.
  Test: `PT_READ_U` with a huge offset; expect −1 and `EIO`.

**ptrace-17** [OSF/1] `PT_WRITE_I` and `PT_WRITE_D` write `data` into the child's address space at the location `address` points to.
  Test: write a value with `PT_WRITE_D`, read back with `PT_READ_D`; equal.

**ptrace-18** [OSF/1] On some machines, where necessary, `PT_WRITE_I` synchronizes any hardware caches; otherwise `PT_WRITE_I` and `PT_WRITE_D` give equal results.
  Test: write a breakpoint instruction with `PT_WRITE_I` and continue; the child traps at it.

**ptrace-19** [OSF/1] On some machines `PT_WRITE_I`/`PT_WRITE_D` return the previous contents of the child's location; on other machines no useful value is returned.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (machine-dependent); record the return value only.

**ptrace-20** [OSF/1] `PT_WRITE_I`/`PT_WRITE_D` fail when `address` points into pure procedure space and a copy cannot be made, when `address` is out of range, and on some machines when `address` is misaligned; they then return −1 and set the parent's `errno` to `EIO`.
  Test: write at an unmapped address; expect −1 and `EIO`.

**ptrace-21** [OSF/1] `PT_WRITE_U` writes `data` into the variable of the child's per-process data area named by `address` (register values and other information); on some machines `address` is subject to alignment constraints; not all locations in the area may be written.
  Test: write a register slot of a stopped child and read it back with `PT_READ_U`.

**ptrace-22** [OSF/1] `PT_WRITE_U` fails when `address` is outside the per-process data area; it returns −1 and sets the parent's `errno` to indicate the error.
  Test: `PT_WRITE_U` with a huge offset; expect −1.
Note: The page does not name the errno for this case (compare ptrace-E6 and ptrace-E7).

**ptrace-23** [OSF/1] `PT_CONTINUE` lets the child resume; when `data` is 0, the signal that stopped the child is cancelled before it resumes.
  Test: child stopped by `SIGUSR1` with a handler; `PT_CONTINUE` with `data` 0; the handler does not run.

**ptrace-24** [OSF/1] When `data` is a valid signal value, the child resumes as though that signal had been received.
  Test: `PT_CONTINUE` with `data` = `SIGUSR2`; the child's `SIGUSR2` handler runs.

**ptrace-25** [OSF/1] When `address` equals 1, execution continues from where it stopped; otherwise `address` is taken as the address at which to resume.
  Test: `PT_CONTINUE` with `address` 1 resumes normally; with `address` set to a function's entry, that function runs.

**ptrace-26** [OSF/1] `PT_CONTINUE` fails when `data` is neither 0 nor a valid signal value; it returns −1 to the parent and sets the parent's `errno` to `EIO`.
  Test: `PT_CONTINUE` with `data` = 9999; expect −1 and `EIO`.

**ptrace-27** [OSF/1] `PT_KILL` terminates the child as if it had called `exit()`.
  Test: `PT_KILL` a stopped child; `wait()` reports it terminated.

**ptrace-28** [OSF/1] `PT_STEP` continues execution like `PT_CONTINUE`, but as soon as possible after at least one instruction executes, the child stops again as if it had received `SIGTRAP`.
  Test: `PT_STEP` a stopped child; `wait()` reports a `SIGTRAP` stop.
Note: The page has no general RETURN VALUES section; success values are given only per request.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**ptrace-E1** `EIO`: `request` is not one of the listed values, or is not valid for the machine type on which the process runs.

**ptrace-E2** `EIO`: the given signal number is invalid.

**ptrace-E3** `EIO`: the specified address is out of bounds or improperly aligned.

**ptrace-E4** `ESRCH`: `process` identifies a child that does not exist or that has not executed `ptrace()` with `PT_TRACE_ME`.

**ptrace-E5** `EPERM`: the specified process cannot be traced.

**ptrace-E6** `EINVAL`: an invalid location was specified for the system's per-process data area.

**ptrace-E7** `EACCES`: the location in the system's per-process data area could not be modified.

**ptrace-29** [DEC] (Environment notes, System V compatibility) To reflect System V behaviour, `PT_WRITE_I`/`PT_WRITE_D` on success return the value written into the child's address space (replacing the "some machines ... no useful value" statement).
  Test: `PT_WRITE_D` value 0x1234; return value is 0x1234.
Note: The page says "PT_WRITE, PT_WRITE_D", apparently meaning `PT_WRITE_I`, `PT_WRITE_D`. The page says these changes "should be made to the descriptions", without stating plainly that this implementation behaves so.

**ptrace-30** [DEC] (Environment notes, System V compatibility) To describe System V behaviour, `PT_CONTINUE` on success returns the signal value to be received by the child.
  Test: `PT_CONTINUE` with `data` = `SIGUSR1`; return value equals `SIGUSR1`.

Related: Functions: exec(2), sigaction(2), wait(2)

### putmsg(2)

Page: `man2/putmsg.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page is headed "Digital" rather than "OSF", and it has no AES Support Level. Nothing in the text itself says the interface is DEC-specific, so the items are tagged [DEC].

**putmsg-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <stropts.h>`; `int putmsg(int fd, struct strbuf *ctlptr, struct strbuf *dataptr, int flags)` (old-style K&R declaration on the page).
  Test: Compile a call with these argument types against `<stropts.h>`.

**putmsg-2** [DEC] `putmsg` builds a message from one or two user buffers and sends it to a STREAMS file.
  Test: Call `putmsg` on a STREAMS pipe/loopback, then read the message at the other end with `getmsg` and compare.

**putmsg-3** [DEC] A message may have a data part, a control part, or both. The two parts are kept apart by being in separate buffers.
  Test: Send only control, only data, and both. Check with `getmsg` that each part arrives in the right buffer.

**putmsg-4** [DEC] The STREAMS module that receives the message decides what each part means.
  Not testable from user space as a general rule: the meaning depends on the module.

**putmsg-5** [DEC] `fd` must be a file descriptor that refers to an open stream.
  Test: See the `EBADF` and `ENOSTR` errors.

**putmsg-6** [DEC] The `strbuf` structure has these fields: `int maxlen` (not used), `int len` (length of the data) and `char *buf` (pointer to the buffer).
  Test: Compile code that sets `maxlen`, `len` and `buf` of a `struct strbuf`.

**putmsg-7** [DEC] `ctlptr` describes the control part, if there is one. Its `buf` points to the control information and its `len` gives the number of bytes to send.
  Test: Send 10 control bytes and check that `getmsg` receives exactly those 10 bytes in its control buffer.

**putmsg-8** [DEC] `putmsg` does not use the `maxlen` field.
  Test: Set `maxlen` to garbage (for example −5 or 0). The send still succeeds and delivers `len` bytes.

**putmsg-9** [DEC] `dataptr` describes the data part, if there is one, in the same way as `ctlptr`.
  Test: Send 10 data bytes and check that `getmsg` receives them in its data buffer.

**putmsg-10** [DEC] `flags` may be 0 or `RS_HIPRI`.
  Test: See putmsg-E6 for other values.

**putmsg-11** [DEC] A data part is sent only when `dataptr` is non-NULL and `dataptr->len` is 0 or greater. A control part is sent only when the same holds for `ctlptr`.
  Test: Send with `dataptr->len` set to 0. A zero-length data part is delivered.

**putmsg-12** [DEC] No data (control) part is sent if `dataptr` (`ctlptr`) is NULL or its `len` is −1.
  Test: Send with `dataptr` NULL, then with `dataptr->len` = −1. The receiver sees no data part.

**putmsg-13** [DEC] With a control part and `flags` = `RS_HIPRI`, a priority message is sent.
  Test: The receiver's `getmsg` reports `RS_HIPRI` in its flags.

**putmsg-14** [DEC] With `flags` = 0, a non-priority message is sent.
  Test: The receiver's `getmsg` reports flags 0.

**putmsg-15** [DEC] With no control part and `flags` = `RS_HIPRI`, `putmsg` fails with `EINVAL`.
  Test: Pass `ctlptr` = NULL, data present, `flags` = `RS_HIPRI`. Expect −1 and `EINVAL`.

**putmsg-16** [DEC] With no control part, no data part and `flags` = 0, no message is sent and 0 is returned.
  Test: Pass both pointers NULL and `flags` 0. Expect 0, and a poll of the other end shows nothing to read.

**putmsg-17** [DEC] A non-priority message blocks when the stream write queue is full because of internal flow control.
  Test: Fill the write queue, then call `putmsg` in a child with flags 0. The call blocks instead of returning.

**putmsg-18** [DEC] A priority message does not block when the write queue is full because of flow control.
  Test: With the write queue full, `putmsg` with `RS_HIPRI` returns at once.

**putmsg-19** [DEC] A non-priority message with `O_NDELAY` set does not block when the write queue is full. The call fails with `EAGAIN` instead.
  Test: Set `O_NDELAY`, fill the queue, call with flags 0. Expect −1 and `EAGAIN`.

**putmsg-20** [DEC] `putmsg` also blocks while it waits for message blocks to become free in the stream. This happens whatever the priority and even with `O_NDELAY` set, "unless prevented by lack of internal resources".
  Not testable from user space in a reliable way: the test cannot control kernel message-block availability.

**putmsg-21** [DEC] No partial message is sent.
  Test: After any failed `putmsg`, the receiver sees either nothing or the whole message.

**putmsg-22** [DEC] `putmsg` also fails if the stream head had processed a STREAMS error message before the call. The error returned is the value carried in that STREAMS error message.
  Test: Have a module or driver send an M_ERROR with a known errno, then call `putmsg`. Expect −1 with that errno. Needs a cooperating STREAMS module.

**putmsg-23** [DEC] On success, `putmsg` returns 0. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: A valid send returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**putmsg-E1** `EAGAIN`: the message is non-priority, the `O_NDELAY` flag is set, and the stream write queue is full because of internal flow control.

**putmsg-E2** `EAGAIN`: buffers could not be allocated for the message that was to be created.

**putmsg-E3** `EBADF`: `fd` is not a valid file descriptor open for writing.

**putmsg-E4** `EFAULT`: `ctlptr` or `dataptr` points outside the allocated address space.

**putmsg-E5** `EINTR`: a signal was caught during the `putmsg` call.

**putmsg-E6** `EINVAL`: `flags` holds an undefined value, or `flags` is `RS_HIPRI` and no control part was supplied.

**putmsg-E7** `EINVAL`: the stream that `fd` refers to is linked below a multiplexor.

**putmsg-E8** `ENOSTR`: no stream is associated with `fd`.

**putmsg-E9** `ENXIO`: a hangup condition was generated downstream for this stream.

**putmsg-E10** `ERANGE`: the size of the data part is outside the range set by the maximum and minimum packet sizes of the topmost stream module. It is also returned if the control part is larger than the maximum configured control-part size, or if the data part is larger than the maximum configured data-part size.

Related: read(2), getmsg(2), poll(2), write(2).

### quotactl(2)

Page: `man2/quotactl.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**quotactl-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `quotactl(char *path, int cmd, int id, char *addr)`, with header `<ufs/quota.h>` (for "ufs" quotas).
  Test: compile and call.
Note: The page gives no return type in the synopsis; RETURN VALUE implies `int`.

**quotactl-2** [OSF/1] `path` is the pathname of any file in the mounted file system; `cmd` is a command for interpreting `id`; `id` is a user or group identifier; `addr` is the address of an optional command-specific structure copied into or out of the system, interpreted per command.
  Test: covered by the command items.

**quotactl-3** [OSF/1] `quotactl()` enables and disables quotas and manipulates disk quotas on file systems where quotas are enabled.
  Test: covered by the command items.

**quotactl-4** [OSF/1] Currently quotas are supported only for the UFS file system.
  Test: on a non-UFS file system, a quota command fails.
Note: The page does not name the error for a non-UFS file system.

**quotactl-5** [OSF/1] For UFS, a command is a primary command combined with a command type that says how to interpret `id`; types exist for user identifiers and group identifiers.
  Test: issue `Q_GETQUOTA` with the user type and with the group type; both are accepted.
Note: The page does not name the type constants or how the command and type are combined.

**quotactl-6** [OSF/1] `Q_QUOTAON` enables quotas for the file system of `path`; the command type gives the quota type; `addr` names the quota file, which must exist (normally created by `quotacheck`); `id` is unused; only superuser can turn quotas on.
  Test: as root, run `quotacheck`, then `Q_QUOTAON` with the quota file; returns 0; as non-root, −1 `EPERM`.

**quotactl-7** [OSF/1] `Q_QUOTAOFF` disables quotas for the file system of `path`; the command type gives the quota type; `addr` and `id` are unused; only superuser can turn quotas off.
  Test: as root, returns 0; as non-root, −1 `EPERM`.

**quotactl-8** [OSF/1] `Q_GETQUOTA` gets quota limits and current usage for the user or group `id` (per command type); `addr` points to a `struct dqblk` defined in `ufs/quota.h`.
  Test: on a quota-enabled file system, get the caller's quota; returns 0 and fills `dqblk`.

**quotactl-9** [OSF/1] `Q_SETQUOTA` sets quota limits for user or group `id`; `addr` points to a `struct dqblk`; its usage fields are ignored; restricted to superuser.
  Test: as root, set limits, read back with `Q_GETQUOTA`; limits match and usage unchanged.

**quotactl-10** [OSF/1] `Q_SETUSE` sets disk usage for user or group `id`; `addr` points to a `struct dqblk`; only its usage fields are used; restricted to superuser.
  Test: as root, set usage, read back; usage matches and limits unchanged.
Note: The page says "Set disk usage limits", though only usage fields are used.

**quotactl-11** [OSF/1] `Q_SYNC` updates the on-disk copy of quota usages; the command type selects which quota type; `id` and `addr` are ignored.
  Test: `Q_SYNC` returns 0 on a quota-enabled file system.

**quotactl-12** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and `errno` set.
  Test: check return values.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**quotactl-E1** `EOPNOTSUPP`: the kernel has not been compiled with the `QUOTA` option.

**quotactl-E2** `EUSERS`: the quota table cannot be expanded.

**quotactl-E3** `EINVAL`: `cmd` or the command type is invalid.

**quotactl-E4** `EINVAL`: a pathname contains a character with the high-order bit set.

**quotactl-E5** `EACCES`: in `Q_QUOTAON`, the quota file is not a plain file.

**quotactl-E6** `EACCES`: search permission is denied for a component of a path prefix.

**quotactl-E7** `ENOTDIR`: a component of a path prefix is not a directory.

**quotactl-E8** `ENAMETOOLONG`: a pathname component exceeded `NAME_MAX`, or the whole pathname exceeded `PATH_MAX`.

**quotactl-E9** `ENOENT`: a filename does not exist.

**quotactl-E10** `ELOOP`: too many symbolic links were encountered in translating a pathname.

**quotactl-E11** `EROFS`: in `Q_QUOTAON`, the quota file is on a read-only file system.

**quotactl-E12** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while reading or writing a file containing quotas.

**quotactl-E13** `EFAULT`: an invalid `addr` was supplied; the structure could not be copied into or out of the kernel.

**quotactl-E14** `EFAULT`: `path` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**quotactl-E15** `EPERM`: the call is privileged and the caller lacks appropriate privilege.

Related: Commands: quota(1), edquota(8), quotacheck(8), quotaon(8), repquota(8)

### read(2), readv(2)

Page: `man2/read.html`; same text as `readv(2)`. AES: Full use (`read()`).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**read-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int read(int filedes, char *buffer, unsigned int nbytes)`; and (with `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/uio.h>`) `int readv(int filedes, struct iovec *iov, int iovcount)`.
  Test: compile calls of both with these types.

**read-2** [OSF/1] `filedes` identifies the object to read; `buffer` receives the data; `nbytes` is the number of bytes to read.
  Test: write "hello" to a file, reopen, `read(fd, b, 5)` returns 5 and `b` holds "hello".

**read-3** [OSF/1] `readv()` does the same as `read()` but scatters the data into the buffers given by the `iovcount` `iovec` structures at `iov`; each entry gives the base address and length of a memory area.
  Test: file "abcdef", two iovecs of 2 and 4 bytes; `readv()` returns 6 with "ab" and "cdef".

**read-4** [OSF/1] `readv()` always fills an area completely before going on to the next.
  Test: file "abc", iovecs of 2 and 4 bytes; first gets "ab", second gets "c".

**read-5** [OSF/1] `struct iovec` is defined in `sys/uio.h` with members `caddr_t iov_base` and `int iov_len`.
  Test: compile code assigning both members.

**read-6** [OSF/1] On regular files and seekable devices, reading starts at the file pointer of `filedes`; on return the file pointer has advanced by the number of bytes actually read.
  Test: after `read(fd, b, 3)` returning 3, `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR) == 3`.

**read-7** [OSF/1] Devices incapable of seeking always read from the current position; the value of their file pointer is undefined.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement for the pointer value (undefined); reading a pipe returns data in order written.

**read-8** [OSF/1] `read()` and `readv()` suspend only the calling thread, not the whole process.
  Test: one thread blocks in `read()` on an empty pipe; another thread keeps running and later writes to the pipe, unblocking it.

**read-9** [OSF/1] On success `read()` returns the number of bytes actually read and placed in the buffer; this is never greater than `nbytes`.
  Test: `read(fd, b, 4)` on a 10-byte file returns 4.

**read-10** [OSF/1] The result may be less than `nbytes` if fewer bytes remain in the file, if the read was interrupted by a signal, or if the file is a pipe, FIFO or special file with fewer than `nbytes` immediately available; for example, a terminal read may return one typed line.
  Test: 3-byte file, `read(fd, b, 10)` returns 3; pipe holding 2 bytes, `read(p, b, 10)` returns 2.

**read-11** [OSF/1] No data is transferred past the current end-of-file; if the start position is at or after end-of-file, 0 is returned.
  Test: `lseek()` to end, `read()` returns 0; `lseek()` past end, `read()` returns 0.

**read-12** [OSF/1] If `nbytes` is 0, `read()` returns 0 and has no other results.
  Test: `read(fd, b, 0) == 0` and the file offset is unchanged.

**read-13** [OSF/1] Empty pipe or FIFO with no writer open: `read()` returns 0 (end-of-file).
