  Test: `pipe()`, close the write end, `read()` returns 0.

**read-14** [OSF/1] Empty pipe or FIFO with a writer, and neither `O_NONBLOCK` nor `O_NDELAY` set: `read()` blocks until data is written or every process that had it open for writing closes it.
  Test: reader blocks; a child writes after 1 s; `read()` returns that data after about 1 s.

**read-15** [OSF/1] Empty pipe or FIFO with a writer, and `O_NONBLOCK` or `O_NDELAY` set: `read()` returns -1 with `EAGAIN`.
  Test: set `O_NONBLOCK` on the read end of an empty pipe with the write end open; `read()` gives -1/`EAGAIN`.

**read-16** [OSF/1] Character special file supporting non-blocking reads (such as a terminal) with no data, and neither `O_NONBLOCK` nor `O_NDELAY` set: `read()` blocks until data is available.
  Test: on a pseudo-terminal slave, `read()` blocks until the master writes a line.

**read-17** [OSF/1] Same case with `O_NONBLOCK` or `O_NDELAY` set: `read()` returns -1 with `EAGAIN` if no data is available; `O_NONBLOCK` has no effect if some data is available.
  Test: pty slave with `O_NONBLOCK`: no data gives -1/`EAGAIN`; after master writes a line, `read()` returns it.

**read-18** [OSF/1] Regular file with enforcement-mode record locking, where part of the region is write- or exclusive-locked by another process, with `O_NDELAY` and `O_NONBLOCK` clear: `read()` blocks until the lock is released or the read is terminated by a signal.
  Test: child holds a write lock on a file with mandatory locking; parent `read()` blocks until the child unlocks.

**read-19** [OSF/1] Same case with `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` set: `read()` returns -1 with `EAGAIN`.
  Test: as above with `O_NONBLOCK`; `read()` gives -1/`EAGAIN`.

**read-20** [OSF/1] If interrupted by a signal before reading any data, `read()` returns -1 with `EINTR`.
  Test: handler for `SIGALRM` installed without restart, `alarm(1)`, `read()` on an empty pipe gives -1/`EINTR`.

**read-21** [OSF/1] If interrupted after reading some data, the result depends on how the handler was installed: without restart, `read()` returns -1 with `EINTR` even if data was already consumed; with restart, it returns the amount of data consumed.
  Test: Not reliably testable from user space (needs a signal arriving mid-transfer); attempt with a slow terminal device.
  Note: The page's rule here (-1 with `EINTR` even after data was consumed) sits uneasily with read-10, which lists an interrupted read as a cause of a short count, and read-22 makes an exception for pipes and FIFOs.

**read-22** [OSF/1] A read from a pipe or FIFO never returns with `EINTR` if it has transferred any data.
  Test: Not reliably testable (needs a signal during a partial pipe transfer).

**read-23** [OSF/1] Any part of an ordinary file before end-of-file that was never written reads as bytes of value 0.
  Test: `lseek()` to 100, write 1 byte, read bytes 0 to 99; all are 0.

**read-24** [OSF/1] On success, `read()` marks the file's `st_atime` for update.
  Test: on a file system that updates access times, `st_atime` after a `read()` is not earlier than the time of the call.

**read-25** [OSF/1] A read from a STREAMS file works in one of three modes: byte-stream (the default), message-nondiscard, and message-discard. The mode is changed with the `I_SRDOPT` `ioctl()` request and tested with `I_GRDOPT`.
  Test: on a STREAMS device, `ioctl(fd, I_GRDOPT, &m)` reports byte-stream mode by default.

**read-26** [OSF/1] Byte-stream mode: `read()` retrieves data until it has `nbytes` bytes or no more data remains; it ignores message boundaries.
  Test: two messages "ab" and "cd" on a stream; `read(fd, b, 4)` returns 4.

**read-27** [OSF/1] Message-nondiscard mode: `read()` stops at `nbytes` or at a message boundary; unread data from the message is put back on the stream for the next `read()` or `getmsg()`.
  Test: message "abcd", `read(fd, b, 2)` gives "ab", then next `read()` gives "cd".

**read-28** [OSF/1] Message-discard mode: like message-nondiscard, but unread data left in the message after `read()` returns is discarded and not available to a later `read()` or `getmsg()`.
  Test: messages "abcd" and "ef"; `read(fd, b, 2)` gives "ab", next `read()` gives "ef".

**read-29** [OSF/1] Zero-byte messages in byte-stream mode: `read()` stops at `nbytes`, at no more data, or at a zero-byte message block; it returns the count read and puts the zero-byte message back on the stream for the next `read()` or `getmsg()`.
  Test: messages "ab", zero-length, "cd"; first `read(fd, b, 10)` returns 2.

**read-30** [OSF/1] In the other two modes, a zero-byte message makes `read()` return 0 and the message is removed from the stream.
  Test: in message-nondiscard mode, a zero-length message gives `read()` == 0, and the next `read()` gets the following message.

**read-31** [OSF/1] When a zero-byte message is the first message on a stream, 0 is returned regardless of the read mode.
  Test: zero-length message first, byte-stream mode: `read()` returns 0.

**read-32** [OSF/1] A STREAMS `read()` can process only data messages; it fails if a protocol message is at the stream head.
  Test: `putmsg()` with a control part; `read()` fails with `EBADMSG`.

**read-33** [OSF/1] A STREAMS `read()` also fails if an error message is received at the stream head; `errno` is set to the value in the error message.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a module that sends `M_ERROR`.

**read-34** [OSF/1] After a hangup on the stream, `read()` works normally until the stream head read queue is empty, then returns 0.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a driver that generates a hangup.

**read-35** [OSF/1] On success `read()` and `readv()` return the number of bytes read into buffers. The system guarantees to read the requested number only if the descriptor references a normal file that has "the same number of bytes left before the End-of-File".
  Test: 10-byte file, `read(fd, b, 10)` returns exactly 10.

**read-36** [OSF/1] On failure -1 is returned, `errno` is set, and the content of `buffer` is indeterminate.
  Test: `read(-1, b, 1)` returns -1.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**read-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not a valid file descriptor open for reading.

**read-E2** `EINVAL`: the file position pointer associated with `filedes` was negative.

**read-E3** `EINVAL`: the sum of the `iov_len` values in the `iov` array was negative or overflowed a 32-bit integer.

**read-E4** `EINVAL`: `iovcount` was not between 1 and 16 inclusive.

**read-E5** `EINVAL`: an attempt was made to read from a stream linked to a multiplexor.

**read-E6** `EAGAIN`: `O_NONBLOCK` is set for the descriptor and the process would be delayed in the read.

**read-E7** `EAGAIN`: enforced record locking is enabled, `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` is set, and another process owns a write lock.

**read-E8** `EAGAIN`: no message is waiting on a stream and `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` is set.

**read-E9** `EFAULT`: `buffer` or part of `iov` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**read-E10** `EINTR`: a `read()` was interrupted by a signal before any data arrived, and the handler was installed with an indication that functions are not to be restarted.

**read-E11** `EIO`: the page lists, separated by commas: the process is a member of a background process attempting to read from its controlling terminal, the process is ignoring or blocking `SIGTTIN`, or the process group is orphaned.
Note: The page's wording is damaged here ("a member of a background process" lacks a word such as "group"), and it does not make clear which of the conditions are alternatives and which must hold together.

**read-E12** `ENOLCK`: the file has mandatory enforcement-mode file locking set and `LOCK_MAX` regions are already locked in the system.

**read-E13** `EDEADLK`: enforcement-mode file locking is enabled, `O_NDELAY` and `O_NONBLOCK` are clear, and a deadlock condition is detected.

**read-E14** `EBADMSG`: the message waiting to be read on a stream is not a data message.

Related: Functions: fcntl(2), lockf(3), lseek(2), open(2), pipe(2), poll(2), socket(2), socketpair(2), creat(2), dup(2), ioctl(2), open(2), pipe(2), getmsg(2), streamio(7), termio(4), opendir(3)

### readlink(2)

Page: `man2/readlink.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**readlink-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <symlink.h>`; `int readlink(const char *path, char *buffer, int buf_size)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types including `<symlink.h>`.

**readlink-2** [OSF/1] `path` gives the pathname; `buffer` points to the user's buffer, which should be at least `buf_size` bytes; `buf_size` is the buffer size.
  Test: see readlink-3.

**readlink-3** [OSF/1] `readlink()` places the contents of the symbolic link named by `path` in `buffer`.
  Test: `symlink("target", "l")`; `readlink("l", b, 100)` returns 6 and `b` starts with "target".

**readlink-4** [OSF/1] If the link's actual length is less than `buf_size`, the string copied into the buffer is null-terminated.
  Test: in the case above, `b[6] == '\0'`.

**readlink-5** [OSF/1] If the link's actual length is greater than `buf_size`, an error is returned.
  Test: `readlink("l", b, 3)` returns -1 with `ERANGE`.
  Note: The page does not say what happens when the length equals `buf_size` exactly.

**readlink-6** [OSF/1] The length of a symbolic link does not exceed `PATH_MAX`.
  Test: `readlink()` of any link returns at most `PATH_MAX`.

**readlink-7** [OSF/1] The caller must have search access to the directory containing the link.
  Test: as non-root, remove search permission from the directory; `readlink()` fails with `EACCES`.

**readlink-8** [OSF/1] On success, returns the number of characters placed in the buffer, not counting any terminating null.
  Test: see readlink-3.

**readlink-9** [OSF/1] On failure the buffer is not modified, -1 is returned, and `errno` is set.
  Test: fill `b` with 'X', call `readlink()` on a regular file; it returns -1 and `b` is still all 'X'.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**readlink-E1** `ENOENT`: the file named by `path` does not exist, or `path` points to an empty string.

**readlink-E2** `EINVAL`: the file named by `path` is not a symbolic link.

**readlink-E3** `ERANGE`: the pathname in the symbolic link is longer than `buf_size`.

**readlink-E4** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix of `path` is not a directory.

**readlink-E5** `EACCES`: search permission is denied on a component of the path prefix of `path`, or read permission is denied on the final component of the path prefix of `path`.

**readlink-E6** `ENAMETOOLONG`: `path` is longer than `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

Related: Functions: link(2), stat(2), symlink(2), unlink(2)

### reboot(2)

Page: `man2/reboot.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**reboot-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `void reboot(int howto)`, with `<sys/reboot.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call against `<sys/reboot.h>`.
Note: The page declares the return type `void` but RETURN VALUES says −1 is returned on failure.

**reboot-2** [OSF/1] `howto` is a mask of options.
  Test: covered by option items (constants defined in `<sys/reboot.h>`).

**reboot-3** [OSF/1] `reboot()` restarts the system. Startup is automatic and brings up `/vmunix` in normal, nonmaintenance mode.
  Test: Not testable from user space without rebooting the machine.

**reboot-4** [OSF/1] The calling process must have superuser privilege to succeed.
  Test: as non-root, `reboot(RB_AUTOBOOT)` returns −1 with `EPERM` and the system keeps running.

**reboot-5** [OSF/1] A reboot is invoked automatically in the event of unrecoverable system failures.
  Test: Not testable from user space.

**reboot-6** [OSF/1] The options are defined in `sys/reboot.h` and are passed to the new kernel or the new bootstrap and `init` programs, as values of `howto`.
  Test: check that `RB_AUTOBOOT`, `RB_ASKNAME`, `RB_DFLTROOT`, `RB_DUMP`, `RB_HALT`, `RB_INITNAME`, `RB_KDB`, `RB_NOSYNC`, `RB_RDONLY`, `RB_SINGLE`, `RB_UNIPROC` are defined in `<sys/reboot.h>`.

**reboot-7** [OSF/1] `RB_AUTOBOOT`: the default; the system reboots in its usual fashion.
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-8** [OSF/1] `RB_ASKNAME`: interpreted by the bootstrap program, which prompts on the console for the file to boot.
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-9** [OSF/1] `RB_DFLTROOT`: use the compiled-in root device. If possible the system uses the device it was booted from as root. (The default depends on the bootstrap program being able to tell which drive it was loaded from, which is not possible on all systems.)
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-10** [OSF/1] `RB_DUMP`: dump kernel memory before rebooting (see `savecore`).
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-11** [OSF/1] `RB_HALT`: the processor is simply halted; no reboot takes place. It "should be used with caution".
  Test: Not testable from user space (halts).

**reboot-12** [OSF/1] `RB_INITNAME`: allows an init program other than `/sbin/init` to be run on reboot. "This switch is not currently available."
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-13** [OSF/1] `RB_KDB`: load the symbol table and enable a built-in debugger. It has no useful function if the kernel is not configured for debugging. Several other options have different meanings combined with it, "although their use may not be possible via the reboot() function".
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-14** [OSF/1] `RB_NOSYNC`: the page says "Normally, the disks are sync'd (see the sync() command) before the processor is halted or rebooted."
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).
Note: The page describes only the normal behaviour; it does not say that `RB_NOSYNC` suppresses the sync, though that is implied by the name.

**reboot-15** [OSF/1] `RB_RDONLY`: initially mount the root file system read-only. This is currently the default, and the option is deprecated as a no-op.
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-16** [OSF/1] `RB_SINGLE`: normally reboot runs an automatic disk consistency check and then multiuser operation; `RB_SINGLE` prevents this and boots with a single-user shell on the console. It is interpreted by the `init` program of the newly booted system.
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-17** [OSF/1] `RB_UNIPROC`: restart the system in uniprocessor mode.
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-18** [OSF/1] With no options (`RB_AUTOBOOT`), the system reboots from file `vmunix` in the root file system of unit 0 of a disk chosen in a processor-specific way; an automatic consistency check of the disks (see `fsck`) is then normally performed.
  Test: Not testable from user space (reboots).

**reboot-19** [OSF/1] "Some options may not be supported on all machines."
  Test: Not testable from user space.

**reboot-20** [OSF/1] If successful, the call does not return; otherwise it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as non-root, the call returns −1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to this):

**reboot-E1** `EPERM`: the calling process does not have appropriate privilege.

Related: Commands: crash(8), halt(8), init(8), reboot(8), savecore(8)

### recv(2)

Page: `man2/recv.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**recv-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int recv(int socket, char *buffer, int length, int flags)`, with `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types against the headers; it builds without warnings.

**recv-2** [OSF/1] `socket` is the socket descriptor; `buffer` is where the message is placed; `length` is the size of the area `buffer` points to.
  Test: send 10 bytes on a connected socket pair, `recv` into a 64-byte buffer with `length` 64; the 10 bytes appear at `buffer`.

**recv-3** [OSF/1] `flags` is formed by logically ORing one or more of the values `MSG_PEEK` and `MSG_OOB`, defined in `sys/socket.h`.
  Test: check both constants are defined in `<sys/socket.h>` and can be ORed.

**recv-4** [OSF/1] `MSG_PEEK` peeks at the incoming message: the data is treated as unread, and the next `recv()` (or similar function) still returns this data.
  Test: send "abc"; `recv(..., MSG_PEEK)` returns "abc"; a following plain `recv` returns "abc" again.

**recv-5** [OSF/1] `MSG_OOB` processes out-of-band data.
  Test: on a TCP connection, peer sends one byte with `send(..., MSG_OOB)`; `recv(..., MSG_OOB)` returns that byte.

**recv-6** [OSF/1] `recv()` receives messages from a connected socket. (`recvfrom()` and `recvmsg()` receive from both connected and unconnected sockets, but are usually used for unconnected sockets only.)
  Test: `recv` on a connected stream socket pair returns data written by the peer.

**recv-7** [OSF/1] `recv()` returns the length of the message. If a message is too long for the supplied buffer, excess bytes "may be truncated depending on the type of socket" that issued the message.
  Test: send a 100-byte datagram on a connected `SOCK_DGRAM` pair, `recv` with `length` 10; record the return value and how many bytes are written (the page says only that excess bytes "may be truncated depending on the type of socket").

**recv-8** [OSF/1] If no messages are available, `recv()` waits for a message to arrive, unless the socket is nonblocking; on a nonblocking socket `errno` is set to `EWOULDBLOCK`.
  Test: blocking `recv` on an empty socket returns only after the peer writes; on a nonblocking socket it returns −1 with `EWOULDBLOCK`.

**recv-9** [OSF/1] `select()` can be used to determine when more data arrives.
  Test: `select` for read on an empty socket times out; after the peer writes, `select` reports it readable.

**recv-10** [OSF/1] NOTES: `recv()` is identical to `recvfrom()` with a zero-valued `address_len` parameter, and to `read()` if no flags are used.
  Test: compare results of `recv(s,b,n,0)`, `read(s,b,n)` and `recvfrom` with zero address length on identical data; all return the same bytes.

**recv-11** [OSF/1] NOTES: because of that, `recv()` is disabled when 4.4BSD behaviour is enabled, that is, when the `_SOCKADDR_LEN` compile-time option is defined.
  Test: compile a program calling `recv` with `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN`; check that `recv` is not available (declaration or link fails).
Note: The page does not say how "disabled" shows itself (missing declaration, link error, or run-time failure).

**recv-12** [OSF/1] On success `recv()` returns the length of the message in bytes; otherwise it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: successful call returns number of bytes received; call on a bad descriptor returns −1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**recv-E1** `EBADF`: the `socket` parameter is not valid.

**recv-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: the `socket` parameter refers to a file, not a socket.

**recv-E3** `EWOULDBLOCK`: the socket is marked nonblocking, and no data is waiting to be received.

**recv-E4** `EINTR`: a signal interrupted `recv()` before any data was available.

**recv-E5** `EFAULT`: the data was directed to be received into a nonexistent or protected part of the process address space; the `buffer` parameter is invalid.

Related: Functions: recvfrom(2), recvmsg(2), send(2), sendmsg(2), sendto(2), select(2), shutdown(2), socket(2), read(2), write(2)

### recvfrom(2)

Page: `man2/recvfrom.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**recvfrom-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int recvfrom(int socket, char *buffer, int length, int flags, struct sockaddr *address, int *address_len)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call including both headers.

**recvfrom-2** [OSF/1] `recvfrom()` receives a message from a socket into `buffer` of `length` bytes; it is normally used on unconnected sockets because it can return the source endpoint of the data.
  Test: send a UDP datagram to a bound socket; `recvfrom` returns its bytes.

**recvfrom-3** [OSF/1] `flags` is formed by ORing one or more of: `MSG_PEEK` (peek at the incoming message) and `MSG_OOB` (process out-of-band data).
  Test: `recvfrom` with `MSG_PEEK` then without; both return the same datagram.
  Note: The page says `flags` "Points to a value", but the synopsis declares it as `int`.

**recvfrom-4** [OSF/1] `address` points to a `sockaddr` whose format depends on the domain; it overlays a `sockaddr_in`, `sockaddr_un` or `sockaddr_ns` according to the active address family.
  Test: for a UDP/IP datagram the returned address has family `AF_INET` and the sender's port.

**recvfrom-5** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined before `<sys/socket.h>` is included, `sockaddr` has 4.4BSD layout with a length field, and the 4.3BSD structure is named `osockaddr`; otherwise the default 4.3BSD `sockaddr` is used, with the address length assumed to be 14 bytes or less.
  Test: compile with and without `_SOCKADDR_LEN`; check `sa_len` exists only with it and `struct osockaddr` exists with it.

**recvfrom-6** [OSF/1] To get the source address, pass a nonzero `address`, with `address_len` set to the size of that buffer; on return `address_len` is set to the actual size in bytes of the address.
  Test: pass `address_len` = `sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)`+16; on return it equals the address size.

**recvfrom-7** [OSF/1] Returns the length of the message written to `buffer`.
  Test: send 10 bytes, `recvfrom` with a 100-byte buffer returns 10.

**recvfrom-8** [OSF/1] When a message is too long for the buffer, excess bytes "may be truncated" depending on the type of the sending socket and on the flags given.
  Test: send 100 bytes on UDP, receive with a 10-byte buffer; returns at most 10.

**recvfrom-9** [OSF/1] If no message is available, `recvfrom()` waits for one, unless the socket is nonblocking, in which case `errno` is set to `EWOULDBLOCK`.
  Test: nonblocking UDP socket with no data: returns -1 with `EWOULDBLOCK`.

**recvfrom-10** [OSF/1] Returns the byte length of the written message on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: see recvfrom-7.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**recvfrom-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not a valid file descriptor.

**recvfrom-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**recvfrom-E3** `EWOULDBLOCK`: the socket is nonblocking and no data is ready to be received.

**recvfrom-E4** `EFAULT`: a valid message buffer was not specified; nonexistent or protected address space is given for the message buffer.

Related: Functions: recv(2), recvmsg(2), send(2), sendmsg(2), sendto(2), select(2), shutdown(2), socket(2), read(2), write(2)

### recvmsg(2)

Page: `man2/recvmsg.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**recvmsg-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis as printed: `int recvmsg(int socket, int flags)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>` and `#include <sys/socket.h>`; PARAMETERS also describes a `message` argument (a `struct msghdr *`).
  Test: compile a call `recvmsg(s, &msg, flags)` after including both headers.
  Note: The page's synopsis omits the `message` parameter that PARAMETERS and RETURN VALUES describe (the original HTML is the same).

**recvmsg-2** [OSF/1] `message` points to a `msghdr` structure; the address format depends on the behaviour requested for the socket.
  Test: receive a datagram into a `msghdr`; the data appears in the `msg_iov` buffers.

**recvmsg-3** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined before `sys/socket.h` is included, `msghdr` has 4.4BSD layout; otherwise the default 4.3BSD `msghdr` is used. If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined, the 4.3BSD structure is named `omsghdr`.
  Test: with `_SOCKADDR_LEN`, `struct msghdr` has `msg_flags` and `struct omsghdr` exists.

**recvmsg-4** [OSF/1] In 4.4BSD layout, `msghdr` has a separate `msg_flags` field for flags from the received message, and `msg_accrights` is generalized into `msg_control`.
  Test: as recvmsg-3.

**recvmsg-5** [OSF/1] `flags` is a logical OR of one or both of: `MSG_PEEK`, which peeks at the incoming message; `MSG_OOB`, which processes out-of-band data.
  Test: `recvmsg` with `MSG_PEEK` returns data; a second `recvmsg` without it returns the same data.

**recvmsg-6** [OSF/1] `recvmsg()` receives messages from unconnected or connected sockets and returns the length of the message.
  Test: send 8 bytes on a UDP socket; `recvmsg` returns 8.

**recvmsg-7** [OSF/1] When a message is too long for the buffer, it "may be truncated" depending on the type of socket.
  Test: on a UDP socket, send 100 bytes and receive into a 10-byte buffer; accept truncation to 10 bytes.

**recvmsg-8** [OSF/1] When no message is available, `recvmsg()` waits for one to arrive.
  Test: a blocking `recvmsg` in a child returns only after the parent sends.

**recvmsg-9** [OSF/1] When the socket is nonblocking and no message is available, `recvmsg()` fails with `errno` `EWOULDBLOCK`.
  Test: set `O_NONBLOCK`, call `recvmsg` on an empty socket: −1 with `EWOULDBLOCK`.

**recvmsg-10** [OSF/1] `select()` can be used to find when more data arrives.
  Test: `select` for reading returns 1 after the peer sends.

**recvmsg-11** [OSF/1] `msg_name` and `msg_namelen` give the address "if the socket is unconnected"; `msg_name` may be a null pointer if no names are wanted.
  Test: on an unconnected UDP socket, `recvmsg` fills `msg_name` with the sender's address; with `msg_name` NULL it still returns the data.
  Note: The page calls this the "destination address"; for a receive it would be the source address.

**recvmsg-12** [OSF/1] `msg_iov` and `msg_iovlen` describe the scatter-gather locations.
  Test: receive 6 bytes into two 3-byte iovecs; each holds 3 bytes in order.

**recvmsg-13** [OSF/1] In 4.3BSD layout, `msg_accrights` is a buffer for passing access rights. In 4.4BSD layout it is expanded into `msg_control`, which carries other protocol control messages or other ancillary data.
  Test: compile code using `msg_accrights` without `_SOCKADDR_LEN` and `msg_control` with it.

**recvmsg-14** [OSF/1] In the 4.4BSD `msghdr`, `msg_flags` holds flags from the received message: besides `MSG_PEEK` and `MSG_OOB`, `MSG_EOR` (data includes the end-of-record marker), `MSG_TRUNC` (data was truncated before delivery) and `MSG_CTRUNC` (control data was truncated before delivery).
  Test: with `_SOCKADDR_LEN`, code naming `MSG_EOR`, `MSG_TRUNC` and `MSG_CTRUNC` compiles; after a `recvmsg`, `msg_flags` contains only these, `MSG_PEEK` or `MSG_OOB`.

**recvmsg-15** [OSF/1] On success `recvmsg()` returns the message length in bytes and fills in the fields of `*message` as appropriate; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: as recvmsg-6.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**recvmsg-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**recvmsg-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**recvmsg-E3** `EWOULDBLOCK`: the socket is nonblocking and no data is ready to be received.

**recvmsg-E4** `EINTR`: the call was interrupted by a signal before any data was available.

**recvmsg-E5** `EFAULT`: `message` is not in a readable or writable part of the user address space.

Related: Functions: recv(2), recvfrom(2), send(2), sendmsg(2), sendto(2), select(2), shutdown(2), socket(2)

### rename(2)

Page: `man2/rename.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**rename-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <stdio.h>`; `int rename(char *from, char *to)`.
  Test: Compile the call.

**rename-2** [OSF/1] `rename()` renames a file or directory within a file system. `from` names the file or directory to rename, and `to` is its new pathname.
  Test: Rename `a` to `b`. Afterwards `b` exists with `a`'s inode and `a` does not exist.

**rename-3** [OSF/1] If `to` is an existing file or an empty directory, it is replaced by `from`. If `to` is a nonempty directory, the call fails.
  Test: Rename a file over an existing file, and a directory over an empty directory: both succeed. Rename a directory over a nonempty one: expect `EEXIST` (rename-E9).

**rename-4** [OSF/1] The caller needs write and search permission on the parent directories of both `from` and `to`.
  Test: Remove write permission from the parent of `to`. Expect `EACCES`.

**rename-5** [OSF/1] If `from` is a directory and the parents of `from` and `to` differ, the caller also needs write and search permission on `from` itself.
  Test: As non-root, move a directory without write permission on itself into another parent. Expect `EACCES`. Moving it within the same parent succeeds.

**rename-6** [OSF/1] If `from` and `to` refer to the same existing file, `rename()` returns successfully and does nothing else.
  Test: Rename `a` to a hard link `b` of the same file. Expect 0, and both names still exist.

**rename-7** [OSF/1] `from` and `to` must be of the same type (both directories or both not) and must be on the same file system.
  Test: See rename-E1, E2 and E5.

**rename-8** [OSF/1] If `to` already exists, it is removed first. A link named `to` is guaranteed to exist throughout the operation, and it refers to the file named by either `to` or `from` before the operation began.
  Test: While one process repeatedly renames files over `to`, another repeatedly calls `stat("to")`. It never gets `ENOENT`.

**rename-9** [OSF/1] If the final component of `from` is a symbolic link, the link itself is renamed, not its target.
  Test: Rename a symlink. `lstat` on the new name shows a symlink with the same contents, and the target is unchanged.

**rename-10** [OSF/1] If the final component of `to` is a symbolic link, that symbolic link is destroyed.
  Test: Rename a file over a symlink. The symlink's target still exists, and `to` is now the regular file.

**rename-11** [OSF/1] When both name directories, `from` must not be an ancestor of `to`. For example, `to` must not contain a path prefix that names `from`.
  Test: `rename("d", "d/sub")` fails with `EINVAL`.

**rename-12** [OSF/1] When both name directories, `from` must be well-formed. Its `.` entry, if present, refers to `from` itself. Exactly one directory has a link to `from`, not counting the self-referential `.`. Its `..` entry, if present, refers to the directory that holds an entry for `from`.
  Not testable from user space in normal use: building a malformed directory needs file-system corruption.

**rename-13** [OSF/1] When both name directories, `to`, if it exists, must also be well-formed in the same sense.
  Not testable from user space in normal use: as for rename-12.

**rename-14** [OSF/1] On success, the `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the parent directory of each file are marked for update.
  Test: Rename between two directories. Both parents' times increased.

**rename-15** [OSF/1] On success, `rename()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1, sets `errno`, and leaves the file or directory name unchanged.
  Test: After a failing rename (for example `EXDEV`), the original name still exists.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**rename-E1** `ENOTDIR`: `from` names a directory and `to` names a nondirectory.

**rename-E2** `EISDIR`: `to` names a directory and `from` names a nondirectory.

**rename-E3** `ENOENT`: a component of either path does not exist, or either path is the empty string, or the file named by `from` does not exist.

**rename-E4** `EACCES`: creating the link requires writing in a directory whose mode denies write permission, or a component of either pathname denies search permission.

**rename-E5** `EXDEV`: the link named by `to` and the file named by `from` are on different file systems.

**rename-E6** `EBUSY`: the directory named by `from` or `to` is currently in use by the system or by another process.

**rename-E7** `EINVAL`: `from` or `to` is not a well-formed directory, or the call tries to rename `.` or `..`, or `from` is an ancestor of `to`.

**rename-E8** `EROFS`: the operation requires writing in a directory on a read-only file system.

**rename-E9** `EEXIST`: `to` is an existing nonempty directory.

**rename-E10** `ENOSPC`: the directory that would hold `to` cannot be extended because the file system is out of space.

**rename-E11** `EDQUOT`: the directory that would hold `to` cannot be extended because the user's disk-block quota on that file system is exhausted.

**rename-E12** `EFAULT`: `to` or `from` is an invalid address.

**rename-E13** `ELOOP`: too many links were met while translating `to` or `from`.

**rename-E14** `ENAMETOOLONG`: `to` or `from` is longer than `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**rename-E15** `EPERM`: the directory that holds the file being renamed has the `S_ISVTX` flag set, and the caller is not the file's owner.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), link(2), mkdir(2), rmdir(2), unlink(2); Commands: chmod(1), mkdir(1), mv(1), mvdir(1)

### rmdir(2)

Page: `man2/rmdir.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**rmdir-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int rmdir(const char *path)`; the page names no header.
  Test: compile and call.

**rmdir-2** [OSF/1] `rmdir()` removes the directory named by `path`, only if it is empty.
  Test: `mkdir("d")`, `rmdir("d")` returns 0 and `stat("d")` fails with `ENOENT`.

**rmdir-3** [OSF/1] The final component of `path` cannot be a symbolic link.
  Test: `symlink(dir, "l")`, `rmdir("l")` fails and `dir` still exists.
  Note: The page does not name the error returned in this case.

**rmdir-4** [OSF/1] The caller must have write access to the parent directory of `path`.
  Test: as non-root, parent mode 0555; `rmdir` fails with `EACCES`.

**rmdir-5** [OSF/1] If the directory's link count becomes 0 and no process has it open, its space is freed and it is no longer accessible.
  Test: after `rmdir` (directory not open), `opendir` on the path fails.

**rmdir-6** [OSF/1] If processes have the directory open when the last link is removed, its `.` and `..` entries, if present, are removed before `rmdir()` returns, and no new entries may be created in it; the directory is not removed until all references are closed.
  Test: `open` the directory, `rmdir` it, then `openat`/`fchdir`+`creat` inside fails; reading it lists no `.`/`..`.

**rmdir-7** [OSF/1] On success, marks `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the parent directory for update.
  Test: record parent times, sleep 1s, `rmdir` a child, check both times advanced.

**rmdir-8** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; on failure returns -1, sets `errno`, and the directory is not deleted.
  Test: failing `rmdir` on a non-empty directory leaves it in place.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**rmdir-E1** `EBUSY`: the directory is in use as a mount point for a file system or as the current directory of the calling process.

**rmdir-E2** `EEXIST`: the directory named by `path` is not empty.

**rmdir-E3** `ENOENT`: the directory named by `path` does not exist, or `path` is an empty string.

**rmdir-E4** `EROFS`: the directory resides on a read-only file system.

**rmdir-E5** `EACCES`: search permission is denied on a component of `path`, or write permission is denied on the parent of the directory to be removed.

**rmdir-E6** `EFAULT`: `path` is an invalid address.

**rmdir-E7** `ELOOP`: too many links were encountered in translating `path`.

**rmdir-E8** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**rmdir-E9** `EPERM`: the `S_ISVTX` flag is set on the parent directory and the caller is not the file owner.

**rmdir-E10** `ENOTDIR`: a component of `path` is not a directory.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), mkdir(2), mknod(2), mkfifo(3), remove(3), rename(2), umask(2), unlink(2)

### select(2)

Page: `man2/select.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**select-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int select(int nfds, fd_set *readfds, fd_set *writefds, fd_set *exceptfds, struct timeval *timeout)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>` and `#include <sys/time.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including both headers.

**select-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis of the macros: `FD_SET(int fd, fd_set *fdset)`, `FD_CLR(int fd, fd_set *fdset)`, `FD_ISSET(int fd, fd_set *fdset)`, `FD_ZERO(fd_set *fdset)`.
  Test: compile code using all four macros.

**select-3** [OSF/1] `nfds` is the number of open objects that may be ready for reading or writing or have exceptions pending; it cannot be greater than `FD_SETSIZE`.
  Test: `select(FD_SETSIZE, ...)` with empty sets and a zero timeout returns 0.
  Note: The page does not say what happens if `nfds` exceeds `FD_SETSIZE`.

**select-4** [OSF/1] `readfds` points to a set of descriptors of objects opened for reading; if it is a null pointer, the read set is ignored.
  Test: `select` with `readfds` NULL and a ready write descriptor returns 1.

**select-5** [OSF/1] `writefds` points to a set of descriptors of objects opened for writing; if it is a null pointer, the write set is ignored.
  Test: `select` with `writefds` NULL and a readable pipe returns 1.

**select-6** [OSF/1] `exceptfds` points to a set of descriptors with an exception pending; if it is a null pointer, the exception set is ignored.
  Test: `select` with `exceptfds` NULL succeeds.

**select-7** [OSF/1] When `timeout` is non-null, the `timeval` it points to gives the maximum time to wait for `select()` to complete.
  Test: with no ready descriptors and a 1-second timeout, `select` returns 0 after about 1 second.

**select-8** [OSF/1] When `timeout` is a null pointer, `select()` blocks indefinitely.
  Test: with `timeout` NULL on an empty pipe, `select` does not return until data is written.

**select-9** [OSF/1] To poll, `timeout` should be non-null and point to a zero-valued `timeval`.
  Test: with a zero `timeval` and nothing ready, `select` returns 0 at once.

**select-10** [OSF/1] `select()` checks the status of objects given by I/O descriptor sets: arrays of bits whose position stands for a descriptor. There is one set each for reading, writing and pending exceptions, pointed to by `readfds`, `writefds` and `exceptfds`.
  Test: covered by the other items.

**select-11** [OSF/1] The status of "nfds - 1" file descriptors in each set is checked when `select()` is called.
  Test: with `nfds` = fd+1 and a ready descriptor `fd`, `select` reports it.
  Note: The page says "nfds - 1 file descriptors"; it presumably means descriptors 0 through `nfds` − 1, but the wording is unclear.

**select-12** [OSF/1] For each set, if a bit for an active descriptor is set on entry and the object is ready for reading, writing, or its exception condition is satisfied, the corresponding bit is set in the returned set.
  Test: put a readable pipe end in `readfds`; on return its bit is set.

**select-13** [OSF/1] On return `select()` replaces the original sets with sets that have a bit set only for each descriptor whose object is ready for the requested operation.
  Test: put a readable and a non-readable pipe in `readfds`; on return only the readable one's bit is set.

**select-14** [OSF/1] `select()` returns the total number of ready objects represented by set bits in all the sets.
  Test: one descriptor readable and another writable, each in its own set: returns 2.

**select-15** [OSF/1] `FD_ZERO(&fdset)` initializes the set to a null value.
  Test: after `FD_ZERO`, `FD_ISSET` is 0 for every fd below `FD_SETSIZE`.

**select-16** [OSF/1] `FD_SET(fd, &fdset)` includes the bit for `fd` in the set.
  Test: after `FD_SET(3, &s)`, `FD_ISSET(3, &s)` is nonzero.

**select-17** [OSF/1] `FD_CLR(fd, &fdset)` clears the bit for `fd` in the set.
  Test: after `FD_SET(3, &s)` and `FD_CLR(3, &s)`, `FD_ISSET(3, &s)` is 0.

**select-18** [OSF/1] `FD_ISSET(fd, &fdset)` returns nonzero when the bit for `fd` is in the set, otherwise 0.
  Test: as select-16 and select-17.

**select-19** [OSF/1] The behaviour of the macros is undefined when `fd` is less than 0 or greater than or equal to `FD_SETSIZE`. `FD_SETSIZE` is normally at least equal to the maximum number of file descriptors the system supports.
  Test: None required ("normally" is not a requirement); do not test out-of-range `fd`.

**select-20** [OSF/1] NOTES: the default `FD_SETSIZE` is currently 256, larger than the current kernel limit on open files.
  Test: compile-time check that `FD_SETSIZE` is 256 by default.
  Note: The page contradicts this in ENVIRONMENT NOTES (select-24), which says `FD_SETSIZE` is set to the kernel limit.

**select-21** [OSF/1] NOTES: a program may define another value for `FD_SETSIZE` before including `sys/types.h`, to use more open files with `select()`. (`getdtablesize()` does not by itself solve sizing the bit field.)
  Test: define `FD_SETSIZE` 1024 before `<sys/types.h>`; `sizeof(fd_set)` holds at least 1024 bits.

**select-22** [OSF/1] On success `select()` returns the number of ready objects; on error it returns −1; when the time limit expires it returns 0.
  Test: as select-7 and select-14.

**select-23** [OSF/1] When `select()` returns an error, including a process interrupt, the sets pointed to by `readfds`, `writefds` and `exceptfds` are left unmodified.
  Test: block in `select` with a set containing a non-ready descriptor, interrupt with a caught signal; it returns −1/`EINTR` and the set still has that bit.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**select-E1** `EBADF`: one of the I/O descriptor sets is invalid.

**select-E2** `EINTR`: a signal was delivered before the time limit expired and before any selected event occurred.

**select-E3** `EINVAL`: the time limit in `timeout` is invalid: one of its components is negative or too large.

**select-24** [DEC] ENVIRONMENT NOTES: `FD_SETSIZE` is set to the current kernel limit on the number of open files.
  Test: compile-time `FD_SETSIZE` equals `getdtablesize()` or the kernel open-file limit.

**select-25** [DEC] ENVIRONMENT NOTES: programs that need another `fd_set` size may define an alternate `FD_SETSIZE` before including `sys/types.h`.
  Test: as select-21.

**select-E4** [DEC] `EAGAIN`: allocation of internal data structures failed; a later call may succeed.

Related: Functions: accept(2), connect(2), send(2), getdtablesize(2), poll(2) read(2), recv(2), write(2)

### semctl(2)

Page: `man2/semctl.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**semctl-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>`, `#include <sys/ipc.h>`, `#include <sys/sem.h>`; `int semctl(int semid, int semnum, int cmd, union semun { int val; struct semid_ds *buf; u_short *array; } arg)`.
  Test: Compile a call that passes each union member.

**semctl-2** [OSF/1] `semid` is the ID of the semaphore set. `semnum` is the number of the semaphore to act on. `cmd` is the command.
  Test: Covered below.

**semctl-3** [OSF/1] `arg` is a user data structure used to set or return semaphore values. If it is used, the caller must allocate it before the call.
  Test: Covered by GETALL and IPC_STAT.

**semctl-4** [OSF/1] `arg.val` is the value `semval` is set to by `SETVAL`.
  Test: See semctl-7.

**semctl-5** [OSF/1] `arg.buf` points to a `semid_ds`. `IPC_STAT` copies the set's `semid_ds` into `arg.buf`. `IPC_SET` copies `arg.buf` into the set's `semid_ds`.
  Test: See semctl-13 and semctl-14.

**semctl-6** [OSF/1] `arg.array` points to an array of `semval` values. `GETALL` returns values into it and `SETALL` sets values from it.
  Test: See semctl-11 and semctl-12.

**semctl-7** [OSF/1] `semctl()` operates on one semaphore, on all semaphores of a set, or on the set's `semid_ds`. It can also remove the set's ID and its `semid_ds`. `cmd` chooses the operation.
  Test: Covered below.

**semctl-8** [OSF/1] `GETVAL` returns `semval` of semaphore `semnum`. It requires read permission.
  Test: After `SETVAL` 3, `GETVAL` returns 3.

**semctl-9** [OSF/1] `SETVAL` sets `semval` to `arg.val`. On success, the kernel clears this semaphore's adjust-on-exit value in all processes. It requires modify permission.
  Test: A child does −1 with `SEM_UNDO`. The parent does `SETVAL` 5 and the child exits. The value stays 5.

**semctl-10** [OSF/1] `GETPID` returns `sempid`, `GETNCNT` returns `semncnt`, and `GETZCNT` returns `semzcnt`. Each requires read permission.
  Test: After `semop` by a child, `GETPID` equals the child's PID. While a child waits, `GETNCNT` or `GETZCNT` is 1.

**semctl-11** [OSF/1] `GETALL` puts every `semval` of the set into `arg.array`. It requires read permission.
  Test: Set 3 values with `SETVAL`. `GETALL` returns all 3.

**semctl-12** [OSF/1] `SETALL` sets every `semval` from `arg.array`. On success, the kernel clears the semaphores' adjust-on-exit values in all processes. It requires modify permission.
  Test: `SETALL` {1,2,3}, then `GETVAL` on each.

**semctl-13** [OSF/1] `IPC_STAT` copies the set's `semid_ds` into `arg.buf`. It requires read permission.
  Test: `sem_nsems` in the buffer equals the size the set was created with.

**semctl-14** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` copies user values from `arg.buf` into the set's `semid_ds`. It is restricted: the effective user ID must have superuser privilege or equal `sem_perm.cuid` or `sem_perm.uid`. It sets `sem_perm.uid` (owner's user ID), `sem_perm.gid` (owner's group ID) and `sem_perm.mode` (access modes), and only the low-order nine bits of the mode are set.
  Test: As owner, `IPC_SET` with mode 07777. `IPC_STAT` shows mode & 0777 == 0777 and the higher bits not set from the input.

**semctl-15** [OSF/1] `IPC_RMID` removes the semaphore ID and destroys the set and its `semid_ds`. It is restricted: the effective user ID must have superuser privilege or equal `sem_perm.cuid` or `sem_perm.uid`.
  Test: After `IPC_RMID`, `GETVAL` fails with `EINVAL`.

**semctl-16** [OSF/1] On success, `GETVAL`, `GETPID`, `GETNCNT` and `GETZCNT` return their values. Every other command returns 0. On failure, −1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: `SETVAL` and `IPC_STAT` return 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**semctl-E1** `EINVAL`: `semid` is not a valid semaphore ID, or `semnum` is less than 0 or greater than `sem_nsems`, or `cmd` is not a valid command.
Note: The page says "greater than `sem_nsems`", not "greater than or equal to", so it does not say whether `semnum` equal to `sem_nsems` is an error.

**semctl-E2** `EACCES`: the caller does not have the required permission.

**semctl-E3** `ERANGE`: `cmd` is `SETVAL` or `SETALL` and the value to set is greater than the system-defined maximum.

**semctl-E4** `EPERM`: `cmd` is `IPC_RMID` and the effective user ID lacks the needed privilege, or `cmd` is `IPC_SET` and the effective user ID is not equal to `sem_perm.cuid` or `sem_perm.uid` of the set.

**semctl-E5** `EFAULT`: `cmd` is `IPC_STAT` or `IPC_SET` and an error occurred while accessing the `arg` structure.

**semctl-E6** `ENOMEM`: the system does not have enough memory to complete the function.

Related: Functions: semget(2), semop(2); Data structures: semid_ds(4)

### semget(2)

Page: `man2/semget.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**semget-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int semget(key_t key, int nsems, int semflg)`, with headers `<sys/types.h>`, `<sys/ipc.h>`, `<sys/sem.h>`.
  Test: compile and call.
Note: The page's synopsis ends with ":" instead of ";".

**semget-2** [OSF/1] `semget()` returns, and possibly creates, the ID of the semaphore set identified by `key`.
  Test: create with `IPC_PRIVATE`; then `semget` with a fixed key twice returns the same ID.

**semget-3** [OSF/1] The `IPC_PRIVATE` key ensures that a new, unused entry in the semaphore table is returned.
  Test: two `semget(IPC_PRIVATE, 1, 0600)` calls return different IDs.

**semget-4** [OSF/1] `nsems` is the number of semaphores to create in the set.
  Test: create with `nsems` 3; `semctl(IPC_STAT)` shows `sem_nsems` 3.

**semget-5** [OSF/1] `IPC_CREAT`: if the key does not exist, a semaphore set is created with that key. The page adds: "If the key does exist, forces an error notification."
  Test: `semget(newkey, 1, IPC_CREAT|0600)` succeeds.
Note: The page's statement that `IPC_CREAT` alone forces an error when the key exists conflicts with semget-E5, which ties the existing-key error to `IPC_EXCL`; the page is unclear.

**semget-6** [OSF/1] `IPC_EXCL`: if the key already exists, `semget()` fails and returns an error.
  Test: see semget-E5.

**semget-7** [OSF/1] Semaphore sets are kept collectively as a system-wide table, one entry per set; the returned ID identifies the set's entry; each set is a `semid_ds` structure defining an array of the set's semaphores; each semaphore is a `sem` structure; semaphores are used mainly for synchronization between processes.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement beyond semget-2 (describes internal layout).

**semget-8** [OSF/1] A semaphore ID, its `semid_ds`, and `nsems` semaphores are created if `key` is `IPC_PRIVATE`, or if `key` is not already in the table and `IPC_CREAT` is set.
  Test: `semget(newkey, 2, 0600)` without `IPC_CREAT` fails `ENOENT`; with it, succeeds.

**semget-9** [OSF/1] On creation, `sem_perm.cuid` and `sem_perm.uid` are set to the caller's effective user ID.
  Test: `semctl(IPC_STAT)`; both equal `geteuid()`.

**semget-10** [OSF/1] On creation, `sem_perm.cgid` and `sem_perm.gid` are set to the caller's effective group ID.
  Test: `semctl(IPC_STAT)`; both equal `getegid()`.

**semget-11** [OSF/1] On creation, the low-order nine bits of `sem_perm.mode` are set to the low-order nine bits of `semflg`.
  Test: create with `IPC_CREAT|0640`; `sem_perm.mode & 0777` is 0640.

**semget-12** [OSF/1] On creation, `sem_nsems` is set to `nsems`.
  Test: see semget-4.

**semget-13** [OSF/1] On creation, `sem_otime` is set to 0 and `sem_ctime` to the current time.
  Test: `semctl(IPC_STAT)`; `sem_otime == 0`, `sem_ctime` within a second of `time(NULL)`.

**semget-14** [OSF/1] `semget()` does not initialize the `sem` structure of each semaphore; semaphores are initialized with `semctl()` `SETVAL` or `SETALL`.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (initial values unspecified); check `SETVAL` then `GETVAL` round-trips.

**semget-15** [OSF/1] On success a semaphore identifier is returned; on failure −1 and `errno` set.
  Test: check return values.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**semget-E1** `EACCES`: a semaphore ID exists for `key`, but the operation permission given by the low-order nine bits of `semflg` was not granted.

**semget-E2** `EINVAL`: `nsems` is less than or equal to 0 or greater than the system-defined limit; or a semaphore ID exists for `key`, the set has fewer semaphores than `nsems`, and `nsems` is not 0.
Note: The page's first clause (`nsems` <= 0 is an error) conflicts with its second (`nsems` 0 allowed for an existing set); the page is unclear for `nsems` 0 with an existing key.

**semget-E3** `ENOENT`: no semaphore ID exists for `key` and `IPC_CREAT` was not set.

**semget-E4** `ENOSPC`: creating a new semaphore ID would exceed the system-wide limit on the size of the semaphore table.

**semget-E5** `EEXIST`: a semaphore ID exists for `key`, but `IPC_CREAT` and `IPC_EXCL` were both given in `semflg`.

Related: Functions: semctl(2), semop(2); Data structures: semid_ds(4)

### semop(2)

Page: `man2/semop.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**semop-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>`, `#include <sys/ipc.h>`, `#include <sys/sem.h>`; `int semop(int semid, struct sembuf *sops, u_int nsops)`.
  Test: Compile the call.

**semop-2** [OSF/1] `semop()` performs operations on semaphores in the set `semid`. The operations are in the array `sops`, which has `nsops` elements of type `struct sembuf`.
  Test: Apply two operations in one call and check both semaphore values with `GETVAL`.

**semop-3** [OSF/1] `sembuf` field: `u_short sem_num` selects one semaphore within the set.
  Test: An operation with `sem_num` 1 changes only semaphore 1.

**semop-4** [OSF/1] `sembuf` field: `short sem_op` is the operation to perform. It is negative, positive or 0, as described in semop-7 to semop-13.
  Test: Compile code that uses the field.

**semop-5** [OSF/1] `sembuf` field: `short sem_flg` holds flags. With `SEM_UNDO`, the kernel adjusts the process's adjust-on-exit value for a semaphore it changes. When the process exits, the kernel uses that value to restore the semaphore to the value it had before the process changed it. This prevents a semaphore staying locked by a process that no longer exists.
  Test: A child does `sem_op` −1 with `SEM_UNDO` and exits. The value goes back to what it was before.

**semop-6** [OSF/1] `sem_flg` flag `IPC_NOWAIT`: the kernel returns an error if a requested operation would make the process sleep. If it returns an error, none of the requested operations is performed.
  Test: In one call, give an operation that succeeds and then one that would block, with `IPC_NOWAIT`. Expect −1 and `EAGAIN`, and the first semaphore is unchanged.

**semop-7** [OSF/1] Negative `sem_op` needs modify permission. If `semval` is at least |`sem_op`|, then |`sem_op`| is subtracted from `semval`. With `SEM_UNDO`, |`sem_op`| is added to the caller's adjust-on-exit value for that semaphore.
  Test: With `semval` 5, `sem_op` −3 leaves `GETVAL` = 2.

**semop-8** [OSF/1] Negative `sem_op`: if `semval` is less than |`sem_op`| and `IPC_NOWAIT` is set, `semop()` returns at once with `EAGAIN`.
  Test: With `semval` 0, `sem_op` −1 and `IPC_NOWAIT` give −1 and `EAGAIN`.

**semop-9** [OSF/1] Negative `sem_op`: if `semval` is less than |`sem_op`| and `IPC_NOWAIT` is clear, `semncnt` is incremented and the caller is suspended.
  Test: While a child blocks, `GETNCNT` returns 1.

**semop-10** [OSF/1] A process suspended by a negative `sem_op` sleeps until one of these happens:
- `semval` becomes at least |`sem_op`|. Then `semncnt` is decremented, |`sem_op`| is subtracted from `semval`, and with `SEM_UNDO` |`sem_op`| is added to the adjust-on-exit value.
- The set is removed. Then −1 is returned with `errno` set to `EIDRM`.
- The process catches a signal. Then `semncnt` is decremented and execution resumes as directed by the `signal()` function.
  Test: Release the blocked child by adding to the value, and `semncnt` drops back to 0. Remove the set with `IPC_RMID` and the child gets `EIDRM`. Signal the child and it gets `EINTR` (semop-E7), and `semncnt` goes back down.

**semop-11** [OSF/1] Positive `sem_op` needs modify permission. It adds `sem_op` to `semval`. With `SEM_UNDO`, `sem_op` is subtracted from the caller's adjust-on-exit value.
  Test: With `semval` 2, `sem_op` +3 gives 5.

**semop-12** [OSF/1] Zero `sem_op` needs read permission. If `semval` is 0, `semop()` returns at once. If `semval` is not 0 and `IPC_NOWAIT` is set, `semop()` returns at once. If `semval` is not 0 and `IPC_NOWAIT` is clear, `semzcnt` is incremented and the caller is suspended.
  Test: With `semval` 0 the call returns at once. With `semval` 1 and no `IPC_NOWAIT`, a child blocks and `GETZCNT` = 1.
Note: The page says that with `IPC_NOWAIT` set and `semval` non-zero, `semop()` "returns immediately", but does not say what it returns.

**semop-13** [OSF/1] A process suspended by a zero `sem_op` sleeps until one of these happens:
- `semval` becomes 0, and then (per the page) `semncnt` is decremented.
- The set is removed. Then −1 is returned with `errno` set to `EIDRM`.
- The process catches a signal. Then (per the page) `semncnt` is decremented and execution resumes as directed by `signal()`.
  Test: Set the value to 0 and the waiting child returns.
Note: The page says `semncnt` is decremented in the zero-wait case, but the wait incremented `semzcnt`. This looks like a mistake for `semzcnt`.

**semop-14** [OSF/1] (Notes.) The operations in one call are atomic: either all are done or none is. If the kernel sleeps partway through, it puts every semaphore in the set back to the value it had when `semop()` started.
  Test: Two operations, where the second would block. While the call is blocked, the first semaphore still has its old value.

**semop-15** [OSF/1] On success, `semop()` returns 0 and sets `sempid` of each semaphore operated on to the caller's process ID. On failure it returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: After success, `semctl(GETPID)` equals `getpid()`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**semop-E1** `EINVAL`: `semid` is not a valid semaphore ID, or the number of semaphores for which `SEM_UNDO` is requested exceeds the system-defined limit.

**semop-E2** `EFBIG`: `sem_num` is less than 0, or is at least the number of semaphores in `semid`.
Note: The page says "less than 0" even though `sem_num` is declared `u_short`.

**semop-E3** `E2BIG`: `nsops` is greater than the system-defined maximum.

**semop-E4** `EACCES`: the caller does not have the required permission.

**semop-E5** `ENOSPC`: the system-defined limit on the number of processes using `SEM_UNDO` was exceeded.

**semop-E6** `ERANGE`: an operation made a `semval` overflow the system-defined limit, or made an adjust-on-exit value exceed the system-defined limit.

**semop-E7** `EINTR`: `semop()` was interrupted by a signal.

**semop-E8** `EIDRM`: the semaphore ID `semid` has been removed from the system.

Related: Functions: exec(2), exit(2), fork(2), semctl(2), semget(2); Data Structures: semid_ds(4)

### send(2)

Page: `man2/send.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**send-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int send(int socket, char *message, int length, int flags)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**send-2** [OSF/1] `socket` names the socket; `message` points to the message; `length` is its length in bytes.
  Test: `send` 5 bytes on a connected socket pair; peer reads those 5 bytes.

**send-3** [OSF/1] `flags` is formed by ORing values defined in `sys/socket.h`.
  Test: compile with both flags.

**send-4** [OSF/1] `MSG_OOB` sends out-of-band data on sockets that support out-of-band communication.
  Test: TCP pair; `send(fd, "x", 1, MSG_OOB)`; peer `recv` with `MSG_OOB` gets 'x'.

**send-5** [OSF/1] `MSG_DONTROUTE` sends without using routing tables; not recommended, for debugging only.
  Test: `send` with `MSG_DONTROUTE` to a directly connected (loopback) peer succeeds.

**send-6** [OSF/1] `send()` sends a message only when the socket is connected; `sendto()` and `sendmsg()` can be used with connected or unconnected sockets.
  Test: `send` on an unconnected `SOCK_DGRAM` socket fails.
  Note: The page lists no errno for the unconnected case.

**send-7** [OSF/1] If the message is too long to pass through the underlying protocol, the system returns an error and does not transmit the message.
  Test: `send` a UDP datagram larger than the maximum; expect `EMSGSIZE` and nothing received.

**send-8** [OSF/1] `send()` implies no indication of failure to deliver; −1 indicates only locally detected errors.
  Test: `send` on a connected UDP socket to a port with no listener; first call returns the byte count.

**send-9** [OSF/1] If no space is available at the sending socket for the message, `send()` blocks unless the socket is in nonblocking I/O mode; `select()` can determine when more data can be sent.
  Test: fill a socket pair's buffer; blocking `send` blocks until the peer reads; nonblocking gives `EWOULDBLOCK`.

**send-10** [OSF/1] `send()` is identical to `sendto()` with a zero-valued `dest_len`, and to `write()` if no flags are used.
  Test: compare results of `send(fd,b,n,0)` and `write(fd,b,n)`; same.

**send-11** [OSF/1] For that reason, `send()` is disabled when 4.4BSD behaviour is enabled (when `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined).
  Test: compile with `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN` and call `send`; check it is not available.
  Note: The page does not say how `send()` is disabled (compile error, link error, or failure at run time).

**send-12** [OSF/1] On success returns the number of characters sent; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: `send` 10 bytes; returns 10.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**send-E1** `EBADF`: The `socket` parameter is not valid.

**send-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**send-E3** `EFAULT`: `message` is not in a readable or writable part of the user address space.

**send-E4** `EMSGSIZE`: The message is too large to be sent all at once, as the socket requires.

**send-E5** `EWOULDBLOCK`: The socket is marked nonblocking, and no space is available for `send()`.

Related: Functions: recv(2), recvfrom(2), recvmsg(2), sendmsg(2), sendto(2), shutdown(2), connect(2), socket(2), getsockopt(2), select(2), setsockopt(2)

### sendmsg(2)

Page: `man2/sendmsg.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sendmsg-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sendmsg(int socket, struct msghdr *message, int flags)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>` and `#include <sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including both headers.

**sendmsg-2** [OSF/1] `socket` is the socket descriptor.
  Test: `sendmsg` on one end of a `socketpair` delivers data to the other end.

**sendmsg-3** [OSF/1] `message` points to a `msghdr` structure (defined with its members in `sys/socket.h`); the address format depends on the behaviour requested for the socket.
  Test: compile code declaring a `struct msghdr` after including `<sys/socket.h>` and pass its address to `sendmsg`.
  Note: The page describes `message` as "containing both the address for the incoming message and the buffers for the source address", wording that fits `recvmsg()` rather than sending.

**sendmsg-4** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined before `sys/socket.h` is included, `msghdr` has 4.4BSD layout; otherwise the default 4.3BSD `msghdr` is used.
  Test: compile with and without `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN`; with it, `struct msghdr` has `msg_flags` and `msg_control`.

**sendmsg-5** [OSF/1] In 4.4BSD layout, `msghdr` has a separate `msg_flags` field for flags from the received message, and `msg_accrights` is generalized into `msg_control`. (See `recvmsg()`.)
  Test: with `_SOCKADDR_LEN`, code naming `msg_flags` and `msg_control` compiles; without it, `msg_accrights` compiles.

**sendmsg-6** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined, the 4.3BSD `msghdr` structure is available under the name `omsghdr`.
  Test: with `_SOCKADDR_LEN`, code declaring `struct omsghdr` compiles.

**sendmsg-7** [OSF/1] `flags` controls transmission and is formed by ORing values from `sys/socket.h`: `MSG_OOB` processes out-of-band data on sockets that support it.
  Test: `sendmsg` with `MSG_OOB` on a TCP connection; the peer sees urgent data.

**sendmsg-8** [OSF/1] `MSG_DONTROUTE` sends without using routing tables; it is "not recommended, for debugging purposes only".
  Test: `sendmsg` with `MSG_DONTROUTE` to a directly connected host succeeds.

**sendmsg-9** [OSF/1] `sendmsg()` sends messages through connected or unconnected sockets using the `msghdr` structure.
  Test: send on a connected TCP socket with `msg_name` null, and on an unconnected UDP socket with `msg_name` set; both deliver.

**sendmsg-10** [OSF/1] To broadcast, the program must first call `setsockopt()` with `SO_BROADCAST` to gain broadcast permission.
  Test: a UDP `sendmsg` to a broadcast address fails without `SO_BROADCAST` and succeeds with it.
  Note: The page does not name the errno for broadcasting without permission.

**sendmsg-11** [OSF/1] On success `sendmsg()` returns the number of characters sent; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: sending 10 bytes in one iovec returns 10.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**sendmsg-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**sendmsg-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**sendmsg-E3** `EMSGSIZE`: the message is too large to be sent all at once, as the socket requires.

**sendmsg-E4** `EWOULDBLOCK`: the socket is marked nonblocking and no space is available for `sendmsg()`.

Related: Functions: recv(2), recvfrom(2), recvmsg(2), send(2), sendto(2), shutdown(2), socket(2), select(2), getsockopt(2), setsockopt(2)

### sendto(2)

Page: `man2/sendto.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sendto-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sendto(int socket, char *message_addr, int length, int flags, struct sockaddr *dest_addr, int dest_len)`, with headers `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with those headers.

**sendto-2** [OSF/1] `socket` names the socket; `message_addr` points to the message; `length` is the message size in bytes.
  Test: send 10 bytes on a UDP socket to a bound peer; peer receives 10 bytes.

**sendto-3** [OSF/1] `flags` is an OR of values from `sys/socket.h`; `MSG_OOB` processes out-of-band data on sockets that support it.
  Test: on a connected TCP socket, `sendto` with `MSG_OOB`; peer sees out-of-band data.

**sendto-4** [OSF/1] `MSG_DONTROUTE` sends without using routing tables (not recommended; for debugging only).
  Test: `sendto` with `MSG_DONTROUTE` to a directly connected address; succeeds.

**sendto-5** [OSF/1] `dest_addr` points to a `sockaddr` whose format depends on the domain and the socket's behaviour; it overlays a `sockaddr_in`, `sockaddr_un` or `sockaddr_ns` according to the active address family.
  Test: send through an `AF_UNIX` datagram socket using a `sockaddr_un` cast to `sockaddr`.

**sendto-6** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined before including `sys/socket.h`, `sockaddr` has 4.4BSD form with a field giving the address length; otherwise the default 4.3BSD `sockaddr` is used, with the address length assumed to be 14 bytes or less.
  Test: compile with and without `-D_SOCKADDR_LEN` and check for the length field (`sizeof` or member access).

**sendto-7** [OSF/1] If `_SOCKADDR_LEN` is defined, the 4.3BSD structure is defined under the name `osockaddr`.
  Test: compile `struct osockaddr x;` with `_SOCKADDR_LEN` defined.

**sendto-8** [OSF/1] `dest_len` is the length of the `sockaddr` structure pointed to by `dest_addr`.
  Test: pass `sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)`; succeeds.

**sendto-9** [OSF/1] `sendto()` sends messages through an unconnected socket by giving a destination address.
  Test: unconnected UDP socket, `sendto` a peer; peer receives the data.

**sendto-10** [OSF/1] To broadcast on a socket, first gain broadcast permission with `setsockopt()` option `SO_BROADCAST`.
  Test: send to a broadcast address without `SO_BROADCAST` (expect failure), then with it (expect success).
Note: The page does not name the error returned without `SO_BROADCAST`.

**sendto-11** [OSF/1] If the sending socket has no room for the message, `sendto()` blocks unless the socket is in nonblocking I/O mode.
  Test: fill a nonblocking socket's send buffer; next `sendto` returns −1 with `EWOULDBLOCK`.

**sendto-12** [OSF/1] `select()` can be used to determine when more data can be sent.
  Test: after `EWOULDBLOCK`, `select()` for writing returns when space is available.

**sendto-13** [OSF/1] On success `sendto()` returns the number of characters sent; otherwise −1 and `errno` set.
  Test: sending 10 bytes returns 10.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**sendto-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**sendto-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**sendto-E3** `EFAULT`: `dest_addr` is not in a writable part of the user address space.
Note: The page says "writable", though `dest_addr` is only read by the call.

**sendto-E4** `EMSGSIZE`: the message is too large to be sent all at once, as the socket requires.

**sendto-E5** `EWOULDBLOCK`: the socket is nonblocking and no space is available for `sendto()`.

Related: Functions: recv(2), recvfrom(2), recvmsg(2), send(2), sendmsg(2), shutdown(2), socket(2), select(2), getsockopt(2), setsockopt(2)

### setgid(2)

Page: `man2/setgid.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setgid-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int setgid(gid_t gid)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>`.
  Test: compile and call.

**setgid-2** [OSF/1] `setgid()` sets the real group ID, effective group ID and saved set-group-ID to `gid`.
  Test: as root, `setgid(100)`; `getgid()` and `getegid()` return 100 (the saved set-group-ID is not directly observable).

**setgid-3** [OSF/1] Without superuser privilege, if `gid` equals the real group ID or the saved set-group-ID, only the effective group ID is set to `gid`; the real and saved IDs are unchanged.
  Test: in a setgid program run by a user, `setgid(getgid())` changes `getegid()`, then `setgid(saved)` restores it.

**setgid-4** [OSF/1] Supplementary group IDs of the caller remain unchanged.
  Test: compare `getgroups()` output before and after `setgid`.

**setgid-5** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: successful call returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**setgid-E1** `EINVAL`: the value of `gid` is invalid.

**setgid-E2** `EPERM`: the process lacks superuser privilege and `gid` matches neither the real group ID nor the saved set-group-ID.

Related: Functions: exec(2), getgid(2), setuid(2)

### setgroups(2)

Page: `man2/setgroups.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setgroups-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int setgroups(int gidsetsize, gid_t grouplist[])`, declared via `<unistd.h>` and `<sys/types.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**setgroups-2** [OSF/1] `gidsetsize` is the number of entries in `grouplist`; it must not be more than `NGROUPS_MAX` (defined in `limits.h`).
  Test: as root, `setgroups(NGROUPS_MAX + 1, list)` fails with `EINVAL`.

**setgroups-3** [OSF/1] `setgroups()` sets the group access list of the current process from the array `grouplist`.
  Test: as root, set {100, 200}; `getgroups()` returns those IDs.

**setgroups-4** [OSF/1] Element `grouplist[0]` becomes the new effective group ID.
  Test: as root, `setgroups(2, {100,200})`; expect `getegid() == 100`.

**setgroups-5** [OSF/1] `setgroups()` fails unless the invoking process has superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, call; expect −1 with `EPERM`.

**setgroups-6** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as above.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**setgroups-E1** `EPERM`: The caller does not have the appropriate system privilege.

**setgroups-E2** `EINVAL`: `gidsetsize` is greater than `NGROUPS_MAX`, or an entry in `grouplist` is not a valid group ID.

**setgroups-E3** `EFAULT`: `grouplist` points outside the allocated address space of the process.

Related: Functions: getgroups(2), initgroups(3)

  Test: compile and call.

**sethostid-2** [OSF/1] `host_id` is the unique 32-bit identifier for the current host; a calling process with a root user ID can set this new identifier (reset the host ID).

**sethostid-3** [OSF/1] The host ID is a unique number that may be used by applications; it is usually set to the primary IP address of the local machine.

  Test: as non-root, call; expect −1 with `EPERM`.

**sethostid-5** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; on failure −1 and `errno` set.
  Test: check return values.

**sethostid-E1** `EPERM`: the calling process does not have the appropriate privilege.

### sethostname(2)

Page: `man2/sethostname.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sethostname-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sethostname(char *name, int name_len)`; no header is listed.
  Test: compile and call.

  Test: as root, `sethostname("abc", 3)`; `gethostname()` returns "abc".

**sethostname-3** [OSF/1] A calling process with root user authority can set the machine's internal hostname.
  Test: as root, set a name and read it back with `gethostname()`.

**sethostname-4** [OSF/1] System hostnames are limited to `MAXHOSTNAMELEN`, defined in `/usr/include/sys/param.h`.

**sethostname-5** [OSF/1] The call fails if the calling process lacks superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, call; expect −1 with `EPERM`.
Note: The page says "The sethostid() function fails ..." on this page, apparently meaning `sethostname()`.

**sethostname-6** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; on failure −1 and `errno` set.
  Test: check return values.

### setpgid(2), setpgrp(2)

Page: `man2/setpgid.html`; same text as `setpgrp(2)`. AES: Full use (`setpgid()`).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setpgid-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>`; `int setpgid(pid_t process_id, pid_t process_group_id)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**setpgid-2** [OSF/1] `setpgid()` either joins an existing process group or creates a new one within the caller's session.
  Test: child calls `setpgid(0, 0)` and gets `getpgrp() == getpid()`; a second child calls `setpgid(0, first_child)` and gets `getpgrp() == first_child`.

**setpgid-3** [OSF/1] The process group ID of a session leader does not change.
  Test: after `setsid()`, `setpgid(0, other_group)` fails with `EPERM` and `getpgrp()` is unchanged.

**setpgid-4** [OSF/1] The process group ID of the process `process_id` is set to `process_group_id`.
  Test: parent calls `setpgid(child, child)`; `getpgid(child)` (or the child's `getpgrp()`) equals `child`.

**setpgid-5** [OSF/1] If `process_id` is 0, the calling process's ID is used.
  Test: `setpgid(0, getpid())` in a child makes it a group leader.

**setpgid-6** [OSF/1] If `process_group_id` is 0, "the process group ID of the indicated process is used".
  Test: in a child, `setpgid(0, 0)` returns 0.
  Note: The page says the process *group* ID of the indicated process is used, which would make the call a no-op; the usual meaning is the process ID. The page also lists `EINVAL` for `process_group_id` "less than or equal to 0", which contradicts this item. A test should only check that `setpgid(0, 0)` does not fail until the intended meaning is settled.

**setpgid-7** [OSF/1] The function is implemented to support job control.
  Test: Not testable (statement of purpose).

**setpgid-8** [Compat] `setpgrp()` is supported for binary compatibility only.
  Test: Not testable from the page; it gives no synopsis or behaviour for `setpgrp()`.

**setpgid-9** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: see setpgid-5.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**setpgid-E1** `EINVAL`: `process_group_id` is less than or equal to 0, or is not a valid process ID.

**setpgid-E2** `EPERM`: `process_group_id` is a valid process ID but that process is not in the caller's session.

**setpgid-E3** `EPERM`: the process given by `process_id` is a session leader.

**setpgid-E4** `EPERM`: `process_id` is a child of the caller and the child is not in the caller's session.

**setpgid-E5** `EPERM`: `process_group_id` is valid but differs from the process ID of the process given by `process_id`, and no process in the caller's session has a process group ID equal to `process_group_id`.

**setpgid-E6** `ESRCH`: `process_id` is neither the caller's process ID nor that of a child of the caller.

**setpgid-E7** `EACCES`: `process_id` is a child of the caller and the child has successfully executed an exec function.

Related: Functions: getpid(2)

### setquota(2)

Page: `man2/setquota.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setquota-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int setquota(char *special, char *file)`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**setquota-2** [OSF/1] `setquota()` enables and disables disk quotas on a file system; `special` names the block special device on which a mounted file system currently exists.
  Test: as superuser, enable quotas on a test file system; expect 0.

**setquota-3** [OSF/1] When `file` has a "positive value", the file it names, in the file system on `special`, is the one from which quotas are taken.
  Test: as superuser, `setquota(dev, "/mnt/quotas")` returns 0 and quotas are enforced.
  Note: The page says "positive value" of a pointer; it presumably means non-null.

**setquota-4** [OSF/1] When `file` is null, quotas are disabled on the file system on `special`.
  Test: `setquota(dev, NULL)` returns 0 and quotas stop being enforced.

**setquota-5** [OSF/1] `setquota()` fails unless the calling process has superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, call; expect −1 with `EPERM`.

**setquota-6** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as above.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**setquota-E1** `ENOTDIR`: A component of either path prefix is not a directory.

**setquota-E2** `EINVAL`: Either pathname contains a character with its high-order bit set.

**setquota-E3** `EINVAL`: The kernel has not been compiled with the `QUOTA` option.

**setquota-E4** `ENAMETOOLONG`: A component of either pathname exceeded `NAME_MAX` characters, or the entire length of either pathname exceeds `PATH_NAME` characters.
  Note: The page says `PATH_NAME`; probably `PATH_MAX` is meant.

**setquota-E5** `ENODEV`: The block special device pointed to by `special` does not exist.

**setquota-E6** `ENOENT`: The file pointed to by `file` does not exist.

**setquota-E7** `ELOOP`: Too many symbolic links were encountered when translating either pathname.

**setquota-E8** `EPERM`: The caller does not have the appropriate privilege.

**setquota-E9** `ENOTBLK`: `special` does not point to a block device.

**setquota-E10** `ENXIO`: The major device number of the block special device named by `special` is out of range (no device driver exists for the associated hardware).

**setquota-E11** `EROFS`: The file named by `file` resides on a read-only file system.

**setquota-E12** `EACCES`: Search permission is denied for a component of either path prefix.

**setquota-E13** `EACCES`: The file named by `file` resides on a file system different from the one on `special`.

**setquota-E14** `EACCES`: The file named by `file` is not a plain file.

**setquota-E15** `EIO`: An I/O error occurred while reading quotas from or writing quotas to the file named by `file`.

**setquota-E16** `EFAULT`: `file` or `special` points outside allocated address space accessible by the process.

Related: Functions: quotactl(2)
