### setreuid(2)

Page: `man2/setreuid.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setreuid-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `setreuid(int ruid, int euid)`; no return type is shown.
  Test: compile a call.

**setreuid-2** [OSF/1] `setreuid()` sets the real and effective user IDs of the process to `ruid` and `euid`.
  Test: as root in a child, `setreuid(100, 200)`; `getuid() == 100`, `geteuid() == 200`.

**setreuid-3** [OSF/1] If `ruid` or `euid` is −1, the system fills in the current uid.
  Test: as root, `setreuid(-1, 200)`; real uid unchanged.

**setreuid-4** [OSF/1] Unprivileged users may change the effective user ID to the real user ID; only superuser processes may make other changes.
  Test: as non-root with real uid R, `setreuid(-1, R)` returns 0; `setreuid(-1, other)` gives `EPERM`.

**setreuid-5** [OSF/1] Such changes are normally done by the system's authentication program (for example, `login`), but not for system daemons.
  Test: none; documentary.

**setreuid-6** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as above.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**setreuid-E1** `EPERM`: The process is not the superuser and a change other than setting the effective user ID to the real user ID was specified.

Related: Functions: getuid(2), setgid(2), setregid(2), setruid(3)

### setsid(2)

Page: `man2/setsid.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setsid-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <unistd.h>`, `#include <sys/types.h>`; `pid_t setsid(void)`.
  Test: Compile a call that assigns the result to a `pid_t`.

**setsid-2** [OSF/1] When the calling process is not a process group leader, `setsid()` creates a new session.
  Test: Fork. In the child (not a group leader), call `setsid()`. Then `getsid`/`getpgrp` show a new session.

**setsid-3** [OSF/1] The caller becomes the session leader of the new session.
  Test: After `setsid()` in the child, the session ID is the child's PID, if the platform can query it.

**setsid-4** [OSF/1] The caller becomes the leader of the new process group, and its process group ID becomes equal to its process ID.
  Test: After `setsid()`, `getpgrp() == getpid()`.

**setsid-5** [OSF/1] The caller has no controlling terminal.
  Test: After `setsid()`, `open("/dev/tty", O_RDWR)` fails (for example with `ENXIO`).

**setsid-6** [OSF/1] The caller is the only process in the new process group and the only process in the new session.
  Test: `kill(-getpid(), 0)` reaches only the caller. Check that no other process has that pgid.

**setsid-7** [OSF/1] On success, the new process group ID is returned. On failure, −1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: The return value equals `getpid()` in the child.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**setsid-E1** `EPERM`: the caller is already a process group leader, or the process group ID of some other process equals the caller's process ID.

Related: Functions: getpid(2), setpgid(2)

### setsockopt(2)

Page: `man2/setsockopt.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setsockopt-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int setsockopt(int socket, int level, int option_name, char *option_value, int option_len)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>` and `#include <sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including both headers.

**setsockopt-2** [OSF/1] `socket` names the socket whose options are set.
  Test: `setsockopt` on a descriptor from `socket()` returns 0 for `SO_REUSEADDR`.

**setsockopt-3** [OSF/1] `level` gives the protocol level of the option: `SOL_SOCKET` for socket-level options, or the protocol number of the controlling protocol for others (for example TCP's number, from `netinet/in.h` or from `getprotobyname()`).
  Test: set an option at `SOL_SOCKET`; set a TCP option with `level` from `getprotobyname("tcp")->p_proto`.

**setsockopt-4** [OSF/1] `option_name` and any option values are passed uninterpreted to the appropriate protocol module for interpretation.
  Test: Not directly testable; see setsockopt-E3 for unknown options.

**setsockopt-5** [OSF/1] `sys/socket.h` defines the socket-level options, which can be enabled or disabled; it defines all options available to `setsockopt()`.
  Test: compile code naming each `SO_` constant listed below after including `<sys/socket.h>`.

**setsockopt-6** [OSF/1] `SO_DEBUG` turns on recording of debugging information, enabling or disabling debugging in the underlying protocol modules. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set `SO_DEBUG` to 1 with `option_len` `sizeof(int)`; expect 0 (may need privilege, which the page does not state).

**setsockopt-7** [OSF/1] `SO_ACCEPTCONN` enables or disables socket listening. It takes an `int`.
  Test: compile a call with `SO_ACCEPTCONN` and an `int` value.

**setsockopt-8** [OSF/1] `SO_BROADCAST` permits sending of broadcast messages. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set `SO_BROADCAST` to 1 on a UDP socket; a send to a broadcast address is then allowed.

**setsockopt-9** [OSF/1] `SO_REUSEADDR` makes the address validation rules used by `bind()` allow reuse of local addresses. It takes an `int`.
  Test: with `SO_REUSEADDR` set on two sockets, the second `bind()` to the same address as a closed TIME_WAIT connection succeeds.

**setsockopt-10** [OSF/1] `SO_KEEPALIVE` keeps connections active by periodically sending messages on a connected socket; if the peer fails to respond, the connection is broken and processes using the socket are notified with a `SIGPIPE` signal.
  Test: set `SO_KEEPALIVE` to 1 on a TCP socket; expect 0. (Peer failure is hard to provoke.)
  Note: The page does not state the value type for this option.

**setsockopt-11** [OSF/1] `SO_DONTROUTE` makes outgoing messages bypass the standard routing facilities; they go to the network interface chosen by the network portion of the destination address.
  Test: set `SO_DONTROUTE` to 1; expect 0.
  Note: The page does not state the value type for this option.

**setsockopt-12** [OSF/1] `SO_USELOOPBACK` is valid only for routing sockets; it decides whether a sending socket receives a copy of its own message.
  Test: set `SO_USELOOPBACK` on a routing socket; expect 0.

**setsockopt-13** [OSF/1] `SO_LINGER` controls what happens on `close()` when unsent messages are queued. If set, the system blocks the process in `close()` until the data is sent or the time expires. If not specified, `close()` lets the process continue as quickly as possible. It takes a `struct linger` (defined in `sys/socket.h`) giving the option state and linger interval.
  Test: set `SO_LINGER` with `l_onoff` 1 and a short interval on a TCP socket whose peer does not read; `close()` takes up to that interval.

**setsockopt-14** [OSF/1] `SO_OOBINLINE` leaves received out-of-band (urgent) data in line. It takes an `int`.
  Test: with `SO_OOBINLINE` set, urgent data sent with `MSG_OOB` is read by plain `recv`.

**setsockopt-15** [OSF/1] `SO_SNDBUF` sets the send buffer size. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set `SO_SNDBUF` to 16384 with `option_len` `sizeof(int)`; expect 0.

**setsockopt-16** [OSF/1] `SO_RCVBUF` sets the receive buffer size. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set `SO_RCVBUF` to 16384 with `option_len` `sizeof(int)`; expect 0.

**setsockopt-17** [OSF/1] `SO_SNDLOWAT` sets the send low-water mark. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set it with an `int` value; expect 0.

**setsockopt-18** [OSF/1] `SO_RCVLOWAT` sets the receive low-water mark. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set it with an `int` value; expect 0.

**setsockopt-19** [OSF/1] `SO_SNDTIMEO` sets the send time-out. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set it with an `int` value; expect 0.

**setsockopt-20** [OSF/1] `SO_RCVTIMEO` sets the receive time-out. It takes an `int`.
  Test: set it with an `int` value; expect 0.

**setsockopt-21** [OSF/1] Options at other protocol levels vary in format and name.
  Test: None; informational.

**setsockopt-22** [OSF/1] To enable a Boolean option, set `option_value` to a nonzero value; to disable it, set it to 0.
  Test: set `SO_REUSEADDR` to 5 and then to 0; both calls return 0, and with 5 a second `bind()` to the same local address is allowed.

**setsockopt-23** [OSF/1] `option_len` holds the size of the buffer pointed to by `option_value`.
  Test: pass `sizeof(int)` for int options and `sizeof(struct linger)` for `SO_LINGER`.

**setsockopt-24** [OSF/1] Options may exist at several protocol levels; the `SO_` options are always present at the uppermost socket level.
  Test: `SO_` options can be set on sockets of every type with `level` `SOL_SOCKET`.

**setsockopt-25** [OSF/1] `setsockopt()` lets a program control socket communication, for example enable debugging at protocol level, allocate buffer space, control time-outs, or permit broadcasts. The caller gives the option's protocol level and name.
  Test: covered by the per-option tests.

**setsockopt-26** [OSF/1] `option_value` and `option_len` identify the buffer holding the option value.
  Test: covered by setsockopt-22 and setsockopt-23.
  Note: The page says this buffer is where the value "is returned", which fits `getsockopt()` rather than `setsockopt()`.

**setsockopt-27** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: a valid `SO_REUSEADDR` call returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**setsockopt-E1** `EBADF`: `socket` is not valid.

**setsockopt-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

**setsockopt-E3** `ENOPROTOOPT`: the option is unknown.

**setsockopt-E4** `EFAULT`: `option_value` is not in a readable part of the user address space.

Related: Functions: bind(2), endprotoent(3), getsockopt(2), getprotobynumber(3), getprotoent(3), setprotoent(3), socket(2)

### setuid(2)

Page: `man2/setuid.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setuid-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int setuid(uid_t uid)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including `<sys/types.h>`.

**setuid-2** [OSF/1] With superuser privilege, `setuid()` sets the real user ID, effective user ID and saved set-user ID to `uid`.
  Test: as root, `setuid(1234)`; then `getuid()` and `geteuid()` return 1234 and `setuid(0)` fails with `EPERM`.

**setuid-3** [OSF/1] Without appropriate privilege, if `uid` equals the real user ID or the saved set-user ID, `setuid()` sets only the effective user ID to `uid`; the real user ID and saved set-user ID stay unchanged.
  Test: in a set-user-ID program (real 100, effective 200), `setuid(100)` succeeds; `geteuid()` is 100, `getuid()` 100, and `setuid(200)` then succeeds again.

**setuid-4** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: `setuid(getuid())` returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**setuid-E1** `EINVAL`: the value of `uid` is invalid and not supported by the implementation.

**setuid-E2** `EPERM`: the process lacks superuser privilege and `uid` matches neither the real user ID nor the saved set-user ID.

Related: Functions: exec(2), getuid(2), getuid(2), setreuid(2)

### shmat(2)

Page: `man2/shmat.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**shmat-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/types.h>`, `<sys/ipc.h>`, `<sys/shm.h>`): `char *shmat(int shmid, caddr_t *addr, int flags)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.
  Note: The page declares `addr` as `caddr_t *` while describing it as an address; the type looks wrong.

**shmat-2** [OSF/1] `shmid` is the region ID, typically returned by a previous `shmget()`.
  Test: `shmat(shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, 4096, 0600), 0, 0)` returns a usable address.

**shmat-3** [OSF/1] `shmat()` attaches the region to the caller's virtual address space; `addr` is the requested address, or 0 to let the kernel choose.
  Test: write through the returned pointer in one process; a second process attaching the same ID reads the value.

**shmat-4** [OSF/1] `SHM_RND`: if `addr` is not 0, the kernel rounds off the address, if necessary.
  Test: attach with `addr` = a valid page-aligned address plus 1 and `SHM_RND`; the call succeeds.

**shmat-5** [OSF/1] `SHM_RDONLY`: if the caller has read permission, the region is attached for reading only.
  Test: attach with `SHM_RDONLY`; a write through the pointer in a child faults.

**shmat-6** [OSF/1] Access is determined by the permission bits in `shm_perm.mode` of the region's `shmid_ds`: 00400 read by user, 00200 write by user, 00040 read by group, 00020 write by group, 00004 read by others, 00002 write by others.
  Test: region mode 0400 owned by caller: attach with `SHM_RDONLY` succeeds.

**shmat-7** [OSF/1] The caller is granted read and write permission if at least one holds: effective UID is superuser; effective UID equals `shm_perm.cuid` or `shm_perm.uid` and bit 0600 of `shm_perm.mode` is set; effective GID equals `shm_perm.cgid` or `shm_perm.gid` and bit 0060 is set; bit 0006 is set.
  Test: region with mode 0006 created by another user: non-root caller attaches read-write successfully.
  Note: The page treats each pair of bits (0600, 0060, 0006) as one "bit" and does not say what is granted when only one of the read or write bits is set.

**shmat-8** [OSF/1] A process with read permission can attach the region read-only by setting `SHM_RDONLY`.
  Test: see shmat-5.

**shmat-9** [OSF/1] On success the starting address of the attached region is returned; on failure -1 is returned, `errno` is set, and the region is not attached.
  Test: `shmat(-1, 0, 0) == (char *)-1`.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**shmat-E1** `EACCES`: the caller does not have the appropriate privilege.

**shmat-E2** `ENOMEM`: not enough data space was available to attach the region.

**shmat-E3** `EINVAL`: `shmid` is not a valid shared memory region ID; or `addr` is not 0 and not a valid address; or `addr` is not 0 and not a valid address, and `SHM_RND` is not set.
Note: The page's second and third conditions are nearly identical; the text seems to have lost a distinction.

**shmat-E4** `EMFILE`: the attach would exceed the maximum number of attached regions allowed for one process.

Related: Functions: exec(2), exit(2), fork(2), shmctl(2), shmdt(2), shmget(2). Data structures: shmid_ds(4)

### shmctl(2)

Page: `man2/shmctl.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**shmctl-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/types.h>`, `<sys/ipc.h>`, `<sys/shm.h>`): `int shmctl(int shmid, int cmd, struct shmid_ds *buf)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**shmctl-2** [OSF/1] `shmid` is the ID of the shared memory region.
  Test: `shmget()` a region, then `shmctl(id, IPC_STAT, &ds)` returns 0.

**shmctl-3** [OSF/1] `IPC_STAT` copies the region's `shmid_ds` structure into `buf`.
  Test: after `shmget(key, 4096, IPC_CREAT|0600)`, `IPC_STAT` gives `ds.shm_perm.mode & 0777 == 0600`.

**shmctl-4** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` copies values from `buf` into the corresponding fields of the region's `shmid_ds`. It is restricted: the effective user ID must be superuser or equal to `shm_perm.cuid` or `shm_perm.uid`.
  Test: as creator, `IPC_SET` mode 0640, then `IPC_STAT` shows 0640; as another non-root user, `IPC_SET` fails with `EPERM`.

**shmctl-5** [OSF/1] `IPC_RMID` removes the region ID and deallocates its `shmid_ds`. It is restricted in the same way as `IPC_SET`.
  Test: after `IPC_RMID`, `IPC_STAT` on the ID fails with `EINVAL`.

**shmctl-6** [OSF/1] `buf` is used only with `IPC_STAT` and `IPC_SET`; the caller must have allocated the structure before the call.
  Test: `shmctl(id, IPC_RMID, NULL)` succeeds.

**shmctl-7** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` sets `shm_perm.uid` to the owner's user ID and `shm_perm.gid` to the owner's group ID, taken from `buf`.
  Test: as root, `IPC_SET` with uid 123, gid 45; `IPC_STAT` shows them.

**shmctl-8** [OSF/1] `IPC_SET` sets `shm_perm.mode` to the access modes; only the low-order nine bits are set.
  Test: `IPC_SET` with mode 07777; `IPC_STAT` shows `mode & 07777 == 0777`.

**shmctl-9** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: see shmctl-2.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to "one or more" of these):

**shmctl-E1** `EINVAL`: `shmid` is not a valid shared memory region ID, or `cmd` is not a valid command.

**shmctl-E2** `EACCES`: `cmd` is `IPC_STAT` and the caller does not have read permission.

**shmctl-E3** `EPERM`: `cmd` is `IPC_RMID` or `IPC_SET` and the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

**shmctl-E4** `EFAULT`: `cmd` is `IPC_STAT` or `IPC_SET` and an error occurred accessing `buf`.

Related: Functions: shmat(2), shmdt(2), shmget(2). Data structures: shmid_ds(4)

### shmdt(2)

Page: `man2/shmdt.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**shmdt-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/types.h>`, `<sys/ipc.h>`, `<sys/shm.h>`): `int shmdt(caddr_t *addr)`.
  Test: compile a call with this type.
  Note: The page declares `addr` as `caddr_t *` while describing it as an address; the type looks wrong.

**shmdt-2** [OSF/1] `addr` is the starting virtual address of the region to detach, as returned by a previous `shmat()`.
  Test: `p = shmat(id, 0, 0)`; `shmdt(p) == 0`; a later access to `p` in a child faults.

**shmdt-3** [OSF/1] Other attachments of the same region at other addresses are unaffected.
  Test: attach the region twice at `p` and `q`, `shmdt(p)`; reading and writing through `q` still works.

**shmdt-4** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; on failure -1, `errno` is set, and the segment is not detached.
  Test: `shmdt(p + 1)` fails, and `p` is still usable.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to this):

**shmdt-E1** `EINVAL`: `addr` is not the starting address of a shared memory region.

Related: Functions: shmat(2), shmctl(2), shmget(2). Data structures: shmid_ds(4)

### shmget(2)

Page: `man2/shmget.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**shmget-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int shmget(key_t key, u_int size, u_int flags)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>`, `<sys/ipc.h>` and `<sys/shm.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types including the three headers.

**shmget-2** [OSF/1] `shmget()` returns, and possibly creates, the ID of the shared memory region identified by `key`.
  Test: create with a key and `IPC_CREAT`, call again with the same key and no flags, expect the same ID.

**shmget-3** [OSF/1] Key `IPC_PRIVATE` assures the return of a new, unused (private, newly created) shared memory region.
  Test: two `shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, 4096, 0600)` calls return two different IDs.

**shmget-4** [OSF/1] `size` is the minimum number of bytes to allocate for the region.
  Test: create with `size` 100, `shmctl(IPC_STAT)` and check `shm_segsz` is 100.

**shmget-5** [OSF/1] `IPC_CREAT`: if `key` does not already exist, a new region is created for the key and its kernel-assigned ID is returned.
  Test: pick an unused key, `shmget(key, 4096, IPC_CREAT|0600)` returns a non-negative ID.
  Note: The page spells the flag `IPC_CREATE` in the PARAMETERS list and `IPC_CREAT` in the DESCRIPTION and ERRORS; it also says under PARAMETERS that if the key does exist the flag "forces an error notification", which contradicts the `EEXIST` entry (error only with `IPC_CREAT` and `IPC_EXCL` together).

**shmget-6** [OSF/1] `IPC_EXCL`: if the key already exists, `shmget()` fails and returns an error.
  Test: create a key, then `shmget(key, 4096, IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL|0600)` fails with `EEXIST`.

**shmget-7** [OSF/1] On creation, `shm_perm.cuid` and `shm_perm.uid` are set to the effective user ID of the caller.
  Test: create, `IPC_STAT`, compare both fields with `geteuid()`.

**shmget-8** [OSF/1] On creation, `shm_perm.cgid` and `shm_perm.gid` are set to the effective group ID of the caller.
  Test: create, `IPC_STAT`, compare both fields with `getegid()`.

**shmget-9** [OSF/1] On creation, the low-order nine bits of `shm_perm.mode` are set to the low-order nine bits of `flags`.
  Test: create with `IPC_CREAT|0640`, `IPC_STAT`, check `shm_perm.mode & 0777` is 0640.

**shmget-10** [OSF/1] On creation, `shm_segsz` is set to `size`.
  Test: see shmget-4.

**shmget-11** [OSF/1] On creation, `shm_lpid`, `shm_nattch`, `shm_atime` and `shm_dtime` are all set to 0.
  Test: create, `IPC_STAT`, check the four fields are 0.

**shmget-12** [OSF/1] On creation, `shm_ctime` is set to the current time.
  Test: compare `shm_ctime` with `time()` taken before and after the call.

**shmget-13** [OSF/1] On creation, `shm_cpid` is set to the process ID of the caller.
  Test: create, `IPC_STAT`, compare `shm_cpid` with `getpid()`.

**shmget-14** [OSF/1] Returns a shared memory identifier on success; on failure returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: a successful call returns a value >= 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**shmget-E1** `EINVAL`: `size` is less than the system-defined minimum or greater than the system-defined maximum.

**shmget-E2** `EINVAL`: a region ID already exists for `key`, but the number of bytes allocated for it is less than `size` and `size` is not 0.

**shmget-E3** `EACCES`: a region ID already exists for `key`, but operation permission as given by the low-order nine bits of `flags` was not granted.

**shmget-E4** `ENOENT`: a region ID does not exist for `key`, and `IPC_CREAT` was used in `flags`.
  Note: The page says "was used"; from the rest of the page this condition would only make sense when `IPC_CREAT` was not used.

**shmget-E5** `ENOSPC`: creating a new region ID would exceed the system-wide limit on the maximum number of IDs.

**shmget-E6** `ENOMEM`: creating a region ID and its `shmid_ds` structure failed because not enough physical memory was available.

**shmget-E7** `EEXIST`: a region ID already exists for `key`, but `IPC_CREAT` and `IPC_EXCL` were used in `flags`.

Related: Functions: shmat(2), shmctl(2), shmdt(2); Data structures: shmid_ds(4)

### shutdown(2)

Page: `man2/shutdown.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**shutdown-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int shutdown(int socket, int how)`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**shutdown-2** [OSF/1] `shutdown()` disables receive and/or send operations on the socket whose file descriptor is `socket`.
  Test: see below.

**shutdown-3** [OSF/1] `how` = 0 disables further receive operations.
  Test: socket pair; `shutdown(a, 0)` returns 0; data later written on `b` is not received on `a`.
  Note: The page does not say what a disabled receive or send returns.

**shutdown-4** [OSF/1] `how` = 1 disables further send operations.
  Test: `shutdown(a, 1)` returns 0; a later `write(a)` delivers no data to `b`.

**shutdown-5** [OSF/1] `how` = 2 disables further send and receive operations.
  Test: `shutdown(a, 2)` returns 0; a later `write(a)` delivers no data to `b`, and data written on `b` is not received on `a`.

**shutdown-6** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as above.
  Note: The page lists no error for an invalid `how` or an unconnected socket.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**shutdown-E1** `EBADF`: The `socket` parameter is not valid.

**shutdown-E2** `ENOTSOCK`: `socket` refers to a file, not a socket.

Page: `man2/sigaction.html`; same text as `signal(2)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigaction-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigaction(int signal, const struct sigaction *action, struct sigaction *o_action)`, with header `<signal.h>`.
  Test: compile and call.

**sigaction-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `void (*signal(int signal, void (*function)(int)))(int)`, with header `<signal.h>`.
  Test: compile and call.

**sigaction-3** [OSF/1] `sigaction()` lets the calling process examine and/or change the action taken when a specific signal is delivered to it.
  Test: set a handler for `SIGUSR1`, raise it; handler runs.

**sigaction-4** [OSF/1] If `action` is not null, it points to a `sigaction` structure describing the action for the signal.
  Test: covered by sigaction-3.

**sigaction-5** [OSF/1] If `o_action` is not null, the signal action in effect at the time of the call is returned in it.
  Test: set handler h, then call with a new action and `o_action`; `o_action.sa_handler == h`.

**sigaction-6** [OSF/1] If `action` is null, signal handling is unchanged, so the call can be used to inquire about the current handling.
  Test: set h, call with `action` null; `o_action.sa_handler == h`; raising the signal still runs h.

**sigaction-7** [OSF/1] Structure field `sa_handler` (`void (*)()`): `SIG_DFL` requests the default action; `SIG_IGN` requests that the signal have no effect on the process; a function pointer requests that the signal be caught by calling the function. These actions are more fully described in `signal.h`.
  Test: set `SIG_IGN` for `SIGUSR1` and raise it; process continues.

**sigaction-8** [OSF/1] Structure field `sa_mask` (`sigset_t`): signals to block, in addition to the process signal mask, while the handler in `sa_handler` runs.
  Test: handler for `SIGUSR1` with `SIGUSR2` in `sa_mask`; inside the handler `sigprocmask` shows `SIGUSR2` blocked.

**sigaction-9** [OSF/1] Structure field `sa_flags` (`int`): may have `SA_ONSTACK`, `SA_RESTART` or `SA_NOCLDSTOP` set for further control of delivery.
  Test: compile using all three constants.

**sigaction-10** [OSF/1] With `SA_ONSTACK`, the handler runs on the signal stack given with `sigstack()`; otherwise it runs on the stack of the process receiving the signal.
  Test: set a signal stack, handler with `SA_ONSTACK` checks the address of a local variable lies in that stack.

**sigaction-11** [OSF/1] If `signal` is `SIGCHLD` and a child of the caller stops, `SIGCHLD` is sent to the caller if and only if `SA_NOCLDSTOP` is not set for `SIGCHLD`.
  Test: with `SA_NOCLDSTOP`, stop a child with `SIGSTOP`; no `SIGCHLD`; without it, `SIGCHLD` arrives.

**sigaction-12** [OSF/1] With `SA_RESTART`, a call interrupted by a caught signal can be restarted; the affected calls are `read()` and `write()` on a slow device (such as a terminal, not a regular file) and `wait()`.
  Test: block in `read()` on a terminal (e.g. a pty), deliver a caught signal with `SA_RESTART`, then write data; `read()` returns the data.

**sigaction-13** [OSF/1] Without `SA_RESTART`, such a call interrupted by a caught signal returns −1 with `errno` `EINTR`.
  Test: same as above without `SA_RESTART`; `read()` returns −1 `EINTR`.

**sigaction-14** [OSF/1] `signal` may be any signal value defined in `signal.h` except `SIGKILL`.
  Test: `sigaction(SIGKILL, &act, NULL)` returns −1 `EINVAL`.
Note: The page's error list also excludes `SIGSTOP` and `SIGCONT` (sigaction-E3), which this sentence does not.

**sigaction-15** [Compat] `signal()` exists for compatibility with older UNIX systems; it sets the action for a signal; `function` takes the same values as `sa_handler`; no handler mask or flags can be given.
  Test: `signal(SIGUSR1, h)` then raise; h runs.

**sigaction-16** [Compat] Without the special libraries `libbsd` or `libsys5`, `signal()` behaves like `sigaction()` with all flags 0.
  Test: install with `signal()`, interrupt a blocking `read()` on a terminal (e.g. a pty); it returns −1 `EINTR`.

**sigaction-17** [Compat] Linked with `libbsd` (`-lbsd`), `signal()` behaves like `sigaction()` with `SA_RESTART` set.
  Test: same program linked `-lbsd`; the `read()` is restarted.

**sigaction-18** [Compat] Linked with `libsys5` (`-lsys5`), the signal is not blocked from delivery when the handler is entered, and its disposition reverts to `SIG_DFL` when the signal is delivered.
  Test: linked `-lsys5`, handler checks the signal is not in the mask and, after return, `sigaction(sig, NULL, &o)` shows `SIG_DFL`.

**sigaction-19** [OSF/1] In a multi-threaded environment, `sigaction()` should be used only for synchronous signals.
  Test: Not testable (advice to programmers).

**sigaction-20** [Compat] `sigvec()` and `signal()` exist for compatibility with old UNIX systems; their function is a subset of `sigaction()`.
  Test: Not testable as a separate requirement.

**sigaction-21** [OSF/1] On success `sigaction()` returns 0; on failure −1 and `errno` set.
  Test: check return values.

**sigaction-22** [OSF/1] On success `signal()` returns the previous signal action; on failure it returns −1 and sets `errno` as `sigaction()` does.
  Test: `signal(SIGUSR1, h1)` then `signal(SIGUSR1, h2)` returns h1; `signal(SIGKILL, h)` returns −1 cast to the function-pointer type.

**sigaction-23** [OSF/1] If `sigaction()` fails, no new signal handler is installed.
  Test: failing call with a bad `signal` leaves the previous handler of other signals intact; failing `EFAULT` call on `o_action` leaves the old handler in place.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set to" these values):

**sigaction-E1** `EFAULT`: `action` or `o_action` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**sigaction-E2** `EINVAL`: `signal` is not a valid signal number.

**sigaction-E3** `EINVAL`: an attempt was made to ignore or supply a handler for `SIGKILL`, `SIGSTOP`, and `SIGCONT`.
Note: The page lists `SIGCONT` here; a test should check `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` and treat `SIGCONT` as stated by the page, which conflicts with sigaction-14.

Related: Functions: acct(2), exit(2), kill(2), pause(3), ptrace(2), setjmp(3), sigblock(2), sigpause(3), sigprocmask(2), sigstack(2), sigsuspend(2), sigvec(2), umask(2), wait(2); Commands: kill(1); Files: signal(4)

### sigblock(2)

Page: `man2/sigblock.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigblock-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: link a program calling `sigblock` with no extra library.

**sigblock-2** [Compat] Synopsis: `int sigblock(int mask)`.
  Test: compile a call with an `int` argument.

**sigblock-3** [Compat] `sigblock()` adds the signals in `mask` to the set currently blocked, by logically ORing `mask` into the process signal mask.
  Test: block `SIGINT` with `sigprocmask`, then `sigblock` with a one-bit mask; `SIGINT` is still blocked and one more signal is now blocked.

**sigblock-4** [Compat] Signal `i` is blocked if the i-th bit of `mask` is 1. Only signals with values 1-31 can be masked with `sigblock()`.
  Test: from an empty mask, `sigblock` with exactly one bit set; a `sigprocmask` query shows exactly one signal in 1..31 blocked (which one depends on the bit numbering, see Note).
  Note: The page does not say whether bit numbering starts at 0 or 1.

**sigblock-5** [Compat] `SIGKILL` cannot be blocked, and the system gives no indication of this.
  Test: `sigblock` with all bits set returns normally; a `sigprocmask` query shows `SIGKILL` not blocked.

**sigblock-6** [Compat] `sigblock()` is provided for compatibility with other UNIX systems; its function is a subset of `sigprocmask()`.
  Test: None; informational.

**sigblock-7** [Compat] On completion `sigblock()` returns the previous set of masked signals.
  Test: from an empty mask, `sigblock(m)` with one bit set for a signal other than `SIGKILL`, then `sigblock(0)` returns `m`.

Note: The page gives no error conditions.

Related: Functions: kill(2), sigaction(2), sigpause(3), sigprocmask(2), sigsuspend(2), sigvec(2)

### sigpending(2)

Page: `man2/sigpending.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigpending-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigpending(sigset_t *set)`, declared in `<signal.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**sigpending-2** [OSF/1] `sigpending()` stores in `*set` the set of signals that are blocked from delivery and pending to the calling process.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1` with `sigprocmask`, `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)`, call `sigpending(&s)`; expect `sigismember(&s, SIGUSR1)` is 1 and an unpending signal is 0.

**sigpending-3** [OSF/1] Applications should call `sigemptyset()` or `sigfillset()` at least once for each `sigset_t` object before any other use; if an uninitialized object is nonetheless passed to `sigpending()`, the results are undefined.
  Test: Not testable (undefined behaviour); a test should always initialise the set first.

**sigpending-4** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: valid call returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**sigpending-E1** `EFAULT`: The `set` parameter points to a location outside the allocated address space of the process.

Related: Functions: sigemptyset(3), sigprocmask(2); Files: signal(4)

### sigprocmask(2), sigsetmask(2)

Page: `man2/sigprocmask.html`; same text as `sigsetmask(2)`. AES: Full use (`sigprocmask()`).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigprocmask-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: link a program calling both functions with no extra library.

**sigprocmask-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigprocmask(int how, sigset_t *set, sigset_t *o_set)`, with `#include <signal.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including `<signal.h>`.

**sigprocmask-3** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigsetmask(int signal_mask)`.
  Test: compile a call with an `int` argument.

**sigprocmask-4** [OSF/1] `sigprocmask()` examines or changes the signal mask of the calling process.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, then `sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, NULL, &old)`; `old` contains `SIGUSR1`.

**sigprocmask-5** [OSF/1] `how` = `SIG_BLOCK`: the new mask is the union of the current mask and `*set`.
  Test: with `SIGINT` blocked, `SIG_BLOCK` a set of `SIGUSR1`; both are now blocked.

**sigprocmask-6** [OSF/1] `how` = `SIG_UNBLOCK`: the new mask is the intersection of the current mask and the complement of `*set`.
  Test: with `SIGINT` and `SIGUSR1` blocked, `SIG_UNBLOCK` `{SIGUSR1}`; only `SIGINT` stays blocked.

**sigprocmask-7** [OSF/1] `how` = `SIG_SETMASK`: the new mask is `*set`.
  Test: `SIG_SETMASK` `{SIGINT}` (the page's own example) then query; the mask is exactly `{SIGINT}`.

**sigprocmask-8** [OSF/1] If `set` is not null, it points to the set used to change the blocked set. If `set` is null, `how` is not significant and the mask is unchanged, so the call can be used to inquire about blocked signals.
  Test: `sigprocmask(12345, NULL, &old)` leaves the mask unchanged (see also sigprocmask-E1).
  Note: The page does not say whether an invalid `how` gives `EINVAL` when `set` is null.

**sigprocmask-9** [OSF/1] If `o_set` is not null, the mask in effect at the time of the call is stored where `o_set` points.
  Test: block `SIGUSR2`, then `SIG_SETMASK` an empty set with `o_set`; `o_set` contains `SIGUSR2`.

**sigprocmask-10** [OSF/1] Typical use: block signals with `SIG_BLOCK` around a critical section, then restore the previous mask, as returned by that call, with `SIG_SETMASK`.
  Test: save the old mask from `SIG_BLOCK`, restore it with `SIG_SETMASK`; the mask equals the original.

**sigprocmask-11** [OSF/1] If any unblocked signals are pending after the call, at least one of them is delivered before `sigprocmask()` returns.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)`, unblock it; the handler has run before `sigprocmask` returns.

**sigprocmask-12** [OSF/1] `sigprocmask()` does not allow `SIGKILL` or `SIGSTOP` to be blocked; an attempt to block them gives no indication of error.
  Test: `SIG_BLOCK` a set with `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` returns 0; a query shows neither blocked.

**sigprocmask-13** [OSF/1] `signal_mask` gives the process signal mask. `sigsetmask()` changes the mask for signal values 1 to 31; signal `i` is blocked if the i-th bit of `signal_mask` is set. `sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK)` does the same for all values.
  Test: `sigsetmask` with a mask having exactly one bit set, then query with `sigprocmask`; exactly one signal in 1..31 is blocked (which one depends on the bit numbering, see Note).
  Note: The page does not say whether bit numbering starts at 0 or 1.

**sigprocmask-14** [OSF/1] On success `sigprocmask()` returns 0. On failure the mask is unchanged, −1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: with an invalid `how` and non-null `set`, the call returns −1 and a query shows the mask unchanged.

**sigprocmask-15** [OSF/1] On success `sigsetmask()` returns the previous signal mask; on failure it returns −1.
  Test: `sigsetmask(m1)` then `sigsetmask(m2)` returns `m1`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; listed for `sigprocmask()`):

**sigprocmask-E1** `EINVAL`: `how` is not one of the defined values.

**sigprocmask-E2** `EFAULT`: `set` or `o_set` points outside the process's allocated address space.

Related: Functions: kill(2), sigaction(2), sigpause(3), sigsuspend(2), sigvec(2)

### sigreturn(2)

Page: `man2/sigreturn.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigreturn-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigreturn(struct sigcontext *scp)`, with `#include <signal.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including `<signal.h>`.

**sigreturn-2** [OSF/1] `scp` points to a `sigcontext` structure holding the processor state to restore; its contents should have been obtained earlier on entry to a signal handler or by `setjmp()` or `sigsetjmp()`.
  Test: in a handler, call `sigreturn` with the handler's context pointer; execution resumes at the interrupted point.

**sigreturn-3** [OSF/1] `sigreturn()` restores the calling process's processor state from the `sigcontext` structure, which holds all application-visible registers and the signal mask.
  Test: in a handler, block an extra signal, then `sigreturn` with the saved context; after resumption the mask equals the one saved in the context.

**sigreturn-4** [OSF/1] The members of `sigcontext` depend on the machine architecture; each machine-dependent member is defined in `signal.h`.
  Test: compile code that declares a `struct sigcontext` from `<signal.h>`.

**sigreturn-5** [OSF/1] The system software uses `sigreturn()` internally to restore processor state on return from a signal handler and from `longjmp()` (restoring the state saved by `setjmp()` or `sigsetjmp()`).
  Test: Not testable from user space as stated (internal use); `longjmp` and handler return working is indirect evidence.

**sigreturn-6** [OSF/1] NOTES: an application should only use `sigreturn()` with great caution.
  Test: None; advisory.

**sigreturn-7** [OSF/1] On success `sigreturn()` does not return. Otherwise it returns −1 and `errno` "may be set".
  Test: a successful call never returns to the next statement.

**sigreturn-8** [OSF/1] If `sigreturn()` fails, the process context remains unchanged.
  Test: call with a bad pointer; afterwards the signal mask and execution continue as before the call.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**sigreturn-E1** `EFAULT`: `scp` points to memory that is not a valid part of the process address space.

**sigreturn-E2** `EINVAL`: the `sigcontext` structure contains unsupported or illegal values.

Related: Functions: setjmp(3), sigaction(2), sigvec(2)

### sigstack(2)

Page: `man2/sigstack.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigstack-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigstack(struct sigstack *instack, struct sigstack *outstack)`, with `#include <signal.h>`.
  Test: compile a call after including `<signal.h>`.

**sigstack-2** [OSF/1] `struct sigstack` member `ss_sp` (type `caddr_t`): the stack pointer of the signal stack.
  Test: set `ss_sp` to the top of a buffer, install; then `sigstack(NULL, &out)` shows the same `ss_sp`.

**sigstack-3** [OSF/1] `struct sigstack` member `ss_onstack` (type `int`): in `instack`, 1 if the process is currently running on that stack, otherwise 0.
  Test: install with `ss_onstack` 0; a later query outside any handler shows 0.

**sigstack-4** [OSF/1] If `instack` is nonzero, it points to a `sigstack` structure whose `ss_sp` gives the new signal stack. If `instack` is 0 (null), the signal stack state is not set.
  Test: `sigstack(NULL, &out)` leaves the stack unchanged; a second query returns the same values.

**sigstack-5** [OSF/1] If `outstack` is nonzero, the current signal stack state is stored in the structure it points to. If it is 0, the previous state is not reported.
  Test: `sigstack(&new, &old)` fills `old` with the previously installed stack.

**sigstack-6** [OSF/1] `sigstack()` defines an alternate stack on which signals are processed. `sigaction()` specifies whether a given handler runs on the signal stack.
  Test: install a signal stack, use `sigaction()` to have a handler run on the signal stack, raise the signal; the address of a local variable in the handler lies within the stack buffer.

**sigstack-7** [OSF/1] When a signal whose handler is to run on the signal stack occurs, the system checks whether the process is already running on that stack. If so, the process "continues to run even after the handler returns". If not, the handler runs on the signal stack and the original stack is restored when the handler returns.
  Test: after the handler returns, a local variable's address in the main code is back on the normal stack.
  Note: The page's wording for the "already on the stack" case is unclear.

**sigstack-8** [OSF/1] CAUTION: a signal stack does not grow automatically as a normal stack does; if it overflows, unpredictable results can occur.
  Test: None; do not test overflow.

**sigstack-9** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: `sigstack(NULL, &out)` returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**sigstack-E1** `EFAULT`: `instack` or `outstack` points outside the process's address space.

Related: Functions: setjmp(3), sigaction(2), sigvec(2)

### sigsuspend(2)

Page: `man2/sigsuspend.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigsuspend-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigsuspend(sigset_t *signal_mask)`, declared via `<signal.h>`; library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile and link a call including `<signal.h>`.

**sigsuspend-2** [OSF/1] `sigsuspend()` replaces the process signal mask with the set pointed to by `signal_mask`, then suspends the process until delivery of a signal whose action is to run a signal-catching function or to terminate the process.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, have a child send it, call `sigsuspend` with an empty mask; the handler runs and the call returns.

**sigsuspend-3** [OSF/1] `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` cannot be blocked by `sigsuspend()`; an attempt to block them gives no indication of error.
  Test: `sigsuspend` with a full mask; another process sends `SIGKILL`; the process dies.

**sigsuspend-4** [OSF/1] If delivery of the signal terminates the process, `sigsuspend()` does not return.
  Test: child calls `sigsuspend` with an empty mask, parent sends `SIGTERM` (default action); `wait` reports death by `SIGTERM`.

**sigsuspend-5** [OSF/1] If a signal-catching function runs, `sigsuspend()` returns after it returns, with the signal mask restored to the mask in effect before the call.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, `sigsuspend(empty)`, after return `sigprocmask` shows `SIGUSR1` still blocked.

**sigsuspend-6** [OSF/1] Setting the mask and waiting are one atomic operation; no signal can occur between them.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, have it already pending, call `sigsuspend(empty)`; it returns at once after the handler.

**sigsuspend-7** [OSF/1] If `sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK)` and `sigpause()` are called separately, a signal arriving between them "might not be noticed" by `sigpause()`.
  Test: informational; not deterministically testable.

**sigsuspend-8** [OSF/1] Typical use: block a signal with `sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, ...)` at the start of a critical section, and if there is no work, wait with `sigsuspend()` using the mask previously returned by `sigprocmask()`.
  Test: informational usage pattern; covered by sigsuspend-6.

**sigsuspend-9** [Compat] `sigpause()` is provided for compatibility with older UNIX systems; its function is a subset of `sigsuspend()`.
  Test: informational.

**sigsuspend-10** [OSF/1] When a signal is caught and the handler returns, the process resumes after `sigsuspend()`, which always returns -1 and sets `errno` to `EINTR`.
  Test: after the handler runs, check return -1 and `errno == EINTR`.

Errors: the page has no ERRORS section; the only error stated is `EINTR` (sigsuspend-10).

Related: Functions: pause(3), sigaction(2), sigblock(2), sigprocmask(2), sigvec(2)

### sigvec(2)

Page: `man2/sigvec.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigvec-1** [Compat] Synopsis: `#include <sys/signal.h>`; `int sigvec(int signal, struct sigvec *in_vec, struct sigvec *out_vec)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**sigvec-2** [Compat] `sigvec()` is provided for compatibility with old UNIX systems; its function is a subset of `sigaction()`. Its use is not recommended; programs should use `sigaction()`.
  Test: Not testable (advice).

**sigvec-3** [Compat] `signal` gives the signal number.
  Test: `sigvec(SIGUSR1, &v, NULL)` installs a handler that runs on `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)`.

**sigvec-4** [Compat] `in_vec` points to a `sigvec` structure giving the action on delivery, the mask used when calling the handler, and flags modifying signal behaviour.
  Test: see sigvec-7 to sigvec-10.

**sigvec-5** [Compat] On success, the structure pointed to by `out_vec` is set to the previous signal action state.
  Test: install handler h1, then call with handler h2 and `out_vec`; `out_vec->sv_handler == h1`.

**sigvec-6** [Compat] `struct sigvec` has members `void (*sv_handler)()`, `int sv_mask`, `int sv_flags`.
  Test: compile code assigning all three.

**sigvec-7** [Compat] `sv_handler` is the action: `SIG_DFL`, `SIG_IGN`, or the address of a handler function (see `sigaction()` for the actions).
  Test: set `SIG_IGN` for `SIGUSR1`, `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)`; process survives.

**sigvec-8** [Compat] `sv_mask` gives signals to block, in addition to those already blocked at delivery, while the handler runs; signal i is blocked if bit i of the mask is set.
  Test: handler for `SIGUSR1` with mask bit for `SIGUSR2`; inside handler `sigprocmask()` shows `SIGUSR2` blocked.
  Note: The page says "the i-th bit"; whether bit numbering starts at 0 or 1 (that is, mask value `1 << i` or `1 << (i-1)`) is not stated.

**sigvec-9** [Compat] Only signals with values 1 to 31 can be masked on entry to a handler set with `sigvec()`.
  Test: Not testable beyond checking that signals 1 to 31 can be masked (the page does not say what happens to higher numbers).

**sigvec-10** [Compat] `sv_flags` holds flags further specifying signal behaviour. If `SV_ONSTACK` is set, the handler runs on the signal stack set by `sigstack()`; otherwise it runs on the stack of the receiving process.
  Test: set a signal stack with `sigstack()`, install with `SV_ONSTACK`; the address of a local variable in the handler is within the signal stack.

**sigvec-11** [Compat] If `SV_INTERRUPT` is set, a system call interrupted by the signal returns -1 with `errno` `EINTR`; otherwise the interrupted system call is restarted.
  Test: `read()` on an empty pipe interrupted by `alarm(1)`: with `SV_INTERRUPT` returns -1/`EINTR`; without it the `read()` keeps blocking after the handler runs.

**sigvec-12** [Compat] If `in_vec` is a null pointer, the handler information is not set; if `out_vec` is null, the previous information is not returned.
  Test: `sigvec(SIGUSR1, NULL, &old)` leaves the handler unchanged and fills `old`.

**sigvec-13** [Compat] A handler, once assigned, stays assigned until another call to `sigvec()`, `signal()`, `sigaction()` or an exec function.
  Test: after two deliveries of `SIGUSR1` the same handler runs both times.

**sigvec-14** [Compat] `sigvec()` does not check the validity of the `sv_handler` pointer; if it points outside the process address space, the process gets a memory fault when the system tries to call the handler; if it points to anything other than a function, the results are unpredictable.
  Test: install handler address 1 in a child, send the signal; the child dies of a memory fault signal.

**sigvec-15** [Compat] The handler can be declared `void handler(int signal)`.
  Test: compile and install such a handler; it receives the signal number.

**sigvec-16** [Compat] On success 0 is returned; on failure -1, `errno` is set, and no new handler is installed.
  Test: `sigvec(SIGUSR1, &v, (struct sigvec *)1)` returns -1; a later `sigvec(SIGUSR1, NULL, &old)` shows the previous handler, not `v.sv_handler`.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**sigvec-E1** `EFAULT`: `in_vec` or `out_vec` points outside the process's address space.

**sigvec-E2** `EINVAL`: `signal` is not a valid signal number.

**sigvec-E3** `EINVAL`: an attempt was made to ignore or supply a handler for `SIGKILL`.

Related: Functions: kill(2), ptrace(2), sigaction(2), sigblock(2), sigpause(3), sigstack(2)

### socket(2)

Page: `man2/socket.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**socket-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`): `int socket(int addr_family, int type, int protocol)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**socket-2** [OSF/1] `addr_family` gives the address family used to interpret addresses in later socket operations; the families are defined in `sys/socket.h`. Commonly used: `AF_UNIX` (UNIX pathnames), `AF_INET` (ARPA Internet addresses), `AF_NS` (Xerox Network Software addresses).
  Test: `socket(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0)` and `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0)` return descriptors ≥ 0.

**socket-3** [OSF/1] `type` gives the communication semantics; the types are defined in `sys/socket.h`.
  Test: compile code referencing `SOCK_STREAM`, `SOCK_DGRAM`, `SOCK_RAW`.

**socket-4** [OSF/1] `SOCK_STREAM` provides sequenced, reliable, two-way byte streams with a transmission mechanism for out-of-band data.
  Test: connect two `AF_INET` stream sockets over loopback; data sent in order arrives in order; `send(..., MSG_OOB)` is accepted.

**socket-5** [OSF/1] `SOCK_DGRAM` provides datagrams: connectionless messages of a fixed maximum length.
  Test: `sendto()` a datagram between two `AF_INET` datagram sockets; `recvfrom()` returns it whole.

**socket-6** [OSF/1] `SOCK_RAW` provides access to internal network protocols and interfaces; it is available only to a process with superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_RAW, 0)` fails with `EPERM`.

**socket-7** [OSF/1] `protocol` names a particular protocol; 0 selects the typical protocol for the requested socket type.
  Test: `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)` succeeds.

**socket-8** [OSF/1] `socket()` creates a socket of the given type in the given family and returns a descriptor (an integer) usable in later socket calls.
  Test: the returned descriptor works with `bind()`.

**socket-9** [OSF/1] Socket-level options control socket operations; `getsockopt()` and `setsockopt()` get and set them, and they are defined in `sys/socket.h`.
  Test: `setsockopt(s, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, ...)` returns 0 and `getsockopt()` reads it back nonzero.

**socket-10** [OSF/1] On success a nonnegative integer (the socket descriptor) is returned; otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: see socket-2.

Errors (the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**socket-E1** `EAFNOSUPPORT`: addresses in the given address family are not available in the kernel.

**socket-E2** `EPROTONOSUPPORT`: the socket in the given address family is not supported.

**socket-E3** `EMFILE`: the per-process descriptor table is full.

**socket-E4** `ENOBUFS`: insufficient system resources were available to complete the call.

**socket-E5** `EPERM`: the process is trying to open a raw socket without superuser privilege.

**socket-E6** [DEC] `ENOMEM`: the system could not allocate kernel memory to enlarge the process descriptor table.

Related: Functions: accept(2), bind(2), connect(2), listen(2), getsockname(2), getsockopt(2), recv(2), recvfrom(2), recvmsg(2), send(2), sendto(2), sendmsg(2), setsockopt(2), shutdown(2), socketpair(2)

### socketpair(2)

Page: `man2/socketpair.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**socketpair-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int socketpair(int domain, int type, int protocol, int socket_vector[2])`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/socket.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `int`.

**socketpair-2** [OSF/1] `domain` is the communications domain; `socketpair()` does not create sockets in the Internet domain.
  Test: `socketpair(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv)` returns −1.
  Note: The page does not say which errno the Internet domain gives.

**socketpair-3** [OSF/1] `type` is the communications method, for example `SOCK_DGRAM` or `SOCK_STREAM`.
  Test: `socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_DGRAM, 0, sv)` and `SOCK_STREAM` both return 0.

**socketpair-4** [OSF/1] `protocol` is an optional identifier of the transport-layer protocol.
  Test: `protocol` 0 succeeds with `AF_UNIX`.

**socketpair-5** [OSF/1] `socketpair()` creates an unnamed pair of connected, identical sockets in the given domain and type, under the optional protocol; their descriptors are returned in `socket_vector[0]` and `socket_vector[1]`.
  Test: `write(sv[0])` is read on `sv[1]` and vice versa.

**socketpair-6** [OSF/1] `sys/socket.h` contains the definitions for socket domains, types and protocols.
  Test: compile using `AF_UNIX`, `SOCK_STREAM` from `<sys/socket.h>`.

**socketpair-7** [OSF/1] Not all protocol families support `socketpair()`.
  Test: see socketpair-2.

**socketpair-8** [OSF/1] On success returns 0; otherwise returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as above.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set):

**socketpair-E1** `EMFILE`: The current process has too many open file descriptors.

**socketpair-E2** `EAFNOSUPPORT`: Addresses in the specified address family cannot be used to create this socket pair.

**socketpair-E3** `EPROTONOSUPPORT`: The specified protocol cannot be used in this system.

**socketpair-E4** `EOPNOTSUPP`: The specified protocol does not permit creation of socket pairs.

**socketpair-E5** `EFAULT`: `socket_vector` is not in a writable part of user address space.

**socketpair-E6** [DEC] `ENOMEM`: The system was unable to allocate kernel memory to increase the process descriptor table. (ENVIRONMENT NOTES, "Digital Extensions"; features not generic to OSF/1.)

Related: Functions: socket(2)

### strmod_add(2)

Page: `man2/strmod_add.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**strmod_add-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `dev_t strmod_add(dev_t devno, struct streamtab *streamtab, struct streamadm *streamadm)` (old-style declaration), with `#include <sys/stream.h>`.
  Test: Not testable from user space: a kernel configuration interface; check only that the declaration compiles in a kernel build.

**strmod_add-2** [OSF/1] `strmod_add()` configures STREAMS modules and drivers into the kernel: drivers add entry points to the character device switch tables; modules are added to the STREAMS modules switch.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel interface).

**strmod_add-3** [OSF/1] `devno` is the device number (`cdevsw` slot) used when adding a driver. It is ignored for modules.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel interface).

**strmod_add-4** [OSF/1] When adding a driver, if `NODEV` is supplied as `devno`, `strmod_add()` uses the first available device switch slot and returns the number actually used.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel interface).

**strmod_add-5** [OSF/1] If the requested device switch slot is already in use, or no slots are available, `NODEV` is returned.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel interface).

**strmod_add-6** [OSF/1] `streamtab` points to a traditional (System V Release 3.2) `streamtab` structure holding pointers to the entry points for the module's read and write queue routines. The structure must be allocated permanently in the driver's data space (as System V Release 3.2 specifies).
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel interface).

**strmod_add-7** [OSF/1] `streamadm` points to a `streamadm` structure with the administration parameters for the module or driver, the additional information required under OSF/1. It is needed only for the duration of the call and need not be allocated permanently.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel interface).

**strmod_add-8** [OSF/1] NOTES: the device number can be built from the major number with the `makedev` macro, defined in `/usr/include/sys/types.h`.
  Test: compile code using `makedev` after including `<sys/types.h>`.

**strmod_add-9** [OSF/1] On success `strmod_add()` returns the device number associated with the device switch table; otherwise it returns `NODEV`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel interface).

### swapon(2)

Page: `man2/swapon.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**swapon-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `swapon(char *path, int flags, int lowat, int hiwat)`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types and treat the result as `int`.
  Note: The page gives no return type and no header file.

**swapon-2** [OSF/1] `swapon()` makes the file or block special device `path` available to the system for allocation of paging and swapping space.
  Test: as root, on a spare file, `swapon(path, 0, 0, 0)` returns 0. Destructive to system state; run only on a test system.

**swapon-3** [OSF/1] `flags`: only one flag is supported, `MS_PREFER`, which makes `path` the preferred paging file or device.
  Test: as root, `swapon(path, MS_PREFER, 0, 0)` returns 0.

**swapon-4** [OSF/1] `lowat` and `hiwat` are the low and high water marks between which the paging file size floats.
  Test: Not testable from user space without system tools to watch the paging file size.

**swapon-5** [OSF/1] If the low water mark is 0, the file does not shrink after paging space is freed.
  Test: Not testable from user space without system tools to watch the paging file size.

**swapon-6** [OSF/1] If the high water mark is 0, the file grows without bounds.
  Test: Not testable from user space without system tools to watch the paging file size.

**swapon-7** [OSF/1] `lowat` and `hiwat` are not used for swapping devices.
  Test: Not testable from user space.

**swapon-8** [OSF/1] The size of the swap area on a block device is calculated when the device is first made available for swapping.
  Test: Not testable from user space.

**swapon-9** [OSF/1] The caller must have superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-root, `swapon` returns −1 with `EPERM`.

**swapon-10** [OSF/1] On success 0 is returned; on error −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: as swapon-2.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**swapon-E1** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

**swapon-E2** `EINVAL`: the pathname contains a character with the high-order bit set; or the device was not specified; or the device given by `path` was not configured into the system as a swap device; or the device does not allow paging.

**swapon-E3** `ENAMETOOLONG`: a pathname component exceeded `NAME_MAX` characters, or the whole pathname exceeded `PATH_MAX` characters.

**swapon-E4** `ENOENT`: the named file or device does not exist.

**swapon-E5** `EACCES`: search permission is denied for a component of the path prefix.

**swapon-E6** `ELOOP`: too many symbolic links were met in translating the pathname.

**swapon-E7** `EPERM`: the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

**swapon-E8** `EBUSY`: the file or device `path` has already been made available for swapping.

**swapon-E9** `ENXIO`: the major device number of `path` is out of range (no device driver exists for the hardware).

**swapon-E10** `EIO`: an I/O error occurred while opening the swap device.

**swapon-E11** `EFAULT`: `path` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**swapon-E12** `EROFS`: an attempt was made to activate a paging file on a read-only file system.

Related: Commands: swapon(8), config(8)

### symlink(2)

Page: `man2/symlink.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**symlink-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int symlink(const char *path1, const char *path2)`, declared via `<symlink.h>`.
  Test: compile a call including `<symlink.h>`.

**symlink-2** [OSF/1] `symlink()` creates a symbolic link named `path2` whose contents are `path1`, referring to the file named by `path1`.
  Test: `symlink("target", "l")`; `readlink("l")` returns "target".

**symlink-3** [OSF/1] Like a hard link, a symbolic link lets a file have multiple names; unlike a hard link, it does not guarantee the file exists: the file named by `path1` need not exist when the link is created.
  Test: `symlink("/nonexistent/x", "l")` returns 0.

**symlink-4** [OSF/1] Unlike hard links, a symbolic link can cross file system boundaries.
  Test: create a link in `/tmp` to a file on another mounted file system and `stat` through it.

**symlink-5** [OSF/1] When a pathname component is a symbolic link rather than a directory, the pathname in the link is resolved: relative to the process root directory if it starts with `/`, otherwise relative to the directory containing the link.
  Test: `d/l` -> "f" resolves to `d/f`; `d/l2` -> "/tmp/f" resolves to `/tmp/f`.

**symlink-6** [OSF/1] If the symbolic link is "the last component" of the original pathname, remaining components of the original pathname are appended to the link contents and resolution continues.
  Test: `l` -> "dir"; `open("l/file")` opens `dir/file`.
  Note: The page says "last component" yet speaks of "remaining components"; it appears to mean a link met before the end of the path.

**symlink-7** [OSF/1] Whether the link is traversed depends on the function; most functions traverse it.
  Test: `stat("l")` reports the target's type.

**symlink-8** [OSF/1] `link()` refers to the link itself: an error is returned if a symbolic link is named by `path2`.
  Test: `link("f", "l")` where `l` is an existing symlink fails.

**symlink-9** [OSF/1] `lstat()` on a symbolic link returns the status of the link itself.
  Test: `lstat("l")` gives `S_ISLNK`.

**symlink-10** [OSF/1] `mknod()` returns an error if a symbolic link is named as the path.
  Test: `mknod("l", S_IFIFO|0600, 0)` on an existing symlink fails.

**symlink-11** [OSF/1] `readlink()` applies only to symbolic links.
  Test: `readlink` on a regular file fails.

**symlink-12** [OSF/1] `remove()` and `unlink()` remove a symbolic link itself.
  Test: `unlink("l")` removes the link; the target still exists.

**symlink-13** [OSF/1] `rename()`: if the file to rename is a symbolic link, the link is renamed; if the new name refers to an existing symbolic link, that link is destroyed.
  Test: `rename("l", "m")`; `lstat("m")` is a link with the same contents and the target is unchanged.

**symlink-14** [OSF/1] `rmdir()` returns an error if a symbolic link is named as the path.
  Test: `rmdir("l")` where `l` -> a directory fails and the directory remains.

**symlink-15** [OSF/1] `symlink()` returns an error if the link named by `path2` already exists; `path1` may refer to another symbolic link.
  Test: `symlink("l", "l2")` where `l` is a link succeeds; repeating it fails with `EEXIST`.

**symlink-16** [OSF/1] Search access to the symbolic link is required to traverse the pathname it contains; normal permission checks are made on each component of the link's pathname during resolution.
  Test: link -> "noaccess/f" where `noaccess` has mode 0; as non-root `open` through it fails.

**symlink-17** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: successful call returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**symlink-E1** `EEXIST`: the path given by `path2` already exists.

**symlink-E2** `EACCES`: the operation requires writing in a directory whose mode denies write permission, or search permission is denied on a component of `path2`.

**symlink-E3** `EROFS`: the operation requires writing in a directory on a read-only file system.

**symlink-E4** `ENOSPC`: the directory to hold the link's entry cannot be extended because no space is left on its file system.

**symlink-E5** `EDQUOT`: the directory to hold the link's entry cannot be extended because the user's quota of disk blocks on its file system is exhausted.

**symlink-E6** `ENOENT`: `path2` points to a null pathname, or a component of `path2` does not exist.

**symlink-E7** `ENOTDIR`: a component of `path2` is not a directory.

**symlink-E8** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of `path1` or `path2` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component of `path2` is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

Related: Functions: link(2), readlink(2), unlink(2); Commands: ln(1)

### umask(2)

Page: `man2/umask.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**umask-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `mode_t umask(mode_t cmask)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/stat.h>`.
  Test: compile a call; check return type `mode_t`.

**umask-2** [OSF/1] `umask()` sets the process's file mode creation mask to `cmask` and returns the previous value of the mask.
  Test: `umask(022)`; then `umask(077)` returns 022.

**umask-3** [OSF/1] `cmask` is built by ORing file permission bits defined in `sys/stat.h`.

**umask-5** [OSF/1] The mask is inherited by child processes.
  Test: `umask(033)`, fork; child's `umask(0)` returns 033.

**umask-6** [OSF/1] On success the previous value of the mask is returned; the page gives no error return.
