### unlink(2)

Page: `man2/unlink.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**unlink-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int unlink(const char *path)`. The page lists no header.
  Test: Compile the call.

**unlink-2** [OSF/1] `unlink()` removes the directory entry named by `path`. If the entry is a hard link, the link count of the file it refers to goes down by one.
  Test: Make a file with two links and unlink one. `stat` on the other shows `st_nlink` == 1, and the removed name gives `ENOENT`.

**unlink-3** [OSF/1] When every link to a file is gone and no process has it open or mapped, all its resources are reclaimed and the file can no longer be reached.
  Not testable from user space directly: the reclaim is a kernel detail, though free space can be watched with `statfs`.

**unlink-4** [OSF/1] If a process has the file open or mapped when the last link is removed, the link is gone before `unlink()` returns. Removal of the file contents waits until every open or map reference is gone.
  Test: Open a file, unlink it, and check that the name is gone. Reads and writes through the open descriptor still work.

**unlink-5** [OSF/1] If `path` names a symbolic link, the link itself is removed, not its target.
  Test: Unlink a symlink to a file. The symlink is gone and the target still exists.

**unlink-6** [OSF/1] Removing a hard link to a directory requires superuser privilege.
  Test: As a non-root user, `unlink` on a directory fails with `EPERM`. See unlink-E3.

**unlink-7** [OSF/1] On success, the `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the directory that held the link are marked for update.
  Test: Record the directory times, sleep, unlink, and check that both increased.

**unlink-8** [OSF/1] If the file's link count is not 0 after the unlink, its `st_ctime` is also marked for update.
  Test: Unlink one of two links. The `st_ctime` of the remaining link increased.

**unlink-9** [OSF/1] On success, `unlink()` returns 0. On failure it returns −1, sets `errno`, and does not change the named file.
  Test: A failing call (for example `EACCES`) leaves the file and its link count unchanged.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**unlink-E1** `ENOENT`: the named file does not exist, or `path` points to an empty string.

**unlink-E2** `EACCES`: search permission is denied on a component of the path prefix, or write permission is denied on the directory that holds the link.

**unlink-E3** `EPERM`: the named file is a directory and the caller does not have superuser privilege.

**unlink-E4** `EPERM`: the directory that holds the file has the `S_ISVTX` flag set, and the caller is not the file's owner.

**unlink-E5** `EBUSY`: the entry is the mount point of a mounted file system.

**unlink-E6** `EROFS`: the entry is on a read-only file system.

**unlink-E7** `EFAULT`: `path` is an invalid address.

**unlink-E8** `ELOOP`: too many links were met while translating `path`.

**unlink-E9** `ENAMETOOLONG`: `path` is longer than `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**unlink-E10** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

**unlink-11** [DEC] (Environment note, System V compatibility.) In the System V habitat, any attempt to unlink a non-empty directory fails with `ENOTEMPTY`, even for a process with superuser privilege. This is there to comply with SVID-2.
  Test: In the System V habitat, as root, unlink a non-empty directory. Expect −1 and `ENOTEMPTY`.

Related: Functions: close(2), link(2), open(2), rmdir(2); Commands: rm(1)

### utime(2), utimes(2)

Page: `man2/utime.html`; same text as `utimes(2)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**utime-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int utime(const char *path, struct utimbuf *times)` and `int utimes(const char *path, struct timeval times[2])`, with `<sys/time.h>`, `<utime.h>` and `<sys/types.h>` included.
  Test: compile calls to both with these argument types against the headers.
Note: The page's synopsis for `utimes` ends with `;` instead of `)`; the text is damaged or misprinted there.

**utime-2** [OSF/1] `path` points to the file. If the final component of `path` names a symbolic link, the link is traversed and pathname resolution continues.
  Test: create symlink `L` -> file `F`; `utime("L", &t)`; `stat("F")` shows the new times and `lstat("L")` times are unchanged.

**utime-3** [OSF/1] `times` points to a `utimbuf` structure for `utime()`, or to an array of `timeval` structures for `utimes()`.
  Test: covered by utime-5 and utime-6.

**utime-4** [OSF/1] `utimes()` sets the access and modification times of the file to the value of `times`, with time specifications accurate to the microsecond; `utime()` also sets them but each time is a single integer accurate only to the nearest second.
  Test: `utimes` with `tv_sec`=1000000, `tv_usec`=500000 then `stat`; `utime` with 1000000 sets exactly 1000000.

**utime-5** [OSF/1] For `utime()`, the `utimbuf` structure is defined in `utime.h`; its first member is the date and time of last access, its second the date and time of last modification. The times are in seconds since the epoch (00:00:00, January 1, 1970, Coordinated Universal Time).
  Test: `utime(p, &{actime=1000, modtime=2000})`; `stat` gives `st_atime`=1000, `st_mtime`=2000.

**utime-6** [OSF/1] For `utimes()`, `times` is an array of `timeval` structures as defined in `sys/time.h`; element 0 is the last access time and element 1 the last modification time. The times are in seconds and microseconds since the epoch, "although rounding towards the nearest second may occur".
  Test: `utimes` with `{1000,0},{2000,0}`; `stat` gives `st_atime`=1000, `st_mtime`=2000.

**utime-7** [OSF/1] If `times` is null, the access and modification times are set to the current time.
  Test: `utime(p, NULL)`; `stat` times are within a second or two of `time(NULL)`.

**utime-8** [OSF/1] With a null `times`, if the file is a remote file, the current time at the remote node, not the local node, is used.
  Test: Not testable without a remote file system with a known clock skew.

**utime-9** [OSF/1] With a null `times`, the process's effective user ID must be the owner of the file, or the process must have write access to the file or superuser privilege.
  Test: as non-owner with write access, `utime(p, NULL)` succeeds; as non-owner without write access it fails with `EACCES`.

**utime-10** [OSF/1] If `times` is not null, the times are set to the values in the structure, whether or not they correlate with the current time; only the owner of the file or a user with superuser privilege can do this.
  Test: as owner set times to 1000/2000, succeeds; as non-owner with write access, fails with `EPERM`.

**utime-11** [OSF/1] On success `utime()` and `utimes()` mark `st_ctime` for update.
  Test: record `st_ctime`, sleep 2 s, `utime(p, &t)`; `st_ctime` has increased.

**utime-12** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success. On failure returns −1, sets `errno`, and the file times are not affected.
  Test: failing call (non-owner with explicit times) leaves `st_atime` and `st_mtime` unchanged.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**utime-E1** `ENOENT`: the named file does not exist, or `path` points to an empty string.

**utime-E2** `EPERM`: `times` is not null and the calling process has write access to the file but neither owns the file nor has the appropriate system privilege.

**utime-E3** `EACCES`: search permission is denied by a component of the path prefix; or `times` is null, the effective user ID is neither the owner of the file nor has appropriate system privilege, and write access is denied.

**utime-E4** `EROFS`: the file system containing the file is mounted read-only.

**utime-E5** `EFAULT`: `path` is an invalid address, or (for `utimes()`) either `path` or `times` is an invalid address.

**utime-E6** `ELOOP`: too many links were encountered in translating `path`.

**utime-E7** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**utime-E8** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

**utime-13** [OSF/1] `utimes()` "can also fail if additional errors occur".
  Test: none beyond the listed errors; the page names no other condition.
Note: The page does not say what the additional errors are.

Related: Functions: stat(2)

### wait(2), wait3(2), wait4(2), waitpid(2)

Page: `man2/wait.html`; same text as `wait3(2)`, `wait4(2)`, `waitpid(2)`. AES: Full use (`wait()`, `waitpid()`).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**wait-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (with `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/wait.h>`): `pid_t wait(int *status_location)`; `pid_t waitpid(pid_t process_id, int *status_location, int options)`.
  Test: compile a program calling both with these argument types and assign the results to `pid_t`.

**wait-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis (additionally with `<sys/resource.h>`): `pid_t wait3(union wait *status_location, int options, struct rusage *resource_usage)`; `pid_t wait4(pid_t process_id, union wait *status_location, int options, struct rusage *resource_usage)`.
  Test: compile (with `_BSD` defined) a call of each with these argument types.
  Note: The page's synopsis of `wait4()` is missing the comma after `pid_t process_id`.

**wait-3** [OSF/1] `status_location` points to a location filled in with the child's termination status, as defined in `sys/wait.h`.
  Test: child calls `exit(3)`; parent `wait(&s)`; `WEXITSTATUS(s)` is 3.

**wait-4** [OSF/1] `resource_usage` specifies where resource utilization information for terminated child processes is stored.
  Test: child burns CPU then exits; `wait4()` fills a nonzero `ru_utime` in the `struct rusage`.

**wait-5** [OSF/1] `wait()` suspends the caller until it receives a signal that is to be caught, or until any one of its child processes stops or terminates.
  Test: fork a child that sleeps 1 s and exits; `wait()` returns after about 1 s with the child's PID.

**wait-6** [OSF/1] `wait()` returns without waiting if a child that has not been waited for already stopped or terminated before the call.
  Test: child exits; parent sleeps 1 s, then `wait()` returns immediately with the child's PID.

**wait-7** [OSF/1] The effect of `wait()` can be modified by the setting of the `SIGCHLD` signal (see `sigaction()`).
  Test: Not testable as stated; the page gives no specific behaviour here (refers to `sigaction()`).

**wait-8** [OSF/1] `waitpid()` behaves identically to `wait()` when `process_id` is -1 and `options` is 0; otherwise its behaviour is modified by `process_id` and `options`.
  Test: `waitpid(-1, &s, 0)` reaps any exited child and returns its PID, like `wait()`.

**wait-9** [OSF/1] `wait()`, `waitpid()`, `wait3()` and `wait4()` suspend only the calling thread, not the whole process.
  Test: in a threaded program, one thread blocks in `wait()`; another thread continues to run and update a counter.

**wait-10** [OSF/1] `process_id` == -1: status is requested for any child process (equivalent to `wait()`).
  Test: two children; `waitpid(-1, ...)` returns whichever exits first.

**wait-11** [OSF/1] `process_id` > 0: it is the PID of a single child for which status is requested.
  Test: children A (exits at once) and B (exits after 1 s); `waitpid(B, ...)` returns B after about 1 s.

**wait-12** [OSF/1] `process_id` == 0: status is requested for any child whose process group ID equals the caller's.
  Test: child A moved to a new process group, child B in caller's group; `waitpid(0, ...)` returns B, not A.

**wait-13** [OSF/1] `process_id` < -1: status is requested for any child whose process group ID equals the absolute value of `process_id`.
  Test: child A in group A; `waitpid(-A, ...)` returns A.

**wait-14** [OSF/1] `waitpid()` and `wait4()` only return the status of a child from the set selected by `process_id`.
  Test: `wait4(B, ...)` with only A exited and `WNOHANG` returns 0, not A.

**wait-15** [OSF/1] `options` for `waitpid()`, `wait3()` and `wait4()` accepts two defined values, `WNOHANG` and `WUNTRACED`, which may be combined with bitwise-inclusive OR.
  Test: `waitpid(pid, &s, WNOHANG|WUNTRACED)` is accepted (does not fail with `EINVAL`).

**wait-16** [OSF/1] `WNOHANG` prevents the caller from being suspended even if there are children to wait for; in that case 0 is returned, meaning no children have stopped or terminated.
  Test: child sleeping 5 s; `waitpid(-1, &s, WNOHANG)` returns 0 immediately.

**wait-17** [OSF/1] With `WUNTRACED`, the call also returns information when children of the current process are stopped because they received `SIGTTIN`, `SIGTTOU`, `SIGSTOP` or `SIGTSTOP`.
  Test: send `SIGSTOP` to a child; `waitpid(pid, &s, WUNTRACED)` returns pid with `WIFSTOPPED(s)` nonzero and `WSTOPSIG(s) == SIGSTOP`.

**wait-18** [OSF/1] When any of the four functions returns because a child's status is available, it returns the child's process ID.
  Test: return value of `wait()` equals the PID returned by `fork()`.

**wait-19** [OSF/1] In that case, if `status_location` is not null, the status is stored at the location it points to.
  Test: `wait(NULL)` succeeds and returns the child's PID; `wait(&s)` stores a value in `s`.

**wait-20** [OSF/1] The stored value is 0 if and only if the status is from a terminated child that returned 0 from `main()` or passed 0 to `_exit()` or `exit()`.
  Test: child `_exit(0)` gives `s == 0`; child `_exit(1)` or killed by signal gives `s != 0`.

**wait-21** [OSF/1] The status macros are defined in `sys/wait.h` and evaluate to integral expressions; their argument `status_value` is the integer pointed to by `status_location`.
  Test: compile `int x = WIFEXITED(s);` etc. for all six macros.

**wait-22** [OSF/1] `WIFEXITED(status_value)` is nonzero if the status is for a child that terminated normally.
  Test: child `exit(0)`: `WIFEXITED(s)` nonzero; child killed by `SIGKILL`: zero.

**wait-23** [OSF/1] If `WIFEXITED` is nonzero, `WEXITSTATUS(status_value)` is the low-order 8 bits of the value the child passed to `_exit()` or `exit()`, or returned from `main()`.
  Test: child `exit(0x1234)` gives `WEXITSTATUS(s) == 0x34`; child returning 7 from `main()` gives 7.

**wait-24** [OSF/1] `WIFSIGNALED(status_value)` is nonzero if the child terminated because of a signal that was not caught.
  Test: kill child with `SIGTERM` (default action); `WIFSIGNALED(s)` nonzero.

**wait-25** [OSF/1] If `WIFSIGNALED` is nonzero, `WTERMSIG(status_value)` is the number of the signal that terminated the child.
  Test: the case above gives `WTERMSIG(s) == SIGTERM`.

**wait-26** [OSF/1] `WIFSTOPPED(status_value)` is nonzero if the status is for a child that is currently stopped.
  Test: see wait-17.

**wait-27** [OSF/1] If `WIFSTOPPED` is nonzero, `WSTOPSIG(status_value)` is the number of the signal that stopped the child.
  Test: stop child with `SIGTSTP`; `WSTOPSIG(s) == SIGTSTP`.
  Note: The page says `SIGTSTOP` (wait-17), which is not a standard signal name; `SIGTSTP` is presumably meant.

**wait-28** [OSF/1] If the status was stored by `waitpid()`, `wait3()` or `wait4()` with `WUNTRACED`, exactly one of `WIFEXITED`, `WIFSIGNALED` and `WIFSTOPPED` is nonzero.
  Test: for stopped, exited and signalled children reaped with `WUNTRACED`, check exactly one macro is nonzero.

**wait-29** [OSF/1] If the status was stored by `waitpid()`, `wait3()` or `wait4()` without `WUNTRACED`, or by `wait()`, exactly one of `WIFEXITED` and `WIFSIGNALED` is nonzero.
  Test: for exited and signalled children reaped by `wait()`, check exactly one of the two is nonzero.

**wait-30** [Compat] `wait3()` is provided for compatibility with BSD systems; a program calling it must be compiled with the `_BSD` switch defined.
  Test: compile a `wait3()` call with `-D_BSD`.

**wait-31** [Compat] With `wait3()`, the argument to the status macros should be the `w_status` member of the union pointed to by `status_location`.
  Test: child `exit(5)`; `wait3(&u, 0, NULL)`; `WEXITSTATUS(u.w_status) == 5`.

**wait-32** [OSF/1] `wait3()` and `wait4()` store resource usage information for the child at the location `resource_usage` points to, as defined in `sys/resource.h`.
  Test: see wait-4, also for `wait3()`.
  Note: The page says "defined in the sys/resource.h function"; it means the header file.

**wait-33** [OSF/1] `wait4()` is like `wait3()` but waits only for the specific child given by `process_id`, instead of all children.
  Test: see wait-11 using `wait4()`.

**wait-34** [OSF/1] If a parent terminates without waiting for all its children, the remaining children get a parent process ID equal to the process ID of `init`.
  Test: child forks grandchild and exits; grandchild later sees `getppid() == 1` (assuming `init` is PID 1).

**wait-35** [Compat] If a program calling `wait()` is compiled with `_BSD` defined and linked with the `libbsd` compatibility library, `status_location` is of type `union wait *` rather than `int *`, as for `wait3()`.
  Test: compile with `-D_BSD`, link `-lbsd`, pass a `union wait *` to `wait()` without warnings.

**wait-36** [OSF/1] Return: when a child's status is available, the child's PID is returned; when the function returns because the caller caught a signal, -1 is returned and `errno` is `EINTR`.
  Test: install a `SIGALRM` handler (no `SA_RESTART`), `alarm(1)`, `wait()` on a long-running child returns -1 with `EINTR`.

**wait-37** [OSF/1] If `WNOHANG` was given and no children are stopped or exited, `waitpid()`, `wait3()` and `wait4()` return 0; otherwise on failure -1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: see wait-16, also for `wait3()` and `wait4()`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may" be set to these):

**wait-E1** `ECHILD`: (any of the four) the calling process has no existing unwaited-for child processes.

**wait-E2** `EINTR`: (any of the four) the function was terminated by receipt of a signal.

**wait-E3** `EFAULT`: (any of the four) `status_location` or `resource_usage` points outside the process's address space.

**wait-E4** `ECHILD`: (`waitpid()`) the process or process group ID given by `process_id` does not exist or is not a child of the caller.

**wait-E5** `EINVAL`: (`waitpid()`, `wait3()`, `wait4()`) the value of `options` is not valid.

Related: Functions: exec(2), exit(2), fork(2), pause(3), ptrace(2), getrusage(2), sigaction(2)

### write(2), writev(2)

Page: `man2/write.html`; same text as `writev(2)`. AES: Full use (`write()`).
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**write-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int write(int filedes, const char *buffer, unsigned int nbytes)`.
  Test: compile a call with these argument types and assign the result to an `int`.

**write-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int writev(int filedes, struct iovec *iov, int iov_count)`, with `#include <sys/types.h>` and `#include <sys/uio.h>`.
  Test: compile a call to `writev` after including both headers.

**write-3** [OSF/1] `filedes` identifies the object to be written; `buffer` holds the data; `nbytes` is the number of bytes to write.
  Test: write 5 bytes from a buffer to a fresh file and read them back.

**write-4** [OSF/1] The `iovec` structure is defined in `sys/uio.h`. Its member `iov_base` (type `caddr_t`) is the base address of a memory area to write from.
  Test: compile code that sets `iov_base` of a `struct iovec` from `<sys/uio.h>`.

**write-5** [OSF/1] The `iovec` member `iov_len` (type `int`) is the length of that memory area.
  Test: compile code that sets `iov_len`; `writev` with one entry of `iov_len` 3 writes 3 bytes.

**write-6** [OSF/1] `iov_count` is the number of `iovec` structures in the array pointed to by `iov`.
  Test: `writev` with `iov_count` 2 writes both areas and no more.

**write-7** [OSF/1] `write()` attempts to write `nbytes` bytes from the buffer pointed to by `buffer` to the file associated with `filedes`.
  Test: `write(fd, "hello", 5)` on a new regular file returns 5 and the file then contains "hello".

**write-8** [OSF/1] If `nbyte` is 0 and the file is a regular file, `write()` returns 0 and has no other results.
  Test: `write(fd, buf, 0)` on a regular file returns 0; file size, offset and `st_mtime` are unchanged.

**write-9** [OSF/1] `writev()` does the same as `write()` but gathers the output from the `iov_count` buffers described by the `iov` array, each entry giving a base address and length.
  Test: `writev` with entries "ab" and "cd" writes "abcd" and returns 4.

**write-10** [OSF/1] `writev()` always writes a complete area before going on to the next.
  Test: after a `writev` of several areas, the file contents are the areas in array order with none interleaved.

**write-11** [OSF/1] `write()` and `writev()` suspend only the calling thread, not the whole process, until the request completes.
  Test: in a two-thread program, one thread blocks writing to a full pipe; the other thread keeps running and can drain the pipe.

**write-12** [OSF/1] For regular files and devices capable of seeking, writing starts at the position given by the file pointer.
  Test: `lseek(fd, 10, SEEK_SET)` then write "x"; byte 10 of the file is "x".

**write-13** [OSF/1] If the incremented file pointer is greater than the file length, the file length is set to that offset.
  Test: on a 5-byte file, seek to 5 and write 3 bytes; `fstat` shows size 8.

**write-14** [OSF/1] On return from `write()`, the file pointer has been incremented by the number of bytes actually written.
  Test: write 7 bytes at offset 0; `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR)` returns 7.

**write-15** [OSF/1] For devices incapable of seeking, writing always starts at the current position, and the value of the file pointer associated with such a device is undefined.
  Test: write to a pipe and check the data arrives in order; do not check the offset.

**write-16** [OSF/1] If there is not enough room for the whole request, fewer bytes than requested can be written, and the number written is returned. The next attempt to write a nonzero number of bytes fails "except as noted" in the page. The limit may be the `ulimit()` limit or the end of the physical medium. Example from the page: with room for 20 more bytes, a 512-byte write returns 20 and the next nonzero write fails.
  Test: set the file size limit with `ulimit()` so 20 bytes remain; `write` of 512 returns 20; the next `write` of 1 byte returns −1.
  Note: The page does not say which later text the "except as noted" refers to, nor which errno the next write gets.

**write-17** [OSF/1] On success `write()` returns the number of bytes actually written to the file, which is never greater than `nbyte`.
  Test: for any successful write, the return value is between 0 and the requested count.

**write-18** [OSF/1] If `O_APPEND` is set in the file status flags, the file offset is set to the end of the file before each write.
  Test: open with `O_APPEND`, seek to 0, write "z"; "z" is appended at the end.

**write-19** [OSF/1] If `O_SYNC` is set and `fildes` refers to a regular file, a successful `write()` does not return until the data has been delivered to the underlying hardware (as described for `open()`).
  Test: Not testable from user space beyond checking that an `O_SYNC` write succeeds; hardware delivery cannot be observed.

**write-20** [OSF/1] A pipe or FIFO has no file offset; each `write()` appends to the end of the pipe.
  Test: two writes to a pipe of "a" then "b"; the reader gets "ab".

**write-21** [OSF/1] A write to a pipe of no more than `PIPE_BUF` bytes is atomic: its data is not interleaved with data written by other processes to the same pipe.
  Test: several processes each write `PIPE_BUF`-byte records of a distinct byte to one pipe; every record read is whole.

**write-22** [OSF/1] A write of more than `PIPE_BUF` bytes to a pipe can have its data interleaved, on arbitrary boundaries, with other processes' writes, whether or not `O_NONBLOCK` or `O_NDELAY` is set.
  Test: Not a requirement; a test may only accept interleaving for such writes, not demand it.

**write-23** [OSF/1] If neither `O_NONBLOCK` nor `O_NDELAY` is set, a write to a full pipe blocks the process until there is enough space for the entire request.
  Test: fill a pipe, start a blocking write of 10 bytes in a child; it does not return until the parent reads at least 10 bytes.

**write-24** [OSF/1] If `O_NONBLOCK` or `O_NDELAY` is set on a pipe, the page says "the write() function does block the process".
  Test: Not separately testable as written; the non-blocking `EAGAIN` results are checked under write-25 and write-26.
  Note: The page says "does block"; the rest of the paragraph (immediate `EAGAIN` returns) suggests "does not block" was meant.

**write-25** [OSF/1] With `O_NONBLOCK` or `O_NDELAY` set, a pipe write of `PIPE_BUF` bytes or fewer either succeeds completely and returns `nbyte`, or returns −1 with `errno` `EAGAIN`.
  Test: on a full non-blocking pipe, `write` of 1 byte returns −1 with `EAGAIN`; on an empty pipe it returns 1.

**write-26** [OSF/1] With `O_NONBLOCK` or `O_NDELAY` set, a pipe write of more than `PIPE_BUF` bytes either transfers what it can and returns the number written, or transfers nothing and returns −1 with `errno` `EAGAIN`.
  Test: on a full non-blocking pipe, a write of 2×`PIPE_BUF` returns −1/`EAGAIN`; on a partly full pipe it returns a positive count no larger than requested.

**write-27** [OSF/1] With `O_NONBLOCK` or `O_NDELAY` set, if a request is greater than `PIPE_BUF` bytes and all data previously written to the pipe has been read, `write()` transfers at least `PIPE_BUF` bytes.
  Test: on an empty non-blocking pipe, write 4×`PIPE_BUF` bytes; the return value is at least `PIPE_BUF`.

**write-28** [OSF/1] When writing to a regular file with enforcement-mode record locking enabled and another process holds a lock on part of the region: if `O_NDELAY` and `O_NONBLOCK` are both clear (the default), the caller blocks until all blocking locks are removed or the write is ended by a signal. `fcntl()` gives more information about record locks.
  Test: enable mandatory locking on a file, have a child lock a region; a blocking write to it waits until the child unlocks.

**write-29** [OSF/1] In the same locking situation, if `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` is set, `write()` returns −1 and sets `errno` to `EAGAIN`.
  Test: same setup with `O_NONBLOCK`; `write` returns −1 with `EAGAIN`.

**write-30** [OSF/1] A successful `write()` marks the file's `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` fields for update.
  Test: note `st_mtime`, sleep 1 s, write 1 byte; `fstat` shows larger `st_mtime` and `st_ctime`.

**write-31** [OSF/1] A successful `write()` to a regular file clears its set-user-ID and set-group-ID attributes.
  Test: create a file with mode 06755, write 1 byte to it; `fstat` shows `S_ISUID` and `S_ISGID` cleared.

**write-32** [OSF/1] If `write()` is interrupted by a signal before it writes any data, it returns −1 with `errno` `EINTR`.
  Test: block on a full pipe, deliver a caught signal (handler without restart); `write` returns −1/`EINTR`.

**write-33** [OSF/1] If `write()` is interrupted by a signal after it has written some data, it returns the number of bytes written.
  Test: interrupt a large blocking pipe write after partial transfer; the return value equals the bytes the reader received.

**write-34** [OSF/1] A write to a pipe or FIFO never returns −1 with `errno` `EINTR` if it has transferred any data and `nbyte` is less than or equal to `PIPE_BUF`.
  Test: hard to provoke since such writes are atomic; check that no `EINTR` is seen with data transferred.

**write-35** [OSF/1] If the signal handler was installed with an indication that functions should not be restarted, `write()` returns −1 and sets `errno` to `EINTR`, even if some data was already written.
  Test: install the handler with `sigaction` without `SA_RESTART`; interrupt a partial pipe write; expect −1/`EINTR`.
  Note: The page contradicts write-33 here; it does not say which rule wins when data was written and the handler does not restart.

**write-36** [OSF/1] If the handler was installed with an indication that functions should be restarted: if no data had been written when the interrupt was handled, `write()` does not return but is restarted; if data had been written, it returns the amount already written.
  Test: with `SA_RESTART`, interrupt a blocked write that has written nothing; the write continues and completes after the pipe is drained.

**write-37** [OSF/1] On success `write()` and `writev()` return the number of bytes actually written; otherwise they return −1 and set `errno`.
  Test: check the return value of a successful `writev` equals the sum of the `iov_len` values written.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**write-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not a valid file descriptor open for writing.

**write-E2** `EINVAL`: the file position pointer associated with `filedes` was negative.

**write-E3** `EINVAL`: `iov_count` was not between 1 and 16, inclusive.

**write-E4** `EINVAL`: one of the `iov_len` values in the `iov` array was negative, or their sum overflowed a 32-bit integer.

**write-E5** `EINVAL`: an attempt was made to write to a stream linked below a multiplexor.

**write-E6** `EFAULT`: `buffer` or part of `iov` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**write-E7** `EPIPE`: an attempt was made to write to a pipe or FIFO not open for reading by any process. A `SIGPIPE` signal is also sent to the process.

**write-E8** `EPERM`: an attempt was made to write to a socket "or type `SOCK_STREAM`" that is not connected to a peer socket.
  Note: The page reads "a socket or type SOCK_STREAM"; "of type" seems meant.

**write-E9** `EAGAIN`: `O_NONBLOCK` is set on the file and the process would be delayed in the write.

**write-E10** `EAGAIN`: an enforcement-mode record lock is outstanding on the part of the file to be written, and `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` is set.

**write-E11** `EAGAIN`: write to a stream that cannot accept data while `O_NDELAY` or `O_NONBLOCK` is set.

**write-E12** `ENOLCK`: enforced record locking is enabled and `LOCK_MAX` regions are already locked in the system.

**write-E13** `EDEADLK`: enforced record locking is enabled, `O_NDELAY` is clear, and a deadlock is detected.

**write-E14** `EFBIG`: an attempt was made to write a file that exceeds the maximum file size.

**write-E15** `ENOSPC`: no free space is left on the file system containing the file.

**write-E16** `EINTR`: a signal was caught during the write and its handler was installed with an indication that functions are not to be restarted.

**write-E17** `EIO`: the process is in a background process group writing to its controlling terminal, `TOSTOP` is set, the process neither ignores nor blocks `SIGTTOU`, and the process group is orphaned.

Related: Functions: open(2), fcntl(2), fcntl(2), lseek(2), open(2), pipe(2), poll(2), select(2), ulimit(3)


## Section 2sv — System V system calls

### mount(2sv)

Page: `man2sv/mount.html`. The page is headed "Digital" rather than "OSF" and documents the SVID-2 `mount()`; all items are tagged [Compat] since the page presents it as the System V alternative to the default BSD `mount()`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**mount.2sv-1** [Compat] Synopsis: `int mount(char *spec, char *dir, int mflag, int fstyp, char *dataptr, int datalen)`, declared via `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/mount.h>`.
  Test: compile a call including both headers and linking `libsys5`.

**mount.2sv-2** [Compat] OSF/1 supports two `mount()` functions: the BSD one (the default, documented in mount(2)) and the SVID-2 one; to use the SVID-2 version, link with the `libsys5` library before `libc`.
  Test: link with `-lsys5` before `-lc` and check the six-argument version is called (e.g. a non-root call returns `EPERM` with these arguments).

**mount.2sv-3** [Compat] `mount()` mounts the removable file system on the block special file `spec` at the mount point directory `dir`.
  Test: as root, mount a block device on an empty directory; `stat(dir)` then shows a different `st_dev`.

**mount.2sv-4** [Compat] `mflag` says whether additional file system data is included; the valid flag is `MS_DATA`.
  Test: check `MS_DATA` is defined in `<sys/mount.h>`.

**mount.2sv-5** [Compat] When the `MS_DATA` bit of `mflag` is off, the file system type defaults to the root file system type; only when it is on should `fstyp` be used to give the file system type number.
  Test: as root, mount a device of the root file system type with `mflag` = 0.

**mount.2sv-6** [Compat] When `MS_DATA` is set, `dataptr` and `datalen` (address and length of a block of file-system-specific data) must be present; the data is interpreted by the file system code and its format depends on the file system type; if a type does not need the data, `dataptr` and `datalen` should both be 0.
  Test: as root, mount with `MS_DATA`, a valid `fstyp`, and `dataptr`=0, `datalen`=0 for a type needing no data.

**mount.2sv-7** [Compat] The low-order bit of `mflag` controls write permission: if it is 1, writing is forbidden; otherwise writing is permitted according to individual file accessibility.
  Test: as root, mount with `mflag` = 1; creating a file under `dir` fails.

**mount.2sv-8** [Compat] After a successful `mount()`, references to `dir` refer to the root directory of the mounted file system.
  Test: see mount.2sv-3.

**mount.2sv-9** [Compat] Only the super-user can invoke `mount()`; it is intended for use by the mount(8) utility.
  Test: non-root call fails with `EPERM`.

**mount.2sv-10** [Compat] Returns 0 when the file system is mounted; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: successful root mount returns exactly 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; this page says `errno` "is set" to one of these):

**mount.2sv-E1** `EPERM`: the effective user ID is not super-user.

**mount.2sv-E2** `ENOENT`: any of the named files does not exist.

**mount.2sv-E3** `ENOTDIR`: a component of a path prefix is not a directory.

**mount.2sv-E4** `EREMOTE`: the file system identified by `spec` is remote and cannot be mounted.

**mount.2sv-E5** `ENOLINK`: the path argument points to a remote machine and the link to it is no longer active.

**mount.2sv-E6** `EMULTIHOP`: components of the path require hopping to multiple remote machines.

**mount.2sv-E7** `ENOTBLK`: `spec` is not a block special device.

**mount.2sv-E8** `ENXIO`: the device associated with `spec` does not exist.

**mount.2sv-E9** `ENOTDIR`: `dir` is not a directory.

**mount.2sv-E10** `EFAULT`: `spec` or `dir` points outside the process's allocated address space.

**mount.2sv-E11** `EBUSY`: `dir` is a user's current working directory, is mounted on a user's current working directory, or is otherwise busy.

**mount.2sv-E12** `EBUSY`: the device associated with `spec` is currently mounted.

**mount.2sv-E13** `EBUSY`: there are no more mount table entries.

**mount.2sv-E14** `EROFS`: `spec` is write protected and `mflag` requests write permission.

**mount.2sv-E15** `ENOSPC`: the file system state in the super-block is not `FsOKAY` and `mflag` requests write permission.

**mount.2sv-E16** `EINVAL`: the super block has an invalid magic number, or `fstyp` is invalid, or `mflag` is not valid.

Related: Command: mount(8); Function: statfs(2); System V Compatibility User's Guide


## Section 3 — library functions

### abort(3)

Page: `man3/abort.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**abort.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `int abort(void)`, with `<stdlib.h>` included.
  Test: compile and link a call to `abort()` against `<stdlib.h>` and libc.
Note: The page declares the return type as `int`.

**abort.3-2** [OSF/1] `abort()` sends a `SIGABRT` signal to the current process. This terminates the process and produces a memory dump, unless the signal is caught and the handler does not return.
  Test: child calls `abort()` with default disposition; parent's `waitpid` shows `WIFSIGNALED` with `WTERMSIG` = `SIGABRT`.

**abort.3-3** [OSF/1] If `SIGABRT` is neither caught nor ignored, and the current directory is writable, the system writes a memory dump to the `core` file in the current directory and prints an error message.
  Test: child in a writable empty directory calls `abort()`; afterwards a file `core` exists there (and `WCOREDUMP` is set if available).

**abort.3-4** [OSF/1] If `abort()` terminates the process, it has the effect of `fclose()` on every open stream.
  Test: child writes "x" with `fputs` to an `fopen`ed file without flushing, then calls `abort()`; the file contains "x".

**abort.3-5** [OSF/1] It then terminates the process with the same result as `_exit()`, except that the status given to `wait()` or `waitpid()` is that of a process terminated by `SIGABRT`.
  Test: as abort.3-2; and the child's pipe write end is closed (parent reads EOF).

**abort.3-6** [OSF/1] If `abort()` terminates the process, all open message catalog descriptors are also closed.
  Test: Not directly observable after termination; check only that the process terminates with `catopen` descriptors open.

**abort.3-7** [OSF/1] NOTES: `abort()` is supported for multi-threaded applications.
  Test: in a program with two threads, one calls `abort()`; the whole process terminates with `SIGABRT`.

Related: Functions: exit(2), kill(2), sigaction(2)

### aio_cancel(3)

Page: `man3/aio_cancel.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**aio_cancel.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int aio_cancel(int fildes, struct aiocb *aiocbp)`, with `<aio.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call against `<aio.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**aio_cancel.3-2** [DEC] `fildes` is the file descriptor whose outstanding asynchronous I/O operations are canceled.
  Test: covered by aio_cancel.3-4.

**aio_cancel.3-3** [DEC] `aiocbp` points to the control block of a particular request to cancel. If `aiocbp` is NULL, all queued outstanding asynchronous I/O requests against `fildes` are canceled.
  Test: queue several `aio_read`s on a pipe with no data, `aio_cancel(fd, NULL)`; each request's `aio_error` gives `ECANCELED`.

**aio_cancel.3-4** [DEC] When an operation is canceled, its error status is set to `ECANCELED`.
  Test: queue an `aio_read` on an empty pipe, cancel it; `aio_error` on its handle returns `ECANCELED`.

**aio_cancel.3-5** [DEC] On success, returns `AIO_CANCELED` if the requested operation was canceled; `AIO_NOTCANCELED` if at least one requested operation is not canceled because it is in progress; `AIO_ALLDONE` if all the operations had already completed.
  Test: cancel a request pending on an empty pipe: `AIO_CANCELED`; cancel after `aio_suspend` reports completion: `AIO_ALLDONE`.

**aio_cancel.3-6** [DEC] On failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: `aio_cancel(-1, NULL)` returns −1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**aio_cancel.3-E1** `EBADF`: `fildes` is not a valid file descriptor.

Related: aio_read(3), aio_write(3)

### aio_error(3)

Page: `man3/aio_error.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**aio_error.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int aio_error(aio_handle_t handle)`, with `<aio.h>` included; the type `aio_handle_t` is defined in `<aio.h>`.
  Test: compile a call with an `aio_handle_t` variable against `<aio.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**aio_error.3-2** [DEC] `handle` identifies the asynchronous operation whose status is queried.
  Test: covered by aio_error.3-3.

**aio_error.3-3** [DEC] `aio_error()` returns the error status associated with `handle`; this is the `errno` value set by the corresponding read or write operation.
  Test: `aio_read` on a descriptor that later fails, or a successful `aio_read` of a regular file; after completion `aio_error(cb.aio_handle)` returns the expected errno (0 for success).

**aio_error.3-4** [DEC] If the operation is in progress, the return value equals `EINPROG`.
  Test: queue `aio_read` on an empty pipe; `aio_error` immediately returns `EINPROG`.

**aio_error.3-5** [DEC] The handle is a unique identifier set when the operation is first submitted. Each separate operation, whether submitted by `aio_read`, `aio_write` or as one item of an `lio_listio` list, has a unique handle. Calling an asynchronous I/O function sets the handle field in the `aiocb` structure.
  Test: submit two `aio_read`s; their `aio_handle` fields differ and were changed by the calls.

**aio_error.3-6** [DEC] If `aio_error()` returns successfully, 0 is returned. On failure, −1 is returned and `errno` is set; the error status corresponds to those described for `aio_read` or `aio_write`.
  Test: after a successful completed `aio_read`, `aio_error` returns 0.
Note: The page is unclear: DESCRIPTION says the function returns the operation's error status (or `EINPROG`), while RETURN VALUES says it returns 0 on success and −1 on failure.

Related: aio_cancel(3), aio_read(3), aio_return(3), aio_write(3), lio_listio(3)

### aio_read(3)

Page: `man3/aio_read.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**aio_read.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int aio_read(int fildes, struct aiocb *aiocbp)`, with `<aio.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call against `<aio.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**aio_read.3-2** [DEC] `fildes` is the descriptor of the file to read from; `aiocbp` points to an `aiocb` structure.
  Test: covered by aio_read.3-3.

**aio_read.3-3** [DEC] `aio_read()` issues a read request and returns when the request is initiated or queued, even when the data cannot be delivered immediately.
  Test: `aio_read` on an empty pipe returns 0 at once; after the peer writes, `aio_suspend` returns and the data is in the buffer.

**aio_read.3-4** [DEC] If an error occurs during queueing, the call returns without initiating the request.
  Test: `aio_read` on a write-only descriptor returns −1 with `EBADF`, and no read occurs.

**aio_read.3-5** [DEC] The `aiocb` control block holds information such as the initial point for the read and a handle used to get the error and return status. Its members are: `int aio_whence`, `off_t aio_offset`, `volatile char *aio_buf`, `size_t aio_nbytes`, `int aio_reqprio`, `struct sigevent aio_event`, `int aio_flag`, `aiohandle_t aio_handle`.
  Test: compile code that assigns each named member of `struct aiocb` with the listed types.
Note: The page spells the handle member's type `aiohandle_t`, while `aio_error(3)` and `aio_return(3)` use `aio_handle_t`.

**aio_read.3-6** [DEC] `aio_whence` and `aio_offset` mean the same as the `whence` and `offset` arguments of `lseek`.
  Test: file "0123456789"; `aio_whence`=`SEEK_SET`, `aio_offset`=4, `aio_nbytes`=3; result is "456".

**aio_read.3-7** [DEC] If `aio_whence` is `SEEK_CUR` and `aio_offset` is zero, no implied `lseek` takes place.
  Test: `lseek(fd, 2, SEEK_SET)`, then `aio_read` with `SEEK_CUR`/0 and 3 bytes; result is "234".

**aio_read.3-8** [DEC] When the I/O completes, the file pointer is updated (using `aio_whence` and `aio_offset`) to the next byte after the bytes that were read.
  Test: after aio_read.3-6 completes, `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR)` returns 7.

**aio_read.3-9** [DEC] `aio_nbytes` and `aio_buf` mean the same as the `nbyte` and `buf` arguments of `read`.
  Test: `aio_nbytes`=5 into a 10-byte buffer; only 5 bytes written, `aio_return` gives 5.

**aio_read.3-10** [DEC] `aio_reqprio` sets the priority of the operation, an indicator of the desired order of execution relative to the process's other asynchronous I/O requests. Requests with equal priority are executed first in, first out.
  Test: queue two reads with equal priority on a pipe; write 2 bytes; the first-queued request gets the first byte.

**aio_read.3-11** [DEC] `aio_reqprio` must be within `AIO_PRIO_MIN` to `AIO_PRIO_MAX`; the default priority is `AIO_PRIO_DFL`. These symbols are defined in `<limits.h>`.
  Test: check the three symbols are defined in `<limits.h>`; an `aio_read` with `aio_reqprio` = `AIO_PRIO_DFL` is accepted.
Note: The page does not say what happens if `aio_reqprio` is out of range.

**aio_read.3-12** [DEC] `aio_event` defines the signal generated when the operation completes. If the `AIO_EVENT` bit in `aio_flag` is zero, no signal is sent.
  Test: set `aio_flag` |= `AIO_EVENT` and `aio_event` to `SIGUSR1` with a handler; the handler runs on completion. With the bit clear, no signal arrives.

**aio_read.3-13** [DEC] Whether the operation fails or succeeds, its error and return status are set and can be retrieved with `aio_error` and `aio_return`.
  Test: after completion, `aio_error` and `aio_return` give 0 and the byte count.

**aio_read.3-14** [DEC] `aio_handle` is a unique identifier set when the operation is first submitted; each operation, submitted by `aio_read` or as one item in an `lio_listio` list, has its own handle, which `aio_error` and `aio_return` use.
  Test: two submissions give different `aio_handle` values.

**aio_read.3-15** [DEC] On `close`, `close` waits for all asynchronous I/O to complete before closing the file.
  Test: queue `aio_read` on a pipe, have another process write after 1 s, `close` the descriptor; `close` returns after about 1 s and the read has completed.

**aio_read.3-16** [DEC] On `_exit` and `fork`, outstanding asynchronous I/O operations are undefined.
  Test: Not testable (the behaviour is undefined).

**aio_read.3-17** [DEC] On success returns 0 and the request is queued; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: valid request returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**aio_read.3-E1** `EAGAIN`: the request was not queued due to system resource limitations.

**aio_read.3-E2** `EBADF`: `fildes` is not a valid file descriptor open for reading.

**aio_read.3-E3** `EFAULT`: `aiocbp` was not a valid address.

**aio_read.3-E4** `EINVAL`: `aio_whence` is not a proper value, or the resulting file pointer is invalid.

**aio_read.3-18** [DEC] If `aio_read` queues the operation but it is later canceled or meets an error, the return status of the operation is one of the values normally returned by `read`, and the error status is `ECANCELED` when the I/O was canceled before completing due to an explicit `aio_cancel` request. Use `aio_error` and `aio_return` to get the error and return status.
  Test: queue a read on an empty pipe, `aio_cancel` it; `aio_error` returns `ECANCELED`.
Note: The page says "errno is set" to `ECANCELED` for the asynchronous failure; the `aio_write(3)` page says instead the value returned by `aio_error` is set.

Related: aio_cancel(3), aio_error(3), aio_return(3), aio_write(3), lio_listio(3)

### aio_return(3)

Page: `man3/aio_return.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**aio_return.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int aio_return(aio_handle_t handle)`, with `<aio.h>` included; `aio_handle_t` is defined in `<aio.h>`.
  Test: compile a call against `<aio.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**aio_return.3-2** [DEC] `handle` identifies the asynchronous operation in status queries.
  Test: covered by aio_return.3-3.

**aio_return.3-3** [DEC] `aio_return()` retrieves the return status for `handle`: the value the corresponding `read` or `write` call would have returned. (`aio_error` gives the error status.)
  Test: `aio_read` 5 bytes from a 10-byte file; after completion `aio_return(cb.aio_handle)` returns 5.

**aio_return.3-4** [DEC] The handle is a unique identifier set when the operation is first submitted; each operation, from `aio_read`, `aio_write` or one item of `lio_listio`, has its own handle, and calling an asynchronous I/O function sets the handle field in the `aiocb`.
  Test: two submissions give different handles.

**aio_return.3-5** [DEC] If the operation has completed, the return status as for `read` or `write` is returned: on success, the number of bytes read or written during the operation. On an unsuccessful call, −1 is returned.
  Test: a completed 4-byte `aio_write` gives 4.
Note: The page does not say what is returned if the operation has not yet completed, nor whether `errno` is set on the −1 return.

Related: aio_cancel(3), aio_error(3), aio_read(3), aio_write(3), lio_listio(3)

### aio_suspend(3)

Page: `man3/aio_suspend.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**aio_suspend.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int aio_suspend(int cnt, struct aiocb *aiocbp[])`, with `<aio.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call against `<aio.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**aio_suspend.3-2** [DEC] `cnt` is the number of elements in the `aiocbp` array, that is, the number of operations; each element points to an `aiocb`.
  Test: covered by aio_suspend.3-5.

**aio_suspend.3-3** [DEC] When `aiocbp` is NULL, the argument is ignored.
  Test: call `aio_suspend(0, NULL)` and record the behaviour.
Note: The page does not say what the call does when the array is ignored.

**aio_suspend.3-4** [DEC] Each `aiocb` in the array must have been used to start a request by `aio_read`, `aio_write` or `lio_listio`.
  Test: Not testable as stated (the page gives no result for a violation).

**aio_suspend.3-5** [DEC] `aio_suspend()` suspends the calling process until at least one operation has completed or a signal or event interrupts it.
  Test: queue a read on an empty pipe; another process writes after 1 s; `aio_suspend` returns 0 after about 1 s.

**aio_suspend.3-6** [DEC] If, at the time of the call, any listed operation has already completed, the function returns without suspending.
  Test: queue a read on a regular file, wait until `aio_error` is not `EINPROG`, then `aio_suspend` returns 0 immediately.

**aio_suspend.3-7** [DEC] Returns 0 if it returns due to an I/O completion; the application can then find which operations finished by examining the status fields, using `aio_error` and `aio_return`.
  Test: as aio_suspend.3-5; then `aio_error` on the completed request is not `EINPROG`.

**aio_suspend.3-8** [DEC] On failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as aio_suspend.3-E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**aio_suspend.3-E1** `EINTR`: a signal or event interrupted `aio_suspend`.

Related: aio_read(3), aio_write(3), lio_listio(3)

### aio_write(3)

Page: `man3/aio_write.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**aio_write.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int aio_write(int fildes, struct aiocb *aiocbp)`, with `<aio.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call against `<aio.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**aio_write.3-2** [DEC] `fildes` is the descriptor of the file to write to; `aiocbp` points to an `aiocb` structure.
  Test: covered by aio_write.3-3.

**aio_write.3-3** [DEC] `aio_write()` issues a write request and returns when it is initiated or queued, even when the data cannot be written immediately.
  Test: `aio_write` 4 bytes to a regular file returns 0; after `aio_suspend`, the file contains the bytes.

**aio_write.3-4** [DEC] If an error occurs during queueing, the call returns without initiating the request.
  Test: `aio_write` on a read-only descriptor returns −1 with `EBADF`; the file is unchanged.

**aio_write.3-5** [DEC] The `aiocb` holds information such as the initial point for the write and a handle for getting error and return status. Members: `int aio_whence`, `off_t aio_offset`, `volatile char *aio_buf`, `size_t aio_nbytes`, `int aio_reqprio`, `struct sigevent aio_event`, `int aio_flag`, `aiohandle_t aio_handle`.
  Test: compile code assigning each member.
Note: The page spells the handle type `aiohandle_t`, while `aio_error(3)` and `aio_return(3)` use `aio_handle_t`.

**aio_write.3-6** [DEC] `aio_whence` and `aio_offset` mean the same as the `whence` and `offset` arguments of `lseek`; if `aio_whence` is `SEEK_CUR` and `aio_offset` is zero, no implied `lseek` takes place.
  Test: `aio_write` "XY" with `SEEK_SET`/3 into "0123456789"; file becomes "012XY56789".

**aio_write.3-7** [DEC] When the I/O completes, the file pointer is updated to the next byte after the bytes transferred.
  Test: after aio_write.3-6, `lseek(fd,0,SEEK_CUR)` returns 5.
Note: The page says "the number of bytes that were read" on this write page, apparently copied from `aio_read(3)`.

**aio_write.3-8** [DEC] `aio_nbytes` and `aio_buf` mean the same as the `nbyte` and `buf` arguments.
  Test: `aio_nbytes`=2 from a 10-byte buffer writes exactly 2 bytes.
Note: The page says these are the arguments "defined by the read routine"; for a write it presumably means `write`, but the page says `read`.

**aio_write.3-9** [DEC] `aio_reqprio` sets the request priority, an indicator of desired order relative to the process's other asynchronous requests; equal priorities run first in, first out. The value must be within the range "AIO_PRIO_MAN and AIO_PRIO_MAX"; the default is `AIO_PRIO_DFL`; the symbols are in `<limits.h>`.
  Test: two writes with equal priority on a pipe arrive in submission order.
Note: The page writes `AIO_PRIO_MAN`, apparently a misprint for `AIO_PRIO_MIN` as on `aio_read(3)`.

**aio_write.3-10** [DEC] `aio_event` defines the signal generated on completion; if the `AIO_EVENT` bit in `aio_flag` is zero, no signal is sent. Whether the operation fails or succeeds, its error and return status are set and can be retrieved with `aio_error` and `aio_return`.
  Test: with `AIO_EVENT` set and `SIGUSR1` in `aio_event`, the handler runs on completion.

**aio_write.3-11** [DEC] `aio_handle` is a unique identifier set when the operation is first submitted; each operation, from `aio_write` or one item of `lio_listio`, has its own handle, used by `aio_error` and `aio_return`.
  Test: two submissions give different handles.

**aio_write.3-12** [DEC] On `close`, `close` waits for all asynchronous I/O to complete before closing the file.
  Test: queue a write to a full pipe, have a reader drain it after 1 s, `close`; `close` returns after the write completes.

**aio_write.3-13** [DEC] On `_exit` and `fork`, outstanding asynchronous I/O operations are undefined.
  Test: Not testable (the behaviour is undefined).

**aio_write.3-14** [DEC] On success returns 0 and the request is queued; on failure returns −1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: valid request returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**aio_write.3-E1** `EAGAIN`: the request was not queued due to system resource limitations.

**aio_write.3-E2** `EBADF`: `fildes` is not a valid file descriptor open for writing.

**aio_write.3-E3** `EFAULT`: `aiocbp` was not a valid address.

**aio_write.3-E4** `EINVAL`: `aio_whence` is not a proper value, or the resulting file pointer is invalid.

**aio_write.3-15** [DEC] If `aio_write` queues the operation but it is later canceled or meets an error, the return status is one of the values normally returned by `write`; the value returned by `aio_error` is `ECANCELED` when the I/O was canceled before completing due to an explicit `aio_cancel` request.
  Test: queue a write to a full pipe, `aio_cancel` it; `aio_error` returns `ECANCELED`.

Related: aio_cancel(3), aio_error(3), aio_read(3), aio_return(3), lio_listio(3)

### alarm(3), ualarm(3)

Page: `man3/alarm.html`; same text as `ualarm(3)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**alarm.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `unsigned int alarm(unsigned int seconds)` and `unsigned int ualarm(unsigned int mseconds, unsigned int interval)`, with `<sys/unistd.h>` included.
  Test: compile and link calls to both against `<sys/unistd.h>` and libc.

**alarm.3-2** [OSF/1] `seconds` is a number of real-time seconds; `mseconds` is a number of real-time microseconds; `interval` is the interval for repeating the timer.
  Test: covered by alarm.3-3 and alarm.3-7.

**alarm.3-3** [OSF/1] `alarm()` gives notification of a timeout after `seconds` real-time seconds: at some time after `seconds` seconds have elapsed, a signal is delivered to the process.
  Test: install a handler on the catchable signals, `alarm(1)`, `pause()`; a signal arrives no sooner than 1 s after the call.
Note: The page does not name the signal delivered.

**alarm.3-4** [OSF/1] Each call resets the timer, until `seconds` is set to 0.
  Test: `alarm(1)` then immediately `alarm(3)`; no signal before about 3 s. `alarm(1)` then `alarm(0)`; no signal within 2 s.

**alarm.3-5** [OSF/1] When the notification signal is caught or ignored, no action takes place; otherwise the calling process is terminated.
  Test: child with default dispositions calls `alarm(1)` and `pause()`; it is terminated by a signal. With the delivered signal caught, it survives 2 s.

**alarm.3-6** [OSF/1] `alarm()` uses the `ITIMER_REAL` interval timer.
  Test: `alarm(5)`, then `getitimer(ITIMER_REAL)` shows about 5 s remaining.

**alarm.3-7** [OSF/1] `ualarm()` gives notification after `mseconds` real-time microseconds. When `interval` is nonzero, timeout notification occurs after `interval` microseconds have been added to `mseconds`.
  Test: `ualarm(200000, 0)` with a handler: one signal after about 0.2 s. With `interval` 100000, count further signals.
Note: The page's wording of the `interval` behaviour ("after the number of microseconds specified by the interval parameter has been added to the mseconds parameter") is unclear about whether the timer repeats.

**alarm.3-8** [OSF/1] For `ualarm()`, when the notification signal is caught or ignored, no action takes place; otherwise the calling process is terminated.
  Test: child with default disposition calls `ualarm(100000,0)` and `pause()`; it is terminated.

**alarm.3-9** [OSF/1] `ualarm()` is the simplified interface to `setitimer()` and uses the `ITIMER_REAL` interval timer.
  Test: `ualarm(500000, 0)` then `getitimer(ITIMER_REAL)` shows about 0.5 s remaining.

**alarm.3-10** [OSF/1] NOTES: `alarm()` is supported for multi-threaded applications; `ualarm()` is not supported for multiple threads.
  Test: call `alarm` from a second thread; a signal is delivered to the process.

**alarm.3-11** [OSF/1] NOTES: `alarm()` is reentrant, but a second call made from a different thread resets the timer, just as a second call from the same thread does.
  Test: thread A calls `alarm(1)`, thread B then `alarm(0)`; no signal arrives.

**alarm.3-12** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise −1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: `alarm(1)` with no prior alarm returns 0.
Note: The page says the return is 0 on success, but the function returns `unsigned int`, so −1 is a large unsigned value; the page does not mention returning the time left on a previous alarm.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to this):

**alarm.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `seconds` specifies a negative value or a value greater than 100,000,000.
Note: The page gives a "negative value" condition though `seconds` is unsigned.

Related: Functions: gettimer(3)

### cfsetispeed(3)

Page: `man3/cfsetispeed.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**cfsetispeed.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `int cfsetispeed(struct termios *termios_p, speed_t speed)`, with `<termios.h>` included.
  Test: compile and link a call against `<termios.h>`.

**cfsetispeed.3-2** [OSF/1] `termios_p` points to a `termios` structure containing the input baud rate; `speed` is the new input baud rate. The function sets the input baud rate stored in the structure to `speed`.
  Test: `cfsetispeed(&t, B1200)`; `cfgetispeed(&t)` returns `B1200`.

**cfsetispeed.3-3** [OSF/1] If the input baud rate is set to 0, the input baud rate is specified by the value of the output baud rate.
  Test: `cfsetospeed(&t, B9600)`, `cfsetispeed(&t, 0)`, `tcsetattr`, `tcgetattr`; `cfgetispeed` gives `B9600` (on a device that accepts it).
Note: The page does not say whether `cfgetispeed` on the structure right after the call returns 0 or the output rate.

**cfsetispeed.3-4** [OSF/1] There is no effect on the baud rates in the hardware until a later successful `tcsetattr()` call on the same `termios` structure.
  Test: `tcgetattr` into `t`, `cfsetispeed(&t, B300)` without `tcsetattr`; a fresh `tcgetattr` shows the old input speed.

**cfsetispeed.3-5** [OSF/1] Returns 0.
  Test: the call returns 0.

Related: Functions: cfgetispeed(3), cfgetospeed(3), cfsetospeed(3), tcsetattr(3); Files: termios(4)

Page: `man3/chdir.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and describes a Fortran library routine in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.

**chdir.3f-1** [Fortran] Synopsis (Fortran): `integer function chdir (dirname)` with `character*(*) dirname`.
  Test: compile a Fortran program calling `chdir('/tmp')` and link with `libU77.a`.

**chdir.3f-2** [Fortran] The default directory for creating and locating files is changed to `dirname`.

**chdir.3f-3** [Fortran] Returns zero on success, and an error code otherwise.

**chdir.3f-4** [Fortran] Files: `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.
  Test: the library file exists.

**chdir.3f-5** [Fortran] RESTRICTIONS: pathnames can be no longer than `MAXPATHLEN` as defined in `<sys/param.h>`.
  Test: a `dirname` longer than `MAXPATHLEN` is not accepted (nonzero return).

**chdir.3f-6** [Fortran] RESTRICTIONS: use of this function "may cause inquire by unit to fail".

### chmod(3)

Page: `man3/chmod.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and describes a Fortran library routine in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.
Origin: This page documents the Fortran library `libU77.a`, not the C function; out of scope, tagged [Fortran].

**chmod.3f-1** [Fortran] Synopsis (Fortran): `integer function chmod (name, mode)` with `character*(*) name, mode`.
  Test: compile a Fortran program calling `chmod('f', 'u+x')` and link with `libU77.a`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [Fortran] for that reason only.

**chmod.3f-2** [Fortran] Changes the file system mode of file `name`. `mode` can be any specification recognized by `chmod(1)`. `name` must be a single pathname.
  Test: `chmod('f', '644')` then `stat` shows mode 0644; `chmod('f', 'u+x')` adds owner execute.

**chmod.3f-3** [Fortran] The normal return value is 0; any other value is a system error number.
  Test: `chmod('/nonexistent', '644')` returns a nonzero value.
Note: The page does not say which error number is returned for which failure.

**chmod.3f-4** [Fortran] Files: `/usr/lib/libU77.a`; `/bin/chmod` is exec'ed to change the mode.
  Test: run with `PATH` irrelevant; temporarily unavailable `/bin/chmod` cannot be arranged from user space without privilege, so check only that the mode changes.

**chmod.3f-5** [Fortran] RESTRICTIONS: pathnames can be no longer than `MAXPATHLEN` as defined in `<sys/param.h>`.
  Test: a `name` longer than `MAXPATHLEN` gives a nonzero return.

### clock_getres(3)

Page: `man3/clock_getres.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**clock_getres.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int clock_getres(int clock_id, struct timespec *res, struct timespec *maxval)`, with `<timers.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call against `<timers.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**clock_getres.3-2** [DEC] `clock_id` is the clock whose resolution is wanted. `CLOCK_REALTIME` is supported and represents the system's time-of-day clock.
  Test: `clock_getres(CLOCK_REALTIME, &r, &m)` returns 0.

**clock_getres.3-3** [DEC] `res` receives the clock's resolution; `maxval` receives the clock's maximum possible time value.
  Test: after clock_getres.3-2, `r` and `m` have been written (pre-fill both with a marker pattern; the marker is gone).

**clock_getres.3-4** [DEC] If `res` or `maxval` is NULL, the corresponding value is not returned.
  Test: `clock_getres(CLOCK_REALTIME, NULL, &m)` and `clock_getres(CLOCK_REALTIME, &r, NULL)` both return 0 and fill the non-null argument.

**clock_getres.3-5** [DEC] These values are the limits that can be used in `clock_settime` to set the current time.
  Test: as root, `clock_settime` with a value greater than `maxval` fails with `EINVAL` (see clock_gettime-E1).

**clock_getres.3-6** [DEC] Returns 0 on success; −1 with `errno` set on failure.
  Test: as clock_getres.3-2.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**clock_getres.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `clock_id` does not specify a known clock.

Related: time(1), clock_gettimedrift(3), clock_settimedrift(3), ctime(3), timer_gettime(3)

### clock_gettime(3), clock_settime(3)

Page: `man3/clock_gettime.html`; same text as `clock_settime(3)`. The page is headed "Digital" (not "OSF") and marked as P1003.4/D10.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**clock_gettime.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `int clock_gettime(int clock_id, struct timespec *tp)` and `int clock_settime(int clock_id, const struct timespec *tp)`, with `<timers.h>` included.
  Test: compile calls to both against `<timers.h>`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [DEC] for that reason only.

**clock_gettime.3-2** [DEC] `clock_id` is the clock read or set; `CLOCK_REALTIME` is supported and represents the system's time-of-day clock. `tp` points to a `timespec` structure.
  Test: `clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME, &ts)` returns 0.

**clock_gettime.3-3** [DEC] `clock_gettime` returns the current time, in seconds and nanoseconds, for the given clock.
  Test: `ts.tv_sec` is within 1 of `time(NULL)` and `0 <= ts.tv_nsec < 1000000000`.

**clock_gettime.3-4** [DEC] `clock_settime` sets the given clock.
  Test: as root, read the clock, set it to the same value plus 1 s, read again; it reads about 1 s ahead. Restore afterwards.

**clock_gettime.3-5** [DEC] `CLOCK_REALTIME` measures time elapsed since 00:00:00:00 January 1, 1970 Greenwich Mean Time (the Epoch).
  Test: as clock_gettime.3-3.

**clock_gettime.3-6** [DEC] Superuser privilege is required to use `clock_settime`.
  Test: as non-root, `clock_settime` returns −1 with `EPERM`.

**clock_gettime.3-7** [DEC] Both return 0 on success; −1 with `errno` set on failure.
  Test: as clock_gettime.3-2.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**clock_gettime.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `clock_id` does not specify a known clock; or the `tp` argument to `clock_settime` is outside the range for the given clock type; or `tp` specified a nanosecond value less than zero or greater than or equal to 1000 million.

**clock_gettime.3-E2** `EPERM`: the requesting process does not have the appropriate privilege to set the given clock.

Related: time(1), clock_getres(3), clock_gettimedrift(3), clock_settimedrift(3), ctime(3), timer_gettime(3)

### ctermid(3)

Page: `man3/ctermid.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**ctermid.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard I/O Package (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `char *ctermid(char *s)`, with `<stdio.h>` included.
  Test: compile and link a call against `<stdio.h>`.

**ctermid.3-2** [OSF/1] `ctermid()` generates the pathname of the controlling terminal for the current process and stores it in a string.
  Test: `ctermid(NULL)` returns a non-empty string.

**ctermid.3-3** [OSF/1] If `s` is a null pointer, the string is stored in an internal static area and its address is returned; the next call overwrites that area.
  Test: `p1 = ctermid(NULL); p2 = ctermid(NULL);` gives `p1 == p2`.

**ctermid.3-4** [OSF/1] If `s` is not null, it points to an array of at least `L_ctermid` bytes; the pathname is placed there and `s` is returned.
  Test: `char b[L_ctermid]; ctermid(b) == b` and `b` holds the same string as `ctermid(NULL)`.

**ctermid.3-5** [OSF/1] `L_ctermid` is defined in `stdio.h` and is greater than 0.
  Test: compile-time check `L_ctermid > 0`.

**ctermid.3-6** [OSF/1] Unlike `ttyname()`, which is given a file descriptor and returns the actual name of its terminal, `ctermid()` returns a string (`/dev/tty`) that refers to the terminal if used as a filename. So `ttyname()` is useful only if the process already has a file open to a terminal.
  Test: `strcmp(ctermid(NULL), "/dev/tty") == 0`.

**ctermid.3-7** [OSF/1] On success returns the address of the generated pathname; otherwise returns an empty string.
  Test: as ctermid.3-4.

**ctermid.3-8** [OSF/1] Access to a pathname returned by `ctermid()` is not guaranteed.
  Test: none; a process without a controlling terminal may fail to open the returned path.

**ctermid.3-9** [OSF/1] `ctermid_r()`, the reentrant version, always returns null if the argument passed is null.
  Test: `ctermid_r(NULL)` returns NULL.
Note: The page mentions `ctermid_r()` only in RETURN VALUES and gives no synopsis for it.

Related: Functions: ttyname(3)

### fork(3)

Page: `man3/fork.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and describes a Fortran library routine in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.
Origin: This page documents the Fortran library `libU77.a`, not the C function; out of scope, tagged [Fortran].

**fork.3f-1** [Fortran] Synopsis (Fortran): `integer function fork()`.
  Test: compile a Fortran program calling `fork()` and link with `libU77.a`.
Note: The page carries a "Digital" heading rather than "OSF"; its items are tagged [Fortran] for that reason only.

**fork.3f-2** [Fortran] `fork` creates a copy of the calling process. The only distinction is the return value: the parent gets the process ID of the copy (the child); the child gets zero.
  Test: parent receives a positive value equal to the child's `getpid()`; child receives 0.

**fork.3f-3** [Fortran] All logical units open for writing are flushed before the fork, so I/O buffer contents are not duplicated in the external files.
  Test: write a record without newline-flush to a unit open on a file, then `fork`; both processes exit; the record appears once.

**fork.3f-4** [Fortran] A negative return indicates an error and is the negation of the system error code (see `perror(3)`).
  Test: Not easily testable (requires exhausting the process limit); under a low process limit, check that the return is negative.

**fork.3f-5** [Fortran] No corresponding exec routine is provided, because open logical units cannot be satisfactorily kept across exec; the usual fork/exec can be done with `system(3)`.
  Test: none (absence of an exec routine in `libU77.a`).

**fork.3f-6** [Fortran] Files: `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.
  Test: the library file exists.
