### pathconf(3), fpathconf(3)

Page: `man3/fpathconf.html`; same text as `pathconf(3)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**fpathconf.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `long pathconf(const char *path, int name)` and `long fpathconf(int filedes, int name)`, with `<unistd.h>` included.
  Test: compile and link calls to both against `<unistd.h>`.

**fpathconf.3-2** [OSF/1] `path` is a pathname; if its final component is a symbolic link, the link is traversed and resolution continues.
  Test: `pathconf` on a symlink to a directory with `_PC_NAME_MAX` returns the same value as on the directory.

**fpathconf.3-3** [OSF/1] `filedes` is an open file descriptor; `name` is the attribute queried. If the attribute is not applicable to the file, the call returns an error.
  Test: `pathconf("/etc/passwd", _PC_MAX_CANON)` (regular file) returns −1 with `EINVAL`.

**fpathconf.3-4** [OSF/1] `pathconf()` reports characteristics of operations supported by the file system holding the file named by `path`. Read, write or execute permission on the file is not required, but every directory in the path must be searchable.
  Test: `pathconf` on a mode-000 file in a searchable directory succeeds; on a file under a mode-000 directory (as non-root) fails with `EACCES`.

**fpathconf.3-5** [OSF/1] `fpathconf()` gives the same information for an open file.
  Test: `fpathconf(fd, _PC_NAME_MAX)` on an open directory equals `pathconf` on its path.

**fpathconf.3-6** [OSF/1] The symbolic values for `name` are defined in `unistd.h`.
  Test: check that all nine `_PC_` names below are defined.

**fpathconf.3-7** [OSF/1] `_PC_LINK_MAX`: maximum number of links to the file. For a directory, the value applies to the directory itself.
  Test: `pathconf(".", _PC_LINK_MAX)` returns a positive value.

**fpathconf.3-8** [OSF/1] `_PC_MAX_CANON`: maximum number of bytes in a canonical input line; applicable only to terminal devices.
  Test: `fpathconf` on a terminal descriptor returns a positive value.

**fpathconf.3-9** [OSF/1] `_PC_MAX_INPUT`: "The number of types allowed in an input queue"; applicable only to terminal devices.
  Test: `fpathconf` on a terminal descriptor returns a positive value.
Note: The page says "types", apparently a misprint for "bytes".

**fpathconf.3-10** [OSF/1] `_PC_NAME_MAX`: maximum number of bytes in a filename, not counting a terminating null. It may be as small as 13 but is never larger than 255. Applicable only to a directory file; the value applies to filenames within the directory.
  Test: `pathconf("/tmp", _PC_NAME_MAX)` returns a value from 13 to 255.

**fpathconf.3-11** [OSF/1] `_PC_PATH_MAX`: maximum number of bytes in a pathname, not counting a terminating null; never larger than 65,535. Applicable only to a directory file; the value is the maximum length of a relative pathname when the directory is the working directory.
  Test: `pathconf("/", _PC_PATH_MAX)` returns a positive value no larger than 65535.

**fpathconf.3-12** [OSF/1] `_PC_PIPE_BUF`: maximum number of bytes guaranteed to be written atomically. Applicable only to a FIFO; the value applies to the referenced object. For a directory, the value applies to any FIFO that exists or can be created within it.
  Test: `pathconf` on a FIFO and on its directory both return a positive value.
Note: The page says "applicable only to a FIFO" and then gives a meaning for directories.

**fpathconf.3-13** [OSF/1] `_PC_CHOWN_RESTRICTED`: applicable only to a directory file; the value applies to any files other than directories that exist or can be created within the directory.
  Test: `pathconf("/tmp", _PC_CHOWN_RESTRICTED)` does not fail with `EINVAL`.
Note: The page does not say what the returned value means.

**fpathconf.3-14** [OSF/1] `_PC_NO_TRUNC`: returns 1 if supplying a component name longer than `NAME_MAX` causes an error, and 0 if long component names are truncated. Applicable only to a directory file.
  Test: if `pathconf("/tmp", _PC_NO_TRUNC)` is 1, `open` of a name longer than `NAME_MAX` with `O_CREAT` fails with `ENAMETOOLONG`.

**fpathconf.3-15** [OSF/1] `_PC_VDISABLE`: always 0; no disabling character is defined. Applicable only to a terminal device.
  Test: `fpathconf` on a terminal descriptor with `_PC_VDISABLE` returns 0.

**fpathconf.3-16** [OSF/1] On success returns the value of the requested parameter; otherwise −1 with `errno` set.
  Test: as fpathconf.3-10; failing call returns −1.

Errors for `pathconf()` (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**fpathconf.3-E1** `EACCES`: search permission is denied for a component of the path prefix.

**fpathconf.3-E2** `ELOOP`: too many links were encountered in translating a pathname.

**fpathconf.3-E3** `EINVAL`: `name` specifies an unknown or inapplicable characteristic.

**fpathconf.3-E4** `EFAULT`: `path` is an invalid address.

**fpathconf.3-E5** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of the path string exceeds `{PATH_MAX}`, or a pathname component is longer than `{NAME_MAX}`.

**fpathconf.3-E6** `ENOENT`: the named file does not exist, or `path` points to an empty string.

**fpathconf.3-E7** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

Errors for `fpathconf()`:

**fpathconf.3-E8** `ELOOP`: too many links were encountered in translating a pathname.
Note: The page lists `ELOOP` for `fpathconf()`, which takes no pathname.

**fpathconf.3-E9** `EINVAL`: `name` specifies an unknown or inapplicable characteristic.

**fpathconf.3-E10** `EBADF`: the `fildes` argument is not a valid file descriptor.
Note: The page calls the argument `fildes` here but `filedes` in the synopsis.

The page has no RELATED INFORMATION section.

### getclock(3)

Page: `man3/getclock.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getclock.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `int getclock(int clktyp, struct timespec *tp)`, with `<sys/timers.h>` included.
  Test: compile and link a call against `<sys/timers.h>`.

**getclock.3-2** [OSF/1] `clktyp` identifies a system-wide clock; `tp` points to where the clock's current value is stored. The function stores the current value of the clock `clktyp` at `tp`.
  Test: `getclock(TIMEOFDAY, &ts)` returns 0 and fills `ts`.

**getclock.3-3** [OSF/1] `clktyp` is a symbolic constant defined in `sys/timers.h`. Only `TIMEOFDAY`, the normal time-of-day clock for system-wide time, is supported.
  Test: `TIMEOFDAY` is defined; any other value (for example −1) gives `EINVAL`.

**getclock.3-4** [OSF/1] For `TIMEOFDAY`, the value is the elapsed time since the epoch, 00:00:00 CUT (Coordinated Universal Time) 1 Jan 1970.
  Test: `ts.tv_sec` is within 1 of `time(NULL)`.

**getclock.3-5** [OSF/1] The `timespec` structure is defined in `sys/timers.h`. Field `tv_sec` (`unsigned long`): elapsed time in seconds since the epoch.
  Test: compile a use of `ts.tv_sec` as `unsigned long`.

**getclock.3-6** [OSF/1] Field `tv_nsec` (`long`): elapsed time as a fraction of a second since the epoch, in nanoseconds.
  Test: `0 <= ts.tv_nsec < 1000000000`.

**getclock.3-7** [OSF/1] The interval expressed by the structure is ((`tv_sec` × 10^9) + `tv_nsec`) nanoseconds.
  Test: two successive calls give non-decreasing values of this expression.
Note: The page text conversion shows "tv_sec * 109"; the original HTML has 10 with superscript 9, that is 10^9.

**getclock.3-8** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise −1 with `errno` set.
  Test: as getclock.3-2.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**getclock.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `clktyp` does not specify a known system-wide clock.

**getclock.3-E2** `EIO`: an error occurred when accessing the system-wide clock given by `clktyp`.

Related: Functions: gettimer(3), setclock(3), time(3)

### getcwd(3)

Page: `man3/getcwd.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getcwd.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `char *getcwd(char *buffer, int size)`.
  Test: compile and link a call with these argument types.
Note: The page gives `size` the type `int` and names no header.

**getcwd.3-2** [OSF/1] `buffer` points to space to hold the pathname; `size` is the length of that space in bytes, and must be at least the length of the pathname plus one byte for the terminating null.
  Test: `chdir("/tmp")`; `getcwd(b, 5)` returns `b` holding "/tmp".

**getcwd.3-3** [OSF/1] If `buffer` is a null pointer, `getcwd()` obtains `size` bytes using `malloc()`, and the returned pointer can be passed to `free()`.
  Test: `p = getcwd(NULL, 1024)`; `p` is non-null, holds the directory, and `free(p)` works.

**getcwd.3-4** [OSF/1] `getcwd()` returns a pointer to a string containing the pathname of the current directory. It calls `getwd` to obtain the pathname.
  Test: after `chdir("/usr")`, the string is "/usr".

**getcwd.3-5** [OSF/1] NOTES: `getcwd()` is supported for multi-threaded applications.
  Test: call from two threads at once with separate buffers; both get the correct path.

**getcwd.3-6** [OSF/1] On success `buffer` is returned; otherwise a null value is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: `getcwd(b, sizeof b) == b`.
Note: The page does not say what is returned on success when `buffer` is null (getcwd.3-3 says the malloc'd pointer).

Errors (the call returns a null pointer and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**getcwd.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `size` is zero or negative.

**getcwd.3-E2** `ERANGE`: `size` is greater than zero but smaller than the length of the pathname + 1.

**getcwd.3-E3** `ENOMEM`: the requested amount of memory could not be allocated.

Related: Functions: malloc(3), getwd(3)

### getpass(3)

Page: `man3/getpass.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getpass.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `char *getpass(const char *prompt)`, with `<stdlib.h>` included.
  Test: compile and link a call against `<stdlib.h>`.

**getpass.3-2** [OSF/1] `prompt` points to the prompt string, which is written to `stderr`.
  Test: run under a pseudo-terminal with `stderr` redirected to a pipe; the prompt appears on the pipe.

**getpass.3-3** [OSF/1] `getpass()` opens `/dev/tty`, flushes output, disables echoing, and reads up to a newline or End-of-File from `/dev/tty`. The terminal state is then restored and `/dev/tty` is closed.
  Test: under a pseudo-terminal, type "secret\n"; the master side sees no echo of "secret", the call returns "secret", and afterwards `ECHO` is set again in `tcgetattr`.
Note: The page does not say whether the newline is kept in the returned string.

**getpass.3-4** [OSF/1] If interrupted by `SIGINT`, the terminal state of `/dev/tty` is restored before the signal is delivered to the calling process.
  Test: under a pseudo-terminal, catch `SIGINT` and in the handler check `tcgetattr` on `/dev/tty` shows `ECHO` set; send the interrupt character during `getpass`.

**getpass.3-5** [OSF/1] On success returns a pointer to a null-terminated string of no more than `PASS_MAX` characters; the data is overwritten by successive calls.
  Test: enter a string longer than `PASS_MAX`; the result has length <= `PASS_MAX`. Two calls return pointers to the same area or the first string is overwritten.

**getpass.3-6** [OSF/1] If `/dev/tty` cannot be opened, a NULL pointer is returned.
  Test: in a process with no controlling terminal (after `setsid`), `getpass("x")` returns NULL.

**getpass.3-7** [OSF/1] Files: `/dev/tty` is the tty device special file.
  Test: as getpass.3-3.

Related: Files: tty(7) termios(4)

### ttyname(3), isatty(3)

Page: `man3/isatty.html`; same text as `ttyname(3)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**isatty.3-1** [OSF/1] Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`). Synopsis: `char *ttyname(int file_descriptor)`, `int isatty(int file_descriptor)`, `int ttyname_r(int file_descriptor, char *buffer, int len)`.
  Test: compile and link calls to all three.
Note: The page names no header file.

**isatty.3-2** [OSF/1] `file_descriptor` is an open file descriptor; `buffer` points to a buffer for the terminal name; `len` is the length of that buffer.
  Test: covered by isatty.3-3 to isatty.3-6.

**isatty.3-3** [OSF/1] `ttyname()` returns a pointer to a string containing the null-terminated pathname of the terminal device associated with `file_descriptor`.
  Test: open a pseudo-terminal slave by name; `ttyname(fd)` returns that same path.

**isatty.3-4** [OSF/1] `ttyname()` returns a pointer to static data overwritten by each call. A null pointer is returned if `file_descriptor` does not describe a terminal device in the directory `/dev`.
  Test: `ttyname` of a regular file descriptor returns NULL; two calls on different terminals return the same pointer.

**isatty.3-5** [OSF/1] `isatty()` returns 1 if the device associated with `file_descriptor` is a terminal, and 0 otherwise.
  Test: `isatty` on a pseudo-terminal slave returns 1; on a pipe returns 0.

**isatty.3-6** [OSF/1] `ttyname_r()` is the reentrant version of `ttyname()`; on success the terminal name is stored as a null-terminated string in `buffer`, and it returns 0. Otherwise it returns −1.
  Test: `ttyname_r(fd, b, sizeof b)` on a terminal returns 0 and `b` equals `ttyname(fd)`.
Note: The page does not say what `ttyname_r()` returns for a descriptor that is not a terminal, beyond −1 on failure.

Errors:

**isatty.3-E1** `EINVAL` (for `ttyname_r()`, which returns −1): `buffer` is a null pointer, or `len` was too short to store the string.

**isatty.3-E2** `ENOTTY` (for `isatty()`): the file associated with the descriptor is not a terminal.
Note: The page says the file "associated with filedes", though the parameter is named `file_descriptor`; and `isatty()` returns 0, not −1, in this case per RETURN VALUES.

### lockf(3)

Page: `man3/lockf.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**lockf.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int lockf(int filedes, int request, off_t size)`, with `<fcntl.h>` included.
  Test: compile a call against `<fcntl.h>`.

**lockf.3-2** [OSF/1] `filedes` is the file to which the lock is applied or from which it is removed; the descriptor is one returned by a successful `open()` or `fcntl()`.
  Test: covered by later items.

**lockf.3-3** [OSF/1] `request` is one of `F_ULOCK`, `F_LOCK`, `F_TLOCK`, `F_TEST`.
  Test: the four constants are defined after including `<fcntl.h>`.

**lockf.3-4** [OSF/1] `F_ULOCK` unlocks a previously locked region.
  Test: lock bytes 0–9, then `F_ULOCK` them; another process's `F_TLOCK` on 0–9 then succeeds.

**lockf.3-5** [OSF/1] `F_LOCK` locks the region for exclusive use. The calling process sleeps if the region overlaps a locked region, and resumes when granted the lock.
  Test: process A locks 0–9; process B's `F_LOCK` on 5–14 blocks until A unlocks (B returns 0 after A's unlock).

**lockf.3-6** [OSF/1] `F_TLOCK` is like `F_LOCK` but returns an error if the region overlaps a locked region.
  Test: A locks 0–9; B's `F_TLOCK` on 5–14 returns −1 at once.
Note: The page does not name the errno for a failed `F_TLOCK`.

**lockf.3-7** [OSF/1] `F_TEST` tests whether another process has already locked a region: returns 0 if the region is unlocked; if locked, returns −1 and sets `errno` to `EACCES`.
  Test: A locks 0–9; B's `F_TEST` on 0–9 returns −1 with `EACCES`; on 20–29 returns 0.

**lockf.3-8** [OSF/1] `size` is the number of bytes to lock or unlock. The region starts at the current file offset and extends forward if `size` is positive and backward if negative.
  Test: `lseek(fd, 10, SEEK_SET)`, A `F_LOCK` with size −5; B's `F_TEST` at offset 5 size 5 returns −1, at offset 10 size 5 returns 0.

**lockf.3-9** [OSF/1] If `size` is 0, the region starts at the current location and extends forward to the maximum possible file size, including unallocated space after end of file.
  Test: A at offset 0 locks with size 0 on a 10-byte file; B's `F_TEST` at offset 1000000 returns −1.

**lockf.3-10** [OSF/1] `lockf()` locks and unlocks sections of an open file; unlike `fcntl()`, it can set only write (exclusive) locks.
  Test: none beyond lockf.3-5 (no request sets a shared lock).

**lockf.3-11** [OSF/1] `lockf()` and `fcntl()` locking are fully integrated: locks obtained from one are honoured and enforced by the other.
  Test: A sets an `fcntl` `F_WRLCK` on 0–9; B's `lockf(F_TEST)` on 0–9 returns −1. A takes `lockf` on 0–9; B's `fcntl(F_GETLK)` reports the lock.

**lockf.3-12** [OSF/1] Each lock is either enforced or advisory, and either a read lock or a write lock.
  Test: none on its own (see lockf.3-13).

**lockf.3-13** [OSF/1] Whether locks on a file are advisory or enforced depends on the file's mode (see `chmod()`); a file can have advisory or enforced locks, but not both. `sys/mode.h` describes the file attributes.
  Test: with an enforcement-enabling mode set (as `sys/mode.h` describes), lock a region and check lockf.3-14; without it, B's `read` of the region succeeds.
Note: The page does not say which mode bits select enforced locking.

**lockf.3-14** [OSF/1] While a process holds an enforced exclusive lock on a section, no other process can access that section with `read()` or `write()`; `open()`, `truncate()` and `ftruncate()` cannot truncate it. Another process that tries to read or modify the locked section "sleeps until the section is unlocked or returns with an error indication".
  Test: on an enforced-lock file, A locks 0–9; B's nonblocking `read` of byte 0 fails or blocks, and B's `ftruncate(fd, 0)` fails.
Note: The page does not say which outcome (sleep or error) occurs when, nor the errno.

**lockf.3-15** [OSF/1] The descriptor on which an exclusive lock is placed must have been opened with write access.
  Test: `lockf(F_LOCK)` on an `O_RDONLY` descriptor does not succeed (returns −1).

**lockf.3-16** [OSF/1] Changing or unlocking part of a file in the middle of a locked section leaves two smaller locked sections, one at each end.
  Test: A locks 0–29, unlocks 10–19; B's `F_TEST` on 0–9 and 20–29 return −1, on 10–19 returns 0.

**lockf.3-17** [OSF/1] All of a process's locks on a file are removed when the process closes any file descriptor for that file.
  Test: A opens the file twice, locks via fd1, closes fd2; B's `F_TLOCK` then succeeds.

**lockf.3-18** [OSF/1] Locks are not inherited by a child process after `fork()`.
  Test: A locks 0–9 and forks; the child's `F_TEST` on 0–9 returns −1 (the lock is the parent's, not its own).

**lockf.3-19** [OSF/1] Locks can start and extend beyond the current end of file, but cannot be negative relative to the beginning of the file.
  Test: on a 10-byte file, lock at offset 100 size 10: returns 0. At offset 5, size −10: returns −1.
Note: The page does not name the errno for a lock reaching before the start of the file.

**lockf.3-20** [OSF/1] "A lock can be set to extend to the end of the file by setting the l_len field to 0", and if `l_start` is 0 and `l_whence` is `SEEK_SET`, the whole file is locked.
  Test: via `fcntl` with `l_start`=0, `l_whence`=`SEEK_SET`, `l_len`=0, lock the file; `lockf(F_TEST)` anywhere in the file from another process returns −1.
Note: The page describes `flock` structure fields (`l_len`, `l_start`, `l_whence`), which belong to `fcntl()`, not to `lockf()`.

**lockf.3-21** [OSF/1] NOTES: buffered I/O does not work properly with file locking; do not use the standard I/O package routines on files that will be locked.
  Test: Not testable (advice).

**lockf.3-22** [OSF/1] NOTES: deadlocks due to file locks in a distributed system are not always detected; programs that may deadlock should set time-out timers.
  Test: Not testable from a single machine.

**lockf.3-23** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise −1 with `errno` set.
  Test: an uncontested `F_LOCK` returns 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**lockf.3-E1** `EACCES`: the file region is locked and `F_TEST` was specified.
Note: The page spells it `[EACESS]`.

**lockf.3-E2** `EINVAL`: the `request` parameter is not valid.

**lockf.3-E3** `EBADF`: `filedes` is not a valid open file descriptor; or `request` is `F_SETLK` or `F_SETLKW`, the lock type (`l_type`) is a shared lock (`F_RDLCK`) and `filedes` is not open for reading; or the lock type is an exclusive lock (`F_WRLCK`) and `filedes` is not open for writing.
Note: The page uses `fcntl()` terms (`F_SETLK`, `F_SETLKW`, `l_type`) that are not `lockf()` requests.

**lockf.3-E4** `EINTR`: the command parameter is `F_SETLKW` and the `fcntl()` function was interrupted by a signal which was caught.
Note: The page describes this error in `fcntl()` terms; for `lockf()` it presumably applies to a blocked `F_LOCK`, but the page does not say so.

**lockf.3-E5** `EDEADLK`: the lock is blocked by a lock from another process, and putting the calling process to sleep waiting for it would cause a deadlock.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), close(2), exec(2), fcntl(2), flock(2), fork(2), open(2), read(2), write(2)

Page: `man3/longjmp.html`; same text as `setjmp(3)`. AES: Full use.

**longjmp.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <setjmp.h>`; `int setjmp(jmp_buf environment)`; `void longjmp(jmp_buf environment, int value)`; `int _setjmp(jmp_buf environment)`; `void _longjmp(jmp_buf environment, int value)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
