  Test: declare a `jmp_buf`, pass it to `setjmp()` and later `longjmp()`; confirm it compiles and works.

**longjmp.3-3** [OSF/1] `setjmp()` saves the current stack context and the signal mask in the buffer given by `environment`.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, call `setjmp()`, unblock `SIGUSR1`, call `longjmp()`; after return from `setjmp()` check with `sigprocmask()` that `SIGUSR1` is blocked again.

**longjmp.3-4** [OSF/1] `longjmp()` restores the stack context and signal mask saved by `setjmp()` in the corresponding `environment` buffer.
  Test: as in longjmp.3-3, verify both control returns to the `setjmp()` point and the mask is restored.

**longjmp.3-5** [OSF/1] After `longjmp()` runs, execution continues as if the corresponding `setjmp()` call had just returned the value of `value`.
  Test: `if ((r = setjmp(env)) == 0) longjmp(env, 42);` then check `r == 42`.

**longjmp.3-6** [OSF/1] The function that called `setjmp()` must not have returned before `longjmp()` completes.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement on the implementation; it is a constraint on the caller (see longjmp.3-13 for the detected-violation behaviour).

**longjmp.3-7** [OSF/1] `setjmp()` and `longjmp()` save and restore the signal mask; `_setjmp()` and `_longjmp()` manipulate only the stack context.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, `_setjmp()`, unblock `SIGUSR1`, `_longjmp()`; check `SIGUSR1` is still unblocked after return.

**longjmp.3-8** [OSF/1] Because it bypasses the usual call and return mechanisms, `longjmp()` executes correctly in contexts of interrupts, signals and their associated functions.
  Test: install a `SIGALRM` handler that calls `longjmp()` to a point set in `main`; raise `SIGALRM`; check control reaches the `setjmp()` point with the passed value.

**longjmp.3-9** [OSF/1] If `longjmp()` is invoked from a nested signal handler (a function invoked by a signal raised while another signal was being handled), the behavior is undefined.
  Test: Not testable; behaviour is undefined.

**longjmp.3-10** [OSF/1] The reentrant versions of `setjmp()` and `longjmp()` are identical in behavior to `_setjmp()` and `_longjmp()`.
  Test: build with the reentrant library and check (as in longjmp.3-7) that the signal mask is not restored.
  Note: The page text is cut off here ("identical in behavior to the _setjmp() and _longjmp()" with no ending), and it does not say how the reentrant versions are selected.

**longjmp.3-11** [Compat] System V versions of `setjmp()` and `longjmp()`, equivalent to `_setjmp()` and `_longjmp()` respectively, are supported for compatibility. To use them, link with the `libsys5` library before linking with libc.
  Test: link with `-lsys5` before libc; check that `longjmp()` does not restore the signal mask.

**longjmp.3-12** [OSF/1] If `longjmp()` is called with an `environment` not previously set by `setjmp()`, or if the function that made the corresponding `setjmp()` call has already returned, the results are undefined.
  Test: Not testable in general; results are undefined (see longjmp.3-13).

**longjmp.3-13** [OSF/1] If `longjmp()` detects such a condition, it calls `longjmperror()`. If `longjmperror()` returns, the program is aborted. The default `longjmperror()` prints an error message to standard error and returns. Users may supply their own `longjmperror()` to exit more gracefully.
  Test: call `setjmp()` in a function that returns, then `longjmp()` to that buffer with a user-defined `longjmperror()` that writes a marker and calls `_exit(3)`; expect exit status 3 (if detection occurs); with the default, expect a message on stderr and abnormal termination.
  Note: The page does not say which invalid uses are detected, so a test can only check the behaviour when detection occurs.

**longjmp.3-14** [OSF/1] `setjmp()` returns 0 on its direct call; when the return is caused by `longjmp()` it returns a nonzero value.
  Test: check the first return is 0 and the return after `longjmp(env, 5)` is 5.

**longjmp.3-15** [OSF/1] `longjmp()` cannot cause `setjmp()` to return 0; if `value` is 0, execution continues as if `setjmp()` had returned 1.
  Test: `longjmp(env, 0)`; check `setjmp()` appears to return 1.

**longjmp.3-16** [OSF/1] All accessible data have values as of the time `longjmp()` is called.
  Test: set a `volatile` global and a `volatile` local after `setjmp()`, then `longjmp()`; check both keep the values assigned before `longjmp()`.

Related: Functions: siglongjmp(3), sigsetjmp(3)

### mkfifo(3)

Page: `man3/mkfifo.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mkfifo.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>`, `#include <sys/stat.h>`; `int mkfifo(const char *path, mode_t mode)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**mkfifo.3-2** [OSF/1] `path` names the new file. If the final component of `path` names a symbolic link, the link is traversed and pathname resolution continues.
  Test: create a symlink `l` pointing to nonexistent `f`; `mkfifo("l", 0666)`; check whether `f` is created as a FIFO (per the page, resolution continues through the link).
  Note: The page does not say what happens when the link's target already exists.

**mkfifo.3-3** [OSF/1] `mode` specifies the type, attributes and access permissions of the file, built by ORing values described in `sys/mode.h`.
  Test: `mkfifo("f", 0640)` with umask 0; `stat()` shows `S_ISFIFO` and permission bits 0640.

**mkfifo.3-4** [OSF/1] `mkfifo()` is an interface to `mknod()` where the file created is a FIFO special file. No special system privileges are required.
  Test: as an unprivileged user, `mkfifo("f", 0666)` returns 0 and `stat()` shows a FIFO.

**mkfifo.3-5** [OSF/1] On success, `mkfifo()` marks `st_atime`, `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the new file for update, and marks `st_ctime` and `st_mtime` of the containing directory for update.
  Test: record the directory's times, sleep 1 s, `mkfifo()`; `stat()` the FIFO and directory and check the times are at least the call time.

**mkfifo.3-6** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: successful call returns 0; a call on an existing name returns -1 with `errno` set.

**mkfifo.3-7** [OSF/1] If `mkfifo()` fails, the new file is not created.
  Test: provoke `EACCES` on a non-writable directory and check with `stat()` that no file exists.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these values):

**mkfifo.3-E1** `EACCES`: a component of the path prefix denies search permission, or write permission is denied on the parent directory of the FIFO.

**mkfifo.3-E2** `EPERM`: `mode` specifies a file type other than `S_IFIFO` and the caller lacks the `DEV_CONFIG` system privilege.

**mkfifo.3-E3** `EEXIST`: the named file exists.

**mkfifo.3-E4** `EROFS`: the directory in which the file would be created is on a read-only file system.

**mkfifo.3-E5** `ENOSPC`: the directory that would contain the new file cannot be extended, or the file system is out of file allocation resources.

**mkfifo.3-E6** `EDQUOT`: the directory cannot be extended because the user's quota of disk blocks or inodes on the file system is exhausted.

**mkfifo.3-E7** `ELOOP`: too many links were encountered in translating `path`.

**mkfifo.3-E8** `ENAMETOOLONG`: the length of `path` exceeds `PATH_MAX`, or a pathname component is longer than `NAME_MAX`.

**mkfifo.3-E9** `ENOENT`: a component of the path prefix does not exist, or `path` points to an empty string.

**mkfifo.3-E10** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix is not a directory.

Related: Functions: chmod(2), mkdir(2), mknod(2), open(2), stat(2), umask(2); Commands: chmod(1), mkdir(1)

### mktimer(3)

Page: `man3/mktimer.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mktimer.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/timers.h>`; `timer_t mktimer(int clock_type, int notify_type, void *reserved)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**mktimer.3-2** [OSF/1] `clock_type` specifies the system-wide clock used as the per-process time base for the new timer.
  Test: `mktimer(TIMEOFDAY, DELIVERY_SIGNALS, NULL)` succeeds.

**mktimer.3-3** [OSF/1] `notify_type` specifies the mechanism by which the process is notified when the timer times out.
  Test: covered by mktimer.3-7.

**mktimer.3-4** [OSF/1] `reserved` is not used; it is specified for future support of other delivery mechanisms.
  Test: pass `NULL` and a non-NULL pointer; both calls behave the same.

**mktimer.3-5** [OSF/1] `mktimer()` allocates a per-process timer using the given clock as its timebase and returns a unique timer ID of type `timer_t`, used to identify the timer in per-process timer requests.
  Test: the returned ID is accepted by `reltimer()` and `rmtimer()`.

**mktimer.3-6** [OSF/1] Each implementation defines a set of usable clocks and one or more notification mechanisms. OSF/1 allows each process to allocate one per-process timer with `clock_type` `TIMEOFDAY` (defined in `timers.h`) and `notify_type` `DELIVERY_SIGNALS`.
  Test: first `mktimer(TIMEOFDAY, DELIVERY_SIGNALS, NULL)` succeeds; a second call fails with `EAGAIN`.

**mktimer.3-7** [OSF/1] With `notify_type` `DELIVERY_SIGNALS`, the system sends `SIGALRM` to the process whenever the timer expires.
  Test: allocate a timer, arm it with `reltimer()` for 100 ms, catch `SIGALRM`, and check it arrives.

**mktimer.3-8** [OSF/1] Per-process timers are not inherited by a child process across `fork()` or `exec()`.
  Test: allocate and arm a timer, `fork()`; in the child check no `SIGALRM` arrives and that `mktimer()` succeeds there; likewise after `exec()`.

**mktimer.3-9** [OSF/1] `mktimer()` is part of the POSIX 1003.4 real time extensions, which is not an approved standard and is liable to change.
  Test: Not testable; informational.

**mktimer.3-10** [OSF/1] On success returns a `timer_t` value that may be passed to a per-process timer call; otherwise returns `(timer_t)-1` and sets `errno`.
  Test: check the error return value equals `(timer_t)-1` with an invalid `clock_type`.

Errors (the call returns `(timer_t)-1` and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**mktimer.3-E1** `EAGAIN`: the calling process has already allocated all available timers.

**mktimer.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `clock_type` or `notify_type` is invalid.

Related: Functions: exec(2), fork(2), getclock(3), gettimer(3), reltimer(3), rmtimer(3), setclock(3)

### mlock(3), munlock(3)

Page: `man3/mlock.html`; same text as `munlock(3)`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**mlock.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <mlock.h>`; `int mlock(void *addr, size_t len)`; `int munlock(void *addr, size_t len)`.
  Test: compile calls with these prototypes.

**mlock.3-2** [DEC] `addr` points to the start of the region to lock or unlock and must be a multiple of the page size returned by `sysconf`.
  Test: `mlock(page_aligned_buf + 1, 1)` fails with `EINVAL`.

**mlock.3-3** [DEC] `len` is the size of the region; it is rounded up to a multiple of the page size.
  Test: as superuser, `mlock(aligned, 1)` returns 0 and a whole page is locked (no error on later `munlock(aligned, pagesize)`).

**mlock.3-4** [DEC] `mlock()` guarantees residency of a region of process address space, given by an address and a length.
  Test: Not testable from user space beyond the return value; residency is not observable directly.

**mlock.3-5** [DEC] A lock is not inherited across a `fork` or an `exec`.
  Test: Not directly testable from user space; residency of the child's pages is not observable.

**mlock.3-6** [DEC] `munlock()` unlocks a previously locked region. A memory lock is also unlocked by an `exec` call or by process termination.
  Test: `mlock()` then `munlock()` on the same region both return 0.

**mlock.3-7** [DEC] All memory locks are removed if an address range associated with the lock is unmapped.
  Test: Not directly testable from user space; lock state is not observable.

**mlock.3-8** [DEC] The caller must have superuser privileges to call `mlock()` or `munlock()`.
  Test: as a non-root user, `mlock()` fails with `EPERM`.

**mlock.3-9** [DEC] `mlock()` returns 0 on success, and the region becomes locked and resident; on failure it returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: as root, `mlock()` of a valid aligned region returns 0.

**mlock.3-10** [DEC] `munlock()` returns 0 on success; on failure it returns -1, none of the memory is unlocked, and `errno` is set.
  Test: as root, `munlock()` of an unaligned address returns -1 with `EINVAL`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says both functions fail under these conditions):

**mlock.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `addr` is not a multiple of the page size returned by `sysconf`.

**mlock.3-E2** `ENOMEM`: the address range given by `addr` and `len` does not all correspond to valid mapped pages in the process's address space.

**mlock.3-E3** `ENOMEM`: the calling process has exceeded an implementation-defined limit on the amount of memory it may lock.

**mlock.3-E4** `EAGAIN`: some or all of the memory could not be locked when the call was made.

**mlock.3-E5** `EPERM`: the calling process does not have the appropriate privileges.

**mlock.3-E6** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 memory locking is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

Related: exec(2), _exit(2), fork(2), mlockall(3), munmap(3), sysconf(3)

### mlockall(3), munlockall(3)

Page: `man3/mlockall.html`; same text as `munlockall(3)`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**mlockall.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <mlock.h>`; `int mlockall(int flags)`; `int munlockall()`.
  Test: compile calls with these prototypes.

**mlockall.3-2** [DEC] `flags` chooses whether the pages locked are those currently mapped, those mapped in the future, or both; it is one or more of `MCL_CURRENT` and `MCL_FUTURE`.
  Test: as root, `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT|MCL_FUTURE)` returns 0.

**mlockall.3-3** [DEC] `mlockall()` locks all pages mapped by the process's address space into memory until unlocked by `munlockall()`, until the process exits, or until it calls `exec`.
  Test: as root, `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT)` returns 0, then `munlockall()` returns 0.

**mlockall.3-4** [DEC] `MCL_CURRENT` locks all pages currently mapped into the address space.
  Test: as root, `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT)` returns 0.

**mlockall.3-5** [DEC] `MCL_FUTURE` locks all pages that become mapped in the future, when those mappings are established.
  Test: as root, `mlockall(MCL_FUTURE)` returns 0, then a new `mmap()` succeeds.

**mlockall.3-6** [DEC] A caller can specify `MCL_CURRENT` and later `MCL_FUTURE` to lock both current and future address space.
  Test: as root, `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT)` then `mlockall(MCL_FUTURE)` both return 0.

**mlockall.3-7** [DEC] `munlockall()` unlocks all currently mapped pages. Pages mapped after a `munlockall()` are not locked unless a later `mlockall()` says so.
  Test: as root, `mlockall(MCL_FUTURE)`, `munlockall()`, then `mmap()`; all succeed (lock state itself is not observable).

**mlockall.3-8** [DEC] A lock is not inherited across a `fork` or an `exec`.
  Test: Not directly testable from user space; lock state is not observable.

**mlockall.3-9** [DEC] All memory locks are removed if an address range associated with the lock is unmapped.
  Test: Not directly testable from user space.

**mlockall.3-10** [DEC] The caller must have superuser privileges to call `mlockall()` or `munlockall()`.
  Test: as a non-root user, `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT)` fails with `EPERM`.

**mlockall.3-11** [DEC] `mlockall()` returns 0 on success and memory is locked; on failure it returns -1, no memory is locked, and `errno` is set.
  Test: as root, `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT)` returns 0.

**mlockall.3-12** [DEC] `munlockall()` returns 0 "if it is supported by the implementation"; otherwise -1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: as root, `munlockall()` returns 0 or -1 with `ENOSYS`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says both functions fail under these conditions):

**mlockall.3-E1** `EAGAIN`: some or all of the memory could not be locked when the call was made.

**mlockall.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `flags` is invalid.

**mlockall.3-E3** `ENOMEM`: the calling process has exceeded an implementation-defined limit on the amount of memory it may lock.

**mlockall.3-E4** `EPERM`: the calling process does not have the appropriate privileges.

**mlockall.3-E5** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 memory locking is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

Related: exec(2), _exit(2), fork(2), mlock(3), munmap(3)

### mount(3)

Page: `man3/mount.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mount.3-1** [Compat] Synopsis: `#include <sys/mount.h>`; `int mount(char *spec, char *dir, int rwflag)`. Library: System V Compatibility Library (`libsys5.a`).
  Test: compile and link against `libsys5` with this prototype.

**mount.3-2** [Compat] OSF/1 supports two `mount()` functions, the BSD one and the System V one; the default is the BSD `mount()`. To use the version on this page, link with `libsys5` before libc.
  Test: link with `-lsys5` before libc and check the three-argument form is used.

**mount.3-3** [Compat] `spec` points to the pathname of the file system to be mounted; `dir` points to the pathname of the directory on which it is mounted.
  Test: as root, mount a block device on an empty directory; `mount()` returns 0.

**mount.3-4** [Compat] `mount()` mounts a removable file system on the block special file `spec` onto the directory `dir`.
  Test: as root, after mounting, `stat()` of `dir` shows a different `st_dev`.

**mount.3-5** [Compat] If `rwflag` is 1, writing is forbidden on the mounted file system; otherwise writing is permitted according to individual file accessibility.
  Test: mount with `rwflag` 1; creating a file under `dir` fails; mount with 0 and it succeeds.

**mount.3-6** [Compat] `mount()` can only be invoked by the superuser.
  Test: as non-root, `mount()` fails with `EPERM`.

**mount.3-7** [Compat] Returns 0 if the file system was mounted; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: see mount.3-3 and the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**mount.3-E1** `EPERM`: the effective user ID of the caller is not root.

**mount.3-E2** `ENOENT`: `spec` or `dir` points to a pathname that does not exist.

**mount.3-E3** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix of `spec` or `dir` is not a directory.

**mount.3-E4** `ENOTBLK`: the device identified by `spec` is not a block-special device.

**mount.3-E5** `ENXIO`: the device identified by `spec` does not exist.

**mount.3-E6** `ENOTDIR`: the pathname pointed to by `dir` is not a directory.

**mount.3-E7** `EBUSY`: `dir` has already been mounted onto, or `dir` is a current working directory of some process, or `dir` is otherwise busy; or `spec` is already mounted; or the system mount table is full.

Related: Commands: mount(8)

### msem_init(3)

Page: `man3/msem_init.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msem_init.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/mman.h>`; `msemaphore *msem_init(msemaphore *sem, int initial_value)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**msem_init.3-2** [OSF/1] `sem` points to an `msemaphore` structure in which the semaphore's state is stored.
  Test: covered by msem_init.3-4.

**msem_init.3-3** [OSF/1] `msem_init()` allocates a new binary semaphore and initializes its state.
  Test: `msem_init(p, MSEM_UNLOCKED)` on a shared mapping returns `p`.

**msem_init.3-4** [OSF/1] If `initial_value` is `MSEM_LOCKED`, the semaphore starts locked; if `MSEM_UNLOCKED`, it starts unlocked.
  Test: after `msem_init(p, MSEM_LOCKED)`, `msem_lock(p, MSEM_IF_NOWAIT)` fails with `EAGAIN`; after `msem_init(p, MSEM_UNLOCKED)` it returns 0.

**msem_init.3-5** [OSF/1] The `msemaphore` structure is located within a mapped file or shared memory region created by a successful `mmap()` and having both read and write access.
  Test: `mmap()` a region with `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE` and `MAP_SHARED`, place the semaphore in it; `msem_init()` succeeds.
  Note: The page does not say what happens if the structure is elsewhere (for example on the stack).

**msem_init.3-6** [OSF/1] In a mapped file region, any reference by a process that has mapped the same file, through a `(struct msemaphore *)` pointer resolving to the same file offset, refers to the same semaphore.
  Test: two processes map the same file at different addresses; one locks the semaphore at offset 0, the other's `msem_lock(..., MSEM_IF_NOWAIT)` at offset 0 fails with `EAGAIN`.

**msem_init.3-7** [OSF/1] In an anonymous shared memory region, any reference by a process sharing the region, through a pointer resolving to the same offset from the region's start, refers to the same semaphore.
  Test: map an anonymous shared region, `fork()`; parent locks, child's `MSEM_IF_NOWAIT` lock fails with `EAGAIN`.

**msem_init.3-8** [OSF/1] Any previous semaphore state stored in the structure is ignored and overwritten.
  Test: lock a semaphore, then `msem_init(p, MSEM_UNLOCKED)`; `msem_lock(p, MSEM_IF_NOWAIT)` returns 0.

**msem_init.3-9** [OSF/1] On success returns a pointer to the initialized `msemaphore` structure; on error returns null and sets `errno`.
  Test: check the return equals `sem`; with an invalid `initial_value` check it returns `NULL` with `EINVAL`.

Errors (the call returns null and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**msem_init.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `initial_value` is not valid.

**msem_init.3-E2** `ENOMEM`: a new semaphore could not be created.

Related: Functions: mmap(2), msem_lock(3), msem_remove(3), msem_unlock(3)

### msem_lock(3)

Page: `man3/msem_lock.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msem_lock.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/mman.h>`; `int msem_lock(msemaphore *sem, int condition)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**msem_lock.3-2** [OSF/1] `sem` points to the `msemaphore` structure of the semaphore to lock; `condition` decides whether the call waits for a currently locked semaphore to unlock.
  Test: covered by msem_lock.3-4 and msem_lock.3-5.

**msem_lock.3-3** [OSF/1] If the semaphore is not currently locked, it is locked and `msem_lock()` returns successfully (0).
  Test: `msem_init(p, MSEM_UNLOCKED)`, then `msem_lock(p, 0)` returns 0.

**msem_lock.3-4** [OSF/1] If the semaphore is locked and `condition` is `MSEM_IF_NOWAIT`, `msem_lock()` returns with an error.
  Test: lock it, then `msem_lock(p, MSEM_IF_NOWAIT)` returns -1 with `EAGAIN`.

**msem_lock.3-5** [OSF/1] If the semaphore is locked and `condition` is 0, `msem_lock()` does not return until the caller locks the semaphore or an error occurs.
  Test: parent holds the lock; child calls `msem_lock(p, 0)` and blocks; parent unlocks after 1 s; child returns 0 after about 1 s.

**msem_lock.3-6** [OSF/1] All `msem_lock()` and `msem_unlock()` calls by multiple processes sharing a common `msemaphore` structure behave as if serialized.
  Test: several processes each do many lock/increment/unlock cycles on a shared counter; final count equals the total number of increments.

**msem_lock.3-7** [OSF/1] If the structure holds any value not resulting from `msem_init()` followed by a (possibly empty) sequence of `msem_lock()` and `msem_unlock()` calls, the results are undefined.
  Test: Not testable; results are undefined.

**msem_lock.3-8** [OSF/1] The address of an `msemaphore` structure may be significant; if the structure holds a value copied from one at a different address, the result is undefined.
  Test: Not testable; results are undefined.

**msem_lock.3-9** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; on error returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: see msem_lock.3-3 and msem_lock.3-4.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**msem_lock.3-E1** `EAGAIN`: `MSEM_IF_NOWAIT` was specified and the semaphore was already locked.

**msem_lock.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `sem` points to a structure specifying a semaphore that has been removed, or `condition` is invalid.

**msem_lock.3-E3** `EINTR`: `msem_lock()` was interrupted by a signal that was caught.

Related: Functions: msem_init(3), msem_remove(3), msem_unlock(3)

### msem_remove(3)

Page: `man3/msem_remove.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msem_remove.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/mman.h>`; `int msem_remove(msemaphore *sem)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**msem_remove.3-2** [OSF/1] `sem` points to the `msemaphore` structure of the semaphore to remove; `msem_remove()` removes that binary semaphore.
  Test: `msem_remove(p)` after `msem_init()` returns 0.

**msem_remove.3-3** [OSF/1] Any later use of the structure before it is again initialized by `msem_init()` has undefined results.
  Test: Not testable; results are undefined (but see msem_remove.3-E1 and msem_lock-E2).

**msem_remove.3-4** [OSF/1] `msem_remove()` causes any process waiting in `msem_lock()` on the removed semaphore to return with an error.
  Test: parent holds the lock; child blocks in `msem_lock(p, 0)`; parent calls `msem_remove(p)`; child's call returns -1.
  Note: The page does not name the `errno` the waiter gets.

**msem_remove.3-5** [OSF/1] If the structure holds any value not resulting from `msem_init()` followed by a (possibly empty) sequence of `msem_lock()` and `msem_unlock()` calls, the result is undefined.
  Test: Not testable; result is undefined.

**msem_remove.3-6** [OSF/1] The address of an `msemaphore` structure may be significant; if it holds a value copied from one at a different address, the result is undefined.
  Test: Not testable; result is undefined.

**msem_remove.3-7** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; on error returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: see msem_remove.3-2 and msem_remove.3-E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to this):

**msem_remove.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `sem` points to a structure specifying a semaphore that has been removed.

Related: Functions: msem_init(3), msem_lock(3), msem_unlock(3), munmap(2)

### msem_unlock(3)

Page: `man3/msem_unlock.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msem_unlock.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/mman.h>`; `int msem_unlock(msemaphore *sem, int condition)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**msem_unlock.3-2** [OSF/1] `sem` points to the structure of the semaphore to unlock; `condition` decides whether the semaphore is unlocked when no other process is waiting to lock it.
  Test: covered by msem_unlock.3-4 to msem_unlock.3-6.

**msem_unlock.3-3** [OSF/1] `msem_unlock()` unlocks a binary semaphore.
  Test: lock, then `msem_unlock(p, 0)` returns 0 and `msem_lock(p, MSEM_IF_NOWAIT)` then returns 0.

**msem_unlock.3-4** [OSF/1] If `condition` is 0, the semaphore is unlocked whether or not other processes are trying to lock it.
  Test: as in msem_unlock.3-3 with no waiters; returns 0.

**msem_unlock.3-5** [OSF/1] If `condition` is `MSEM_IF_WAITERS` and another process is waiting to lock the semaphore, or it cannot be reliably determined whether one is waiting, the semaphore is unlocked.
  Test: child blocks in `msem_lock(p, 0)`; parent calls `msem_unlock(p, MSEM_IF_WAITERS)`, which returns 0, and the child then acquires the lock.

**msem_unlock.3-6** [OSF/1] If `condition` is `MSEM_IF_WAITERS` and no process is waiting, the semaphore is not unlocked and an error is returned.
  Test: lock with no waiters; `msem_unlock(p, MSEM_IF_WAITERS)` returns -1 with `EAGAIN`, and `msem_lock(p, MSEM_IF_NOWAIT)` still fails with `EAGAIN`.
  Note: The page also allows the semaphore to be unlocked when waiting "cannot be reliably determined", so a conforming system may return 0 here.

**msem_unlock.3-7** [OSF/1] All `msem_lock()` and `msem_unlock()` calls by multiple processes sharing a common structure behave as if serialized.
  Test: see msem_lock-6.

**msem_unlock.3-8** [OSF/1] If the structure holds any value not resulting from `msem_init()` followed by a (possibly empty) sequence of `msem_lock()` and `msem_unlock()` calls, the results are undefined.
  Test: Not testable; results are undefined.

**msem_unlock.3-9** [OSF/1] The address of an `msemaphore` structure may be significant; if it holds a value copied from one at a different address, the result is undefined.
  Test: Not testable; result is undefined.

**msem_unlock.3-10** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; on error returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: see msem_unlock.3-3 and msem_unlock.3-6.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**msem_unlock.3-E1** `EAGAIN`: `MSEM_IF_WAITERS` was specified and there were no waiters.

**msem_unlock.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `sem` points to a structure specifying a semaphore that has been removed, or `condition` is invalid.

Related: Functions: msem_init(3), msem_lock(3), msem_remove(3)

### nanosleep(3)

Page: `man3/nanosleep.html`. The page also documents `nanosleep_getres`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**nanosleep.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <timers.h>`; `int nanosleep(const struct timespec *rqtp, struct timespec *rmtp)`; `int nanosleep_getres(struct timespec *res, struct timespec *max)`.
  Test: compile calls with these prototypes.

**nanosleep.3-2** [DEC] `rqtp` points to a `timespec` giving the interval during which the caller is suspended.
  Test: `nanosleep({0, 200000000}, &rem)` returns 0 after at least 200 ms.

**nanosleep.3-3** [DEC] `rmtp` points to a `timespec` that receives the time remaining in the requested interval, or zero if the full interval has elapsed.
  Test: after an uninterrupted sleep, check `rem` is zero.

**nanosleep.3-4** [DEC] `nanosleep()` suspends the process until the interval in `rqtp` has elapsed, or a signal is delivered whose action is to call a signal-catching function or to terminate the process.
  Test: sleep 5 s with a 1 s `alarm()` and a `SIGALRM` handler; the call returns after about 1 s.

**nanosleep.3-5** [DEC] The suspension may be longer than requested, because the argument is rounded up to an integer multiple of the sleep resolution, or because of scheduling of other activity.
  Test: request 1 ns; check the elapsed time is at least the resolution reported by `nanosleep_getres()`.

**nanosleep.3-6** [DEC] `nanosleep_getres()` returns the resolution and the maximum value supported by `nanosleep()`, via `res` and `max`.
  Test: call with two `timespec` pointers; both structures are filled in.

**nanosleep.3-7** [DEC] If either argument pointer of `nanosleep_getres()` is NULL, the corresponding value is not returned.
  Test: `nanosleep_getres(NULL, &max)` and `nanosleep_getres(&res, NULL)` succeed and fill only the non-NULL argument.

**nanosleep.3-8** [DEC] When `nanosleep()` returns because the requested time elapsed, it returns 0.
  Test: see nanosleep.3-2.

**nanosleep.3-9** [DEC] When `nanosleep()` is interrupted by a signal, it returns +1 and stores the unslept time in `rmtp`.
  Test: as in nanosleep.3-4; check return value 1 and that `rem` is about 4 s.
  Note: The page says +1, not -1 with `EINTR`; a test should follow the page.

**nanosleep.3-10** [DEC] On failure `nanosleep()` returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: see nanosleep.3-E1.

**nanosleep.3-11** [DEC] `nanosleep_getres()` does not fail.
  Test: call it with valid pointers and with NULLs; it never returns -1.
  Note: The page does not state `nanosleep_getres()`'s return value on success.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**nanosleep.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `rqtp` specified a nanosecond value less than zero or greater than or equal to 1000 million.

**nanosleep.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `rqtp` specified a time that exceeds the maximum time supported by `nanosleep()`.

Related: sleep(1)

### nice(3)

Page: `man3/nice.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**nice.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int nice(int increment)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`), Berkeley Compatibility Library (`libbsd.a`).
  Test: compile and link a call with this prototype.

**nice.3-2** [OSF/1] `increment` is added to the current process priority. Negative values may be given, but values exceeding the high or low limit are truncated.
  Test: `nice(1000)` does not fail and leaves the nice value at the high limit; as root, `nice(-1000)` leaves it at the low limit.

**nice.3-3** [OSF/1] `nice()` adds `increment` to the nice value of the calling process. The nice value is nonnegative; raising it gives the process lower CPU priority.
  Test: `nice(5)` from a default process; `getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0)` reflects an increase of 5.

**nice.3-4** [OSF/1] System V priorities are in the range 0 to 39 and BSD ones in -20 to 20, so OSF/1 supports two versions of `nice()`. The default (libc) version behaves like System V: `increment` modifies a value in the range 0 to 39.
  Test: link with libc only; check results stay within the expected range.
  Note: The page says "-20 to 20" for BSD, not "-20 to 19".

**nice.3-5** [Compat] For BSD behavior, use the Berkeley Compatibility Library (`libbsd.a`); then `increment` modifies a value in the range -20 to 20.
  Test: link with `-lbsd`; check `nice(1)` behaves per the BSD range.
  Note: The page says "compile with" the library; it means link with it.

**nice.3-6** [OSF/1] On success, `nice()` returns the new nice value minus `NZERO`; otherwise -1 and `errno` is set.
  Test: from a process at the default nice value, `nice(3)` returns 3 (if the default equals `NZERO`).
  Note: The page does not say how a legitimate return of -1 is told apart from an error.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**nice.3-E1** `EPERM`: (libc version) the calling process does not have appropriate privilege.

**nice.3-E2** (libbsd version) `errno` may be set to the same values as `setpriority()`.

Related: Functions: exec(2), getpriority(2)

### pause(3)

Page: `man3/pause.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**pause.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int pause(void)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**pause.3-2** [OSF/1] `pause()` suspends the calling process until it receives a signal whose action is to run a signal-catching function or to terminate the process.
  Test: install a `SIGALRM` handler, `alarm(1)`, `pause()`; returns after about 1 s.

**pause.3-3** [OSF/1] "The signal must not be one that is not acknowledged by the calling process."
  Test: Not testable as written; see pause.3-2 (an ignored signal, whose action is neither to catch nor to terminate, does not end `pause()`).
  Note: The page's double negative is unclear.

**pause.3-4** [OSF/1] `pause()` does not affect the action taken when a signal is received.
  Test: after `pause()` returns, `sigaction()` shows the handler unchanged.

**pause.3-5** [OSF/1] `pause()` is redefined so that only the calling thread is suspended.
  Test: in a threaded program, one thread calls `pause()` while another keeps incrementing a counter; the counter advances.

**pause.3-6** [OSF/1] `pause()` is not supported for multi-threaded applications.
  Test: Not testable; it is a statement of non-support.
  Note: The page contradicts itself: pause.3-5 describes thread behaviour while this NOTE says multithreaded use is unsupported.

**pause.3-7** [OSF/1] If the signal causes the process to end, `pause()` does not return.
  Test: child calls `pause()`; parent sends `SIGTERM` (default action); `wait()` shows termination by `SIGTERM`.

**pause.3-8** [OSF/1] If the signal is caught and the handler returns, the process resumes from the point of suspension and `pause()` returns -1 with `errno` set to `EINTR`.
  Test: as in pause.3-2, check return -1 and `errno == EINTR`.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to this):

**pause.3-E1** `EINTR`: the signal is caught by the calling process and control is returned from the signal-catching function.

Related: Functions: alarm(3), kill(2), sigaction(2), sigvec(2), wait(2)

### pthread_cancel(3)

Page: `man3/pthread_cancel.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (DCE Threads), so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**pthread_cancel.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <pthread.h>`; `int pthread_cancel(pthread_t thread)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**pthread_cancel.3-2** [DEC] `thread` is the thread that receives the cancel request. The routine sends a cancel to that thread. A cancel asks the target (which may be the caller itself) to terminate as quickly as possible.
  Test: create a thread blocked in `pthread_cond_wait()`, `pthread_cancel()` it, `pthread_join()` it; join completes.

**pthread_cancel.3-3** [DEC] Issuing a cancel does not guarantee that the cancelled thread receives or handles it. The target may delay processing a received cancel, for example to finish an operation that cannot be interrupted where the cancel was requested.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement; it only permits delay.

**pthread_cancel.3-4** [DEC] Because of communication delays, the caller can only rely on the cancel eventually becoming pending in the target, provided the target does not terminate first. The caller has no guarantee that a pending cancel is delivered, because delivery is controlled by the target.
  Test: target loops calling `pthread_testcancel()`; after `pthread_cancel()`, the target eventually terminates.

**pthread_cancel.3-5** [DEC] When a cancel is delivered, termination processing is similar to `pthread_exit`: outstanding cleanup routines run in the context of the target thread, and a status of -1 is made available to any thread joining the target.
  Test: target pushes a cleanup handler that records `pthread_self()`, then waits; cancel and join; check the handler ran with the target's identity and the join status is `(pthread_addr_t)-1`.

**pthread_cancel.3-6** [DEC] This routine is preferred for implementing Ada's abort statement and any other language or software construct for requesting thread cancellation.
  Test: Not testable; advice.

**pthread_cancel.3-7** [DEC] The results are unpredictable if `thread` refers to a thread that does not currently exist.
  Test: Not testable; results are unpredictable.
  Note: The page also lists `ESRCH` for a nonexistent thread, which conflicts with "unpredictable".

**pthread_cancel.3-8** [DEC] Returns 0 on success; on error returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: see pthread_cancel.3-2; check the return is 0.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**pthread_cancel.3-E1** `EINVAL`: the specified thread is invalid.

**pthread_cancel.3-E2** `ESRCH`: `thread` does not specify an existing thread.

Related: pthread_exit(3), pthread_join(3), pthread_setasynccancel(3), pthread_setcancel(3), pthread_testcancel(3)

### pthread_create(3)

Page: `man3/pthread_create.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (DCE Threads), so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**pthread_create.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <pthread.h>`; `int pthread_create(pthread_t *thread, pthread_attr_t attr, pthread_startroutine start_routine, pthread_addr_t arg)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype (note `attr` is passed by value).

**pthread_create.3-2** [DEC] `thread` receives the thread object created.
  Test: after success, `thread` can be passed to `pthread_join()`.

**pthread_create.3-3** [DEC] `attr` is a thread attributes object defining the new thread's characteristics; if `pthread_attr_default` is given, default attributes are used.
  Test: `pthread_create(&t, pthread_attr_default, f, 0)` returns 0.
  Note: The page spells the default both `pthread_attr_default` (PARAMETERS) and `PTHREAD_ATTR_DEFAULT` (DESCRIPTION).

**pthread_create.3-4** [DEC] `start_routine` is the function run as the new thread's start routine; `arg` is an address value copied and passed to it.
  Test: pass `&x`; in the start routine check the argument equals `&x`.

**pthread_create.3-5** [DEC] The routine creates a thread object and a thread. A thread is a single, sequential flow of control within a program: the active execution of a designated routine, including nested calls. A thread object defines and controls the executing thread.
  Test: Not separately testable; definitional.

**pthread_create.3-6** [DEC] Calling it creates an internal thread object describing the thread; creates the executable thread with the attributes in `attr` (or defaults if `PTHREAD_ATTR_DEFAULT` is given); stores the new thread in `thread`; and `start_routine` is called when this routine successfully completes.
  Test: start routine sets a flag; join the thread; check the flag is set.

**pthread_create.3-7** [DEC] The thread is created in the ready state and might immediately begin running `start_routine`.
  Test: Not deterministic; informational.

**pthread_create.3-8** [DEC] The new thread begins running before `pthread_create` completes if it follows `SCHED_RR` or `SCHED_FIFO`, or has a higher priority than the creator, or both. Otherwise it runs at its turn, which with enough processors might also be before `pthread_create` returns.
  Test: on a uniprocessor, create a `SCHED_FIFO` thread with higher priority that sets a flag; check the flag is set when `pthread_create` returns.

**pthread_create.3-9** [DEC] `start_routine` is passed a copy of `arg`. "The value of the arg parameter is unspecified."
  Test: see pthread_create.3-4.
  Note: The page's sentence "The value of the arg parameter is unspecified" is unclear as written.

**pthread_create.3-10** [DEC] The thread object exists until `pthread_detach` is called or the thread terminates, whichever occurs last.
  Test: create a thread that exits, then `pthread_join()` it before detaching; the join succeeds and returns the status.

**pthread_create.3-11** [DEC] Synchronization between the creator and the new thread is through `pthread_join` (or any mutexes or condition variables they agree to use).
  Test: Not separately testable; informational.

**pthread_create.3-12** [DEC] A thread terminates when it returns from its start routine, when it calls `pthread_exit`, or when it is cancelled.
  Test: create three threads ending each way; each `pthread_join()` returns.

**pthread_create.3-13** [DEC] On termination by return from the start routine or by `pthread_exit`, the return value is copied into the thread object. If the start routine is a procedure that returns no value, the result obtained by `pthread_join` is unpredictable.
  Test: start routine returns `(pthread_addr_t)7`; join yields 7.

**pthread_create.3-14** [DEC] If the thread was cancelled, -1 is copied into the thread object as its return value. Other threads retrieve the return value with `pthread_join`.
  Test: cancel a waiting thread; join yields `(pthread_addr_t)-1`.

**pthread_create.3-15** [DEC] On termination, each per-thread context destructor is removed from the thread's list of destructors and then called, destroying all per-thread context of the thread.
  Test: create a key with a destructor, set a value in a thread, let it exit; check the destructor ran with that value.

**pthread_create.3-16** [DEC] On termination, each cleanup handler declared by `pthread_cleanup_push` and not yet removed by `pthread_cleanup_pop` is called, most recently pushed first.
  Test: push handlers A then B, call `pthread_exit`; check B runs before A.
  Note: The page lists destructors before cleanup handlers in the order of termination actions; it does not say outright that this is the required order.

**pthread_create.3-17** [DEC] On termination, a flag is set in the thread object showing the thread has terminated; this flag must be set for `pthread_join` callers to return.
  Test: join returns only after the target has terminated.

**pthread_create.3-18** [DEC] On termination, a broadcast is made so that all threads waiting in `pthread_join` on it can return.
  Test: two threads join the same target; both return when it exits.

**pthread_create.3-19** [DEC] On termination, the thread object is marked as no longer needed by the thread itself; if `pthread_detach` has been called, the object is deallocated.
  Test: Not testable from user space beyond absence of leaks.

**pthread_create.3-20** [DEC] Returns 0 on success. On error, no thread is created, the contents of `thread` are undefined, and the routine returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: check the return is 0 on success.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**pthread_create.3-E1** `EAGAIN`: the system lacks the necessary resources to create another thread.

**pthread_create.3-E2** `ENOMEM`: insufficient memory exists to create the thread attributes object; this is not a temporary condition.

Related: pthread_attr_create(3), pthread_cancel(3), pthread_detach(3), pthread_exit(3), pthread_join(3)

### pthread_exit(3)

Page: `man3/pthread_exit.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (DCE Threads), so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**pthread_exit.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <pthread.h>`; `void pthread_exit(pthread_addr_t status)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**pthread_exit.3-2** [DEC] `status` is an address value copied and returned to the caller of `pthread_join`.
  Test: thread calls `pthread_exit((pthread_addr_t)9)`; join yields 9.

**pthread_exit.3-3** [DEC] The routine terminates the calling thread and makes the status available to any thread that calls `pthread_join` on it.
  Test: code after `pthread_exit()` in the thread never runs; join returns the status.

**pthread_exit.3-4** [DEC] Returning from the start routine issues an implicit `pthread_exit`; the function's return value is the thread's exit status.
  Test: start routine returns `(pthread_addr_t)4`; join yields 4.

**pthread_exit.3-5** [DEC] The process exits when the last running thread calls `pthread_exit`.
  Test: main thread calls `pthread_exit()` after creating a thread that sleeps 1 s then calls `pthread_exit()`; the process ends after about 1 s.
  Note: The page does not state the process's exit status in this case.

**pthread_exit.3-6** [DEC] No return value.
  Test: Not applicable; the call does not return.

Related: pthread_create(3), pthread_detach(3), pthread_join(3)

### pthread_intro(3)

Page: `man3/pthread_intro.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (DCE Threads), so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**pthread_intro.3-1** [DEC] DCE Threads are a set of routines for building a multithreaded program; multithreading is used to improve a program's performance.
  Test: Not testable; informational.

**pthread_intro.3-2** [DEC] The routines are grouped as: Threads; Attributes Object; Mutex; Condition Variable; Per-Thread Context; Thread Cancellation; Thread Priority and Scheduling; Cleanup.
  Test: Not testable; organisational.

**pthread_intro.3-3** [DEC] Threads routines: `pthread_create` creates a thread; `pthread_delay_np` makes a thread wait for a period of time; `pthread_detach` marks a thread for deletion; `pthread_exit` terminates the calling thread; `pthread_join` makes the caller wait for a given thread to terminate; `pthread_once` calls an initialization routine to be executed only once; `pthread_self` obtains the current thread's identifier; `pthread_yield` tells the scheduler the current thread will release its processor to other threads of the same or higher priority.
  Test: link a program referencing each of these names from `<pthread.h>`.

**pthread_intro.3-4** [DEC] Attributes Object routines: `pthread_attr_create`, `pthread_attr_delete` (create and delete a thread attributes object); `pthread_attr_getinheritsched`, `pthread_attr_setinheritsched` (inherit scheduling attribute); `pthread_attr_getprio`, `pthread_attr_setprio` (scheduling priority attribute); `pthread_attr_getsched`, `pthread_attr_setsched` (scheduling policy attribute); `pthread_attr_getstacksize`, `pthread_attr_setstacksize` (stacksize attribute); `pthread_condattr_create`, `pthread_condattr_delete` (condition variable attributes object); `pthread_mutexattr_create`, `pthread_mutexattr_delete` (mutex attributes object); `pthread_mutexattr_getkind_np`, `pthread_mutexattr_setkind_np` (obtain and specify the mutex type attribute).
  Test: link a program referencing each of these names.

**pthread_intro.3-5** [DEC] Mutex routines: `pthread_lock_global_np` locks a global mutex; `pthread_mutex_destroy` deletes a mutex; `pthread_mutex_init` creates a mutex; `pthread_mutex_lock` locks a mutex and waits if it is already locked; `pthread_mutex_trylock` locks a mutex and returns if it is already locked; `pthread_mutex_unlock` unlocks a mutex; `pthread_unlock_global_np` unlocks a global mutex.
  Test: link a program referencing each of these names.

**pthread_intro.3-6** [DEC] Condition Variable routines: `pthread_cond_broadcast` wakes all threads waiting on a condition variable; `pthread_cond_destroy` deletes one; `pthread_cond_init` creates one; `pthread_cond_signal` wakes one waiting thread; `pthread_cond_timedwait` waits for a signal or broadcast for a specified period of time; `pthread_cond_wait` waits for a signal or broadcast; `pthread_get_expiration_np` obtains a value representing a desired expiration time.
  Test: link a program referencing each of these names.

**pthread_intro.3-7** [DEC] Per-thread Context routines: `pthread_getspecific` obtains the per-thread context associated with a key; `pthread_keycreate` generates a unique per-thread context key value; `pthread_setspecific` sets the per-thread context associated with a key.
  Test: link a program referencing each of these names.

**pthread_intro.3-8** [DEC] Thread Cancellation routines: `pthread_cancel` lets a thread request termination; `pthread_setasynccancel` enables or disables the current thread's asynchronous cancellability; `pthread_setcancel` enables or disables its general cancellability; `pthread_testcancel` requests delivery of a pending cancel.
  Test: link a program referencing each of these names.

**pthread_intro.3-9** [DEC] Priority and Scheduling routines: `pthread_getprio` obtains a thread's current priority; `pthread_getscheduler` obtains its current scheduling policy; `pthread_setprio` changes its current priority; `pthread_setscheduler` changes its current scheduling policy and priority.
  Test: link a program referencing each of these names.

**pthread_intro.3-10** [DEC] Cleanup routines: `pthread_cleanup_pop` removes a cleanup handler from the stack; `pthread_cleanup_push` establishes a cleanup handler.
  Test: compile a function using the push/pop pair.

### pthread_setasynccancel(3)

Page: `man3/pthread_setasynccancel.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (DCE Threads), so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <pthread.h>`; `int pthread_setasynccancel(int state)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-2** [DEC] `state` is the asynchronous cancellability state to set for the calling thread: `CANCEL_ON` (enabled) or `CANCEL_OFF` (disabled).
  Test: `pthread_setasynccancel(CANCEL_ON)` and `pthread_setasynccancel(CANCEL_OFF)` do not fail.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-3** [DEC] The routine enables or disables the current thread's asynchronous cancellability and returns the previous state "to the state parameter" ("On return, receives the prior state").
  Test: `pthread_setasynccancel(CANCEL_ON)` in a new thread; a following `pthread_setasynccancel(CANCEL_OFF)` reports a prior state of `CANCEL_ON` (the page does not make clear how it is reported; see Note).
  Note: The page is unclear: `state` is an `int` passed by value, so it cannot receive a value, and RETURN VALUES says 0 is returned on success. The page does not say how the previous state reaches the caller.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-4** [DEC] When general cancellability is `CANCEL_OFF`, a cancel cannot be delivered, even if a cancellable routine is called or asynchronous cancellability is enabled.
  Test: `pthread_setcancel(CANCEL_OFF)`, `pthread_setasynccancel(CANCEL_ON)`, receive a cancel, spin 1 s and call `pthread_testcancel()`; the thread is still running.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-5** [DEC] When general cancellability is `CANCEL_ON`, cancellability depends on asynchronous cancellability.
  Test: see pthread_setasynccancel.3-6 and -7.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-6** [DEC] With general `CANCEL_ON` and asynchronous `CANCEL_OFF`, the thread can only receive a cancel at cancellation points (for example condition waits, thread joins and calls to `pthread_testcancel`).
  Test: thread in a pure compute loop with no cancellation points is not cancelled for 1 s; once it calls `pthread_testcancel()` it terminates.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-7** [DEC] With both general and asynchronous cancellability `CANCEL_ON`, the thread can be cancelled at any point in its execution.
  Test: thread enables asynchronous cancel and spins in a pure loop; after `pthread_cancel()` it terminates and join returns -1.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-8** [DEC] A newly created thread's asynchronous cancellability is `CANCEL_OFF`.
  Test: in a new thread, `pthread_setasynccancel(CANCEL_OFF)` reports a previous state of `CANCEL_OFF`.

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-9** [DEC] When enabling asynchronous cancels, call the routine in a region where asynchronous delivery was disabled by a previous call. Threads routines should not be called where asynchronous delivery is enabled. The previous state can later be restored by another call.
  Test: Not testable; usage advice (restore is covered by pthread_setasynccancel.3-3).

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-10** [DEC] Returns 0 on success; on error returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: see pthread_setasynccancel.3-E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**pthread_setasynccancel.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `state` is not `CANCEL_ON` or `CANCEL_OFF`.

Related: pthread_cancel(3), pthread_setcancel(3), pthread_testcancel(3)

### pthread_setcancel(3)

Page: `man3/pthread_setcancel.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (DCE Threads), so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**pthread_setcancel.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <pthread.h>`; `int pthread_setcancel(int state)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**pthread_setcancel.3-2** [DEC] `state` is the general cancelability state to set for the calling thread: `CANCEL_ON` (enabled) or `CANCEL_OFF` (disabled).
  Test: both values are accepted.

**pthread_setcancel.3-3** [DEC] The routine enables or disables the current thread's general cancelability and returns the previous state "to the state parameter" ("On return, receives the prior state").
  Test: in a new thread, `pthread_setcancel(CANCEL_OFF)` reports a prior state of `CANCEL_ON` (the page does not make clear how; see Note).
  Note: The page is unclear in the same way as pthread_setasynccancel: `state` is passed by value, and RETURN VALUES says 0 on success.

**pthread_setcancel.3-4** [DEC] When general cancelability is `CANCEL_OFF`, a cancel cannot be delivered, even if a cancelable routine is called or asynchronous cancelability is enabled.
  Test: disable, receive a cancel, wait on a condition variable with a 1 s timeout; the wait ends by timeout, not cancel.

**pthread_setcancel.3-5** [DEC] A newly created thread's general cancelability is `CANCEL_ON`.
  Test: in a new thread, `pthread_setcancel(CANCEL_ON)` reports a previous state of `CANCEL_ON`.

**pthread_setcancel.3-6** [DEC] When cancelability is disabled, no routine is cancelable; waits must complete normally before a cancel can be delivered. The page warns that the program can then stop working with no way for the user to cancel, and advises disabling only where no long waits can occur or deferral is needed for other reasons.
  Test: disable, receive a cancel, then re-enable and call `pthread_testcancel()`; the thread terminates only then.

**pthread_setcancel.3-7** [DEC] Returns 0 on success; on error returns -1 and sets `errno`.
  Test: see pthread_setcancel.3-E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**pthread_setcancel.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `state` is not `CANCEL_ON` or `CANCEL_OFF`.

Related: pthread_cancel(3), pthread_setasynccancel(3), pthread_testcancel(3)

### pthread_testcancel(3)

Page: `man3/pthread_testcancel.html`. The page is headed "Digital" (DCE Threads), so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**pthread_testcancel.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <pthread.h>`; `void pthread_testcancel()`. No parameters.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**pthread_testcancel.3-2** [DEC] The routine requests delivery of a pending cancel to the current thread. The cancel is delivered only if one is pending and general cancel delivery is not disabled (a thread disables it with `pthread_setcancel`).
  Test: with a cancel pending and general cancel enabled, `pthread_testcancel()` does not return and join gives -1; with no cancel pending it returns.

**pthread_testcancel.3-3** [DEC] Called within very long loops, it ensures a pending cancel is noticed within a reasonable time.
  Test: see pthread_setasynccancel-6.

**pthread_testcancel.3-4** [DEC] No return value.
  Test: Not applicable.

Related: pthread_cancel(3), pthread_setasynccancel(3), pthread_setcancel(3)

### raise(3)

Page: `man3/raise.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**raise.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/signal.h>`; `int raise(int signal)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**raise.3-2** [OSF/1] `signal` is a signal number; `raise()` sends that signal to the executing program.
  Test: install a `SIGUSR1` handler that sets a flag; `raise(SIGUSR1)`; check the flag is set after the call.

**raise.3-3** [OSF/1] `raise()` is equivalent to `error = kill(getpid(), signal);`.
  Test: compare results of `raise(0)` and `kill(getpid(), 0)`, and of an invalid signal number with both.

**raise.3-4** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise returns a nonzero value and sets `errno`.
  Test: `raise(SIGUSR1)` with a handler returns 0; `raise(-1)` returns nonzero.
  Note: The page says "a nonzero value", not -1, on failure.

Errors (the call returns a nonzero value and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to this):

**raise.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `signal` is an invalid or unsupported signal number.

Related: Functions: kill(2), sigaction(2)

### reltimer(3)

Page: `man3/reltimer.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**reltimer.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/timers.h>`; `int reltimer(timer_t tmrid, struct itimerspec *val, struct itimerspec *oval)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**reltimer.3-2** [OSF/1] `tmrid` gives the per-process timer to access; `val` points to an `itimerspec` with the initial and offset timeout intervals; `oval` points to an `itimerspec` where the current timeout interval and time-to-go are stored.
  Test: arm with `val`, then call again and check `oval` holds the earlier interval and a time-to-go not greater than it.

**reltimer.3-3** [OSF/1] `reltimer()` establishes initial and offset timeout intervals for timer `tmrid`. While active, after the initial interval times out, all later timeouts are controlled by the offset value, which is used as the interval as long as `tmrid` continues to operate.
  Test: initial 100 ms, offset 50 ms; count `SIGALRM` over 1 s; expect about 19 signals.
  Note: The page does not say what a zero initial or offset value does (for example, disarm or one-shot).

**reltimer.3-4** [OSF/1] The current timeout interval and time-to-go are returned in the location `oval` points to.
  Test: see reltimer.3-2.
  Note: The page does not say whether `oval` may be NULL.

**reltimer.3-5** [OSF/1] The `itimerspec` structure, used for both `val` and `oval`, is defined in `sys/timers.h`.
  Test: compile code declaring `struct itimerspec` after including `<sys/timers.h>`.
  Note: The page does not name the structure's fields.

**reltimer.3-6** [OSF/1] Time values smaller than the timer's resolution are rounded up to the resolution. Time values larger than the timer's maximum timeout are rounded down to that maximum.
  Test: arm with 1 ns, then read back with `oval` (or `gettimer()`); the interval equals the resolution.

**reltimer.3-7** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: see reltimer.3-3 and reltimer.3-E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**reltimer.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `tmrid` does not specify an allocated per-process timer.

**reltimer.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `val` points to a nanosecond value less than zero or greater than or equal to 1000 million.

Note: The page names the parameter `timerid` in ERRORS but `tmrid` in the synopsis.

Related: Functions: alarm(3), getclock(3), gettimer(3), mktimer(3)

### sched_get_priority_max(3), sched_get_priority_min(3)

Page: `man3/sched_get_priority_max.html`; same text as `sched_get_priority_min(3)`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**sched_get_priority_max.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sched.h>`; `int sched_get_priority_max(int policy)`; `int sched_get_priority_min(int policy)`.
  Test: compile calls with these prototypes.

**sched_get_priority_max.3-2** [DEC] The functions return the maximum or minimum priority for `policy`, which must be one of `SCHED_FIFO`, `SCHED_RR` or `SCHED_OTHER` as defined in `<sched.h>`.
  Test: for each of the three policies, both calls succeed (do not return -1).

**sched_get_priority_max.3-3** [DEC] No special privileges are needed.
  Test: run the calls as an unprivileged user; they succeed.

**sched_get_priority_max.3-4** [DEC] On success the requested value is returned; on failure -1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: see sched_get_priority_max.3-2 and -E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**sched_get_priority_max.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `policy` does not represent a defined scheduling policy.

**sched_get_priority_max.3-E2** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 priority scheduling is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).
