### sched_get_rr_interval(3)

Page: `man3/sched_get_rr_interval.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**sched_get_rr_interval.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sched.h>`; `int sched_get_rr_interval(struct timespec *min)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**sched_get_rr_interval.3-2** [DEC] The function stores in `min` the current quantum for process execution under `SCHED_RR`.
  Test: call it with a valid pointer; returns 0 and `min` is filled in.

**sched_get_rr_interval.3-3** [DEC] A process running under round-robin that runs without blocking or yielding for more than this time "may be preempted" by another runnable process at the same priority.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement; the page says only that preemption "may" occur.

**sched_get_rr_interval.3-4** [DEC] No special privileges are needed.
  Test: run as an unprivileged user; succeeds.

**sched_get_rr_interval.3-5** [DEC] Returns 0 on success; -1 with `errno` set on failure.
  Test: see -2 and -E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**sched_get_rr_interval.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `min` is NULL.

**sched_get_rr_interval.3-E2** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 priority scheduling is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

Related: sched_getscheduler(3), sched_get_sched_param(3), sched_setscheduler(3), sched_set_sched_param(3)

### sched_get_sched_param(3)

Page: `man3/sched_get_sched_param.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sched.h>`; `int sched_get_sched_param(pid_t pid, struct sched_param *param)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-2** [DEC] `pid` is the process whose scheduling parameters are returned; if `pid` is zero, those of the calling process are returned.
  Test: results for `pid` 0 and `getpid()` are equal.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-3** [DEC] `param` points to a `sched_param` structure (defined in `<sched.h>`) that receives the scheduling parameters; its `priority` field is the current priority of the process `pid`.
  Test: after `sched_set_sched_param()` to priority P, `sched_get_sched_param()` reports `priority == P`.
  Note: The page says `param` "contains the scheduling parameters of the calling process", which is wrong when `pid` names another process.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-4** [DEC] Use `sched_set_sched_param` to change the parameters.
  Test: see sched_get_sched_param.3-3.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-5** [DEC] Currently the `sched_param` structure contains only a `priority` field.
  Test: compile code that uses `param.priority`.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-6** [DEC] A process's priority is inherited across `fork` and `exec`.
  Test: set a priority, `fork()`; the child reports the same priority; likewise after `exec()`.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-7** [DEC] A portable application must initialize all fields of `sched_param` before the call.
  Test: Not testable; advice to callers.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-8** [DEC] No special privileges are needed.
  Test: run as an unprivileged user on its own pid; succeeds.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-9** [DEC] Returns 0 on success; on failure returns -1, sets `errno`, and "the specified priority is unchanged".
  Test: see -E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**sched_get_sched_param.3-E1** `ESRCH`: no process can be found corresponding to `pid`.

**sched_get_sched_param.3-E2** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 priority scheduling is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

**sched_get_sched_param.3-E3** `EINVAL`: `param` is NULL, or one or more of the parameters in it is outside the valid range for the specified scheduling policy.
  Note: The page applies a range check to `param`, an output structure, without saying what is checked on input.

Related: getpid(2), sched_getscheduler(3), sched_set_sched_param(3), sched_setscheduler(3)

### sched_getscheduler(3)

Page: `man3/sched_getscheduler.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**sched_getscheduler.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sched.h>`; `int sched_getscheduler(pid_t pid)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**sched_getscheduler.3-2** [DEC] `pid` is the process whose scheduling policy is obtained; if zero, the calling process's policy is obtained.
  Test: `sched_getscheduler(0) == sched_getscheduler(getpid())`.

**sched_getscheduler.3-3** [DEC] The function returns the current scheduling policy of a process; possible values are defined in `<sched.h>`.
  Test: as root, after `sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_FIFO, ...)` succeeds, `sched_getscheduler(0)` returns `SCHED_FIFO`.

**sched_getscheduler.3-4** [DEC] `sched_setscheduler` changes a process's policy and priority, which lets an application determine more effectively when a process will run.
  Test: see sched_setscheduler.

**sched_getscheduler.3-5** [DEC] The policies are `SCHED_FIFO` (first-in, first-out), `SCHED_RR` (round-robin) and `SCHED_OTHER` (standard timesharing).
  Test: compile code using all three constants from `<sched.h>`.

**sched_getscheduler.3-6** [DEC] `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR` are fixed-priority: the process specifies a priority and the scheduler does not adjust it. A `SCHED_FIFO` process can run as soon as ready, for as long as it needs, since it preempts lower-priority processes.
  Test: as root, a `SCHED_FIFO` process at high priority spinning on a uniprocessor is not interrupted by a lower-priority spinning process.

**sched_getscheduler.3-7** [DEC] Round-robin is like FIFO but imposes a quantum on execution time; `sched_get_rr_interval` gives the current quantum.
  Test: see sched_get_rr_interval-3.

**sched_getscheduler.3-8** [DEC] The scheduler adjusts priorities of processes under the timesharing policy.
  Test: Not directly testable; informational.

**sched_getscheduler.3-9** [DEC] No special privileges are needed.
  Test: run as an unprivileged user on its own pid; succeeds.

**sched_getscheduler.3-10** [DEC] On success the process's scheduling policy is returned; on error -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: see sched_getscheduler.3-3.
  Note: The page also says "The call returns 0 if there is no error", which contradicts returning the policy (unless the policy value is 0).

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**sched_getscheduler.3-E1** `EPERM`: the caller does not have permission to determine the scheduling policy of the specified process.

**sched_getscheduler.3-E2** `ESRCH`: no process can be found corresponding to `pid`.

**sched_getscheduler.3-E3** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 priority scheduling is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

Related: getpid(2), sched_get_sched_param(3), sched_setscheduler(3), sched_set_sched_param(3)

### sched_set_sched_param(3)

Page: `man3/sched_set_sched_param.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sched.h>`; `int sched_set_sched_param(pid_t pid, struct sched_param *param)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-2** [DEC] `pid` is the process whose parameters are set; if zero, the calling process's are set.
  Test: set via `pid` 0, read via `getpid()`; values match.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-3** [DEC] `param` points to a `sched_param` holding the parameters; currently only a `priority` field. The priority may be any integer within the priority range for the current policy of process `pid`.
  Test: as root, set priority to `sched_get_priority_min(policy)` and to `sched_get_priority_max(policy)`; both succeed.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-4** [DEC] The function changes the scheduling parameters of a process. Giving the most critical process the highest priority lets applications determine more effectively when a process will run.
  Test: set, then read with `sched_get_sched_param()`.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-5** [DEC] At runtime a process starts with an initial priority of `SCHED_PRIO_USER_MAX`.
  Test: a fresh process's `sched_get_sched_param()` priority equals `SCHED_PRIO_USER_MAX`.
  Note: The page also says priority is inherited across fork and exec (sched_set_sched_param.3-10) and does not reconcile this with "starts out".

**sched_set_sched_param.3-6** [DEC] A call that raises a process's priority also raises its maximum priority. This higher maximum lasts for the life of the process or until raised again by another `sched_set_sched_param` call. The maximum cannot be adjusted downward, but later `sched_set_sched_param` or `sched_setscheduler` calls can make the process run at a lower priority.
  Test: as root, raise priority to P > `SCHED_PRIO_USER_MAX`, then lower it to P-1; both calls return 0 and `sched_get_sched_param()` reflects each value.
  Note: The page does not say whether the raised maximum lets a process without privilege later return to it.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-7** [DEC] Superuser privileges are required to set the priority above the maximum.
  Test: as non-root, set priority to `SCHED_PRIO_USER_MAX + 1`; expect -1 with `EPERM`.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-8** [DEC] The target process, running or not, resumes after all other runnable processes of equal or greater priority are scheduled. If the target is set above the caller and is ready, it preempts the caller. If the caller sets its own priority below another process, that process preempts the caller. In either case the caller might not learn the change completed until the target has executed.
  Test: on a uniprocessor as root (`SCHED_FIFO`), raise a ready spinning child above the caller; the child writes a timestamp before the caller's call returns.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-9** [DEC] The parameters of process `pid` are obtained with `sched_get_sched_param`.
  Test: see sched_set_sched_param.3-4.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-10** [DEC] A process's priority is inherited across `fork` and `exec`.
  Test: set priority, `fork()` and `exec()` a program that prints its priority; values match.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-11** [DEC] Returns 0 on success; on failure returns -1, sets `errno`, and the specified priority is unchanged.
  Test: attempt an out-of-range priority; expect -1 with `EINVAL` and the priority unchanged.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**sched_set_sched_param.3-E1** `EINVAL`: one or more requested parameters is outside the range defined for the scheduling policy of `pid`.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-E2** `EPERM`: the caller lacks permission to set the parameters as requested for the process, or lacks permission to invoke the function.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-E3** `ESRCH`: no process can be found corresponding to `pid`.

**sched_set_sched_param.3-E4** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 priority scheduling is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

Related: getpid(2), sched_getscheduler(3), sched_get_sched_param(3), sched_setscheduler(3)

### sched_setscheduler(3)

Page: `man3/sched_setscheduler.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**sched_setscheduler.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sched.h>`; `int sched_setscheduler(pid_t pid, int policy, struct sched_param *param)`.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**sched_setscheduler.3-2** [DEC] `pid` is the process whose policy and priority are set; if zero, the calling process's are set.
  Test: as root, `sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_RR, &p)`; `sched_getscheduler(getpid())` returns `SCHED_RR`.

**sched_setscheduler.3-3** [DEC] `policy` is the policy to set: `SCHED_FIFO`, `SCHED_RR` or `SCHED_OTHER`.
  Test: as root, set each in turn; `sched_getscheduler()` reflects each.

**sched_setscheduler.3-4** [DEC] `param` points to a `sched_param`; currently only a `priority` field, which gives the priority level and must be within the inclusive range of the minimum and maximum for the policy used.
  Test: as root, priority `sched_get_priority_max(SCHED_FIFO) + 1` fails with `EINVAL`.

**sched_setscheduler.3-5** [DEC] The function changes the scheduling policy and priority of a process; doing so lets an application determine more effectively when a process will run.
  Test: see -2 and -3.

**sched_setscheduler.3-6** [DEC] A process starts with an initial priority of `SCHED_PRIO_USER_MAX`. Either `sched_set_sched_param` or `sched_setscheduler` can raise or lower a process's priority. Raising it above the initial priority makes the new priority the process's maximum; this maximum lasts for the life of the process or until raised again by `sched_set_sched_param`. The maximum cannot be adjusted downward, but later calls can make the process run at a lower priority.
  Test: as root, raise above `SCHED_PRIO_USER_MAX`, then lower; both calls succeed and `sched_get_sched_param()` reflects each.

**sched_setscheduler.3-7** [DEC] `SCHED_FIFO` is fixed-priority FIFO: processes waiting at a priority level are chosen from a list ordered by time spent on the list without running; generally the head has waited longest and the tail shortest.
  Test: on a uniprocessor as root, start three `SCHED_FIFO` children at the same priority that each record order of first running; they run in the order they became ready.

**sched_setscheduler.3-8** [DEC] `SCHED_RR` is fixed-priority round-robin: like `SCHED_FIFO`, with the added condition that execution time is subject to a quantum.
  Test: see sched_get_rr_interval-3.

**sched_setscheduler.3-9** [DEC] `SCHED_OTHER` is standard timesharing: like `SCHED_FIFO`, but the scheduler adjusts process priorities, and recalculation of priorities results in preemption.
  Test: two spinning `SCHED_OTHER` processes on one CPU both make progress.

**sched_setscheduler.3-10** [DEC] Three policies are supported: two fixed-priority (`SCHED_FIFO`, `SCHED_RR`) and one timesharing (`SCHED_OTHER`). Under fixed-priority, only the user sets and adjusts priorities; under timesharing, the scheduler adjusts them automatically by resource usage and other factors.
  Test: a `SCHED_FIFO` process that spins for 2 s reports an unchanged priority afterwards.

**sched_setscheduler.3-11** [DEC] Priorities with FIFO let a critical process run as soon as ready, for as long as needed, as it preempts lower-priority processes. The page says this matters where scheduling must be as fast and as precise as possible.
  Test: see sched_getscheduler-6.

**sched_setscheduler.3-12** [DEC] `sched_get_priority_max` and `sched_get_priority_min` give the allowed range per policy. The `priority` field may be any integer within the inclusive range for the current policy, as defined in `<sched.h>`. Higher numbers mean higher priority.
  Test: a `SCHED_FIFO` process at max preempts one at min on a uniprocessor.

**sched_setscheduler.3-13** [DEC] A process's scheduling policy is inherited across `fork` and `exec`.
  Test: set `SCHED_RR`, `fork()` and `exec()` a program that prints `sched_getscheduler(0)`; it reports `SCHED_RR`.

**sched_setscheduler.3-14** [DEC] A portable application must initialize all fields of `sched_param` before the call.
  Test: Not testable; advice to callers.

**sched_setscheduler.3-15** [DEC] Superuser privileges are required to call `sched_setscheduler`.
  Test: as non-root, the call fails with `EPERM`.

**sched_setscheduler.3-16** [DEC] On success the former scheduling policy is returned. On failure -1 is returned, `errno` is set, and the process's policy and parameters are unchanged.
  Test: from `SCHED_OTHER`, set `SCHED_FIFO`; the return equals `SCHED_OTHER`. On an invalid policy, `sched_getscheduler()` is unchanged.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`):

**sched_setscheduler.3-E1** `EINVAL`: invalid `policy`, or `param` is NULL, or one or more parameters in it is outside the valid range for the policy.

**sched_setscheduler.3-E2** `EPERM`: the caller lacks permission to set the priority, the policy, or both, for the process.

**sched_setscheduler.3-E3** `ESRCH`: no process can be found corresponding to `pid`.

**sched_setscheduler.3-E4** `ENOSYS`: P1003.4/D10 priority scheduling is not configured in this implementation (see the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

Related: getpid(2), sched_getscheduler(3), sched_get_sched_param(3), sched_set_sched_param(3)

### sched_yield(3)

Page: `man3/sched_yield.html`. The page is headed "Digital" and the NAME line says "(P1003.4/D10)", so its items are tagged [DEC].
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**sched_yield.3-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sched.h>`; `void sched_yield(void)`. It takes no arguments.
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**sched_yield.3-2** [DEC] `sched_yield` yields execution to another process; it is useful under `SCHED_FIFO` to let another process at the same priority run.
  Test: on a uniprocessor as root, two `SCHED_FIFO` processes at the same priority alternate when each calls `sched_yield()` in a loop.

**sched_yield.3-3** [DEC] The yielding process goes to the end of the queue for its priority.
  Test: as in -2, check strict alternation of a shared counter's writers.

**sched_yield.3-4** [DEC] If no other process is runnable at the caller's priority, the caller continues to run.
  Test: a lone `SCHED_FIFO` process calling `sched_yield()` returns promptly.

**sched_yield.3-5** [DEC] Higher-priority processes may preempt the running process anyway, so `sched_yield` has no effect on scheduling of higher- or lower-priority processes.
  Test: a lower-priority spinning `SCHED_FIFO` process makes no progress while a higher one loops on `sched_yield()` on a uniprocessor.

**sched_yield.3-6** [DEC] No special privileges are needed.
  Test: call as an unprivileged user.

**sched_yield.3-7** [DEC] It returns no value and never generates an error ("No diagnostics are generated").
  Test: `errno` set to 0 before the call is still 0 after.

Related: sched_getscheduler(3), sched_setscheduler(3)

### setclock(3)

Page: `man3/setclock.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setclock.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/timers.h>`; `int setclock(int clktyp, struct timespec *val)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile a call with this prototype.

**setclock.3-2** [OSF/1] `clktyp` gives a system-wide clock whose symbolic name must be `TIMEOFDAY` (defined in `sys/timers.h`).
  Test: `setclock(TIMEOFDAY + 1, &v)` fails with `EINVAL`.

**setclock.3-3** [OSF/1] `val` points to the time value to set into the clock. `setclock()` sets that value into the clock named by `clktyp`.
  Test: as root, read the clock with `getclock()`, set it to the same value plus 1 s, read it back; it is about 1 s later. Restore afterwards.

**setclock.3-4** [OSF/1] The value is the time since the epoch, 00:00:00 GMT 1 Jan 1970.
  Test: as in -3; `time(NULL)` after the call matches `val.tv_sec`.

**setclock.3-5** [OSF/1] `timespec` (defined in `sys/timers.h`) has member `tv_sec` (`unsigned long`): time of day since the epoch in seconds.
  Test: compile code assigning `val.tv_sec`.
  Note: The page gives `tv_sec` the type `unsigned long`.

**setclock.3-6** [OSF/1] `timespec` has member `tv_nsec` (`long`): the fraction of a second, in nanoseconds.
  Test: compile code assigning `val.tv_nsec`.

**setclock.3-7** [OSF/1] Returns 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: see -3 and the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to these):

**setclock.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `clktyp` does not specify a known system-wide clock; or the value at `val` is outside the permissible range for the clock; or `val` specifies a nanosecond value less than zero or greater than or equal to 1000 million.

**setclock.3-E2** `EIO`: an error occurred while accessing the clock specified by `clktyp`.

**setclock.3-E3** `EPERM`: the caller does not have the appropriate privilege to set the clock.

Related: Functions: getclock(3), gettimer(3), time(3)

### setegid(3), setrgid(3)

Page: `man3/setegid.html`; same text as `setrgid(3)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**setegid.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>`; `int setrgid(gid_t rgid)`; `int setegid(gid_t egid)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile calls with these prototypes.

**setegid.3-2** [OSF/1] `setegid()` sets the effective group ID to `egid` if `egid` equals the current real, effective, or saved group ID.
  Test: as non-root, `setegid(getgid())` returns 0 and `getegid() == getgid()`.

**setegid.3-3** [OSF/1] `setrgid()` sets the real group ID to `rgid`.
  Test: as root, `setrgid(G)` returns 0 and `getgid() == G`.

**setegid.3-4** [OSF/1] Only the superuser may change the real or effective group ID to a value other than the current real or saved group ID.
  Test: as non-root, `setegid(G)` for G not the real or saved GID fails with `EPERM`.
  Note: The page is inconsistent: DESCRIPTION lets `setegid()` use the current effective GID, but this sentence and `EPERM` allow only the real or saved GID.

**setegid.3-5** [OSF/1] Both functions return 0 on success; on failure -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: see -2 and -E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to this):

**setegid.3-E1** `EPERM`: `rgid` or `egid` is not equal to the real or saved group ID, and the caller lacks superuser privilege.

Related: Functions: getgroups(2), setgroups(2), setregid(2); Commands: setgroups(1)

### seteuid(3), setruid(3)

Page: `man3/seteuid.html`; same text as `setruid(3)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**seteuid.3-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>`; `int setruid(uid_t ruid)`; `int seteuid(uid_t euid)`. Library: Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile calls with these prototypes.

**seteuid.3-2** [OSF/1] `setruid()` resets the process's real user ID; `seteuid()` resets the effective user ID.
  Test: as root, `seteuid(U)` gives `geteuid() == U`; as root, `setruid(U)` gives `getuid() == U`.

**seteuid.3-3** [OSF/1] A process with superuser privilege can set either ID to any value.
  Test: as root, `seteuid(12345)` returns 0.

**seteuid.3-4** [OSF/1] An unprivileged process can set the effective user ID only if `euid` equals its real, effective, or saved user ID.
  Test: as non-root, `seteuid(getuid())` returns 0; `seteuid(0)` fails with `EPERM`.

**seteuid.3-5** [OSF/1] An unprivileged process cannot set the real user ID.
  Test: as non-root, `setruid(getuid())` fails.
  Note: The page does not name the `errno` for an unprivileged `setruid()` with the current real UID; `EPERM` names only `euid`.

**seteuid.3-6** [OSF/1] Both functions return 0 on success; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: see -3 and -E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`; the page says `errno` "may be set" to this):

**seteuid.3-E1** `EPERM`: `euid` is not equal to the real or saved user ID, and the caller does not have appropriate privilege.

Related: Functions: getuid(2), setreuid(2)

### sigemptyset(3), sigfillset(3), sigaddset(3), sigdelset(3), sigismember(3)

Page: `man3/sigaddset.html`; same text as `sigdelset(3)`, `sigemptyset(3)`, `sigfillset(3)`, `sigismember(3)`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigaddset.3-1** [OSF/1] The functions are in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`) and are declared in `<signal.h>`.
  Test: compile and link a program that includes `<signal.h>` and calls all five functions with only the default C library.

**sigaddset.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigemptyset(sigset_t *set)`; `int sigfillset(sigset_t *set)`; `int sigaddset(sigset_t *set, int sig_number)`; `int sigdelset(sigset_t *set, int sig_number)`; `int sigismember(sigset_t *set, int sig_number)`.
  Test: compile calls with these argument types and assign each result to an `int` without warnings.

**sigaddset.3-3** [OSF/1] The functions operate on data objects addressed by the application, not on any set of signals known to the system (such as the process's blocked set or pending set).
  Test: get the mask with `sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, NULL, &old)`, call `sigfillset` on a local set, read the mask again and expect it unchanged.

**sigaddset.3-4** [OSF/1] `sigemptyset()` initializes the set pointed to by `set` so that all signals are excluded.
  Test: after `sigemptyset(&s)`, `sigismember(&s, n)` returns 0 for every valid signal `n`.

**sigaddset.3-5** [OSF/1] `sigfillset()` initializes the set pointed to by `set` so that all signals are included.
  Test: after `sigfillset(&s)`, `sigismember(&s, n)` returns 1 for every valid signal `n`.

**sigaddset.3-6** [OSF/1] Either `sigfillset()` or `sigemptyset()` must be called at least once on each `sigset_t` object before any other use of that object.
  Test: Not testable from user space as a requirement on the implementation (it is a requirement on the application).

**sigaddset.3-7** [OSF/1] `sigaddset()` adds the signal `sig_number` to the set `set`.
  Test: `sigemptyset(&s); sigaddset(&s, SIGINT);` then `sigismember(&s, SIGINT)` is 1 and `sigismember(&s, SIGQUIT)` is 0.

**sigaddset.3-8** [OSF/1] `sigdelset()` deletes the signal `sig_number` from the set `set`.
  Test: `sigfillset(&s); sigdelset(&s, SIGINT);` then `sigismember(&s, SIGINT)` is 0 and `sigismember(&s, SIGQUIT)` is 1.

**sigaddset.3-9** [OSF/1] `sigismember()` tests whether `sig_number` is a member of the set pointed to by `set`; on success it returns 1 if it is a member and 0 if it is not.
  Test: check both return values as in sigaddset.3-7.

**sigaddset.3-10** [OSF/1] On success, `sigemptyset()`, `sigfillset()`, `sigaddset()` and `sigdelset()` return 0.
  Test: call each with valid arguments and expect 0.

**sigaddset.3-11** [OSF/1] For all five functions, if an error is detected, -1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: call `sigaddset(&s, -1)`; if it reports an error, the result is -1 and `errno` has been set.

**sigaddset.3-12** [OSF/1] Example given by the page: a mask that blocks only `SIGINT` is built with `sigemptyset` and `sigaddset` and installed with `sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, ...)`.
  Test: build the set, install it, then read back the mask and expect only `SIGINT` blocked.
Note: The page's example passes `newset` (not `&newset` or `newset_p`) to `sigemptyset` and `sigaddset`, which does not match the synopsis's `sigset_t *` parameter.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**sigaddset.3-E1** `EINVAL`: the value of `sig_number` is not a valid signal number. The page says this applies to `sigfillset()`, `sigdelset()`, `sigismember()` or `sigaddset()` and that `errno` "may be set" to this value.
Note: The page lists `sigfillset()` among the functions that can give `EINVAL` for `sig_number`, but `sigfillset()` has no `sig_number` parameter.

Related: Functions: sigaction(2), sigprocmask(2), sigsuspend(2), sigvec(2); Files: signal(4)

### sigset(3), sighold(3), sigrelse(3), sigignore(3)

Page: `man3/sighold.html`; same text as `sigignore(3)`, `sigrelse(3)`, `sigset(3)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sighold.3-1** [Compat] The functions are in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`), declared in `<signal.h>`, and are described as "Compatibility interfaces for signal management".
  Test: compile and link calls to all four functions with only the default C library.

**sighold.3-2** [Compat] Synopsis: `void (*sigset(int signal, void (*function)(int)))(int)`; `int sighold(int signal)`; `int sigrelse(int signal)`; `int sigignore(int signal)`.
  Test: compile assignments of each return value to a matching type without warnings.

**sighold.3-3** [Compat] The `signal` parameter can be any of the signals defined in `signal.h`.
  Test: call `sighold` on each catchable signal defined in `<signal.h>` and expect 0.

**sighold.3-4** [Compat] The `function` parameter of `sigset()` is one of `SIG_DFL`, `SIG_IGN`, `SIG_HOLD`, or the address of a signal-catching function; it is of type pointer to function returning void.
  Test: call `sigset` with each of the three constants and with a handler address, expecting no `SIG_ERR`.

**sighold.3-5** [Compat] `SIG_DFL` means system default handling of the signal.
  Test: `sigset(SIGUSR1, SIG_DFL)` then `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)` in a child; parent sees the child killed by `SIGUSR1`.

**sighold.3-6** [Compat] `SIG_IGN` ignores the signal: any pending signal of that type is discarded, and the system signal action is set to ignore future occurrences of that signal.
  Test: hold `SIGUSR1`, send it, then `sigset(SIGUSR1, SIG_IGN)`; `sigpending` no longer shows it; a later `kill` has no effect.

**sighold.3-7** [Compat] `SIG_HOLD` holds the signal: any pending signal of this type remains held, and only one signal of each type is held.
  Test: `sigset(SIGUSR1, SIG_HOLD)`, send `SIGUSR1` three times, install a counting handler with `sigset`; the handler runs once.

**sighold.3-8** [Compat] With a handler address, on receipt of the signal the process executes the handler; any pending signal of this type is released when the handler is installed.
  Test: hold `SIGUSR1`, send it, then `sigset(SIGUSR1, handler)`; the handler runs at once.

**sighold.3-9** [Compat] The handler address is kept across calls to `sighold()` and `sigrelse()`.
  Test: `sigset(SIGUSR1, h); sighold(SIGUSR1); sigrelse(SIGUSR1);` then send `SIGUSR1`; `h` runs.

**sighold.3-10** [Compat] The signal number is passed as the only argument to the signal-catching function.
  Test: the handler records its argument; after `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR2)` it equals `SIGUSR2`.

**sighold.3-11** [Compat] Before the handler is entered, the action for the caught signal is set to `SIG_HOLD`.
  Test: inside the handler, `sigset(sig, SIG_HOLD)` (or another query) returns `SIG_HOLD` as the previous action; or the same signal sent inside the handler is not delivered until it returns.

**sighold.3-12** [Compat] On normal return from the handler, the system signal action is restored to `function` and any held signal of this type is released.
  Test: send the signal again from inside the handler; it is delivered right after the handler returns, to the same handler.

**sighold.3-13** [Compat] If a nonlocal goto (see `setjmp()`) is taken out of the handler, `sigrelse()` must be called to restore the system signal action and release any held signal of this type.
  Test: `longjmp` out of the handler, send the signal (it stays held), call `sigrelse`; the handler then runs.

**sighold.3-14** [Compat] On return from the handler, the process resumes where it was interrupted, "except for implementation-defined signals where this may not be true".
  Test: a loop counter keeps increasing after a handler runs and returns.

**sighold.3-15** [Compat] After the handler runs, the interrupted routine "may" return -1 with `errno` set to `EINTR` when the caught signal occurs during a nonatomic operation such as `read()`, `write()`, `open()` or `ioctl()` on a slow device (such as a terminal); during `pause()` or `sigsuspend()`; or during a wait function that does not return immediately.
  Test: with a handler set by `sigset`, block in `pause()` and send the signal; `pause` returns -1 with `EINTR`.

**sighold.3-16** [Compat] `sigset()` specifies the system signal action to be taken on receipt of `signal`.
  Test: covered by sighold.3-5 to sighold.3-8.

**sighold.3-17** [Compat] `sighold()` defers (holds) a signal until a later call to `sigrelse()`; the two establish critical regions of code.
  Test: `sighold(SIGUSR1)`, send it, check the handler has not run, then `sigrelse(SIGUSR1)` and check it has.

**sighold.3-18** [Compat] `sigrelse()` restores the system signal action to the one previously specified by `sigset()`.
  Test: `sigset(SIGUSR1, h); sighold(SIGUSR1); sigrelse(SIGUSR1);` then sending the signal runs `h`.

**sighold.3-19** [Compat] `sigignore()` sets the action for `signal` to `SIG_IGN`.
  Test: `sigignore(SIGUSR1)`, then `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)`; the process survives.

**sighold.3-20** [Compat] `signal()` should not be used together with these routines for a particular signal type.
  Test: Not testable (advice to applications).

**sighold.3-21** [Compat] NOTES: these interfaces are provided for compatibility only; new programs should use `sigaction()` and `sigprocmask()`.
  Test: Not testable (advice to applications).

**sighold.3-22** [Compat] On success, `sigset()` returns the previous system signal action for the signal; otherwise it returns `SIG_ERR` and sets `errno`.
  Test: `sigset(SIGUSR1, h1)` then `sigset(SIGUSR1, h2)` returns `h1`; `sigset(SIGKILL, h1)` returns `SIG_ERR`.

**sighold.3-23** [Compat] `sighold()`, `sigrelse()` and `sigignore()` return 0 on success and -1 with `errno` set otherwise.
  Test: call each on `SIGUSR1` and expect 0; on `SIGKILL` expect -1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; `sigset()` returns `SIG_ERR`):

**sighold.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `signal` is an illegal signal number, or is `SIGKILL`, or the default handling of `signal` cannot be changed. Applies to `sigset()`, `sighold()`, `sigrelse()` and `sigignore()`.

Related: Functions: kill(2), setjmp(3), sigaction(2), sigprocmask(2), wait(2); Files: signal(4)

### siginterrupt(3)

Page: `man3/siginterrupt.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**siginterrupt.3-1** [Compat] The function is in the Berkeley Compatibility Library (`libbsd.a`).
  Test: link a program calling `siginterrupt` with `-lbsd`.

**siginterrupt.3-2** [Compat] Synopsis: `int siginterrupt(int sig, int flag)`.
  Test: compile a call with two `int` arguments and assign the result to `int`.

**siginterrupt.3-3** [Compat] `siginterrupt()` changes the restart behaviour of a system call when it is interrupted by the signal `sig`.
  Test: see siginterrupt.3-4 and -5.

**siginterrupt.3-4** [Compat] When `flag` is FALSE (0), restart is enabled: system calls restart when interrupted by `sig` and no data has yet been transferred.
  Test: catch `SIGALRM`, `siginterrupt(SIGALRM, 0)`, `alarm(1)`, `read` from an empty pipe that a child fills after 2 s; `read` returns the data rather than -1.

**siginterrupt.3-5** [Compat] When `flag` is TRUE (1), restart is disabled: a system call interrupted by `sig` with no data transferred returns -1 with `errno` set to `EINTR`.
  Test: as siginterrupt.3-4 but with `siginterrupt(SIGALRM, 1)`; `read` returns -1 with `EINTR`.

**siginterrupt.3-6** [Compat] With restart disabled, an interrupted system call that has started transferring data returns the number of bytes actually transferred.
  Test: Not reliably testable from user space (needs a signal to arrive mid-transfer).

**siginterrupt.3-7** [Compat] System call interrupt is the default behaviour unless the program has been linked with the `libbsd` library.
  Test: without `-lbsd` and without `siginterrupt`, a handler installed by `sigaction` with no flags makes a blocked `read` return -1 with `EINTR`.
Note: The page does not say what the default is when linked with `libbsd`; it implies restart.

**siginterrupt.3-8** [Compat] `siginterrupt()` does not affect signal-handling semantics in any other way.
  Test: after `siginterrupt`, the handler still runs and the mask is unchanged.

**siginterrupt.3-9** [Compat] Programs may switch between restartable and interruptible operation as often as desired.
  Test: alternate `siginterrupt(sig, 0)` and `(sig, 1)` and check the behaviour each time as in -4 and -5.

**siginterrupt.3-10** [Compat] A `siginterrupt()` call made during a signal handler takes effect when the next instance of the signal is caught.
  Test: call `siginterrupt(SIGALRM, 1)` inside the `SIGALRM` handler; the next interrupted `read` returns `EINTR`.

**siginterrupt.3-11** [Compat] The function is provided for compatibility with BSD systems; programs using it should be linked with `libbsd`; `sigaction()` is the recommended method.
  Test: Not testable (advice to applications).

**siginterrupt.3-12** [Compat] On success it returns 0; otherwise it returns -1 to indicate that an invalid signal value was used.
  Test: `siginterrupt(SIGINT, 1)` returns 0; `siginterrupt(-1, 1)` returns -1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**siginterrupt.3-E1** `EINVAL`: the value of `sig` does not represent a valid signal (`errno` "may be set").

### siglongjmp(3)

Page: `man3/siglongjmp.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**siglongjmp.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`) and declared in `<setjmp.h>`.
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**siglongjmp.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `void siglongjmp(sigjmp_buf env, int value)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**siglongjmp.3-3** [OSF/1] `value` is any nonzero value; `env` is the address of a `sigjmp_buf` structure.
  Test: covered by siglongjmp.3-6.

**siglongjmp.3-4** [OSF/1] `siglongjmp()` restores the environment saved by the most recent `sigsetjmp()` in the same process with the corresponding `sigjmp_buf`.
  Test: `if (sigsetjmp(b,0)==0) siglongjmp(b,5);` control returns to the `sigsetjmp` point.

**siglongjmp.3-5** [OSF/1] All accessible objects have their values as of the time `siglongjmp()` was called, except that automatic objects changed between the `sigsetjmp()` and `siglongjmp()` calls have indeterminate values.
  Test: a global (static storage) object changed between `sigsetjmp` and `siglongjmp` keeps its new value after the jump; automatic objects are not checked.

**siglongjmp.3-6** [OSF/1] After `siglongjmp()`, execution continues as if the corresponding `sigsetjmp()` had just returned `value`.
  Test: `siglongjmp(b, 7)` makes `sigsetjmp` return 7.

**siglongjmp.3-7** [OSF/1] `siglongjmp()` cannot make `sigsetjmp()` return 0; if `value` is 0, `sigsetjmp()` returns 1.
  Test: `siglongjmp(b, 0)` makes `sigsetjmp` return 1.

**siglongjmp.3-8** [OSF/1] Because it bypasses the usual call and return mechanisms, `siglongjmp()` works correctly from interrupts, signals and their associated functions.
  Test: from a `SIGALRM` handler call `siglongjmp`; control reaches the `sigsetjmp` point.

**siglongjmp.3-9** [OSF/1] If `siglongjmp()` is called from a nested signal handler (a handler invoked for a signal raised while handling another signal), the behaviour is undefined.
  Test: Not testable (undefined behaviour).

**siglongjmp.3-10** [OSF/1] `siglongjmp()` restores the saved signal mask if and only if `env` was initialized by `sigsetjmp()` with a nonzero `savemask`.
  Test: `sigsetjmp(b,1)` with empty mask, block `SIGUSR1`, `siglongjmp`; mask is empty again. With `sigsetjmp(b,0)`, `SIGUSR1` stays blocked.

Related: Functions: setjmp(3), sigprocmask(2), sigsetjmp(3), sigsuspend(2)

### signal(3) (Fortran)

Page: `man3/signal.html`.
Note: The page is the Fortran 77 (`f77`, `libU77.a`) interface, headed "Digital", not the C `signal()` function.
Origin: This page documents the Fortran library `libU77.a`, not the C function; out of scope, tagged [Fortran].

**signal.3f-1** [Fortran] Synopsis (Fortran): `integer function signal(signum, proc, flag)` with `integer signum, flag` and `external proc`.
  Test: compile a Fortran program declaring and calling `signal` this way, linked with `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.

**signal.3f-2** [Fortran] The routine is in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.
  Test: check the symbol is defined in `/usr/lib/libU77.a` (for example with `nm`).

**signal.3f-3** [Fortran] When a process incurs a signal the default action is "usually to clean up and abort"; a call to `signal` specifies an alternative action.
  Test: install a handler for `SIGUSR1` with `signal`, send it with `kill`, and check the handler ran.

**signal.3f-4** [Fortran] `signum` is the signal number.
  Test: covered by signal.3f-3.

**signal.3f-5** [Fortran] If `flag` is negative, `proc` must be the name of the user signal handling routine.
  Test: `signal(SIGUSR1, h, -1)` then raise `SIGUSR1`; `h` runs.

**signal.3f-6** [Fortran] If `flag` is zero or positive, `proc` is ignored and `flag` is passed to the system as the signal action definition; this is how saved actions are restored.
  Test: save the return value of one call, change the action, then call with the saved value as `flag`; the original action is back.

**signal.3f-7** [Fortran] `flag` 0 means "use the default action" (see signal.3f-11); `flag` 1 means "ignore this signal".
  Test: `signal(SIGUSR1, h, 1)` then raise `SIGUSR1`; the process continues and `h` does not run.

**signal.3f-8** [Fortran] A positive return value is the previous action definition; a value greater than 1 is the address of the routine previously set for the signal.
  Test: set `h` with flag -1, then call again; the return value is greater than 1.

**signal.3f-9** [Fortran] The returned value can be used in later calls to `signal` to restore a previous action definition.
  Test: covered by signal.3f-6.

**signal.3f-10** [Fortran] A negative return value is the negation of a system error code (see `perror(3)`).
  Test: whenever a call returns a negative value, its negation is a valid system error code (for example, try an invalid signal number).

**signal.3f-11** [Fortran] NOTES: `f77` traps certain signals when a process starts; the only way to restore the default `f77` action is to save the value returned from the first call to `signal`.
  Test: save the value returned by the first call for a signal, change the action, then pass the saved value back as `flag`; the original action is in effect again.
Note: The page does not say which signals `f77` traps.

**signal.3f-12** [Fortran] When the user handler is called it is passed the signal number as an integer argument.
  Test: the handler stores its argument; it equals the signal sent.

Related: kill(3), kill(1)

### sigpause(3)

Page: `man3/sigpause.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigpause.3-1** [Compat] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`) and declared in `<signal.h>`.
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**sigpause.3-2** [Compat] Synopsis: `int sigpause(int signal_mask)`.
  Test: compile a call with an `int` argument.

**sigpause.3-3** [Compat] `sigpause()` blocks the signals in `signal_mask`, then suspends the process until delivery of a signal whose action is to run a signal-catching function or to end the process.
  Test: with a `SIGUSR1` handler, a child sends `SIGUSR1` after 1 s; `sigpause(0)` returns after the handler runs.

**sigpause.3-4** [Compat] Signal number `i` is blocked if the `i`-th bit of the mask is set.
  Test: `sigpause(1 << (SIGUSR2-1))` (or the page's bit numbering) with `SIGUSR2` then `SIGUSR1` sent; only the `SIGUSR1` handler runs during the pause.
Note: The page does not say whether bit numbering starts at 0 or 1 for signal 1.

**sigpause.3-5** [Compat] Only signals with values 1 to 31 can be blocked with `sigpause()`.
  Test: Not directly testable unless signals above 31 exist.

**sigpause.3-6** [Compat] `sigpause()` does not allow `SIGKILL`, `SIGSTOP` or `SIGCONT` to be blocked; an attempt to block them gives no indication of error.
  Test: `sigpause` with the `SIGCONT` bit set; a `SIGCONT` with a handler still wakes it, and the call does not fail for that reason.

**sigpause.3-7** [Compat] Setting the mask and waiting is one atomic operation; no signal can occur between the two.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, send it, then `sigpause(0)`; it returns at once after the handler runs.

**sigpause.3-8** [Compat] `sigpause()` is provided for compatibility with older UNIX systems; it is a subset of `sigsuspend()`.
  Test: Not testable (descriptive).

**sigpause.3-9** [Compat] If a signal is caught and the handler returns, the process resumes after `sigpause()`, which always returns -1 with `errno` set to `EINTR`.
  Test: as sigpause.3-3; expect -1 and `EINTR`.

**sigpause.3-10** [Compat] If delivery of a signal ends the process, `sigpause()` does not return.
  Test: in a child, `sigpause(0)` and send `SIGTERM` (default action); the parent sees it killed by `SIGTERM`.

**sigpause.3-11** [Compat] When a handler runs, `sigpause()` returns after the handler returns, with the signal mask restored to the one in effect before the call.
  Test: block `SIGQUIT`, `sigpause(0)`, after return check that `SIGQUIT` is blocked and nothing else changed.

Related: Functions: pause(3), sigaction(2), sigblock(2), sigprocmask(2), sigsuspend(2), sigvec(2)

### sigwait(3)

Page: `man3/sigwait.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sigwait.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Threads Library (`libpthreads.a`) and declared in `<signal.h>`.

**sigwait.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int sigwait(sigset_t *set)`.
  Test: compile a call with a `sigset_t *` and assign the result to `int`.

**sigwait.3-3** [OSF/1] `sigwait()` suspends the calling thread until at least one signal in `set` is in the thread's set of pending signals.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, start a thread that sends it after 1 s; `sigwait` returns after about 1 s while other threads keep running.

**sigwait.3-4** [OSF/1] When this happens, one of those signals is atomically chosen and removed from the pending set, and its number is returned.
  Test: after `sigwait` returns `SIGUSR1`, `sigpending` no longer shows `SIGUSR1`.

**sigwait.3-5** [OSF/1] The effect is unspecified if any signal in `set` is not blocked when `sigwait()` is called.
  Test: Not testable (unspecified).

**sigwait.3-6** [OSF/1] `set` is built using `sigemptyset()`, `sigfillset()`, `sigaddset()` and `sigdelset()`.
  Test: Not testable (advice to applications).

**sigwait.3-7** [OSF/1] On success the signal number of the pending signal is returned; otherwise -1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: covered by sigwait.3-4 and sigwait.3-E1.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**sigwait.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `set` contains an invalid or unsupported signal number (`errno` "may be set").

### tcdrain(3)

Page: `man3/tcdrain.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**tcdrain.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`) and declared in `<termios.h>`.
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**tcdrain.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int tcdrain(int filedes)`.
  Test: compile a call with an `int` argument.

**tcdrain.3-3** [OSF/1] `tcdrain()` waits until all output written to the object referred to by `filedes` has been transmitted.
  Test: on a pseudo-terminal master/slave pair, write to the slave, call `tcdrain` on it from a thread; it returns only after the master side has read the data.

**tcdrain.3-4** [OSF/1] A process group is sent `SIGTTOU` if `tcdrain()` is called from one of its member processes; if the caller is blocking or ignoring `SIGTTOU`, the operation is allowed and no signal is sent.
  Test: from a background process group on the controlling terminal, call `tcdrain` with a `SIGTTOU` handler and see the handler run; repeat with `SIGTTOU` ignored and expect 0 and no signal.
Note: The page does not say "background" process group here, although the `tcsetattr` page does; read literally it would apply to any process group.

**tcdrain.3-5** [OSF/1] `tcdrain()` suspends the calling process until the request completes, and is redefined so that only the calling thread is suspended.
  Test: while one thread is blocked in `tcdrain` on a pty whose master is not read, another thread keeps running.

**tcdrain.3-6** [OSF/1] On success it returns 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: `tcdrain` on a pty slave with no pending output returns 0.
Note: The page's example `rc = tcdrain(stdout);` passes the `FILE *` `stdout`, not a file descriptor.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; `errno` "may be set"):

**tcdrain.3-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` does not specify a valid file descriptor.

**tcdrain.3-E2** `EINTR`: a signal interrupted `tcdrain()`.

**tcdrain.3-E3** `ENOTTY`: the file associated with `filedes` is not a terminal.

Related: Functions: tcflow(3), tcflush(3), tcsendbreak(3)

Page: `man3/tcflow.html`. AES: Full use.

**tcflow.3-4** [OSF/1] `TCOOFF` suspends output.
  Test: on a pty slave, `tcflow(fd, TCOOFF)`, write data; the master reads nothing (non-blocking read gives no data).

**tcflow.3-5** [OSF/1] `TCOON` restarts suspended output.
  Test: after tcflow.3-4, `tcflow(fd, TCOON)`; the master now reads the data.

  Test: as tcdrain-4, using `tcflow(fd, TCOON)`.
Note: The page does not say "background" process group here.

**tcflow.3-9** [OSF/1] On success it returns 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: covered by tcflow.3-4 and the errors.

**tcflow.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `action` is not a supported value.

**tcflow.3-E3** `ENOTTY`: the file associated with `filedes` is not a terminal.

**tcflush.3-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` does not specify a valid file descriptor.

**tcflush.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `queue_selector` does not specify a proper value.

**tcflush.3-E3** `ENOTTY`: the file associated with `filedes` is not a terminal.

### tcsendbreak(3)

Page: `man3/tcsendbreak.html`. AES: Full use.

**tcsendbreak.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`) and declared in `<termios.h>`.

  Test: `tcsendbreak` on a pty slave returns 0 promptly.

**tcsendbreak.3-6** [OSF/1] A process group is sent `SIGTTOU` if `tcsendbreak()` is called from one of its member processes; if the caller is blocking or ignoring `SIGTTOU`, the operation is allowed and no signal is sent.

Note: The page does not say "background" process group here.

**tcsendbreak.3-7** [OSF/1] On success it returns 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: covered by tcsendbreak.3-5 and the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**tcsendbreak.3-E1** `EBADF`: `filedes` does not specify a valid open file descriptor.

### tcsetattr(3)

Page: `man3/tcsetattr.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**tcsetattr.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`) and declared in `<termios.h>`.
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**tcsetattr.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int tcsetattr(int file_des, int optional_actions, struct termios *termios_p)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**tcsetattr.3-3** [OSF/1] `tcsetattr()` sets the parameters of the terminal referred to by `file_des` from the `termios` structure at `termios_p`; `optional_actions` says how.
  Test: clear `ECHO` with `tcsetattr`, then `tcgetattr` shows it cleared.

**tcsetattr.3-4** [OSF/1] `TCSANOW`: the change occurs immediately.
  Test: `tcsetattr(fd, TCSANOW, &t)` followed at once by `tcgetattr` shows the new value.

**tcsetattr.3-5** [OSF/1] `TCSADRAIN`: the change occurs after all output written to `file_des` has been transmitted; it should be used when changing parameters that affect output.
  Test: on a pty, suspend output with `TCOOFF`, write, call `TCSADRAIN` in a thread; it does not complete until output is resumed and read.

**tcsetattr.3-6** [OSF/1] `TCSAFLUSH`: the change occurs after all output written has been transmitted, and all input received but not read is discarded before the change.
  Test: write "abc\n" to the pty master, `tcsetattr(slave, TCSAFLUSH, &t)`; a non-blocking read on the slave returns no data.

**tcsetattr.3-7** [OSF/1] If the output baud rate in the structure is `B0`, the modem control lines are no longer asserted; normally this disconnects the line.
  Test: Not testable from user space without modem hardware (on a pty, check only that the call is accepted).

**tcsetattr.3-8** [OSF/1] If the input baud rate in the structure is zero, the input baud rate given to the hardware is the same as the output baud rate in the structure.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware (the page does not say what `tcgetattr` reports afterwards).

**tcsetattr.3-9** [OSF/1] Calling `tcsetattr()` from a member of a background process group on its controlling terminal sends `SIGTTOU` to the process group; if the caller is blocking or ignoring `SIGTTOU`, the operation is allowed and no signal is sent.
  Test: from a background process group with a `SIGTTOU` handler, `tcsetattr` triggers the handler; with `SIGTTOU` ignored it returns 0.

**tcsetattr.3-10** [OSF/1] On success it returns 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: covered by tcsetattr.3-3 and the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; `errno` "may be set"):

**tcsetattr.3-E1** `EBADF`: `file_des` is not a valid file descriptor.

**tcsetattr.3-E2** `EINVAL`: `optional_actions` is not a proper value, or an attempt was made to change an attribute in the `termios` structure to an unsupported value.

**tcsetattr.3-E3** `ENOTTY`: the file associated with `file_des` is not a terminal.

Related: Functions: cfgetispeed(3), tcgetattr(3)

Page: `man3/tcsetpgrp.html`. AES: Full use.

**tcsetpgrp.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`); the synopsis includes `<sys/types.h>`.

**tcsetpgrp.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int tcsetpgrp(int filedes, pid_t pgrp_id)`.

**tcsetpgrp.3-3** [OSF/1] If the process has a controlling terminal, `tcsetpgrp()` sets the terminal's foreground process group ID to `pgrp_id`.

**tcsetpgrp.3-4** [OSF/1] The file for `filedes` must be the calling process's controlling terminal, and that terminal must currently be associated with the caller's session.
  Test: see tcsetpgrp.3-E3.

**tcsetpgrp.3-5** [OSF/1] `pgrp_id` must match the process group ID of a process in the same session as the caller.
  Test: see tcsetpgrp.3-E4.

**tcsetpgrp.3-6** [OSF/1] On success it returns 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.

**tcsetpgrp.3-E3** `ENOTTY`: the caller has no controlling terminal, or the file is not the controlling terminal, or the controlling terminal is no longer associated with the caller's session.

**tcsetpgrp.3-E4** `EPERM`: `pgrp_id` is valid but matches a process ID or process group ID of a process in another session.

### timer_create(3)

Page: `man3/timer_create.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**timer_create.3-1** [DEC] Described as P1003.4/D10; declared in `<timers.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<timers.h>` and calls `timer_create`.

**timer_create.3-2** [DEC] Synopsis: `timer_t timer_create(int clock_id, struct sigevent *evp)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types and assign the result to `timer_t`.

**timer_create.3-3** [DEC] `clock_id` is the type of clock on which the timer is based; the `CLOCK_REALTIME` clock is supported.
  Test: `timer_create(CLOCK_REALTIME, NULL)` does not return -1.

**timer_create.3-4** [DEC] `timer_create()` allocates a per-process timer using the given clock as the timing base and returns a timer ID used to identify the timer in timer requests.
  Test: the returned ID is accepted by `timer_gettime`, `timer_settime` and `timer_delete`.

**timer_create.3-5** [DEC] The timer ID is unique within the calling process for the life of that process.
  Test: create several timers (deleting some in between) and check every returned ID differs from all earlier ones.
Note: The page's wording suggests an ID is never reused in the process, even after `timer_delete`.

**timer_create.3-6** [DEC] The timer is disarmed when first returned from `timer_create()`.
  Test: `timer_gettime` on a new timer gives zero `it_value`.

**timer_create.3-7** [DEC] `evp` points to a `sigevent` structure (defined in `<signal.h>`) that gives the signal number sent to the calling process when the timer expires.
  Test: create with `SIGUSR1` in `evp`, arm for 100 ms; the `SIGUSR1` handler runs.

**timer_create.3-8** [DEC] DEC OSF/1 does not support the P1003.4/D10 Realtime Signals Extension, so the `sevt_value` member of `sigevent` must be NULL.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement on the implementation (it is a requirement on the caller).

**timer_create.3-9** [DEC] If `evp` is NULL, the default signal `SIGALRM` is sent on expiration.
  Test: create with `evp == NULL`, arm for 100 ms; the `SIGALRM` handler runs.

**timer_create.3-10** [DEC] The maximum number of timers per process, `TIMER_MAX`, is defined in `limits.h`.
  Test: `TIMER_MAX` is defined after including `<limits.h>`; a process never holds more than `TIMER_MAX` timers at once (further `timer_create` calls return -1).

**timer_create.3-11** [DEC] Timers are not inherited across `fork` or `exec`.
  Test: arm a timer, `fork`; the child receives no expiry signal (likewise after `exec`).

**timer_create.3-12** [DEC] On success a timer ID (`timer_t`) is returned, usable with the per-process timer calls; on failure -1 is returned and `errno` is set.
  Test: covered by timer_create.3-4 and the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**timer_create.3-E1** `EMTIMERS`: the calling process has already allocated all the timers this implementation allows it.

**timer_create.3-E2** `EINVAL`: the specified clock type is not defined.

**timer_create.3-E3** `EAGAIN`: the system lacks sufficient signal queuing resources to honor the request.

Related: clock_getres(3), clock_gettime(3), clock_settime(3), timer_delete(3), timer_getres(3), timer_gettime(3), timer_settime(3)

### timer_delete(3)

Page: `man3/timer_delete.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**timer_delete.3-1** [DEC] Described as P1003.4/D10; declared in `<timers.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<timers.h>` and calls `timer_delete`.

**timer_delete.3-2** [DEC] Synopsis: `int timer_delete(timer_t timerid)`.
  Test: compile a call with a `timer_t` argument.

**timer_delete.3-3** [DEC] `timer_delete()` frees a per-process timer allocated by `timer_create()`.
  Test: after `timer_delete(id)`, `timer_gettime(id, &v)` fails with `EINVAL`.

**timer_delete.3-4** [DEC] If the timer is armed, it is disarmed and then removed; no signal is sent when a timer is deallocated with `timer_delete()`.
  Test: arm a timer for 200 ms, delete it at once, wait 500 ms; no signal arrives.

**timer_delete.3-5** [DEC] On success it returns 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: covered by timer_delete.3-3 and the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**timer_delete.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `timerid` is not a valid timer ID.

**timer_delete.3-E2** [DEC] `ENOSYS`: the configuration does not support P1003.4/D10 Timers (the page refers to the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide for installing the realtime software).

Related: timer_create(3)

### timer_getres(3)

Page: `man3/timer_getres.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**timer_getres.3-1** [DEC] Described as P1003.4/D10; declared in `<timers.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<timers.h>` and calls `timer_getres`.

**timer_getres.3-2** [DEC] Synopsis: `int timer_getres(timer_t timerid, int abstime, struct timespec *res, struct timespec *max)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types.

**timer_getres.3-3** [DEC] `timer_getres()` returns the resolution of the timer in `*res` and the maximum possible time value in `*max`.
  Test: with a valid timer, the call returns 0 and writes both structures (pre-filled with a marker value).

**timer_getres.3-4** [DEC] If `res` or `max` is NULL, the corresponding value is not returned.
  Test: `timer_getres(id, 0, NULL, &m)` and `timer_getres(id, 0, &r, NULL)` both return 0.

**timer_getres.3-5** [DEC] If `abstime` is zero, the values are the limits for setting a relative timer; if nonzero, they are the resolution and maximum for an absolute timer.
  Test: call with 0 and 1 and expect 0 from both.

**timer_getres.3-6** [DEC] These values are "not necessarily the same" as those of `clock_getres`, and the values for zero and nonzero `abstime` "may differ".
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (permission only).

**timer_getres.3-7** [DEC] On success it returns 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: covered above and by the error.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**timer_getres.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `timerid` does not correspond to an ID returned by `timer_create` and not yet removed by `timer_delete`.

Related: alarm(3), clock_gettime(3), timer_create(3), timer_gettime(3), timer_settime(3)

### timer_settime(3), timer_gettime(3)

Page: `man3/timer_gettime.html`; same text as `timer_settime(3)`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**timer_gettime.3-1** [DEC] Described as P1003.4/D10; declared in `<timers.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<timers.h>` and calls both functions.

**timer_gettime.3-2** [DEC] Synopsis: `int timer_gettime(timer_t timerid, struct itimerspec *value)`; `int timer_settime(timer_t timerid, int abstime, const struct itimerspec *value, struct itimerspec *ovalue)`.
  Test: compile calls with these types.

**timer_gettime.3-3** [DEC] `timer_gettime()` returns in `*value` the time remaining in the current interval before the timer expires.
  Test: arm for 2 s, wait 0.5 s; `timer_gettime` gives an `it_value` between 1 and 1.5 s.

**timer_gettime.3-4** [DEC] `timer_gettime()` can be used to find whether a timer is still active; if the timer is disabled, zero is returned.
  Test: on a disarmed timer, `it_value` is zero.
Note: The page does not say exactly what "zero is returned" refers to (the function result or the `it_value` member).

**timer_gettime.3-5** [DEC] `timer_settime()` sets the expiration time of the timer, sets whether it is absolute or relative, returns the time remaining (if any) on the previous setting in `*ovalue`, and arms the timer.
  Test: arm for 5 s, then re-arm for 1 s with `ovalue`; `ovalue.it_value` is close to 5 s.

**timer_gettime.3-6** [DEC] Structure `itimerspec` has members `struct timespec it_interval` and `struct timespec it_value`.
  Test: compile code that sets both members.

**timer_gettime.3-7** [DEC] Structure `timespec` has members `time_t tv_sec` and `long tv_nsec`.
  Test: compile code that sets both members.

**timer_gettime.3-8** [DEC] The values of these members determine the duration of the timer intervals and the start and end times.
  Test: covered by the items below.

**timer_gettime.3-9** [DEC] If `abstime` is zero, the timer is relative: it expires `it_value` seconds and nanoseconds after the call.
  Test: arm with `abstime` 0 and `it_value` 200 ms; the signal arrives after at least 200 ms.

**timer_gettime.3-10** [DEC] If `abstime` is nonzero, the timer is absolute: it expires when the timer's clock reaches `it_value`.
  Test: read `clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME)`, add 300 ms, arm with `abstime` 1; the signal arrives after about 300 ms.

**timer_gettime.3-11** [DEC] Setting `it_value` to zero and calling `timer_settime()` disarms the timer.
  Test: arm for 200 ms, then call with zero `it_value`; no signal arrives within 500 ms.

**timer_gettime.3-12** [DEC] The reload value is set from `it_interval`; zero gives a one-shot timer, nonzero a periodic timer.
  Test: `it_value` 100 ms, `it_interval` 100 ms; about 5 signals in 550 ms. With `it_interval` zero, exactly one.

**timer_gettime.3-13** [DEC] `timer_getoverrun` is not supported for this release.
  Test: Not testable as a behaviour (statement of absence).

**timer_gettime.3-14** [DEC] On success both functions return 0; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: covered above and by the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**timer_gettime.3-E1** `EINVAL`: `timerid` does not correspond to an ID returned by `timer_create` and not yet removed by `timer_delete`.

**timer_gettime.3-E2** `EINVAL` (`timer_settime` only): a `value` structure specified a nanosecond value less than zero or greater than or equal to 1000 million.

**timer_gettime.3-E3** `EINVAL` (`timer_settime` only): a `value` structure specified a time that exceeds the maximum time for the timer.

**timer_gettime.3-E4** [DEC] `ENOSYS`: the configuration does not support P1003.4/D10 Timers (the page refers to the DEC OSF/1 Realtime Installation Guide).

Note: The page says the `itimerspec` structure "points to" a `timespec` structure; its members are `timespec` structures, not pointers.

Related: alarm(3), clock_gettime(3), timer_create(3), timer_getres(3)

### times(3)

Page: `man3/times.html`. AES: Full use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**times.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`); the synopsis includes `<sys/types.h>` and `<sys/times.h>`.
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**times.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `time_t times(struct tms *buffer)`.
  Test: compile a call with a `struct tms *` argument.
Note: The page gives the return type as `time_t` in the synopsis but speaks of `clock_t` values in RETURN VALUES.

**times.3-3** [OSF/1] `times()` fills the `tms` structure at `buffer` with time-accounting information; all values are in hardware-dependent clock ticks.
  Test: burn 1 s of CPU; `tms_utime` increases by about `sysconf(_SC_CLK_TCK)` ticks.

**times.3-4** [OSF/1] The `tms` structure is defined in `sys/times.h`.
  Test: compile code using `struct tms` after including `<sys/times.h>`.

**times.3-5** [OSF/1] Field `time_t tms_utime`: user time, the CPU time charged while executing user instructions of the calling process.
  Test: increases after a CPU loop.

**times.3-6** [OSF/1] Field `time_t tms_stime`: system time, the CPU time charged during system execution on behalf of the calling process.
  Test: increases after many `getpid`-like system calls or large `write`s to `/dev/null`.

**times.3-7** [OSF/1] Field `time_t tms_cutime`: user time of children, the sum of `tms_utime` and `tms_cutime` of the child processes.
  Test: a child burns 1 s CPU then exits; after `wait`, `tms_cutime` has grown by about 1 s of ticks.

**times.3-8** [OSF/1] Field `time_t tms_cstime`: system time of children, the sum of `tms_stime` and `tms_cstime` of the child processes.
  Test: a child does heavy system work then exits; after `wait`, `tms_cstime` has grown.

**times.3-9** [OSF/1] A terminated child's times are added to the parent's `tms_cutime` and `tms_cstime` when `wait()` or `waitpid()` returns that child's process ID.
  Test: `tms_cutime` read after the child exits but before `wait` is unchanged; after `wait` it has grown.

**times.3-10** [OSF/1] If a child process does not wait for its own children, their times are not included in its times.
  Test: a grandchild burns CPU and exits; the child exits without waiting; the parent's `tms_cutime` after `wait` reflects only the child's own CPU.

**times.3-11** [OSF/1] The information comes from the calling process and each terminated child for which a `wait()` function has been executed.
  Test: covered by times.3-9 and times.3-10.

**times.3-12** [OSF/1] On success `times()` returns the elapsed real time in clock ticks since an arbitrary fixed reference time in the past (for example, system start-up); the reference does not change between calls.
  Test: two calls 1 s apart differ by about `sysconf(_SC_CLK_TCK)`.

**times.3-13** [OSF/1] The return value "may overflow" the range of `clock_t`.
  Test: Not testable (permission only).

**times.3-14** [OSF/1] On failure `times()` returns -1.
  Test: Not testable from user space (no failure condition is documented).

Related: Functions: exec(2), fork(2), getrusage(2), profil(2), stime(3), sysconf(3), time(3), wait(2); Commands: cc(1)

### ttyslot(3)

Page: `man3/ttyslot.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**ttyslot.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**ttyslot.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `int ttyslot(void)`.
  Test: compile a call and assign the result to `int`.

**ttyslot.3-3** [OSF/1] `ttyslot()` scans `/etc/utmp` for the name of the terminal associated with file descriptor 0, 1 or 2, and returns the index of the current user's entry in `/etc/utmp`.
  Test: from a login session, the returned index selects a `utmp` record whose `ut_line` matches `ttyname(0)` without `/dev/`.

**ttyslot.3-4** [OSF/1] If an error occurs while searching for the terminal name, or none of descriptors 0, 1 and 2 is a terminal device, 0 is returned.
  Test: run with all three descriptors redirected to `/dev/null`; expect 0.

Related: Functions: getutent(3), ttyname(3)

### ulimit(3)

Page: `man3/ulimit.html`. AES: Trial use.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**ulimit.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`) and declared in `<ulimit.h>`.
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**ulimit.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `long ulimit(int command, off_t new_limit, ...)`.
  Test: compile a call with these types and assign the result to `long`.

**ulimit.3-3** [OSF/1] `ulimit()` controls process limits; `command` gives the form of control and the meaning of `new_limit` depends on `command`.
  Test: covered by the items below.

**ulimit.3-4** [OSF/1] `UL_GETFSIZE` returns the process file size limit, in units of `UBSIZE` blocks (see `sys/param.h`).
  Test: `ulimit(UL_GETFSIZE, 0)` returns a nonnegative value; after `ulimit(UL_SETFSIZE, n)` with a lower `n` it returns `n`.

**ulimit.3-5** [OSF/1] The file size limit is inherited by child processes.
  Test: lower it with `UL_SETFSIZE`, `fork`; the child's `UL_GETFSIZE` gives the lowered value.

**ulimit.3-6** [OSF/1] Files of any size can be read regardless of the file size limit.
  Test: lower the limit to 1 block, then read a larger existing file fully.

**ulimit.3-7** [OSF/1] `UL_SETFSIZE` sets the process file size limit for output operations to `new_limit` and returns the new limit.
  Test: `ulimit(UL_SETFSIZE, 10)` returns 10; writing past 10 blocks then fails.

**ulimit.3-8** [OSF/1] Any process can decrease the limit; only a process with the `SEC_LIMIT` system privilege can increase it.
  Test: unprivileged, lower then try to raise; the raise fails with `EPERM`.

**ulimit.3-9** [OSF/1] `GET_GETBREAK` returns the maximum possible break value (see `brk()` and `sbrk()`).
  Test: the returned value is greater than or equal to `sbrk(0)`.
Note: The page spells this command `GET_GETBREAK`; the name may be damaged or a misprint. The page also writes each command with "()" after it.

**ulimit.3-10** [OSF/1] With remote files, the `ulimit()` values of the client node (local node) are used.
  Test: with the limit lowered, writing a large file on an NFS mount fails at the same size as on a local file system.

**ulimit.3-11** [OSF/1] `ulimit()` is implemented in terms of `setrlimit()`; the two should not be used in the same program; the result of doing so is undefined.
  Test: Not testable (using both interfaces in one program is undefined).

**ulimit.3-12** [OSF/1] The page's example `rc = ulimit(1006, ulimit(1005, 0) - 2048);` is said to grow the stack segment by 2048 bytes and set `rc` to the new lowest valid stack address.
  Test: Not testable as stated (commands 1005 and 1006 are not documented on the page).
Note: The page does not define commands 1005 and 1006 anywhere else.

**ulimit.3-13** [OSF/1] On success a nonnegative value is returned; on failure -1 is returned, `errno` is set, and the limit remains unchanged.
  Test: after a failed raise (ulimit.3-8), `UL_GETFSIZE` still returns the old value.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; `errno` "may be set"):

**ulimit.3-E1** `EPERM`: a process without appropriate system privilege attempts to increase the file size limit.

**ulimit.3-E2** `EINVAL`: the `command` parameter is invalid.

Related: Functions: brk(2), getrlimit(2), pathconf(3), write(2)

### umount(3)

Page: `man3/umount.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**umount.3-1** [Compat] This `umount()` is in the System V Compatibility Library (`libsys5.a`) and declared in `<sys/mount.h>`.
  Test: link a program calling `umount` with `-lsys5` placed before `-lc`.

**umount.3-2** [Compat] Synopsis: `int umount(char *spec)`.
  Test: compile a call with a `char *` argument.

**umount.3-3** [Compat] `spec` points to the pathname of the special file or file system to be unmounted.
  Test: covered by umount.3-4.

**umount.3-4** [Compat] `umount()` unmounts a previously mounted file system contained on the block special file named by `spec`; afterwards the mount-point directory returns to its normal interpretation.
  Test: as superuser, mount a file system on a block device, call `umount(dev)`; a file created on it is no longer visible under the mount point.

**umount.3-5** [Compat] `umount()` can only be invoked by the superuser.
  Test: as a non-root user, expect -1 with `EPERM`.

**umount.3-6** [Compat] OSF/1 supports two `umount()` functions, the BSD one and the System V one; the default is the BSD `umount()`; to get the version on this page, link with `libsys5` before `libc`.
  Test: link with and without `-lsys5` and check that the `libsys5` version accepts a block-device path.

**umount.3-7** [Compat] It returns 0 if the file system was unmounted; otherwise -1 with `errno` set.
  Test: covered by umount.3-4 and the errors.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise; `errno` "may be set"):

**umount.3-E1** `EPERM`: the effective user ID of the calling process is not root.

**umount.3-E2** `ENOENT`: `spec` points to a pathname that does not exist.

**umount.3-E3** `ENOTDIR`: a component of the path prefix of `spec` is not a directory.

**umount.3-E4** `ENOTBLK`: the device identified by `spec` is not a block-special device.

**umount.3-E5** `ENXIO`: the device identified by `spec` does not exist.

**umount.3-E6** `EBUSY`: a file on the device pointed to by `spec` is busy.

**umount.3-E7** `EINVAL`: the device pointed to by `spec` is not mounted.

Related: Commands: mount(8)

### unlink(3) (Fortran)

Page: `man3/unlink.html`.
Note: The page is the Fortran 77 (`libU77.a`) interface, headed "Digital", not the C `unlink()` call.
Origin: This page documents the Fortran library `libU77.a`, not the C function; out of scope, tagged [Fortran].

**unlink.3f-1** [Fortran] Synopsis (Fortran): `integer function unlink(name)` with `character*(*) name`.
  Test: compile a Fortran program calling `unlink` this way, linked with `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.

**unlink.3f-2** [Fortran] The routine is in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.
  Test: check the symbol is defined in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.

**unlink.3f-3** [Fortran] `unlink` removes the directory entry named by the pathname `name`.
  Test: create a file, call `unlink`; the file no longer exists.

**unlink.3f-4** [Fortran] If this was the last link to the file, the file's contents are lost.
  Test: unlink a file with one link; no other name gives access to its data.

**unlink.3f-5** [Fortran] The returned value is zero on success and a system error code otherwise.
  Test: unlinking a nonexistent file returns `ENOENT`'s value (positive).

**unlink.3f-6** [Fortran] RESTRICTIONS: pathnames can be no longer than `MAXPATHLEN` as defined in `<sys/param.h>`.
  Test: a name longer than `MAXPATHLEN` gives a nonzero result.

Related: unlink(2), link(3), perror(3)

### usleep(3)

Page: `man3/usleep.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**usleep.3-1** [OSF/1] The function is in the Standard C Library (`libc.a`).
  Test: compile and link a call with only the default C library.

**usleep.3-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `unsigned usleep(unsigned mseconds)`.
  Test: compile a call with an `unsigned` argument.

**usleep.3-3** [OSF/1] `usleep()` suspends the current process for `mseconds` microseconds; the actual suspension "may be longer" because of other system activity or the time spent processing the call.
  Test: `usleep(200000)` takes at least 0.2 s of wall time.

**usleep.3-4** [OSF/1] `usleep()` sets an interval timer and pauses until it occurs; the previous state of this timer is saved and restored.
  Test: `setitimer(ITIMER_REAL)` for 5 s, `usleep(100000)`; afterwards `getitimer` shows about 4.9 s remaining.

**usleep.3-5** [OSF/1] If the sleep time exceeds the time to expiry of the previous timer, the process sleeps only until that signal would have occurred, and the signal is sent a short time later.
  Test: `setitimer` for 0.2 s with a `SIGALRM` handler, `usleep(1000000)`; it returns after about 0.2 s and the handler then runs.

**usleep.3-6** [OSF/1] `usleep()` uses `setitimer()` and requires eight system calls each time it is invoked.
  Test: Not testable from user space without system-call tracing.

**usleep.3-7** [OSF/1] A similar, less compatible function can be made with a single `select`; it would not restart after signals but would not interfere with other uses of `setitimer()`.
  Test: Not testable (advice to applications).

Note: The page does not give a RETURN VALUES section, so the meaning of the `unsigned` result is not stated.

Related: Functions: alarm(3), getitimer(2), sigaction(2), sigvec(2), sleep(3)

### wait(3) (Fortran)

Page: `man3/wait.html`.
Note: The page is the Fortran 77 (`libU77.a`) interface, headed "Digital", not the C `wait()` call.
Origin: This page documents the Fortran library `libU77.a`, not the C function; out of scope, tagged [Fortran].

**wait.3f-1** [Fortran] Synopsis (Fortran): `integer function wait(status)` with `integer status`.
  Test: compile a Fortran program calling `wait` this way, linked with `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.

**wait.3f-2** [Fortran] The routine is in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.
  Test: check the symbol is defined in `/usr/lib/libU77.a`.

**wait.3f-3** [Fortran] `wait` suspends the caller until a signal is received or one of its child processes terminates.
  Test: start a child that sleeps 1 s and exits; `wait` returns after about 1 s.

**wait.3f-4** [Fortran] If any child has terminated since the last wait, return is immediate.
  Test: let a child exit, sleep 1 s, then `wait`; it returns at once with the child's ID.

**wait.3f-5** [Fortran] If there are no children, return is immediate with an error code.
  Test: with no children, `wait` returns at once with a negative value.

**wait.3f-6** [Fortran] A positive return value is the child's process ID, and `status` is its termination status (see `wait(2)`).
  Test: the child exits with code 3; the returned value equals the child's pid and `status` encodes exit code 3 as `wait(2)` does.

**wait.3f-7** [Fortran] A negative return value is the negation of a system error code.
