  Test: with no children, the return value is negative and its negation is a valid system error code.

Related: wait(2), signal(3), kill(3), perror(3)


## Section 4 — file formats and headers

### acct(4)

Page: `man4/acct.html`.
Note: The page's NAME line is "acct.h - Account include files".
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**acct.4-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/acct.h>` and `#include <utmp.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes both headers and declares `struct acct` and `struct utmp` variables.

**acct.4-2** [OSF/1] `/usr/include/sys/acct.h` defines the `acct` structure used in records of the accounting files, which have various fixed formats.
  Test: compile code using `struct acct` after including `<sys/acct.h>`.

**acct.4-3** [OSF/1] The accounting files monitor system use and performance, pass charges to users, and are the permanent billing record for each process, CPU real time, allocated resources and services; the `acct` command is used to produce them.
  Test: Not testable (descriptive).

**acct.4-4** [OSF/1] `/usr/include/utmp.h` defines the record format written to `/var/adm/wtmp` whenever any user logs in or out.
  Test: after a login and a logout, `/var/adm/wtmp` has grown by whole `sizeof(struct utmp)` records naming the user's terminal line.

**acct.4-5** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `char ut_user[32]`: the user login name listed in `/etc/passwd`.
  Test: `sizeof(((struct utmp*)0)->ut_user) == 32`.

**acct.4-6** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `char ut_id[14]`: the user identification from the `/etc/inittab` ID file.
  Test: `sizeof(((struct utmp*)0)->ut_id) == 14`.

**acct.4-7** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `char ut_line[32]`: the device name (for example `console` or `tty43`).
  Test: `sizeof(((struct utmp*)0)->ut_line) == 32`.

**acct.4-8** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `short ut_type`: a flag giving the type of entry.
  Test: compile code assigning each constant in acct.4-9 to `ut_type`.

**acct.4-9** [OSF/1] `ut_type` values: `EMPTY` — no valid entry; `RUN_LVL` — run level changed by `init`; `BOOT_TIME` — boot time entry generated by `init`; `OLD_TIME` and `NEW_TIME` — used by `date` when the system time is changed; `INIT_PROCESS` — process spawned by `init`; `LOGIN_PROCESS` — a `getty` process waiting for login; `USER_PROCESS` — a user process; `DEAD_PROCESS` — terminated process; `ACCOUNTING` — private flag for accounting programs.
  Test: all ten names are defined by `<utmp.h>` and have distinct values.

**acct.4-10** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `pid_t ut_pid`: process ID number.
  Test: compile code using `ut_pid` as a `pid_t`.

**acct.4-11** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `short ut_exit.e_termination`: termination status of a process whose `ut_type` is `DEAD_PROCESS`.
  Test: compile code reading `u.ut_exit.e_termination`.

**acct.4-12** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `short ut_exit.e_exit`: exit status of a process whose `ut_type` is `DEAD_PROCESS`.
  Test: compile code reading `u.ut_exit.e_exit`.
Note: The page writes "DEAD PROCESS" with a space in these two fields.

**acct.4-13** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `time_t ut_time`: time that the entry was made.
  Test: the newest `wtmp` record's `ut_time` is close to `time(NULL)` right after a login.

**acct.4-14** [OSF/1] `utmp` field `char ut_host[64]`: host machine name.
  Test: `sizeof(((struct utmp*)0)->ut_host) == 64`.

**acct.4-15** [OSF/1] `sys/acct.h` defines the record format written to the process accounting file when a process completes.
  Test: as superuser enable accounting with `acct()`, run and end a process; a new `struct acct` record appears.

**acct.4-16** [OSF/1] `acct` field `char ac_flag`: accounting flag for the process.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_flag`.

**acct.4-17** [OSF/1] `ac_flag` value `AFORK`: the process was created by `fork()` and has not yet completed an `exec()`; `exec()` resets `AFORK`.
  Test: with accounting on, a child that exits without `exec` has `AFORK` set; one that `exec`s has it clear.

**acct.4-18** [OSF/1] `ac_flag` value `ASU`: superuser privileges were invoked.
  Test: a process run as root that uses privilege has `ASU` set in its record.

**acct.4-19** [OSF/1] `ac_flag` value `ACOMPAT`: compatibility mode used.
  Test: `ACOMPAT` is defined by `<sys/acct.h>`.

**acct.4-20** [OSF/1] `ac_flag` value `ACORE`: dumped core.
  Test: a process killed by `SIGQUIT` that dumps core has `ACORE` set.

**acct.4-21** [OSF/1] `ac_flag` value `AXSIG`: process killed by a signal.
  Test: a process killed by `SIGKILL` has `AXSIG` set.

**acct.4-22** [OSF/1] `acct` field `char ac_stat`: exit status, a flag indicating how the process terminated.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_stat`.

**acct.4-23** [OSF/1] `acct` field `uid_t ac_uid`: user ID of the process.
  Test: the record's `ac_uid` equals the process's uid.

**acct.4-24** [OSF/1] `acct` field `gid_t ac_gid`: group ID of the process.
  Test: the record's `ac_gid` equals the process's gid.

**acct.4-25** [OSF/1] `acct` field `dev_t ac_tty`: the terminal from which the process was started.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_tty` as `dev_t`.

**acct.4-26** [OSF/1] `acct` field `time_t ac_btime`: the time at which the process began.
  Test: the record's `ac_btime` is close to the process's start time.

**acct.4-27** [OSF/1] `acct` field `comp_t ac_utime`: user time used, in compressed format.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_utime` as `comp_t`.

**acct.4-28** [OSF/1] `acct` field `comp_t ac_stime`: system time used, in compressed format.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_stime`.

**acct.4-29** [OSF/1] `acct` field `comp_t ac_etime`: elapsed time since the command ran, in compressed format.
  Test: a process that sleeps 2 s has an expanded `ac_etime` of about 2 s.

**acct.4-30** [OSF/1] `acct` field `short ac_mem`: average amount of memory used by the process.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_mem` as `short`.

**acct.4-31** [OSF/1] `acct` field `comp_t ac_io`: number of characters transferred, in compressed format.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_io`.

**acct.4-32** [OSF/1] `acct` field `comp_t ac_rw`: number of blocks read or written, in compressed format.
  Test: compile code reading `ac_rw`.

**acct.4-33** [OSF/1] `acct` field `char ac_comm[8]`: name of the command that started the process; a child created by `fork()` receives up to 8 bytes from the parent; `exec()` changes the name.
  Test: `sizeof(ac_comm) == 8`; a forked child without `exec` has the parent's name; one that `exec`s a program of a different name has a changed `ac_comm`.

**acct.4-34** [OSF/1] Compressed data is a condensed floating-point representation and "may be expanded" to normal floating point with the `expacct()` routine.
  Test: `expacct()` is callable on a `comp_t` value.

**acct.4-35** [OSF/1] The `tacct` structure is not part of `utmp.h` or `sys/acct.h`; it is defined in a private `tacct.h`; it stores all information from `/var/adm/wtmp` and `/var/adm/pacct` and is used by accounting commands to produce reports (see `acctmerg`).
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-36** [OSF/1] `tacct` members declared as arrays of two `double` hold prime-time and non-prime-time values.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-37** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `uid_t ta_uid`: user ID.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-38** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `char ta_name[NSZ]`: login name, with `NSZ` the same number of characters as `ut_user` in `utmp`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-39** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `double ta_cpu[2]`: cumulative CPU time in minutes.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-40** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `double ta_kcore[2]`: cumulative Kcore minutes.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-41** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `double ta_io[2]`: cumulative number of characters transferred, in blocks of 512 bytes.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-42** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `double ta_rw[2]`: cumulative number of blocks read and written.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-43** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `double ta_con[2]`: cumulative connect time in minutes.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-44** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `double ta_du`: cumulative disk usage time in minutes.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-45** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `long ta_qsys`: queueing system (printer) fee in number of pages.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-46** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `double ta_fee`: special services fee.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-47** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `long ta_pc`: count of processes.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-48** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `unsigned short ta_sc`: count of login sessions.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-49** [OSF/1] `tacct` field `unsigned short ta_dc`: count of disk samples.
  Test: Not testable from user space (private header).

**acct.4-50** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/include/sys/acct.h` and `/usr/include/utmp.h` are the accounting header files; `/var/adm/wtmp` is the active login/logoff database; `/var/adm/pacct` is the active process accounting database.
  Test: the two headers exist at those paths; `/var/adm/wtmp` exists on a running system.

Related: Commands: acct/*, acctcms, acctcom, acctcon, acctdisk, acctmerg, acctprc, runacct, sa; Functions: acct(), fork(), exec(), expacct()

### core(4)

Page: `man4/core.html`.
Note: The page is headed "Digital" and says the "RICS/os system" writes the file; "RICS/os" appears to be a misprint (perhaps of RISC/os).
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

**core.4-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <sys/param.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/param.h>` and uses `UPAGES` and `NBPG`.

**core.4-2** [DEC] The system writes a memory image of a terminated process when any of various errors occur (see `sigvec(2)`); the most common are memory violations, illegal instructions, bus errors and user-generated quit signals.
  Test: a child that sends itself `SIGQUIT` leaves a file `core` in its working directory.

**core.4-3** [DEC] The file is called `core` and is written in the process's working directory, if it can be; normal access controls apply.
  Test: a child in a directory it cannot write to that sends itself `SIGQUIT` leaves no `core` file.

**core.4-4** [DEC] The maximum size of a core file is limited; files that would be larger than the limit are not created.
  Test: set `RLIMIT_CORE` to 0 (if that is the limit meant), cause a core dump; no `core` file appears.
Note: The page does not name the limit.

**core.4-5** [DEC] The file starts with the u. area, whose size in pages is `UPAGES` from `<sys/param.h>`; the u. area starts with a `user` structure as given in `<sys/user.h>`.
  Test: read the first `sizeof(struct user)` bytes of a core file and check fields such as the command name.

**core.4-6** [DEC] After the u. area come the data pages and then the stack pages of the process image.
  Test: a program with a known data pattern in a global variable dumps core; the pattern is found at offset `UPAGES*NBPG` plus its offset in the data segment.

**core.4-7** [DEC] The amount of data image, in pages, is given by `u_dsize` in the u. area; the amount of stack image, in pages, by `u_ssize`.
  Test: file size equals `(UPAGES + u_dsize + u_ssize) * NBPG`.

**core.4-8** [DEC] The size of a page is the constant `NBPG` from `<sys/param.h>`.
  Test: `NBPG` is defined after including `<sys/param.h>`.

**core.4-9** [DEC] In general the debugger `dbx(1)` is sufficient to deal with core images.
  Test: Not testable (advice).

Related: sigvec(2), dbx(1)

### dir(4)

Page: `man4/dir.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**dir.4-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/types.h>` and `#include <dirent.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes both headers.

**dir.4-2** [OSF/1] A directory behaves like an ordinary file except that no user may write into a directory.
  Test: `open(dir, O_WRONLY)` fails, even for the superuser.
Note: The page does not say which error is returned.

**dir.4-3** [OSF/1] That a file is a directory is shown by a bit in the flag word of its inode entry (see `fs`).
  Test: `stat` on a directory gives `S_ISDIR(st_mode)` true.

**dir.4-4** [OSF/1] Directory entries are returned in variable-length directory entry structures, described as "the POSIX standard way".
  Test: entries read with `getdirentries` have varying record lengths.

**dir.4-5** [OSF/1] Each entry starts with a `struct direct` holding the inode number, the length of the entry and the length of the name.
  Test: for each entry, the record length is at least the header size plus the name length plus 1.

**dir.4-6** [OSF/1] The name follows, padded with null bytes to a 4-byte boundary; all names are guaranteed null-terminated.
  Test: every record length is a multiple of 4 and the byte after each name is 0.

**dir.4-7** [OSF/1] The maximum length of a name in a directory is `_D_NAME_MAX`.
  Test: `_D_NAME_MAX` is defined by the headers; no name returned by `readdir` is longer than it.

**dir.4-8** [OSF/1] By convention, the first two entries are `.` (the directory itself) and `..` (the parent directory).
  Test: the first two names from `readdir` on a new directory are `.` and `..`, with `.` having the directory's own inode.

**dir.4-9** [OSF/1] In the root directory `/` of the master file system, `..` has the same meaning as `.`.
  Test: `stat("/..")` gives the same `st_ino` and `st_dev` as `stat("/")`.

Related: Functions: opendir(3); Files: fs(4)

### fstab(4)

Page: `man4/fstab.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**fstab.4-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: the file `/etc/fstab` and `#include <fstab.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<fstab.h>` and uses `struct fstab`.

**fstab.4-2** [OSF/1] `/etc/fstab` describes the known file systems; it is only read by programs and not written; by convention the administrator creates and maintains it.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement on the implementation (convention).

**fstab.4-3** [OSF/1] Each file system is on a separate line; fields are separated by tabs or spaces.
  Test: an `/etc/fstab` with tab-separated and space-separated lines gives the same `getfsent` results.

**fstab.4-4** [OSF/1] The order of records matters because `fsck`, `mount` and `umount` go through `/etc/fstab` sequentially.
  Test: `getfsent` returns the records in file order.

**fstab.4-5** [OSF/1] Field 1 (`fs_spec`): the block special device or remote file system to be mounted.
  Test: `getfsent()->fs_spec` equals the first field of the first line.

**fstab.4-6** [OSF/1] For `ufs` file systems, the special file name is the block special name, not the character special name; a program needing the character name must create it by putting the letter `r` after the last `/` of the name.
  Test: Not testable as an interface behaviour (convention for file contents and programs).

**fstab.4-7** [OSF/1] Field 2 (`fs_file`): the mount point; for swap partitions it should be `none`.
  Test: `getfsent()->fs_file` equals the second field.
Note: The page's example uses `swap1` and `swap2`, not `none`, as the second field of the swap lines.

**fstab.4-8** [OSF/1] Field 3 (`fs_vfstype`): the file system type; four types are supported: `ufs` (a local UNIX file system), `nfs` (a Network File System), `swap` (a disk partition used for swapping), `s5fs` (a System V file system).
  Test: `getfsent()->fs_vfstype` equals the third field.
Note: The page's example uses `ufs` with option `sw` for swap lines rather than the type `swap`.

**fstab.4-9** [OSF/1] Field 4 (`fs_mntops`): a comma-separated list of mount options containing at least the type of mount (see `fs_type`) plus options for the file system type.
  Test: for a line with `rw,bg`, `fs_mntops` is `"rw,bg"`.

**fstab.4-10** [OSF/1] If `userquota` and/or `groupquota` are given, the file system is processed by `quotacheck` and quotas are enabled with `quotaon`.
  Test: Not testable from a user program (depends on system startup commands).

**fstab.4-11** [OSF/1] By default quotas are kept in `quota.user` and `quota.group` at the root of the file system; this can be overridden with `=` and an absolute pathname after the option, for example `userquota=/var/quotas/tmp.user`.
  Test: Not testable from a user program (depends on the quota commands).

**fstab.4-12** [OSF/1] The type of mount is extracted from `fs_mntops` and stored separately in `fs_type`; it is not deleted from `fs_mntops`.
  Test: for a line with options `rw,bg`, `fs_type` is `"rw"` and `fs_mntops` still begins with `rw`.

**fstab.4-13** [OSF/1] If `fs_type` is `rw` or `ro`, the file system named in `fs_file` is normally mounted read-write or read-only on the special file.
  Test: Not testable from a user program (describes `mount`).

**fstab.4-14** [OSF/1] If `fs_type` is `sw`, the special file is made available as swap space by `swapon` at the end of the reboot procedure; the fields other than `fs_spec` and `fs_type` are unused.
  Test: Not testable from a user program (describes system startup).

**fstab.4-15** [OSF/1] If `fs_type` is `xx`, the entry is ignored; this is useful to show unused disk partitions.
  Test: a line with `xx` is skipped by `mount -a` (not by `getfsent`, which the page does not say).
Note: The page does not say whether `getfsent()` returns `xx` entries.

**fstab.4-16** [OSF/1] Field 5 (`fs_freq`) is used by `dump` to decide which file systems to dump; if absent, a value of zero is returned and `dump` assumes no dump is needed.
  Test: a line with only four fields gives `fs_freq == 0` from `getfsent`.

**fstab.4-17** [OSF/1] Field 6 (`fs_passno`) is used by `fsck` to order checks at reboot; root should have 1 and other file systems 2; file systems on one drive are checked sequentially and those on different drives at the same time.
  Test: `getfsent()->fs_passno` equals the sixth field.

**fstab.4-18** [OSF/1] If field 6 is absent or zero, a value of zero is returned and `fsck` assumes the file system need not be checked.
  Test: a line with five fields gives `fs_passno == 0`.

**fstab.4-19** [OSF/1] Constants: `FSTAB_RW` is `"rw"` (read-write device), `FSTAB_RO` is `"ro"` (read-only device), `FSTAB_SW` is `"sw"` (swap device), `FSTAB_XX` is `"xx"` (ignore totally).
  Test: `strcmp(FSTAB_RW, "rw") == 0` and likewise for the other three.

**fstab.4-20** [OSF/1] `struct fstab` field `char *fs_spec`: block special device name.
  Test: compile code reading `fs_spec`.

**fstab.4-21** [OSF/1] `struct fstab` field `char *fs_file`: file system path prefix.
  Test: compile code reading `fs_file`.

**fstab.4-22** [OSF/1] `struct fstab` field `char *fs_vfstype`: type of file system.
  Test: compile code reading `fs_vfstype`.

**fstab.4-23** [OSF/1] `struct fstab` field `char *fs_mntops`: comma-separated mount options.
  Test: compile code reading `fs_mntops`.

**fstab.4-24** [OSF/1] `struct fstab` field `char *fs_type`: `rw`, `ro`, `sw` or `xx`.
  Test: compile code reading `fs_type`.

**fstab.4-25** [OSF/1] `struct fstab` field `int fs_freq`: dump frequency, in days.
  Test: compile code reading `fs_freq` as `int`.

**fstab.4-26** [OSF/1] `struct fstab` field `int fs_passno`: commented as "pass number on parallel dump".
  Test: compile code reading `fs_passno` as `int`.
Note: The page's structure comment says "parallel dump", but the text says `fs_passno` is used by `fsck`.

**fstab.4-27** [OSF/1] Records should be read with `getfsent()`, `getfsspec()`, `getfstype()` and `getfsfile()`.
  Test: `getfsfile("/")` returns the entry whose `fs_file` is `/`.

**fstab.4-28** [DEC] ENVIRONMENT NOTES (ULTRIX Compatibility): field 3 also supports the type `cdfs`, an ISO 9660 or High Sierra Formatted (CD-ROM) file system.
  Test: a line with type `cdfs` gives `fs_vfstype == "cdfs"` from `getfsent`.

**fstab.4-29** [OSF/1] Example from the page: `/dev/rz2a / ufs rw 1 1`; `/dev/rz0g /usr ufs rw 1 2`; `/dev/rz2b swap1 ufs sw 0 2`; `/dev/rz0b swap2 ufs sw 0 2`; `/dev/rz2g /var ufs rw 1 2`; `/dev/rz3c /usr/users ufs rw 1 2`; `/usr/share/man@rabbit /usr/share/man nfs rw,bg 0 0`.
  Test: with this file as `/etc/fstab`, `getfsent` returns seven records with these fields.

Related: Commands: getfsent, fsck(8), mount(8), umount(8)

### inittab(4)

Page: `man4/inittab.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**inittab.4-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: the file is `/etc/inittab`.
  Test: check that `/etc/inittab` exists and is a regular file.

**inittab.4-2** [OSF/1] The `inittab` file supplies the `init` program with instructions for creating and running initialization processes.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires running `init` at boot); inspect the file's contents only.

**inittab.4-3** [OSF/1] The `init` command reads the `inittab` file each time `init` is invoked.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires invoking `init`).

**inittab.4-4** [OSF/1] The file "typically" contains instructions for the default initialization, for creating and controlling processes at each run level, and for the line process `getty`, which controls the activation of terminal lines.
  Test: read `/etc/inittab` and check for entries that run `getty`.

**inittab.4-5** [OSF/1] The file is made of lines; each line has four fields separated by colons, in the order `Identifier:Runlevel:Action:Command`.
  Test: parse every non-comment line of `/etc/inittab` and expect exactly four colon-separated fields.

**inittab.4-6** [OSF/1] There is no limit to the number of lines in the `inittab` file.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init` to read a very long file).

**inittab.4-7** [OSF/1] `Identifier` is a fourteen-character field that uniquely identifies an object.
  Test: parse `/etc/inittab`; expect every identifier to be at most 14 characters and unique.
  Note: The page spells the field heading "Indentifier".

**inittab.4-8** [OSF/1] `Runlevel` is a twenty-character field that defines the run levels in which the object is to be processed.
  Test: parse `/etc/inittab`; expect every run-level field to be at most 20 characters.

**inittab.4-9** [OSF/1] A run level corresponds to a configuration of processes in a system; each process spawned by `init` is assigned one or more run levels in which it is allowed to exist.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires changing `init` run levels).

**inittab.4-10** [OSF/1] The run levels are represented by the characters `0`, `2`, `3`, `S` and `s`.
  Test: parse `/etc/inittab`; expect run-level fields to contain only these characters.

**inittab.4-11** [OSF/1] The `Runlevel` field can name several run levels for a process, using more than one run-level character in any combination.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init` to act on such an entry).

**inittab.4-12** [OSF/1] `Action` is a twenty-character field that tells `init` how to treat the specified process.
  Test: parse `/etc/inittab`; expect every action field to be one of the actions in inittab.4-13 to inittab.4-22.

**inittab.4-13** [OSF/1] `respawn`: if the process does not exist or dies, `init` starts it; if the process exists, `init` does nothing and continues scanning the `inittab` file.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init`); could be checked by killing a respawned `getty` as root and seeing it restarted.

**inittab.4-14** [OSF/1] `wait`: when `init` enters a run level that matches the entry's run level, it starts the process and waits for it to end; while `init` stays in that run level, it does not act on later reads of the entry.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init`).

**inittab.4-15** [OSF/1] `once`: when `init` enters a run level that matches the line's run level, it starts the process and does not wait for it to end. When the process stops, `init` does not restart it. If `init` enters a new run level while the process is still running from an earlier run-level change, `init` does not restart the process.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init`).

**inittab.4-16** [OSF/1] `boot`: the entry is processed when `init` first executes and reads the `inittab` file; `init` starts the process, does not wait for it to end, and does not restart it when it stops. The entry's run level "should be the default run level, or it must match" the run level at which `init` operates at boot time.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires booting).

**inittab.4-17** [OSF/1] `bootwait`: the entry is processed when `init` first executes and reads the `inittab` file; `init` starts the process, waits for it to end and, when it dies, does not restart it.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires booting).

**inittab.4-18** [OSF/1] `powerfail`: when `init` receives the `SIGPWR` power-fail signal, it executes the process on this line.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires sending `SIGPWR` to `init`).
  Note: The page names `SIGPWR`, which the signal table in signal.h(4) of this manual does not list.

**inittab.4-19** [OSF/1] `powerwait`: when `init` receives the `SIGPWR` power-fail signal, it executes the process on this line and waits until it ends before continuing any processing of the `inittab` file.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires sending `SIGPWR` to `init`).

**inittab.4-20** [OSF/1] `off`: if the process on this line is running, `init` sends the warning signal `SIGTERM` and waits 20 seconds before sending the kill signal `SIGKILL`; if the process does not exist, `init` ignores the line.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init`).

**inittab.4-21** [OSF/1] `initdefault`: a line with this action is processed when `init` is first invoked; `init` uses it to choose the run level to enter first, by taking the highest run level in the run-level field as its initial state.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires booting).

**inittab.4-22** [OSF/1] For `initdefault`, an empty run-level field is interpreted as `0s23`, so `init` enters run level 3.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires booting).

**inittab.4-23** [OSF/1] If `init` finds no `initdefault` line in the `inittab` file, it requests an initial run level from the operator.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires booting).

**inittab.4-24** [OSF/1] `sysinit`: such entries are executed before `init` tries to access the console; this line is expected to be used only to initialize devices on which `init` might try to request a run level.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires booting).

**inittab.4-25** [OSF/1] `Command` is a 1024-character field holding the `sh` command to be executed.
  Test: parse `/etc/inittab`; expect every command field to be at most 1024 characters.

**inittab.4-26** [OSF/1] The entry in the command field is prefixed with `exec`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init` to run an entry).

**inittab.4-27** [OSF/1] Any legal `sh` syntax can appear in the command field.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init` to run an entry).

**inittab.4-28** [OSF/1] Comments can be inserted with the `#comment` syntax.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init` to read the file).

**inittab.4-29** [OSF/1] A line continuation character may be placed at the end of a line.
  Test: Not testable from user space (requires `init` to read the file).
  Note: the page text is damaged here; the character appears as `\\*O` (an unexpanded formatter escape, also in the original HTML), so which character is meant cannot be read.

**inittab.4-30** [OSF/1] Files: `/etc/getty` specifies the command that initializes and controls terminal lines.
  Test: check that `/etc/getty` exists.

Related: Commands: init(8); Functions: kill(2)

### limits(4)

Page: `man4/limits.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page carries the "Digital" title label (a Digital-supplied page, see intro(7)).

**limits.4-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <limits.h>`, `#include <float.h>`, `#include <sys/limits.h>`.
  Test: compile a program that includes all three headers; expect success.

**limits.4-2** [DEC] The header `<limits.h>` specifies the sizes of integral types as required by the proposed ANSI C standard.
  Test: compile a program that uses `CHAR_BIT`, `INT_MAX`, `LONG_MAX` etc. from `<limits.h>`; expect it to build and the values to match the types.

**limits.4-3** [DEC] The header `<float.h>` specifies the characteristics of floating types as required by the proposed ANSI C standard.
  Test: compile a program that uses `FLT_MAX`, `DBL_EPSILON` etc. from `<float.h>`; expect it to build.

**limits.4-4** [DEC] The `<float.h>` constants that refer to long doubles are not specified, because long doubles are not implemented.
  Test: compile a program that tests `#ifdef LDBL_MAX`; expect it not to be defined.

**limits.4-5** [DEC] The header `<sys/limits.h>` is a list of magnitude limitations imposed by a specific implementation of the operating system.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/limits.h>`; expect success.

**limits.4-6** [DEC] All values in the files are specified in decimal.
  Test: scan the three header files; expect the limit constants to be written as decimal numbers.

**limits.4-7** [DEC] Files: `/usr/include/limits.h`, `/usr/include/float.h`, `/usr/include/sys/syslimits.h`.
  Test: check that the three files exist.
  Note: The page's SYNOPSIS names `<sys/limits.h>` but its FILES section names `/usr/include/sys/syslimits.h`; it is unclear which file is meant.

### msqid_ds(4)

Page: `man4/msqid_ds.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**msqid_ds.4-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/msg.h>` declares `struct msqid_ds` with the fields `struct ipc_perm msg_perm; struct msg *msg_first; struct msg *msg_last; u_short msg_cbytes; u_short msg_qnum; u_short msg_qbytes; u_short msg_lspid; ushort msg_lrpid; time_t msg_stime; time_t msg_rtime; time_t msg_ctime;`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/msg.h>` and refers to every field; expect success.
  Note: The page gives `msg_lrpid` the type `ushort` but the other short fields `u_short`.

**msqid_ds.4-2** [OSF/1] The `msqid_ds` structure defines a message queue associated with a message queue ID; there is one queue per message queue ID.
  Test: create two queues with `msgget()`; expect two different IDs whose `msgctl(IPC_STAT)` results are independent.

**msqid_ds.4-3** [OSF/1] Collectively, the queues are stored as an array, with message queue IDs serving as an index into the array.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel storage layout).

**msqid_ds.4-4** [OSF/1] A message queue is implemented as a linked list of messages, with `msg_first` and `msg_last` pointing to the first and last messages on the queue.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel pointers); only check that the fields exist.

**msqid_ds.4-5** [OSF/1] The IPC permissions for the message queue are implemented in a separate, but associated, `ipc_perm` structure.
  Test: after `msgctl(IPC_STAT)`, read `msg_perm.uid` and `msg_perm.mode`; expect the creator's values.

**msqid_ds.4-6** [OSF/1] A message queue is created indirectly via `msgget()`. If `msgget()` is called with a non-existent message queue ID, the kernel allocates a new `msqid_ds` structure, initializes it, and returns the message queue ID to be associated with the queue.
  Test: call `msgget(IPC_PRIVATE, IPC_CREAT|0600)`; expect a valid ID and `msgctl(IPC_STAT)` to succeed on it.
  Note: The page says "non-existent message queue ID", although `msgget()` is called with a key; the page is unclear here.

**msqid_ds.4-7** [OSF/1] `msg_perm`: the `ipc_perm` structure that defines permissions for message operations (see msqid_ds.4-18 onward).
  Test: `msgctl(IPC_STAT)` and check `msg_perm.mode & 0777` equals the creation mode.

**msqid_ds.4-8** [OSF/1] `msg_first`: a pointer to the first message on the queue.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel pointer).

**msqid_ds.4-9** [OSF/1] `msg_last`: a pointer to the last message on the queue.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel pointer).

**msqid_ds.4-10** [OSF/1] `msg_cbytes`: the current number of bytes on the queue.
  Test: send a 10-byte message to an empty queue; expect `msg_cbytes` to be 10.

**msqid_ds.4-11** [OSF/1] `msg_qnum`: the number of messages currently on the queue.
  Test: send two messages; expect `msg_qnum` to be 2; receive one; expect 1.

**msqid_ds.4-12** [OSF/1] `msg_qbytes`: the maximum number of bytes allowed on the queue.
  Test: lower `msg_qbytes` with `msgctl(IPC_SET)` and read it back with `IPC_STAT`.

**msqid_ds.4-13** [OSF/1] `msg_lspid`: the process ID of the last process that called `msgsnd()` for the queue.
  Test: `msgsnd()` from a child; expect `msg_lspid` to equal the child's PID.

**msqid_ds.4-14** [OSF/1] `msg_lrpid`: the process ID of the last process that called `msgrcv()` for the queue.
  Test: `msgrcv()` from a child; expect `msg_lrpid` to equal the child's PID.

**msqid_ds.4-15** [OSF/1] `msg_stime`: the time of the last `msgsnd()` operation.
  Test: call `msgsnd()`; expect `msg_stime` to be within a second of `time()`.

**msqid_ds.4-16** [OSF/1] `msg_rtime`: the time of the last `msgrcv()` operation.
  Test: call `msgrcv()`; expect `msg_rtime` to be within a second of `time()`.

**msqid_ds.4-17** [OSF/1] `msg_ctime`: the time of the last `msgctl()` operation that changed a member of the `msqid_ds` structure.
  Test: wait 2 seconds, `msgctl(IPC_SET)`; expect `msg_ctime` updated to about `time()`.

**msqid_ds.4-18** [OSF/1] The `msg_perm` field identifies the associated `ipc_perm` structure, from the `sys/ipc.h` header file, which defines the permissions for operations on the queue.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/ipc.h>` and uses `struct ipc_perm`; expect success.

**msqid_ds.4-19** [OSF/1] `ipc_perm.uid` (`ushort`): the owner's user ID.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` a new queue; expect `uid` to equal `geteuid()`.

**msqid_ds.4-20** [OSF/1] `ipc_perm.gid` (`ushort`): the owner's group ID.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` a new queue; expect `gid` to equal `getegid()`.

**msqid_ds.4-21** [OSF/1] `ipc_perm.cuid` (`ushort`): the creator's user ID.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` a new queue; expect `cuid` to equal `geteuid()`.

**msqid_ds.4-22** [OSF/1] `ipc_perm.cgid` (`ushort`): the creator's group ID.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` a new queue; expect `cgid` to equal `getegid()`.

**msqid_ds.4-23** [OSF/1] `ipc_perm.mode` (`ushort`): access modes.
  Test: create with mode 0640; expect `mode & 0777` to be 0640.

**msqid_ds.4-24** [OSF/1] `ipc_perm.seq` (`ushort`): slot usage sequence number.
  Test: compile a program that reads `msg_perm.seq`; expect success.

**msqid_ds.4-25** [OSF/1] `ipc_perm.key` (`key_t`): the key.
  Test: create a queue with key 0x1234; expect `msg_perm.key` to be 0x1234.

**msqid_ds.4-26** [OSF/1] The `mode` field is a 9-bit field holding the permissions for message operations: the first three bits are owner permissions, the second three group permissions, the last three other permissions. In each group the first bit means read permission, the second write permission, and the third bit is not used.
  Test: create a queue with mode 0600; from another non-root user, expect `msgsnd()`/`msgrcv()` to fail.

Related: Functions: msgctl(2), msgget(2), msgrcv(2), msgsnd(2)

### semid_ds(4)

Page: `man4/semid_ds.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**semid_ds.4-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/sem.h>` declares `struct semid_ds` with the fields `struct ipc_perm sem_perm; struct sem *sem_base; u_short sem_nsems; time_t sem_otime; time_t sem_ctime;`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/sem.h>` and refers to every field; expect success.

**semid_ds.4-2** [OSF/1] The `semid_ds` structure defines a semaphore set associated with a semaphore ID; there is one semaphore set per semaphore ID.
  Test: create two sets with `semget()`; expect different IDs with independent `IPC_STAT` results.

**semid_ds.4-3** [OSF/1] A semaphore set is implemented as an array of `sem_nsems` semaphores, with `sem_base` pointing to the first semaphore in the set.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel pointer); check `sem_nsems` only.

**semid_ds.4-4** [OSF/1] The IPC permissions for a semaphore set are implemented in a separate, but associated, `ipc_perm` structure.
  Test: `semctl(IPC_STAT)` and read `sem_perm.uid`, `sem_perm.mode`.

**semid_ds.4-5** [OSF/1] A semaphore set is created indirectly via `semget()`. If `semget()` is called with a non-existent semaphore ID, the kernel allocates a new `semid_ds` structure, initializes it, and returns the semaphore ID to be associated with the set.
  Test: call `semget(IPC_PRIVATE, 3, IPC_CREAT|0600)`; expect a valid ID and `sem_nsems` of 3.
  Note: The page says "non-existent semaphore ID", although `semget()` is called with a key; the page is unclear here.

**semid_ds.4-6** [OSF/1] `sem_perm`: the `ipc_perm` structure that defines permissions for semaphore operations.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` and check `sem_perm.mode & 0777` equals the creation mode.

**semid_ds.4-7** [OSF/1] `sem_base`: a pointer to the first semaphore in the set; individual semaphores are defined using the `sem` structure.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel pointer).

**semid_ds.4-8** [OSF/1] `sem_nsems`: the number of semaphores in the set.
  Test: create a set of 5; expect `sem_nsems` to be 5.

**semid_ds.4-9** [OSF/1] Each semaphore in the set is referenced by a unique integer. A semaphore number is sometimes called `sem_num`, but this is not a field in any of the relevant data structures. Semaphore numbers run sequentially from zero to `sem_nsems`-1.
  Test: with a set of 5, `semctl(id, 4, GETVAL)` succeeds and `semctl(id, 5, GETVAL)` fails.

**semid_ds.4-10** [OSF/1] `sem_otime`: the time of the last `semop()` operation on the set.
  Test: call `semop()`; expect `sem_otime` to be within a second of `time()`.

**semid_ds.4-11** [OSF/1] `sem_ctime`: the time of the last `semctl()` operation that changed a semaphore in the set.
  Test: wait 2 seconds, `semctl(SETVAL)`; expect `sem_ctime` to be about `time()`.

**semid_ds.4-12** [OSF/1] The `sem_perm` field identifies the associated `ipc_perm` structure from the `sys/ipc.h` header file, with fields `ushort uid` (owner's user ID), `ushort gid` (owner's group ID), `ushort cuid` (creator's user ID), `ushort cgid` (creator's group ID), `ushort mode` (access modes), `ushort seq` (slot usage sequence number), `key_t key` (key).
  Test: `IPC_STAT` a new set; expect `uid`/`cuid` = `geteuid()`, `gid`/`cgid` = `getegid()`, `key` = the key used.

**semid_ds.4-13** [OSF/1] The `mode` field is a 9-bit field holding the permissions for semaphore operations: owner, group and other in three groups of three bits; in each group the first bit means read, the second write, and the third is not used.
  Test: create a set with mode 0600; as another non-root user, expect `semop()` to fail.

**semid_ds.4-14** [OSF/1] Individual semaphores are implemented with the `sem` structure from `sys/sem.h`: `u_short semval; short sempid; u_short semncnt; u_short semzcnt;`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/sem.h>` and uses `struct sem` fields; expect success.
  Note: The page spells "implimented".

**semid_ds.4-15** [OSF/1] `semval`: a nonnegative integer that is the current value of the semaphore.
  Test: `semctl(SETVAL, 7)` then `GETVAL`; expect 7.

**semid_ds.4-16** [OSF/1] `sempid`: the process ID of the last process to perform an operation on the semaphore.
  Test: `semop()` in a child; expect `semctl(GETPID)` to return the child's PID.

**semid_ds.4-17** [OSF/1] `semncnt`: the number of processes currently suspended waiting for an operation to increment the current `semval` value.
  Test: block a child in `semop()` decrementing a zero semaphore; expect `semctl(GETNCNT)` to be 1.

**semid_ds.4-18** [OSF/1] `semzcnt`: the number of processes currently suspended waiting for `semval` to go to zero.
  Test: block a child waiting for zero on a semaphore of value 1; expect `semctl(GETZCNT)` to be 1.

Related: Functions: semctl(2), semget(2), semop(2)

### shmid_ds(4)

Page: `man4/shmid_ds.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**shmid_ds.4-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/shm.h>` declares `struct shmid_ds` with the fields `struct ipc_perm shm_perm; int shm_segsz; u_short shm_lpid; u_short shm_cpid; u_short shm_nattch; time_t shm_atime; time_t shm_dtime; time_t shm_ctime;`.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/shm.h>` and refers to every field; expect success.

**shmid_ds.4-2** [OSF/1] The `shmid_ds` structure defines a shared memory region associated with a shared memory region ID; there is one shared memory region per ID.
  Test: create two regions; expect different IDs with independent `IPC_STAT` results.

**shmid_ds.4-3** [OSF/1] Collectively, the regions are kept in a shared memory table, with the region IDs identifying the entries in the table.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel storage layout).

**shmid_ds.4-4** [OSF/1] The IPC permissions for shared memory regions are implemented in a separate, but associated, `ipc_perm` structure.
  Test: `shmctl(IPC_STAT)` and read `shm_perm.uid`, `shm_perm.mode`.

**shmid_ds.4-5** [OSF/1] A shared memory region is created indirectly via `shmget()`. If `shmget()` is called with a non-existent shared memory region ID, the kernel allocates a new `shmid_ds` structure, initializes it, and returns the ID to be associated with the region.
  Test: `shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, 4096, IPC_CREAT|0600)`; expect a valid ID and `shm_segsz` of 4096.
  Note: The page says "non-existent shared memory region ID", although `shmget()` is called with a key; the page is unclear here.

**shmid_ds.4-6** [OSF/1] The kernel allocates the actual memory of `shm_segsz` bytes only when a process attaches a region to its address space.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel allocation timing).

**shmid_ds.4-7** [OSF/1] Attached regions are kept in a separate region table; entries in the shared memory table point to the associated attached regions in the region table.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel tables).

**shmid_ds.4-8** [OSF/1] The same shared memory region can be attached several times, by the same or different processes; each attachment creates a new entry in the region table.
  Test: `shmat()` the same ID twice in one process; expect both calls to succeed and a write through one attachment to be visible through the other.

**shmid_ds.4-9** [OSF/1] After a process attaches a region, the region becomes part of the process's virtual address space, and the process accesses it with the same machine instructions used for any virtual address.
  Test: `shmat()` and store/load through the returned pointer; expect the value in a second attaching process.

**shmid_ds.4-10** [OSF/1] `shm_perm`: the `ipc_perm` structure that defines permissions for shared memory operations.
  Test: `IPC_STAT` and check `shm_perm.mode & 0777` equals the creation mode.

**shmid_ds.4-11** [OSF/1] `shm_segsz`: the size of the region, in bytes.
  Test: create with size 8192; expect `shm_segsz` 8192.

**shmid_ds.4-12** [OSF/1] `shm_cpid`: the process ID of the process that created the region ID.
  Test: create in a child; expect `shm_cpid` = child's PID.

**shmid_ds.4-13** [OSF/1] `shm_lpid`: the process ID of the last process that did a `shmat()` or `shmdt()` operation on the region.
  Test: `shmat()` in a child; expect `shm_lpid` = child's PID.

**shmid_ds.4-14** [OSF/1] `shm_nattch`: the number of processes that currently have this region attached.
  Test: attach in two processes; expect `shm_nattch` 2; detach one; expect 1.
  Note: The page says "number of processes", but shmid_ds.4-8 says one process can attach a region more than once; how such attachments are counted is not stated.

**shmid_ds.4-15** [OSF/1] `shm_atime`: the time of the last `shmat()` operation.
  Test: `shmat()`; expect `shm_atime` within a second of `time()`.

**shmid_ds.4-16** [OSF/1] `shm_dtime`: the time of the last `shmdt()` operation.
  Test: `shmdt()`; expect `shm_dtime` within a second of `time()`.

**shmid_ds.4-17** [OSF/1] `shm_ctime`: the time of the last `shmctl()` operation that changed a member of the `shmid_ds` structure.
  Test: wait 2 seconds, `shmctl(IPC_SET)`; expect `shm_ctime` about `time()`.

**shmid_ds.4-18** [OSF/1] The `shm_perm` field identifies the associated `ipc_perm` structure from the `sys/ipc.h` header file, with fields `ushort uid` (owner's user ID), `ushort gid` (owner's group ID), `ushort cuid` (creator's user ID), `ushort cgid` (creator's group ID), `ushort mode` (access modes), `ushort seq` (slot usage sequence number), `key_t key` (key).
  Test: `IPC_STAT` a new region; expect `uid`/`cuid` = `geteuid()`, `gid`/`cgid` = `getegid()`, `key` = the key used.

**shmid_ds.4-19** [OSF/1] The `mode` field is a nine-bit field holding the permissions for shared memory operations: owner, group and other in three groups of three bits; in each group the first bit means read, the second write, and the third is not used.
  Test: create with mode 0600; as another non-root user, expect `shmat()` to fail.

Related: Functions: shmat(2), shmdt(2), shmctl(2), shmget(2)

### signal.h(4), signal(4)

Page: `man4/signal.h.html`; same text as `signal(4)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**signal.h.4-1** [OSF/1] The file `/usr/include/signal.h` defines the signals listed in signal.h.4-2 to signal.h.4-32, with the numbers given.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<signal.h>` and checks each constant's value.

**signal.h.4-2** [OSF/1] `SIGHUP` is 1: hangup.
  Test: expect `SIGHUP == 1`; default action terminates a child.

**signal.h.4-3** [OSF/1] `SIGINT` is 2: interrupt.
  Test: expect `SIGINT == 2`; default action terminates a child.

**signal.h.4-4** [OSF/1] `SIGQUIT` is 3: quit; default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGQUIT == 3`; send to a child; expect `WCOREDUMP` and a `core` file under the conditions of signal.h.4-38.

**signal.h.4-5** [OSF/1] `SIGILL` is 4: invalid instruction (not reset when caught); default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGILL == 4`; catch it twice with a handler installed once; expect the handler to run both times.

**signal.h.4-6** [OSF/1] `SIGTRAP` is 5: trace trap (not reset when caught); default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGTRAP == 5`; catch it twice with a handler installed once; expect the handler to run both times.

**signal.h.4-7** [OSF/1] `SIGABRT` is 6: end process (see `abort()`); default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGABRT == 6`; child calls `abort()`; expect termination by signal 6 with core.

**signal.h.4-8** [OSF/1] `SIGEMT` is 7: EMT instruction.
  Test: expect `SIGEMT == 7`; default action terminates a child without core.

**signal.h.4-9** [OSF/1] `SIGFPE` is 8: arithmetic exception, integer divide by 0, or floating-point exception; default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGFPE == 8`; send to a child; expect termination with core.

**signal.h.4-10** [OSF/1] `SIGKILL` is 9: kill (cannot be caught or ignored).
  Test: expect `SIGKILL == 9`; `sigaction(SIGKILL, ...)` with a handler or `SIG_IGN` must not stop a later `kill(pid, SIGKILL)` from terminating the child.

**signal.h.4-11** [OSF/1] `SIGBUS` is 10: specification exception; default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGBUS == 10`; send to a child; expect termination with core.

**signal.h.4-12** [OSF/1] `SIGSEGV` is 11: segmentation violation; default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGSEGV == 11`; child dereferences an invalid pointer; expect termination by signal 11 with core.

**signal.h.4-13** [OSF/1] `SIGSYS` is 12: invalid parameter to system call; default action includes a core dump.
  Test: expect `SIGSYS == 12`; send to a child; expect termination with core.

**signal.h.4-14** [OSF/1] `SIGPIPE` is 13: write on a pipe when there is no process to read it.
  Test: expect `SIGPIPE == 13`; child writes to a pipe whose read end is closed; expect termination by signal 13.

**signal.h.4-15** [OSF/1] `SIGALRM` is 14: alarm clock.
  Test: expect `SIGALRM == 14`; child calls `alarm(1)` and `pause()`; expect termination by signal 14.

**signal.h.4-16** [OSF/1] `SIGTERM` is 15: software termination signal.
  Test: expect `SIGTERM == 15`; default action terminates a child.

**signal.h.4-17** [OSF/1] `SIGURG` is 16: urgent condition on I/O channel; default action is to ignore it.
  Test: expect `SIGURG == 16`; send to a child; expect the child to keep running.

**signal.h.4-18** [OSF/1] `SIGSTOP` is 17: stop (cannot be caught or ignored); default action stops the process.
  Test: expect `SIGSTOP == 17`; send to a child; expect `waitpid(WUNTRACED)` to report it stopped.

**signal.h.4-19** [OSF/1] `SIGTSTP` is 18: interactive stop; default action stops the process.
  Test: expect `SIGTSTP == 18`; send to a child; expect it stopped.

**signal.h.4-20** [OSF/1] `SIGCONT` is 19: continue if stopped (cannot be caught or ignored); default action restarts or continues the process.
  Test: expect `SIGCONT == 19`; stop a child then send `SIGCONT`; expect it to resume.
  Note: The page says `SIGCONT` "cannot be caught or ignored"; elsewhere it only says it cannot be ignored (signal.h.4-49).

**signal.h.4-21** [OSF/1] `SIGCHLD` is 20: sent to the parent on child stop or exit; default action is to ignore it.
  Test: expect `SIGCHLD == 20`; with a handler installed, expect it to run when a child exits.

**signal.h.4-22** [OSF/1] `SIGTTIN` is 21: background read attempted from control terminal; default action stops the process.
  Test: expect `SIGTTIN == 21`; send to a child; expect it stopped.

**signal.h.4-23** [OSF/1] `SIGTTOU` is 22: background write attempted from control terminal; default action stops the process.
  Test: expect `SIGTTOU == 22`; send to a child; expect it stopped.

**signal.h.4-24** [OSF/1] `SIGIO` is 23: input/output possible or completed; default action is to ignore it.
  Test: expect `SIGIO == 23`; send to a child; expect it to keep running.

**signal.h.4-25** [OSF/1] `SIGXCPU` is 24: CPU time limit exceeded (see `setrlimit()`).
  Test: expect `SIGXCPU == 24`; child sets `RLIMIT_CPU` to 1 second and loops; expect it to receive signal 24.

**signal.h.4-26** [OSF/1] `SIGXFSZ` is 25: file size limit exceeded (see `setrlimit()`).
  Test: expect `SIGXFSZ == 25`; child sets a small `RLIMIT_FSIZE` and writes past it; expect signal 25.

**signal.h.4-27** [OSF/1] `SIGVTALRM` is 26: virtual time alarm (see `setitimer()`).
  Test: expect `SIGVTALRM == 26`; arm `ITIMER_VIRTUAL` and loop; expect signal 26.

**signal.h.4-28** [OSF/1] `SIGPROF` is 27: profiling time alarm (see `setitimer()`).
  Test: expect `SIGPROF == 27`; arm `ITIMER_PROF` and loop; expect signal 27.

**signal.h.4-29** [OSF/1] `SIGWINCH` is 28: window size change; default action is to ignore it.
  Test: expect `SIGWINCH == 28`; send to a child; expect it to keep running.

**signal.h.4-30** [OSF/1] `SIGINFO` is 29: information request; default action is to ignore it.
  Test: expect `SIGINFO == 29`; send to a child; expect it to keep running.

**signal.h.4-31** [OSF/1] `SIGUSR1` is 30: user-defined signal 1.
  Test: expect `SIGUSR1 == 30`; default action terminates a child.

**signal.h.4-32** [OSF/1] `SIGUSR2` is 31: user-defined signal 2.
  Test: expect `SIGUSR2 == 31`; default action terminates a child.

**signal.h.4-33** [OSF/1] Table notes: mark 1 means the default action includes creating a core dump file; mark 2 means the default action is to ignore the signal; mark 3 means the default action is to stop the receiving process; mark 4 means the default action is to restart or continue the receiving process. Marks: 1 for `SIGQUIT`, `SIGILL`, `SIGTRAP`, `SIGABRT`, `SIGFPE`, `SIGBUS`, `SIGSEGV`, `SIGSYS`; 2 for `SIGURG`, `SIGCHLD`, `SIGIO`, `SIGWINCH`, `SIGINFO`; 3 for `SIGSTOP`, `SIGTSTP`, `SIGTTIN`, `SIGTTOU`; 4 for `SIGCONT`.
  Test: for each signal, send it to a child with default disposition and check the outcome class (core, ignored, stopped, continued, or plain termination).

**signal.h.4-34** [OSF/1] Three kinds of action can be associated with a signal: `SIG_DFL`, `SIG_IGN`, or a pointer to a function.
  Test: install each kind with `sigaction()` and read it back.

**signal.h.4-35** [OSF/1] `SIG_DFL` is the signal-specific default action.
  Test: see signal.h.4-33.

**signal.h.4-36** [OSF/1] Except for signals marked 2, 3 or 4, the default action ends the receiving process with all the consequences described for `_exit()`.
  Test: send `SIGTERM` to a child; expect `WIFSIGNALED` with `WTERMSIG == SIGTERM`.

**signal.h.4-37** [OSF/1] In addition, for a signal marked 1, a memory image file is created in the current directory of the receiving process if the conditions in signal.h.4-38 are met.
  Test: send `SIGQUIT` to a child in a writable directory; expect a file `core` there.

**signal.h.4-38** [OSF/1] The core-file conditions are: the effective user ID and the real user ID of the receiving process are equal; and an ordinary file named `core` exists in the current directory and is writable, or it can be created.
  Test: in a child with different real and effective UIDs, send `SIGQUIT`; expect no `core` file. In a directory where `core` cannot be created, expect no `core` file.

**signal.h.4-39** [OSF/1] If the `core` file must be created, it has access permission code 0666 (0x1B6) modified by the file creation mask (see `umask()`), a file owner ID equal to the effective user ID of the receiving process, and a file group ID equal to the effective group ID of the receiving process.
  Test: with `umask(022)`, make a child dump core; expect `core` mode 0644, owner `geteuid()`, group `getegid()`.

**signal.h.4-40** [OSF/1] For signals marked 4, the default action is to restart the receiving process if it is stopped, or to continue its execution.
  Test: stop a child with `SIGSTOP`, send `SIGCONT`; expect it to run again.

**signal.h.4-41** [OSF/1] For signals marked 3, the default action is to stop the execution of the receiving process temporarily.
  Test: send `SIGTSTP` to a child; expect `waitpid(WUNTRACED)` to report it stopped.

**signal.h.4-42** [OSF/1] When a process stops, a `SIGCHLD` signal is sent to its parent process, unless the parent process has set the `SA_NOCLDSTOP` bit.
  Test: stop a child; expect the parent's `SIGCHLD` handler to run; repeat with `SA_NOCLDSTOP` set; expect no `SIGCHLD`.

**signal.h.4-43** [OSF/1] While a process is stopped, any further signals sent to it are not delivered until it is continued; the exceptions are `SIGKILL`, which always terminates the receiving process, and `SIGCONT`, which always causes it to restart or continue.
  Test: stop a child that catches `SIGUSR1`, send `SIGUSR1`; expect the handler not to run until `SIGCONT`; send `SIGKILL` to a stopped child; expect it to die.

**signal.h.4-44** [OSF/1] A process whose parent has ended "shall be sent a `SIGKILL` signal" if the `SIGTSTP`, `SIGTTIN` or `SIGTTOU` signals are generated for that process.
  Test: create a grandchild whose parent exits; send it `SIGTSTP`; expect it to be killed by `SIGKILL`.

**signal.h.4-45** [OSF/1] For signals marked 2, the default action is to ignore the signal, and delivery has no effect on the receiving process.
  Test: send `SIGWINCH` to a child; expect it to continue unaffected.

**signal.h.4-46** [OSF/1] If a signal's action is set to `SIG_DFL` while the signal is pending, the signal remains pending.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, install a handler, send it, set `SIG_DFL`; expect `sigpending()` still to include it.

**signal.h.4-47** [OSF/1] `SIG_IGN` ignores the signal: delivery has no effect on the receiving process.
  Test: set `SIG_IGN` for `SIGTERM` and send it; expect the process to continue.

**signal.h.4-48** [OSF/1] If a signal's action is set to `SIG_IGN` while the signal is pending, the pending signal is discarded.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, send it, set `SIG_IGN`; expect `sigpending()` not to include it.

**signal.h.4-49** [OSF/1] The `SIGKILL`, `SIGSTOP` and `SIGCONT` signals cannot be ignored.
  Test: try `sigaction(sig, SIG_IGN)` for each and send the signal to a child; expect it still to be killed, stopped or continued.

**signal.h.4-50** [OSF/1] With a pointer to a function, the signal is caught: on delivery the receiving process runs that signal-catching function.
  Test: install a handler for `SIGUSR1`, `kill(getpid(), SIGUSR1)`; expect the handler to run.

**signal.h.4-51** [OSF/1] The handler can be declared as `void handler(signal) int signal;`; the `signal` parameter is the signal number.
  Test: handler records its argument; send `SIGUSR2`; expect it to receive 31.

**signal.h.4-52** [OSF/1] A new signal mask is calculated and installed for the duration of the signal-catching function (or until `sigprocmask()` or `sigsuspend()` calls are made). It is the union of the process signal mask, the mask associated with the action for the signal being delivered, and a mask for the signal being delivered.
  Test: install a `SIGUSR1` handler with `sa_mask` containing `SIGUSR2`; inside it, call `sigprocmask()` to read the mask; expect `SIGUSR1`, `SIGUSR2` and the previously blocked signals.

**signal.h.4-53** [OSF/1] The mask associated with the signal-catching function is not allowed to block signals that cannot be ignored; the kernel enforces this without indicating an error.
  Test: install a handler with `sa_mask` containing `SIGKILL`; expect `sigaction()` to succeed and, inside the handler, the mask not to contain `SIGKILL`.

**signal.h.4-54** [OSF/1] If and when the signal-catching function returns, the original signal mask is restored (modified by any `sigprocmask()` calls made since the function was called), and the process resumes execution where it was interrupted.
  Test: read the mask before and after a handler runs; expect equality.

**signal.h.4-55** [OSF/1] The signal-catching function can make the process resume in a different context by calling `longjmp()`. When `longjmp()` is called, the process leaves the signal stack if it is on it, and restores the process signal mask to its state when the corresponding `setjmp()` call was made.
  Test: `setjmp()` with an empty mask, `longjmp()` out of a `SIGUSR1` handler; expect the mask not to contain `SIGUSR1` afterwards.

**signal.h.4-56** [OSF/1] Once an action is installed for a signal, it stays installed until another action is explicitly requested (by another `sigaction()` call) or until one of the `exec` calls is made.
  Test: install a handler, deliver the signal twice; expect the handler both times.

**signal.h.4-57** [OSF/1] If a signal action is set to a pointer to a function while the signal is pending, the signal remains pending.
  Test: block `SIGUSR1`, send it, install a handler; expect it still pending, and the handler to run on unblocking.

**signal.h.4-58** [OSF/1] When signal-catching functions are invoked asynchronously with process execution, the behavior of some functions defined by this standard is unspecified if they are called from a signal-catching function.
  Test: Not testable (unspecified behavior).

**signal.h.4-59** [OSF/1] The following functions are reentrant with respect to signals and can be called without restriction from signal-catching functions: `_exit()`, `access()`, `alarm()`, `chdir()`, `chmod()`, `chown()`, `close()`, `creat()`, `dup2()`, `dup()`, `exec()`, `fcntl()`, `fork()`, `fstat()`, `getegid()`, `geteuid()`, `getgid()`, `getgroups()`, `getpgrp()`, `getpid()`, `getppid()`, `getuid()`, `kill()`, `link()`, `lseek()`, `mkdir()`, `mkfifo()`, `open()`, `pause()`, `pipe()`, `read()`, `rename()`, `rmdir()`, `setgid()`, `setpgrp()`, `setuid()`, `sigaction()`, `sigaddset()`, `sigdelset()`, `sigfillset()`, `siginitset()`, `sigismember()`, `signal()`, `sigpending()`, `sigprocmask()`, `sigsuspend()`, `sleep()`, `statx()`, `tcdrain()`, `tcflow()`, `tcflush()`, `tcgetattr()`, `tcgetprgp()`, `tcsendbreak()`, `tcsetattr()`, `tcsetpgrp()`, `time()`, `times()`, `umask()`, `uname()`, `unlink()`, `ustat()`, `utime()`, `wait2()`, `wait()`, `write()`.
  Test: from a handler for a frequent timer signal, call each listed function while the main program calls the same functions; expect correct results.
  Note: The page lists `tcgetprgp()`, apparently a misspelling of `tcgetpgrp()` (the list also has `tcsetpgrp()`); `sigemptyset()` is not listed although `sigaddset()`, `sigdelset()` and `sigfillset()` are.

**signal.h.4-60** [OSF/1] All other system calls should not be called from signal-catching functions, since their behavior is undefined.
  Test: Not testable (undefined behavior).

Related: Functions: sigaction(2), sigblock(2), sigemptyset(3), siginterrupt(3), siglongjmp(3), sigpause(3), sigpending(2), sigprocmask(2), sigreturn(2), sigset(3), sigsetjmp(3), sigstack(2), sigsuspend(2), sigvec(2), sigwait(3)

### termios.h(4), termios(4)

Page: `man4/termios.h.html`; same text as `termios(4)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**termios.h.4-1** [OSF/1] The header `/usr/include/termios.h` contains information used by system calls that apply to terminal files.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<termios.h>` and declares `struct termios`; expect success.

**termios.h.4-2** [OSF/1] The definitions, values and structure in this file are required for compatibility with the IEEE P1003.1 POSIX standard.
  Test: compile a program using `tcgetattr()`, `tcsetattr()` and the POSIX constants; expect success.

**termios.h.4-3** [OSF/1] General terminal interface information is in the `termio.h` header file; its `termio` structure defines the basic input, output, control and line-discipline modes.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<termio.h>` and declares `struct termio`; expect success.

**termios.h.4-4** [OSF/1] If a calling program is identified as requiring POSIX compatibility, the `termios` structure and the additional POSIX control packet information in `termios.h` are implemented.
  Test: Not testable as stated (the page does not say how a program is identified).
  Note: The page is unclear on how a program is "identified as requiring POSIX compatibility".

**termios.h.4-5** [OSF/1] Window and terminal size operations use the `winsize` structure, defined in the `ioctl.h` header file.
  Test: compile a program that includes `<sys/ioctl.h>` and declares `struct winsize`; expect success.

**termios.h.4-6** [OSF/1] The `termios` structure contains the fields `c_iflag`, `c_oflag`, `c_cflag`, `c_lflag` and `c_cc`.
  Test: compile a program that refers to each field; expect success.

**termios.h.4-7** [OSF/1] `c_iflag` describes the basic terminal input control; its initial value is all bits clear.
  Test: open a pty slave fresh and `tcgetattr()`; compare `c_iflag` with 0.
  Note: The initial values on this page are tested on a freshly opened terminal; other pages (getty, pty) may set modes before a program sees them.

**termios.h.4-8** [OSF/1] `IGNBRK`: if set, the break condition is ignored: it is not put on the input queue and so not read by any process.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a serial line that can send a break.

**termios.h.4-9** [OSF/1] `BRKINT`: if set, the break condition generates an interrupt signal and flushes both the input and output queues.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a serial line that can send a break.

**termios.h.4-10** [OSF/1] `IGNPAR`: if set, characters with other framing and parity errors are ignored.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a serial line that can produce parity errors.

**termios.h.4-11** [OSF/1] `PARMRK`: if set, a character with a framing or parity error that is not ignored is read as the three-character sequence 0377, 0, x, where x is the data of the character received in error.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a serial line that can produce parity errors.

**termios.h.4-12** [OSF/1] With `PARMRK` set and `ISTRIP` not set, a valid character of 0377 is read as 0377, 0377 to avoid ambiguity.
  Test: on a pty with `PARMRK` set and `ISTRIP` and `ICANON` clear, write byte 0377 to the master; expect to read 0377 0377 from the slave.

**termios.h.4-13** [OSF/1] If `PARMRK` is not set, a framing or parity error that is not ignored is read as the null character.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a serial line that can produce parity errors.

**termios.h.4-14** [OSF/1] `INPCK`: if set, input parity checking is enabled; if not set, it is disabled, which allows output parity generation without input parity errors.
  Test: set `INPCK` with `tcsetattr()` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-15** [OSF/1] `ISTRIP`: if set, valid input characters are first stripped to 7 bits; otherwise all 8 bits are processed.
  Test: on a pty with `ISTRIP` set and `ICANON` clear, write 0xC1 to the master; expect 0x41 at the slave.

**termios.h.4-16** [OSF/1] `INLCR`: if set, a received NL character is translated into a CR character.
  Test: on a pty with `INLCR` set and `ICANON` clear, write `\n` to the master; expect `\r` at the slave.

**termios.h.4-17** [OSF/1] `IGNCR`: if set, a received CR character is ignored (not read).
  Test: on a pty with `IGNCR` set and `ICANON` clear, write `a\rb`; expect `ab` at the slave.

**termios.h.4-18** [OSF/1] `ICRNL`: if set, a received CR character is translated into an NL character.
  Test: on a pty with `ICRNL` set, write `\r`; expect `\n` at the slave.

**termios.h.4-19** [OSF/1] `IUCLC`: if set, a received uppercase alphabetic character is translated into the corresponding lowercase character.
  Test: on a pty with `IUCLC` set, write `AB\n`; expect `ab\n`.

**termios.h.4-20** [OSF/1] `IXON`: if set, a received STOP character suspends output and a received START character restarts output; the START and STOP characters perform flow control but are not read.
  Test: on a pty with `IXON` set, write the STOP character to the master; expect slave writes not to reach the master until START is written, and neither character to be read by the slave.

**termios.h.4-21** [OSF/1] `IXANY`: if set, any input character restarts output that was suspended.
  Test: with `IXON` and `IXANY` set, stop output with STOP, then write `x` to the master; expect output to resume.

**termios.h.4-22** [OSF/1] `IXOFF`: if set, the system transmits a STOP character when the input queue is nearly full, and a START character when enough input has been read that the queue is nearly empty again.
  Test: on a pty with `IXOFF` set, fill the slave's input queue from the master; expect a STOP character to be read on the master.

**termios.h.4-23** [OSF/1] `IMAXBEL`: if set, the ASCII BEL character is echoed if the input stream overflows; further input is not stored, but input already present is not lost. If not set, BEL is not echoed and the input in the input queue is discarded on overflow.
  Test: on a pty with `IMAXBEL` and `ECHO` set, overflow the slave's input queue; expect BEL on the master and the earlier input still readable.

**termios.h.4-24** [OSF/1] `c_oflag` specifies how the system treats output; its initial value is all bits clear.
  Test: open a pty slave fresh and `tcgetattr()`; compare `c_oflag` with 0.

**termios.h.4-25** [OSF/1] `OPOST`: if set, output characters are processed as the remaining flags say; otherwise they are transmitted without change.
  Test: with `ONLCR` set and `OPOST` clear, write `\n` on the slave; expect `\n` alone on the master.

**termios.h.4-26** [OSF/1] `OLCUC`: if set, a lowercase alphabetic character is transmitted as the corresponding uppercase character; it is often used with the `IUCLC` input mode.
  Test: with `OPOST|OLCUC`, write `ab` on the slave; expect `AB` on the master.

**termios.h.4-27** [OSF/1] `ONLCR`: if set, the NL character is transmitted as the CR-NL character pair.
  Test: with `OPOST|ONLCR`, write `\n` on the slave; expect `\r\n` on the master.

**termios.h.4-28** [OSF/1] `OCRNL`: if set, the CR character is transmitted as the NL character.
  Test: with `OPOST|OCRNL`, write `\r` on the slave; expect `\n` on the master.

**termios.h.4-29** [OSF/1] `ONOCR`: if set, no CR character is transmitted at column 0 (first position).
  Test: with `OPOST|ONOCR`, write `\r` at column 0 on the slave; expect nothing on the master.

**termios.h.4-30** [OSF/1] `ONLRET`: if set, NL is assumed to do the carriage-return function: the column pointer is set to 0 and the carriage-return delay is used. Otherwise NL is assumed to do only the line-feed function, and the column pointer is unchanged. The column pointer is also set to 0 if a CR character is actually transmitted.
  Test: with `OPOST|ONLRET|ONOCR`, write `x\n\r`; expect the `\r` to be suppressed (column 0 after NL).

**termios.h.4-31** [OSF/1] The delay bits specify how long transmission stops to allow for mechanical or other movement when certain characters are sent to the terminal; the actual delays depend on line speed and system load.
  Test: Not testable reliably from user space (timing depends on hardware and load).

**termios.h.4-32** [OSF/1] `OFILL`: if set, fill characters are transmitted for a delay instead of a timed delay; this is useful for high-baud-rate terminals that need only a minimal delay.
  Test: with `OPOST|OFILL|NL1`, write `\n` on the slave; expect two fill characters after it on the master.

**termios.h.4-33** [OSF/1] `OFDEL`: if set, the fill character is DEL; if not set, the fill character is null.
  Test: as termios.h.4-32, with and without `OFDEL`; expect fill bytes 0177 and 0 respectively.

**termios.h.4-34** [OSF/1] `NLDLY` is the mask that selects newline delays, used before comparing with `NL0` and `NL1`.
  Test: expect `(NL1 & NLDLY) == NL1` and `(NL0 & NLDLY) == NL0`.

**termios.h.4-35** [OSF/1] `NL0`: no delay.
  Test: set `NL0` and read it back with `tcgetattr()`.

**termios.h.4-36** [OSF/1] `NL1`: one delay of approximately 0.10 seconds. If `ONLRET` is set, the carriage-return delays are used instead of the newline delays. If `OFILL` is set, two fill characters are transmitted.
  Test: see termios.h.4-32.

**termios.h.4-37** [OSF/1] `CRDLY` is the mask that selects carriage-return delays, used before comparing with `CR0`, `CR1`, `CR2` and `CR3`.
  Test: expect each of `CR0`..`CR3` to lie within `CRDLY`.

**termios.h.4-38** [OSF/1] `CR0`: no delay.
  Test: set `CR0` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-39** [OSF/1] `CR1`: the delay depends on the current column position; if `OFILL` is set, it transmits two fill characters.
  Test: with `OPOST|OFILL|CR1`, write `x\r`; expect two fill characters after `\r`.

**termios.h.4-40** [OSF/1] `CR2`: one delay of approximately 0.10 seconds; if `OFILL` is set, it transmits four fill characters.
  Test: with `OPOST|OFILL|CR2`, write `x\r`; expect four fill characters after `\r`.

**termios.h.4-41** [OSF/1] `CR3`: one delay of approximately 0.15 seconds.
  Test: set `CR3` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-42** [OSF/1] `TABDLY` is the mask that selects horizontal-tab delays, used before comparing with `TAB0`, `TAB1`, `TAB2` and `TAB3`. If `OFILL` is set, any of these delays transmits two fill characters.
  Test: with `OPOST|OFILL|TAB2`, write `\t`; expect two fill characters after it.
  Note: The page says "any of these delays" transmits two fill characters, which would include `TAB0` (no delay) and `TAB3` (expansion); it is unclear.

**termios.h.4-43** [OSF/1] `TAB0`: no delay.
  Test: set `TAB0` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-44** [OSF/1] `TAB1`: the delay depends on the current column position; if `OFILL` is set, two fill characters are transmitted.
  Test: with `OPOST|OFILL|TAB1`, write `\t`; expect two fill characters.

**termios.h.4-45** [OSF/1] `TAB2`: one delay of approximately 0.10 seconds.
  Test: set `TAB2` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-46** [OSF/1] `TAB3`: tabs are expanded into spaces.
  Test: with `OPOST|TAB3`, write `\t` at column 0; expect spaces (no tab) on the master.

**termios.h.4-47** [OSF/1] `BSDLY` is the mask that selects backspace delays, used before comparing with `BS0` and `BS1`.
  Test: expect `BS1` to lie within `BSDLY`.

**termios.h.4-48** [OSF/1] `BS0`: no delay.
  Test: set `BS0` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-49** [OSF/1] `BS1`: one delay of approximately 0.05 seconds; if `OFILL` is set, it transmits one fill character.
  Test: with `OPOST|OFILL|BS1`, write `\b`; expect one fill character after it.

**termios.h.4-50** [OSF/1] `VTDLY` is the mask that selects vertical-tab delays, used before comparing with `VT0` and `VT1`.
  Test: expect `VT1` to lie within `VTDLY`.

**termios.h.4-51** [OSF/1] `VT0`: no delay.
  Test: set `VT0` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-52** [OSF/1] `VT1`: one delay of approximately 2 seconds.
  Test: with `OPOST|VT1`, time a write of `\v` followed by `tcdrain()`; expect roughly 2 seconds (timing may be unreliable on a pty).

**termios.h.4-53** [OSF/1] `FFDLY` is the mask that selects formfeed delays, used before comparing with `FF0` and `FF1`.
  Test: expect `FF1` to lie within `FFDLY`.

**termios.h.4-54** [OSF/1] `FF0`: no delay.
  Test: set `FF0` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-55** [OSF/1] `FF1`: one delay of approximately 2 seconds.
  Test: with `OPOST|FF1`, time a write of `\f` followed by `tcdrain()`; expect roughly 2 seconds (timing may be unreliable on a pty).

**termios.h.4-56** [OSF/1] `c_cflag` describes the hardware control of the terminal.
  Test: `tcgetattr()` on a terminal and read `c_cflag`.
  Note: The page says this field "uses the following control characters"; the items listed are flag bits, not characters.

**termios.h.4-57** [OSF/1] `CBAUD`: these bits specify the baud rate of a connection. For any particular hardware, impossible speed changes are ignored.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware; on a pty, set a rate and read it back.

**termios.h.4-58** [OSF/1] `B0`: the zero baud rate hangs up the connection; with `B0` the 'data terminal ready' signal is not asserted, which normally disconnects the line.
  Test: Not testable from user space without modem hardware (the page says only that this "normally" disconnects the line); set `B0` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-59** [OSF/1] Baud-rate values: `B50` 50 baud, `B75` 75 baud, `B110` 110 baud, `B134` 134.5 baud, `B150` 150 baud, `B200` 200 baud, `B300` 300 baud, `B600` 600 baud, `B1200` 1200 baud, `B1800` 1800 baud, `B2400` 2400 baud, `B4800` 4800 baud, `B9600` 9600 baud, `B19200` 19200 baud, `B38400` 38400 baud.
  Test: compile a program that uses each constant; set each with `cfsetospeed()` on a pty and read it back.
  Note: The page lists `B600` twice and writes "75 iaud" for `B75`.

**termios.h.4-60** [OSF/1] `EXTA`: external A; `EXTB`: external B.
  Test: compile a program that uses `EXTA` and `EXTB`; expect success.

**termios.h.4-61** [OSF/1] `CSIZE`: these bits specify the character size in bits for both transmit and receive; the size does not include the parity bit, if any.
  Test: expect `CS5`..`CS8` to lie within `CSIZE`.

**termios.h.4-62** [OSF/1] `CS5` 5 bits, `CS6` 6 bits, `CS7` 7 bits, `CS8` 8 bits.
  Test: set each with `tcsetattr()` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-63** [OSF/1] `CSTOPB`: if set, 2 stop bits are sent; otherwise only 1 stop bit is sent.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware; set and read back.

**termios.h.4-64** [OSF/1] The page states that higher baud rates require 2 stop bits, and that at 110 baud, for example, 2 stop bits are required.
  Test: Not testable from user space (hardware statement).
  Note: The page gives 110 baud, one of the lowest rates it lists, as its example of "higher baud rates"; the page is inconsistent here.

**termios.h.4-65** [OSF/1] `CREAD`: if set, the receiver is enabled; otherwise characters are not received.
  Test: on a pty slave with `CREAD` clear, write to the master; expect nothing to be readable on the slave (if the pty honors `CREAD`).

**termios.h.4-66** [OSF/1] `PARENB`: if set, parity generation and detection is enabled and a parity bit is added to each character.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware; set and read back.

**termios.h.4-67** [OSF/1] `PARODD`: if parity is enabled, specifies odd parity; if not set, even parity is used.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware; set and read back.

**termios.h.4-68** [OSF/1] `HUPCL`: if set, the line is disconnected when the last process closes the line or when the process terminates (when the 'data terminal ready' signal drops).
  Test: with `HUPCL` set on a pty slave, close the last slave descriptor; expect the master to see a hangup.

**termios.h.4-69** [OSF/1] `CLOCAL`: if set, the line is assumed to have a local, direct connection with no modem control; if not set, modem control (dialup) is assumed.
  Test: Not testable from user space without modem hardware; set and read back.

**termios.h.4-70** [OSF/1] `CIBAUD`: specifies the input baud rate if it differs from the output rate.
  Test: compile a program that uses `CIBAUD`; set different input and output speeds and read them back.

**termios.h.4-71** [OSF/1] `PAREXT`: specifies extended parity for mark and space parity.
  Test: compile a program that uses `PAREXT`; expect success.

**termios.h.4-72** [OSF/1] The initial hardware control value after an open is `B300`, `CS8`, `CREAD` and `HUPCL`.
  Test: open a terminal fresh and `tcgetattr()`; expect `c_cflag` to contain exactly these settings.

**termios.h.4-73** [OSF/1] `c_lflag` controls various terminal functions; its initial value after an open is all bits clear.
  Test: open a pty slave fresh and `tcgetattr()`; compare `c_lflag` with 0.

**termios.h.4-74** [OSF/1] `ISIG`: if set, each input character is checked against the INTR and QUIT special control characters; on a match the associated function is performed. If not set, no checking is done.
  Test: with `ISIG` set, write the INTR character to the master; expect `SIGINT` in the slave's foreground process group; with `ISIG` clear, expect the character to be read as data.

**termios.h.4-75** [OSF/1] `ICANON`: if set, canonical processing is on, which enables the erase and kill edit functions and assembles input into lines delimited by NL, EOF and EOL.
  Test: with `ICANON` set, write `ab<ERASE>c\n`; expect the slave to read `ac\n`.

**termios.h.4-76** [OSF/1] If `ICANON` is not set, read requests are satisfied directly from the input queue, and a read is not satisfied until either the minimum number of characters given by MIN has been received, or the time-out given by TIME has expired since the last character was received. This allows bursts of input to be read while still allowing single-character input.
  Test: with `ICANON` clear, MIN 3, TIME 0, write 2 bytes; expect `read()` to block; write a third; expect 3 bytes.

**termios.h.4-77** [OSF/1] The MIN and TIME values are stored in the positions for the EOF and EOL characters, respectively; the TIME value is in tenths of seconds.
  Test: set `c_cc[VEOF]`=1 and `c_cc[VEOL]`=10 with `ICANON` clear; expect `read()` to return after 1 byte, or after about 1 second from the last byte.

**termios.h.4-78** [OSF/1] `XCASE`: if set along with `ICANON`, an uppercase letter (or the uppercase letter translated to lowercase by the `IUCLC` input mode) is accepted on input by preceding it with a `\` (backslash); the output is then preceded by a backslash.
  Test: with `ICANON|XCASE|IUCLC`, write `\a\n`; expect the slave to read `A\n`.
