**termios.h.4-79** [OSF/1] `ECHO`: if set, characters are displayed on the terminal as they are received.
  Test: with `ECHO` set, write `x` to the master; expect `x` echoed back on the master.

**termios.h.4-80** [OSF/1] `ECHOE`: if `ECHO` and `ECHOE` are both set and `ECHOPRT` is not set, the erase character is echoed as backspace, space, backspace (ASCII BS-SP-BS), clearing the last character from the screen. If `ECHOE` is set but `ECHO` is not set, the erase character is echoed as ASCII SP-BS.
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHO|ECHOE`, write `a<ERASE>`; expect `a\b \b` on the master.

**termios.h.4-81** [OSF/1] `ECHOK`: if `ECHOK` is set and `ECHOKE` is not set, a newline function is performed after a KILL character is received, to clear the line and emphasize that it is deleted.
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHO|ECHOK`, write `ab<KILL>`; expect a newline echoed after the kill.

**termios.h.4-82** [OSF/1] An escape character preceding the ERASE or KILL character removes any special function.
  Test: with `ICANON`, write `a\<ERASE>\n`; expect the ERASE character to be read as data.

**termios.h.4-83** [OSF/1] `ECHONL`: if set, the line is cleared when a newline function is performed, whether or not `ECHO` is set; this is useful for terminals set to local echo (half-duplex).
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHONL` and `ECHO` clear, write `a\n`; expect only `\n` echoed.

**termios.h.4-84** [OSF/1] Unless an escape character precedes an EOF, the EOF character is not displayed; because ASCII EOT is the default end-of-file character, this prevents terminals that respond to EOT from hanging up. (Stated under both `ECHONL` and `ECHOCTL`.)
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHO|ECHOCTL`, write the EOF character; expect nothing echoed.

**termios.h.4-85** [OSF/1] `NOFLSH`: if set, the normal flushing of the input and output queues on the quit and interrupt characters is not done.
  Test: with `ISIG|NOFLSH|ICANON`, write `abc` then INTR then `\n`; expect the slave still to read `abc\n`.

**termios.h.4-86** [OSF/1] The page states that the `ICANON`, `XCASE`, `ECHO`, `ECHOE`, `ECHOK`, `ECHONL` and `NOFLSH` special input functions are possible only if the `ISIG` function is set.
  Test: with `ISIG` clear and `ICANON|ECHO` set, write `ab<ERASE>c\n`; per the page, expect no line editing.
  Note: The page's statement conflicts with its own description of `ISIG` (termios.h.4-74), which concerns only the INTR and QUIT characters; the page appears to be wrong here.

**termios.h.4-87** [OSF/1] These functions can be disabled individually by changing the value of the control character to an unlikely or impossible value (for example, 0377 octal or 0xFF).
  Test: set `c_cc[VERASE]` to 0377; write the old erase character; expect it read as data.

**termios.h.4-88** [OSF/1] `ECHOCTL`: control characters are echoed as `^X`, where X is the character formed by adding 100 octal to the control character's code. ASCII DEL is echoed as `^?`. ASCII TAB, NL and START characters are not echoed.
  Test: with `ECHO|ECHOCTL`, write 001 to the master; expect `^A` echoed; write 0177; expect `^?`.
  Note: The page says TAB and NL are "not echoed" under `ECHOCTL`; it probably means not echoed in `^X` form, but the page is unclear.

**termios.h.4-89** [OSF/1] `ECHOPRT`: the first ERASE or WERASE character in a sequence is echoed as `\` (backslash), and the characters are then erased; later ERASE and WERASE characters echo the characters being erased, in reverse order.
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHO|ECHOPRT`, write `ab<ERASE><ERASE>`; expect `\ba` echoed after `ab`.

**termios.h.4-90** [OSF/1] `ECHOKE`: the kill character is echoed by erasing each character on the line from the screen.
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHO|ECHOKE`, write `ab<KILL>`; expect the echo to erase both characters from the screen (the page does not give the byte sequence).

**termios.h.4-91** [OSF/1] `FLUSHO`: when this bit is set by typing the FLUSH character, data written to the terminal is discarded; a terminal can cancel the effect of the FLUSH character by clearing this bit.
  Test: set `FLUSHO` with `tcsetattr()`, write on the slave; expect nothing on the master; clear it and expect output again.

**termios.h.4-92** [OSF/1] `PENDIN`: any input not yet read is reprinted when the next character arrives as input.
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHO`, write `ab`, set `PENDIN`, write `c`; expect `abc` echoed again.

**termios.h.4-93** [OSF/1] `IEXTEN`: enables extended (implementation-defined) functions to be recognized from the input data. If not set, implementation-defined functions are not recognized, and the corresponding input characters are processed as described for `ICANON`, `ISIG`, `IXON` and `IXOFF`.
  Test: Not testable as stated (the page does not say which functions are implementation-defined); set and clear `IEXTEN` and read it back.

**termios.h.4-94** [OSF/1] `TOSTOP`: a `SIGTTOU` signal is sent when a process in a background process group tries to write to its controlling terminal; `SIGTTOU` stops the members of the process group. If job control is not supported, this symbol is ignored.
  Test: with `TOSTOP` set, have a background process group write to the controlling pty; expect it to be stopped by `SIGTTOU`.

**termios.h.4-95** [OSF/1] `c_cc` is an array that defines the special control characters; each function has a relative position (index) and an initial value, as in termios.h.4-96 to termios.h.4-110.
  Test: compile a program that uses every `V*` index; open a terminal fresh and compare `c_cc` with the initial values.

**termios.h.4-96** [OSF/1] `VINTR` indexes the INTR control character (initial value Ctrl-Backspace), which sends `SIGINT` "to stop all processes controlled by this terminal".
  Test: with `ISIG`, write `c_cc[VINTR]` to the master; expect `SIGINT` in the foreground process group.
  Note: The page gives the INTR default as "Ctrl-Backspace", which is unusual; the value cannot be checked from the page.

**termios.h.4-97** [OSF/1] `VQUIT` indexes the QUIT control character (initial value Ctrl-v or Ctrl-|), which sends `SIGQUIT` to stop all processes controlled by the terminal and writes a core image file into the current working directory.
  Test: with `ISIG`, write `c_cc[VQUIT]` to the master; expect `SIGQUIT` and a `core` file in the receiver's directory.
  Note: The page gives Ctrl-v for both QUIT and LNEXT (termios.h.4-110); one of these is probably wrong.

**termios.h.4-98** [OSF/1] `VERASE` indexes the ERASE character (initial value Backspace), which erases the preceding character; it does not erase beyond the start of the line (delimited by NL, EOL, EOF or EOL2).
  Test: with `ICANON`, write `a\n` then `<ERASE><ERASE>b\n`; expect reads of `a\n` and `b\n`.

**termios.h.4-99** [OSF/1] `VKILL` indexes the KILL character (initial value Ctrl-u), which deletes the entire line (delimited by NL, EOL, EOF or EOL2).
  Test: with `ICANON`, write `abc<KILL>d\n`; expect `d\n`.

**termios.h.4-100** [OSF/1] `VEOF` indexes the EOF character (initial value Ctrl-d), which generates an end-of-file at the terminal. When it is received, all characters waiting to be read are passed to the program at once without waiting for a newline, and the EOF is discarded. If EOF is at the start of a line (no characters waiting), zero characters are passed back, which is the standard end-of-file.
  Test: with `ICANON`, write `ab<EOF>`; expect `read()` to return `ab` (2 bytes); write `<EOF>` alone; expect `read()` to return 0.

**termios.h.4-101** [OSF/1] `VEOL` indexes the EOL character (initial value Ctrl-@ or ASCII null), an additional line delimiter not normally used.
  Test: set `c_cc[VEOL]`='x' with `ICANON`; write `abx`; expect `read()` to return `abx`.

**termios.h.4-102** [OSF/1] `VEOL2` indexes the EOL2 character (initial value Ctrl-@ or ASCII null), an additional line delimiter not normally used.
  Test: set `c_cc[VEOL2]`='y' with `ICANON`; write `aby`; expect `read()` to return `aby`.

**termios.h.4-103** [OSF/1] `VSTART` indexes the START character (initial value Ctrl-q), which resumes output suspended by a STOP character; START characters are ignored if output is not suspended.
  Test: with `IXON`, write START when output is not stopped; expect it neither read nor to change anything.

**termios.h.4-104** [OSF/1] `VSUSP` indexes the SUSP character (initial value Ctrl-z), which sends `SIGTSTP` to all foreground processes controlled by the terminal; it is recognized during input if `ISIG` is enabled. If job control is not supported, it is ignored.
  Test: with `ISIG`, write `c_cc[VSUSP]` to the master; expect the foreground process group to be stopped by `SIGTSTP`.

**termios.h.4-105** [OSF/1] `VDSUSP` indexes the DSUSP character (initial value Ctrl-y), which sends `SIGTSTP` to all foreground processes controlled by the terminal; it is recognized when the process attempts to read the DSUSP character. If job control is not supported, it is ignored.
  Test: with `ISIG|IEXTEN`, write `c_cc[VDSUSP]` and have the foreground process read; expect `SIGTSTP` at the read, not at input time.

**termios.h.4-106** [OSF/1] `VSTOP` indexes the STOP character (initial value Ctrl-s), which temporarily suspends output; it is recognized during both input and output if the `IXOFF` (input control) or `IXON` (output control) flag is set.
  Test: see termios.h.4-20.

**termios.h.4-107** [OSF/1] `VREPRINT` indexes the REPRINT character (initial value Ctrl-r), which reprints all characters that are preceded by an NL character and have not been read.
  Test: with `ICANON|ECHO|IEXTEN`, write `ab<REPRINT>`; expect `ab` echoed again.

**termios.h.4-108** [OSF/1] `VDISCRD` indexes the DISCARD character (initial value Ctrl-o), which causes all output to be discarded until another DISCARD is typed, more input is received, or a program clears the condition.
  Test: with `IEXTEN`, write DISCARD to the master; expect slave output to be dropped until a second DISCARD.

**termios.h.4-109** [OSF/1] `VWERASE` indexes the WERASE character (initial value Ctrl-w), which erases the preceding word; it does not erase beyond the start of the line (delimited by NL, EOL, EOF or EOL2).
  Test: with `ICANON|IEXTEN`, write `ab cd<WERASE>e\n`; expect `ab e\n`.

**termios.h.4-110** [OSF/1] `VLNEXT` indexes the LNEXT (literal next) character (initial value Ctrl-v), which makes the special meaning of the next character be ignored, so that characters can be input without being interpreted by the system.
  Test: with `ICANON|IEXTEN`, write `<LNEXT><ERASE>\n`; expect the ERASE character read as data.

**termios.h.4-111** [OSF/1] The character values for INTR, QUIT, SWTCH, ERASE, KILL, EOF and EOL can be changed. The ERASE, KILL and EOF characters can also be escaped (preceded with a backslash) so that no special processing is done.
  Test: set `c_cc[VKILL]`='#', write `ab#c\n`; expect `c\n`; write `ab\#c\n`; expect `ab#c\n` (or with the backslash, as the implementation keeps it).
  Note: The page names a SWTCH character that has no index in the `c_cc` list above.

**termios.h.4-112** [OSF/1] `tcsetattr()` `optional_actions` value `TCSANOW`: the terminal's parameters are set immediately from the referenced `termios` structure.
  Test: `tcsetattr(fd, TCSANOW, &t)` then `tcgetattr()`; expect the new values.

**termios.h.4-113** [OSF/1] `TCSADRAIN`: waits until all output written to the object file has been transmitted before setting the parameters.
  Test: write data on the slave without reading the master, call `tcsetattr(TCSADRAIN)` in a thread or child; expect it to block until the master reads.

**termios.h.4-114** [OSF/1] `TCSAFLUSH`: waits until all output written to the object file has been transmitted and all input received but not read has been discarded, before setting the parameters.
  Test: write input to the master, `tcsetattr(slave, TCSAFLUSH)`; expect the pending input to be gone.

**termios.h.4-115** [OSF/1] `tcflush()` `queue_selector` value `TCIFLUSH`: flushes data received but not read.
  Test: write to the master, `tcflush(slave, TCIFLUSH)`; expect no input on the slave.

**termios.h.4-116** [OSF/1] `TCOFLUSH`: flushes data written but not transmitted.
  Test: stop output, write on the slave, `tcflush(slave, TCOFLUSH)`, restart output; expect nothing on the master.

**termios.h.4-117** [OSF/1] `TCIOFLUSH`: flushes both data received but not read and data written but not transmitted.
  Test: combine the tests of termios.h.4-115 and termios.h.4-116 with `TCIOFLUSH`.

**termios.h.4-118** [OSF/1] `tcflow()` `action` value `TCOOFF`: suspends output of data by the object file named in `tcflow()`.
  Test: `tcflow(slave, TCOOFF)`, write on the slave; expect nothing on the master.

**termios.h.4-119** [OSF/1] `TCOON`: restarts data output suspended by `TCOOFF`.
  Test: after termios.h.4-118, `tcflow(slave, TCOON)`; expect the data on the master.

**termios.h.4-120** [OSF/1] `TCIOFF`: transmits a stop character to stop data transmission by the terminal device.
  Test: `tcflow(slave, TCIOFF)`; expect the STOP character to be readable on the master.

**termios.h.4-121** [OSF/1] `TCION`: transmits a start character to start or restart data transmission by the terminal device.
  Test: `tcflow(slave, TCION)`; expect the START character readable on the master.

**termios.h.4-122** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/include/sys/termios.h` is "the path to the termios.h header file".
  Test: check that `/usr/include/sys/termios.h` exists.
  Note: The page's DESCRIPTION names `/usr/include/termios.h` but FILES names `/usr/include/sys/termios.h`.

Related: Functions: ioctl(2), sigvec(2); Commands: csh(1), getty(1), sh(1), stty(1), tset(1)

### ttys(4)

Page: `man4/ttys.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page carries the "Digital" title label (a Digital-supplied page, see intro(7)).

**ttys.4-1** [DEC] The `/etc/ttys` file identifies which terminal and pseudoterminal lines are secure, that is, allow root logins.
  Test: check that `/etc/ttys` exists and parse it.

**ttys.4-2** [DEC] To allow root logins on a line, add the `secure` keyword to the status field; to disallow them, remove the `secure` keyword.
  Test: Not testable from user space without root and `login`; could be checked by `login` as root on a pty listed without `secure` and expecting refusal.

**ttys.4-3** [DEC] By default, only the console terminal line is marked secure.
  Test: on a freshly installed system, parse `/etc/ttys`; expect `secure` only on the `console` line.

**ttys.4-4** [DEC] The file is created when the system is installed and can be updated at any time.
  Test: Not testable from user space (installation behavior).

**ttys.4-5** [DEC] Each line has the format `name none type { secure }`.
  Test: parse each line of `/etc/ttys`; expect three fields plus an optional `secure`.

**ttys.4-6** [DEC] `name` is the name of the terminal's special file in the `/dev` directory, for example `console`, `ttyd0`, `ttyd1`.
  Test: for each line, expect `/dev/<name>` to exist.

**ttys.4-7** [DEC] `none` (second field) is a nonoperative placeholder.
  Test: parse each line; expect the second field to be `none`.

**ttys.4-8** [DEC] `type` is `none` for terminal lines, or `network` for pseudoterminal lines.
  Test: parse each line; expect the third field to be `none` or `network`.

**ttys.4-9** [DEC] `secure` allows the root user to log in on the terminal line.
  Test: see ttys.4-2.

**ttys.4-10** [DEC] Examples: `console none none secure` and `tty00 none none secure` permit root login on the console and on `tty00`; `ttyp0 none network secure` and `ttyp1 none network` show network pseudoterminals.
  Test: feed these lines to the parser; expect the stated fields.

**ttys.4-11** [DEC] Files: `/etc/ttys` is the full pathname of the file.
  Test: check that `/etc/ttys` exists.

Related: login(1), getty(8), init(8), inittab(4); Guide to System Administration


## Section 5 — miscellany

### environ(5)

Page: `man5/environ.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**environ.5-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `extern char **environ;`
  Test: compile a program that declares `extern char **environ` and prints its entries; expect success.

**environ.5-2** [OSF/1] An array of strings called the environment is made available by the `execve()` function when a process begins.
  Test: `execve()` a child with envp `{"A=1", NULL}`; expect the child's `environ` to hold exactly `A=1`.

**environ.5-3** [OSF/1] By convention these strings have the form `name=value`.
  Test: Not a requirement (a convention); check that the entries set by `login` (e.g. `HOME`, `PATH`) have the form `name=value`.

**environ.5-4** [OSF/1] `EXINIT`: a startup list of commands read by `ex`, `edit` and `vi`.
  Test: run `ex` with `EXINIT="set number"` and check the option is on.

**environ.5-5** [OSF/1] `HOME`: the user's login directory, set by `login` from the password file `passwd`.
  Test: after login, expect `HOME` to equal the user's `pw_dir`.

**environ.5-6** [OSF/1] `PATH`: the sequence of directories, separated by colons, searched by `csh`, `sh`, `system`, `execvp`, etc. when looking for an executable file.
  Test: set `PATH=/tmp/x:/bin`, put a program in `/tmp/x`, `execvp()` it by name; expect it found.

**environ.5-7** [OSF/1] `PATH` is set to `:/usr/ucb:/bin:/usr/bin` initially by `login`.
  Test: after login with no profile, expect `PATH` to be `:/usr/ucb:/bin:/usr/bin`.

**environ.5-8** [OSF/1] `PRINTER`: the name of the default printer used by `lpr`, `lpq` and `lprm`.
  Test: Not testable without a printer setup; check `lpq` honors `PRINTER`.

**environ.5-9** [OSF/1] `SHELL`: the full pathname of the user's login shell.
  Test: after login, expect `SHELL` to equal the user's `pw_shell`.

**environ.5-10** [OSF/1] `TERM`: the kind of terminal for which output is to be prepared; it is used by commands such as `nroff` which may exploit special terminal capabilities.
  Test: Not testable as a system interface (used by commands).

**environ.5-11** [OSF/1] `TERMCAP`: the string describing the terminal named in `TERM`, or, if it begins with `/` (slash), the name of the termcap file.
  Test: set `TERMCAP=/tmp/tc` with a custom entry and call `tgetent()`; expect the entry from `/tmp/tc`.

**environ.5-12** [OSF/1] `TERMPATH`: a sequence of termcap file pathnames, separated by colons or spaces, searched in the order listed for terminal descriptions.
  Test: set `TERMPATH="/tmp/a /tmp/b"` with an entry only in `/tmp/b`; expect `tgetent()` to find it.

**environ.5-13** [OSF/1] Having no `TERMPATH` is equivalent to a `TERMPATH` of `$HOME/.termcap:/etc/termcap`.
  Test: unset `TERMPATH`, put an entry in `$HOME/.termcap`; expect `tgetent()` to find it.

**environ.5-14** [OSF/1] `TERMPATH` is ignored if `TERMCAP` contains a full pathname.
  Test: set both, with the entry only in the `TERMCAP` file; expect `tgetent()` to find it.

**environ.5-15** [OSF/1] `USER`: the login name of the user.
  Test: after login, expect `USER` to equal the login name.

**environ.5-16** [OSF/1] Further names may be put in the environment by the `export` command and `name=value` arguments in `sh`, or by the `setenv` command in `csh`.
  Test: run `sh -c 'X=1; export X; env'`; expect `X=1` in the output.

**environ.5-17** [OSF/1] It is unwise to change certain `sh` variables that `.profile` files often export, such as `MAIL`, `PS1`, `PS2` and `IFS`.
  Test: Not testable (advice).

Related: Functions: exec(2), system(3); Commands: csh(1), ex(1), login(1), sh(1)

### hier(5)

Page: `man5/hier.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**hier.5-1** [OSF/1] The page describes the file system hierarchy and, as a general rule, lists only directories.
  Test: for every directory below, `stat()` the path and expect `S_ISDIR`.

**hier.5-2** [OSF/1] `/` is the root directory of the file system.
  Test: `stat("/")`; expect a directory.

**hier.5-3** [OSF/1] `/dev/` holds block and character device files.
  Test: expect `/dev` to be a directory containing `S_ISCHR`/`S_ISBLK` files.

**hier.5-4** [OSF/1] `/etc/` holds system configuration files and databases, which are nonexecutable files.
  Test: expect `/etc` to be a directory.

**hier.5-5** [OSF/1] `/etc/nls/` holds National Language Support databases.
  Test: expect `/etc/nls` to be a directory.

**hier.5-6** [OSF/1] `/lost+found/` holds files located by `fsck`.
  Test: expect `/lost+found` to be a directory.

**hier.5-7** [OSF/1] `/opt/` holds optional application packages.
  Test: expect `/opt` to be a directory.

**hier.5-8** [OSF/1] `/sbin/` holds commands essential for the system to boot; they do not depend on shared libraries or the loader and can have other versions in `/usr/bin` or `/usr/sbin`.
  Test: expect `/sbin` to be a directory and its programs to be statically linked.

**hier.5-9** [OSF/1] `/sbin/init.d/` holds system state rc files.
  Test: expect `/sbin/init.d` to be a directory.

**hier.5-10** [OSF/1] `/sbin/rc0.d/`, `/sbin/rc2.d/` and `/sbin/rc3.d/` hold rc files executed for system-state 0, 2 and 3 respectively.
  Test: expect the three directories to exist.

**hier.5-11** [OSF/1] `/stand/` holds standalone programs.
  Test: expect `/stand` to be a directory.

**hier.5-12** [OSF/1] `/tmp/` holds system-generated temporary files; its contents are "usually not preserved across a system reboot".
  Test: expect `/tmp` to be a directory.

**hier.5-13** [OSF/1] `/usr/` contains the majority of user utilities and applications.
  Test: expect `/usr` to be a directory.

**hier.5-14** [OSF/1] `/usr/bin/` holds common utilities and applications.
  Test: expect `/usr/bin` to be a directory.

**hier.5-15** [OSF/1] `/usr/ccs/` is the C compilation system (tools and libraries used to generate C programs); `/usr/ccs/bin/` holds development binaries (including `cc`, `ld`, `make`, etc.); `/usr/ccs/lib/` holds development libraries and backends.
  Test: expect the three directories, and `/usr/ccs/bin/cc`, `ld`, `make` to exist.

**hier.5-16** [OSF/1] `/usr/include/` holds program header (include) files; not all subdirectories are listed.
  Test: expect `/usr/include` to be a directory.

**hier.5-17** [OSF/1] Subdirectories of `/usr/include/`: `mach/` (Mach-specific C include files), `machine/` (machine-specific), `net/` (miscellaneous network), `netimp/` (IMP protocols), `netinet/` (Internet standard protocols), `netns/` (XNS standard protocols), `nfs/` (Network File System), `protocols/` (Berkeley service protocols), `rpc/` (remote procedure calls), `servers/` (servers), `streams/` (Streams), `sys/` (system C include files, kernel data structures), `tli/` (Transport Layer Interface), `ufs/` (UFS).
  Test: expect each of these subdirectories to exist.

**hier.5-18** [OSF/1] `/usr/lbin/` holds back-end executables; `/usr/lbin/spell/` is the spell back-end.
  Test: expect both directories to exist.

**hier.5-19** [OSF/1] `/usr/lib/` consists of links to libraries located elsewhere (`/usr/ccs/lib`, `/usr/lbin`, `/usr/share/lib`, `/X11/lib`), "and includes" `/usr/lib/uucp/`, which holds UUCP programs.
  Test: expect `/usr/lib` and `/usr/lib/uucp` to exist and library entries in `/usr/lib` to be links (the page does not say hard or symbolic).
  Note: The page lists `/X11/lib`, probably meaning a path under `/usr`; the page is unclear here.

**hier.5-20** [OSF/1] `/usr/sbin/` holds system administration utilities and system utilities.
  Test: expect `/usr/sbin` to be a directory.

**hier.5-21** [OSF/1] `/usr/share/` holds architecture-independent ASCII text files; `/usr/share/dict/` holds word lists.
  Test: expect both directories.

**hier.5-22** [OSF/1] `/usr/share/lib/` has subdirectories `me/` (macros for the ME macro package), `ms/` (macros for the MS macro package), `tabset/` (tab description files for a variety of terminals, used in `/etc/termcap`), `terminfo/` (terminal information database), `tmac/` (text processing macros).
  Test: expect each subdirectory to exist.

**hier.5-23** [OSF/1] `/usr/share/man/` holds online reference pages: `man1/` user commands, `man2/` system calls, `man3/` library routines, `man4/` file formats, `man5/` miscellaneous, `man7/` devices, `man8/` administrator commands (each "Source for" those pages), and `cat1-8`, formatted versions of the pages in `man1` through `man8`.
  Test: expect the `man1`..`man8` directories listed to exist.
  Note: The page writes `cat1-8` as one entry, meaning directories `cat1` through `cat8`; no `man6` is listed.

**hier.5-24** [OSF/1] `/usr/shlib/` holds binary loadable shared libraries, the shared versions of the libraries in `/usr/ccs/lib`.
  Test: expect `/usr/shlib` to be a directory.

**hier.5-25** [OSF/1] `/var/` holds multipurpose log, temporary, transient, varying and spool files.
  Test: expect `/var` to be a directory.

**hier.5-26** [OSF/1] `/var/adm/` holds common administrative files and databases; its subdirectories are `crash/` (for saving kernel crash dumps), `cron/` (files used by `cron`), `sendmail/` (sendmail configuration and database files), `syslog/` (files generated by `syslog`).
  Test: expect each directory to exist.

**hier.5-27** [OSF/1] `/var/spool/` holds miscellaneous printer and mail spooling directories, including `lpd/` (line printer spooling), `mail/` (incoming mail messages), `mqueue/` (undelivered mail queue), `uucp/` (UUCP spool).
  Test: expect each directory to exist.

**hier.5-28** [OSF/1] `/var/tmp/` holds application-generated temporary files that are kept between system reboots.
  Test: expect `/var/tmp` to be a directory.

**hier.5-29** [OSF/1] `/var/run/` holds files created when daemons are running.
  Test: expect `/var/run` to be a directory.

**hier.5-30** [OSF/1] `/vmunix` is the pure kernel executable, the operating system loaded into memory at boot time.
  Test: expect `/vmunix` to be a regular file.

Related: Commands: ls(1), apropos(1), whatis(1), whereis(1), finger(1), which(1), find(1), grep(1), fsck(8)


## Section 7 — special files

### clone(7)

Page: `man7/clone.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page carries the "Digital" title label (a Digital-supplied page, see intro(7)).

**clone.7-1** [DEC] `clone` is a STREAMS software driver that finds and opens an unused major/minor device on another STREAMS driver.
  Test: open `/dev/streams/log` (a clone node, see log(7)) twice; expect two descriptors with different `st_rdev` from `fstat()`.

**clone.7-2** [DEC] The major device number passed to `clone` during open corresponds to the clone driver, and the minor device number corresponds to the target driver.
  Test: `stat()` a clone node; expect its major to be the clone driver's and its minor to be the target driver's major.

**clone.7-3** [DEC] Each open results in a separate stream to a previously unused major/minor device.
  Test: see clone.7-1.

**clone.7-4** [DEC] The clone driver consists only of an open function, which does all the necessary work so that later system calls, including `close(2)`, need no further involvement of `clone`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (driver internals); `close()` on a cloned descriptor must succeed.

**clone.7-5** [DEC] Multiple opens of the same major/minor device cannot be done through the clone interface.
  Test: open a clone node twice; expect two different minor numbers.

**clone.7-6** [DEC] Running `stat(2)` on the file system node of a cloned device gives a different result from running `fstat(2)` on a descriptor obtained by opening the node.
  Test: compare `stat()` of the node with `fstat()` of an open descriptor; expect the results to differ (the page does not say in which field).

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**clone.7-E1** `ENXIO`: the major/minor device number given does not correspond to a valid major/minor device, or the driver indicated is not a STREAMS driver. The device is not opened.

Related: Commands: log(7).

### console(7)

Page: `man7/console.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page carries the "Digital" title label (a Digital-supplied page, see intro(7)).

**console.7-1** [DEC] One returns to the monitor by halting the machine from the operating system or by pressing the HALT button on the rear panel.
  Test: Not testable from user space (hardware console).

**console.7-2** [DEC] Entering `help` at the console prompt (`>>`) gives a description of valid console commands.
  Test: Not testable from user space (firmware console).

**console.7-3** [DEC] The `/dev/console` device is valid for all operating system accesses to the character tty device.
  Test: `stat("/dev/console")`; expect a character special file; as root, `open()` it and `write()` a line; expect success.

**console.7-4** [DEC] Files: `/dev/console`.
  Test: check that `/dev/console` exists.

Related: tty(7), MAKEDEV(8)

### fd(7), stdin(7)

Page: `man7/fd.html`; same text as `stdin(7)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

Note: The page's NAME line also names `stdout` and `stderr`.

**fd.7-1** [OSF/1] The files `/dev/fd/0` through `/dev/fd/#` refer to file descriptors that can be accessed through the file system.
  Test: `stat("/dev/fd/0")`; expect it to exist.

**fd.7-2** [OSF/1] If the file descriptor is open and the mode the file is being opened with is a subset of the existing descriptor's mode, `fd = open("/dev/fd/0", mode);` is equivalent to `fd = fcntl(0, F_DUPFD, 0);`.
  Test: with descriptor 0 open read-only on a file, `open("/dev/fd/0", O_RDONLY)`; expect the lowest free descriptor, sharing the file offset with descriptor 0 (`lseek` on one moves the other).
  Note: The page does not say what happens when the descriptor is not open or the mode is not a subset.

**fd.7-3** [OSF/1] Opening `/dev/stdin`, `/dev/stdout` and `/dev/stderr` is equivalent to `fcntl(STDIN_FILENO, F_DUPFD, 0)`, `fcntl(STDOUT_FILENO, F_DUPFD, 0)` and `fcntl(STDERR_FILENO, F_DUPFD, 0)` respectively.
  Test: open `/dev/stdout` with `O_WRONLY`; write to it; expect the data where descriptor 1 goes and a shared offset.

**fd.7-4** [OSF/1] Flags to `open()` other than `O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY` and `O_RDWR` are ignored.
  Test: `open("/dev/fd/0", O_RDONLY|O_TRUNC|O_CREAT|O_EXCL)` with descriptor 0 open on a non-empty file; expect success and the file not truncated.

**fd.7-5** [OSF/1] Files: `/dev/fd/#` are the file descriptor files, where `#` is the descriptor number; `/dev/stdin`, `/dev/stdout` and `/dev/stderr` are special files for the standard input, standard output and standard error devices.
  Test: check that `/dev/stdin`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr` and `/dev/fd/0`..`/dev/fd/2` exist.

Related: Files: tty(7)

### log(7)

Page: `man7/log.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page carries the "Digital" title label (a Digital-supplied page, see intro(7)).

**log.7-1** [DEC] `log` is a STREAMS software device driver that provides an interface for the STREAMS error logging and event tracing processes (`strerr(1)`, `strace(1)`).
  Test: open `/dev/streams/log`; expect success.

**log.7-2** [DEC] `log` presents two interfaces: a kernel function call interface through which STREAMS drivers and modules submit log messages, and a subset of `ioctl(2)` calls and STREAMS messages for a user-level error logger, a trace logger, or processes that submit their own log messages.
  Test: see log.7-9 onward.

**log.7-3** [DEC] Kernel log messages are generated by calls to `strlog(mid, sid, level, flags, fmt, arg1, ...)` with `short mid, sid; char level; ushort flags; char *fmt; unsigned arg1;`; the required definitions are in `<sys/strlog.h>`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel function); compile a program that includes `<sys/strlog.h>`.

**log.7-4** [DEC] `mid` is the STREAMS module ID number of the module or driver submitting the message; `sid` is an internal sub-ID number, usually identifying a particular minor device of a driver.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel function).

**log.7-5** [DEC] `level` is a tracing level that allows low-priority messages to be screened out selectively from the tracer.
  Test: see log.7-12.

**log.7-6** [DEC] `flags` is any combination of `SL_ERROR` (the message is for the error logger), `SL_TRACE` (the message is for the tracer), `SL_FATAL` (advisory notification of a fatal error) and `SL_NOTIFY` (request that a copy of the message be mailed to the system administrator).
  Test: compile a program that uses the four constants; send a message with `SL_ERROR` and expect the error logger to receive it.

**log.7-7** [DEC] `fmt` is a `printf(3)`-style format string, except that the `%s`, `%e`, `%E`, `%g` and `%G` conversion specifications are not handled.
  Test: Not testable from user space (`strlog` is a kernel function).

**log.7-8** [DEC] Up to `NLOGARGS` (currently 3) numeric or character arguments can be given.
  Test: compile a program that checks `NLOGARGS == 3`.

**log.7-9** [DEC] `log` is opened via the clone interface, `/dev/streams/log`; each open of `/dev/log` obtains a separate stream to `log`.
  Test: open `/dev/streams/log` twice; expect two independent streams (both can become loggers of different types).
  Note: The page names both `/dev/streams/log` and `/dev/log` for the same device; FILES gives only `/dev/streams/log`.

**log.7-10** [DEC] To receive log messages, a process must first tell `log` whether it is an error logger or a trace logger, with a STREAMS `I_STR` ioctl. For the error logger the `ic_cmd` field is `I_ERRLOG` with no data. For the trace logger the `ic_cmd` field is `I_TRCLOG`, with a data buffer holding an array of one or more `struct trace_ids` elements.
  Test: issue `I_STR` with `I_ERRLOG`, `ic_len` 0; expect success.

**log.7-11** [DEC] Each `trace_ids` structure gives an `mid`, `sid` and `level` from which messages are accepted (fields `ti_mid`, `ti_sid`, `ti_level` in the EXAMPLES).
  Test: compile a program that sets `ti_mid`, `ti_sid`, `ti_level`; expect success.

**log.7-12** [DEC] Messages are accepted whose `mid` and `sid` exactly match those in a `trace_ids` structure and whose `level` is less than or equal to the structure's `level`.
  Test: register a trace logger with mid 2, sid 0, level 1; submit (from a driver) messages at levels 1 and 2; expect only level 1 to arrive.
  Note: The page says "strlog accepts" the messages; it presumably means `log`.

**log.7-13** [DEC] A value of −1 in any `trace_ids` field means any value is accepted for that field.
  Test: register `ti_sid = -1`, `ti_level = -1`; expect messages from any sub-ID and level of that mid.

**log.7-14** [DEC] At most one trace logger and one error logger can be active at a time.
  Test: see log.7-E1.

**log.7-15** [DEC] Once the logger has identified itself via the ioctl, `log` begins sending up messages, subject to the restrictions above; they are obtained with the `getmsg(2)` system call.
  Test: as error logger, `putmsg()` a message with `SL_ERROR` from another stream; expect `getmsg()` on the logger to return it.

**log.7-16** [DEC] The control part of each message received holds a `log_ctl` structure giving the `mid`, `sid`, `level`, `flags`, the time in ticks since boot when the message was submitted, the corresponding time in seconds since Jan. 1, 1970, and a sequence number.
  Test: receive a message as in log.7-15; expect `level` and `flags` as sent and the seconds field within a second of `time()`.

**log.7-17** [DEC] The time in seconds since 1970 is given so that the date and time of the message can be computed; the time in ticks since boot is given so that the relative timing of messages can be determined.
  Test: send two messages a second apart; expect the ticks field to increase.

**log.7-18** [DEC] Separate sequence numbers are kept for the error and trace logging streams, so that gaps in the sequence of messages can be detected.
  Test: send two error messages; expect consecutive sequence numbers on the error logger independent of trace messages.

**log.7-19** [DEC] During times of high message traffic some messages "may not be delivered" by the logger, to avoid hogging system resources.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement (permitted loss); check that any gap shows in the sequence numbers.

**log.7-20** [DEC] The data part of a received message holds the unexpanded text of the format string (null-terminated), followed by `NLOGARGS` words for the format string's arguments, aligned on the first word boundary after the format string.
  Test: send `"x %d"` with argument 7; expect data `"x %d\0"`, padding to a word boundary, then 3 words, the first 7.

**log.7-21** [DEC] A process may also send a message of the same structure to `log` even if it is not an error or trace logger.
  Test: from a non-logger stream, `putmsg()` a `log_ctl` and format string; expect the error logger to receive it.

**log.7-22** [DEC] In the control part of a message sent to `log`, only the `level` and `flags` fields of `log_ctl` are accepted; `log` fills in all other fields before forwarding the message to the appropriate logger.
  Test: send a message with `mid` set to 999; expect the logger to receive a different, `log`-assigned `mid`, with the sent `level` and `flags`.

**log.7-23** [DEC] The data portion of a message sent must contain a null-terminated format string, and any arguments (up to `NLOGARGS`) must be packed one word each, on the next word boundary after the end of the format string.
  Test: send a format string with 2 packed word arguments; expect the logger to receive them at the same offsets.

**log.7-24** [DEC] Incorrectly formatted log messages sent to the driver by a user process are silently ignored; no error results.
  Test: `putmsg()` a message with a control part shorter than `log_ctl`; expect `putmsg()` to succeed and nothing to reach the logger.

**log.7-25** [DEC] In the EXAMPLES, `ic_timout = 0` gives the default timeout, noted as 15 seconds.
  Test: issue the `I_ERRLOG` `I_STR` with `ic_timout` 0; expect success.

**log.7-26** [DEC] EXAMPLES: I_ERRLOG notification uses `ic_cmd = I_ERRLOG`, `ic_len = 0`, `ic_dp = NULL`; I_TRCLOG notification uses `ic_cmd = I_TRCLOG`, `ic_len = 2 * sizeof(struct trace_ids)`, `ic_dp` pointing at the array; submitting a message uses `putmsg(log, &ctl, &dat, 0)` with `ctl` holding a `log_ctl` (`level` 0, `flags` `SL_ERROR|SL_NOTIFY`) and `dat` holding the message text.
  Test: compile and run the three examples against `/dev/streams/log`; expect each `ioctl()`/`putmsg()` to succeed.
  Note: The submit example sets `dat.len` to `strlen(message)`, which leaves out the null terminator that log.7-23 requires.

**log.7-27** [DEC] Files: `/dev/streams/log`, `<sys/strlog.h>`.
  Test: check that both exist.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**log.7-E1** `ENXIO`: an `I_TRCLOG` or `I_ERRLOG` is issued when a logging process of that type already exists.

**log.7-E2** `ENXIO`: an `I_TRCLOG` ioctl is issued without any `trace_ids` structures.

**log.7-E3** `ENXIO`: an unrecognized `I_STR` ioctl call is issued.

Related: strace(1), strerr(1), getmsg(2), putmsg(2), clone(7)

### null(7)

Page: `man7/null.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**null.7-1** [OSF/1] Data written on a null special file are discarded.
  Test: `write()` 100 bytes to `/dev/null`; expect a return of 100.

**null.7-2** [OSF/1] Reads from a null special file always return 0 (zero) bytes.
  Test: `read()` from `/dev/null`; expect 0.

**null.7-3** [OSF/1] Examples: `dd if=/dev/rz1c of=/dev/null` reads a device and discards the data; `cat > foo < /dev/null` creates a zero-length file.
  Test: run `cat > foo < /dev/null`; expect `foo` to have size 0.

**null.7-4** [OSF/1] Files: `/dev/null`.
  Test: `stat("/dev/null")`; expect a character special file.

### pty(7)

Page: `man7/pty.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**pty.7-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (configuration): `pseudo-device pty [ count ]`.
  Test: Not testable from user space (kernel configuration).

**pty.7-2** [OSF/1] The `pty` driver supports a device pair called a pseudo terminal: a pair of character devices, a master device and a slave device.
  Test: open `/dev/ptyp0` and then `/dev/ttyp0`; expect both opens to succeed and both to be character special files.

**pty.7-3** [OSF/1] The slave device provides an interface identical to that described in the tty reference page; instead of a hardware device behind it, another process manipulates it through the master half.
  Test: `tcgetattr()` on the slave; expect success.

**pty.7-4** [OSF/1] Anything written on the master device is given to the slave device as input, and anything written on the slave device is presented as input on the master device.
  Test: write `hi\n` on the master, read it on the slave; write `ok` on the slave, read it on the master.

**pty.7-5** [OSF/1] When configuring, if the optional count is given, that many pseudo terminal pairs are configured; the default count is 32.
  Test: Not testable from user space (configuration); with the default, expect 32 pairs of `/dev/pty*`/`/dev/tty*` nodes to work.

**pty.7-6** [OSF/1] The ioctl calls in pty.7-7 to pty.7-23 apply only to pseudo terminals.
  Test: issue `TIOCPKT` on a non-pty terminal; expect it to have no packet-mode effect (the page does not say whether the call fails).

**pty.7-7** [OSF/1] `TIOCSTOP` stops output to a terminal (like entering Ctrl-S); it takes no parameter.
  Test: `ioctl(master, TIOCSTOP)`, write on the slave; expect nothing readable on the master.

**pty.7-8** [OSF/1] `TIOCSTART` restarts output stopped by `TIOCSTOP` or by typing Ctrl-S; it takes no parameter.
  Test: after pty.7-7, `ioctl(master, TIOCSTART)`; expect the slave's data on the master.

**pty.7-9** [OSF/1] `TIOCPKT` enables or disables packet mode: a nonzero parameter (passed by reference) enables it and a zero parameter disables it.
  Test: `int on = 1; ioctl(master, TIOCPKT, &on)`; expect success; repeat with 0.

**pty.7-10** [OSF/1] In packet mode on the master side, each later `read()` returns either data written on the slave, preceded by a zero byte (`TIOCPKT_DATA`), or a single byte giving control status information.
  Test: in packet mode, write `abc` on the slave; expect master `read()` to return `\0abc`.

**pty.7-11** [OSF/1] The control status byte is an inclusive OR of zero or more of the bits `TIOCPKT_FLUSHREAD`, `TIOCPKT_FLUSHWRITE`, `TIOCPKT_STOP`, `TIOCPKT_START`, `TIOCPKT_DOSTOP`, `TIOCPKT_NOSTOP`.
  Test: compile a program that uses all six constants; expect them to be distinct nonzero bits.

**pty.7-12** [OSF/1] `TIOCPKT_FLUSHREAD` is set whenever the terminal's read queue is flushed.
  Test: in packet mode, `tcflush(slave, TCIFLUSH)`; expect a master read of one byte with `TIOCPKT_FLUSHREAD` set.

**pty.7-13** [OSF/1] `TIOCPKT_FLUSHWRITE` is set whenever the terminal's write queue is flushed.
  Test: in packet mode, `tcflush(slave, TCOFLUSH)`; expect a status byte with `TIOCPKT_FLUSHWRITE`.

**pty.7-14** [OSF/1] `TIOCPKT_STOP` is set whenever output to the terminal is stopped by Ctrl-S.
  Test: in packet mode with `IXON`, write Ctrl-S to the master; expect a status byte with `TIOCPKT_STOP`.

**pty.7-15** [OSF/1] `TIOCPKT_START` is set whenever output to the terminal is restarted.
  Test: after pty.7-14, write Ctrl-Q; expect a status byte with `TIOCPKT_START`.

**pty.7-16** [OSF/1] `TIOCPKT_DOSTOP` is set whenever `t_stopc` is Ctrl-S and `t_startc` is Ctrl-Q.
  Test: in packet mode, set STOP/START to Ctrl-S/Ctrl-Q on the slave; expect a status byte with `TIOCPKT_DOSTOP`.

**pty.7-17** [OSF/1] `TIOCPKT_NOSTOP` is set whenever the start and stop characters are not Ctrl-S and Ctrl-Q.
  Test: in packet mode, change STOP to another character; expect a status byte with `TIOCPKT_NOSTOP`.

**pty.7-18** [OSF/1] While packet mode is in use, the presence of control status information to be read from the master side can be detected by a `select()` for exceptional conditions.
  Test: in packet mode, flush the slave's queue; expect `select()` with the master in the exception set to report it ready.

**pty.7-19** [OSF/1] Packet mode is used by `rlogin` and `rlogind` to implement a remote-echoed, locally Ctrl-S/Ctrl-Q flow-controlled remote login with proper back-flushing of output, and can be used by other similar programs.
  Test: Not testable (usage statement).

**pty.7-20** [OSF/1] `TIOCUCNTL` enables or disables a mode that lets a small number of simple user ioctl commands pass through the pseudo terminal, using a protocol like that of `TIOCPKT`. It is enabled from the master side by a nonzero parameter (by reference) and disabled by a zero parameter. `TIOCUCNTL` and `TIOCPKT` modes are mutually exclusive.
  Test: `int on = 1; ioctl(master, TIOCUCNTL, &on)`; expect success; then enable `TIOCPKT` and check that `TIOCUCNTL` is no longer in effect (or that the enable fails).
  Note: The page does not say what happens when one tries to enable both modes.

**pty.7-21** [OSF/1] In `TIOCUCNTL` mode, each later `read()` from the master returns data written on the slave preceded by a zero byte, or a single byte giving a user control operation on the slave side. A user control command is a special ioctl with no data, given as `UIOCCMD(n)` with `n` in the range 1-255; the value `n` is received as a single byte on the next `read()` from the master. `UIOCCMD(0)` is a no-op that may be used to probe for the facility. As with `TIOCPKT`, command operations can be detected with `select()` for exceptional conditions.
  Test: enable `TIOCUCNTL`; `ioctl(slave, UIOCCMD(5))`; expect `select()` exceptional readiness and a master `read()` returning the single byte 5; `ioctl(slave, UIOCCMD(0))` succeeds and returns nothing on the master.

**pty.7-22** [OSF/1] `TIOCREMOTE` is a mode for the master half of a pseudo terminal, independent of `TIOCPKT`. It makes input to the pseudo terminal flow controlled and not input-edited, regardless of the terminal mode.
  Test: set `TIOCREMOTE` on the master; with `ICANON` on the slave, write `ab<ERASE>c`; expect the slave to read the bytes unedited.

**pty.7-23** [OSF/1] In `TIOCREMOTE` mode, each write to the control terminal produces a record boundary for the process reading the terminal: a write of data is like a line typed on the terminal, and a write of 0 (zero) bytes is like typing an end-of-file character.
  Test: with `TIOCREMOTE`, write `abc` (no newline) on the master; expect the slave's canonical `read()` to return `abc`; write 0 bytes; expect the next slave `read()` to return 0.

**pty.7-24** [OSF/1] `TIOCREMOTE` can be used for remote line editing in a window manager, or whenever flow-controlled input is required.
  Test: Not testable (usage statement).

**pty.7-25** [OSF/1] Files: `/dev/pty[p-r][0-9a-f]` are the master pseudo terminals and `/dev/tty[p-r][0-9a-f]` are the slave pseudo terminals.
  Test: check that `/dev/ptyp0` and `/dev/ttyp0` exist as character special files.

### streamio(7)

Page: `man7/streamio.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page's header line reads "Digital" (not "OSF"); the page does not otherwise say that its contents are specific to DEC, so items are tagged `[DEC]`.

**streamio.7-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `#include <stropts.h>`; `int ioctl(fildes, command, arg)` with `int fildes, command;` (the type of `arg` is not declared in the synopsis).
  Test: compile a program that includes `<stropts.h>` and calls `ioctl(fd, I_FIND, "name")`; it builds and links.

**streamio.7-2** [DEC] STREAMS ioctl commands are a subset of `ioctl(2)` that perform control functions on streams; `command` and `arg` are passed to the file designated by `fildes` and are interpreted by the stream head.
  Test: on a stream fd, call `ioctl(fd, I_LOOK, buf)` after `I_PUSH`; the stream head answers without a driver-specific ioctl.

**streamio.7-3** [DEC] Certain combinations of `command` and `arg` "may be passed to a module or driver in the stream".
  Test: send an `I_STR` with a driver-specific `ic_cmd` to a test driver and check the driver receives it.

**streamio.7-4** [DEC] `fildes` is an open file descriptor that refers to a stream; `command` selects the control function; `arg` carries additional information whose type depends on the command, and is generally an integer or a pointer to a command-specific data structure.
  Test: covered by the per-command tests below.

**streamio.7-5** [DEC] Because these commands are a subset of `ioctl`, they are subject to the errors described in `ioctl(2)`.
  Test: call `ioctl(-1, I_FIND, "x")`; expect −1 with the `ioctl(2)` error for a bad descriptor.

**streamio.7-6** [DEC] Modules and drivers can detect errors; a module or driver then sends an error message containing an error value to the stream head, and this causes subsequent system calls to fail with `errno` set to that value.
  Test: have a test driver send an M_ERROR-style error message with `EPROTO`; a later `read` on the stream fails with −1 and `errno == EPROTO`.

**streamio.7-7** [DEC] Unless a command's description says otherwise, `ioctl` returns 0 on success and −1 on failure with `errno` set as indicated.
  Test: `ioctl(fd, I_SRDOPT, RNORM)` on a stream returns 0.

**streamio.7-8** [DEC] All the listed commands apply to all STREAMS files.
  Test: issue `I_GRDOPT` on a STREAMS pipe and on a STREAMS device; both succeed.

**streamio.7-9** [DEC] `I_PUSH` pushes the module whose name is pointed to by `arg` onto the top of the current stream, just below the stream head, and then calls the open routine of the newly pushed module.
  Test: `I_PUSH` a known module, then `I_LOOK` returns that module's name.

**streamio.7-10** [DEC] `I_POP` removes the module just below the stream head of the stream referred to by `fildes`; `arg` should be 0.
  Test: push module A then B, `I_POP` with arg 0, then `I_LOOK` returns A.

**streamio.7-11** [DEC] `I_LOOK` retrieves the name of the module just below the stream head and places it, as a null-terminated string, in the buffer pointed to by `arg`; the buffer should be at least `FMNAMESZ+1` bytes long, and `#include <sys/conf.h>` is required.
  Test: after `I_PUSH` of a module, `I_LOOK` into a `FMNAMESZ+1` buffer returns 0 and a null-terminated name equal to the pushed name.

**streamio.7-12** [DEC] `I_FLUSH` flushes input and/or output queues according to `arg`: `FLUSHR` flushes read queues, `FLUSHW` flushes write queues, `FLUSHRW` flushes read and write queues.
  Test: write data into one end of a STREAMS pipe, `I_FLUSH` the other end with `FLUSHR`, then `I_NREAD` reports no messages.

Note: The page text repeats the descriptions of `I_POP`, `I_LOOK` and `I_FLUSH` (with their error lists) a second time, word for word, after the first `I_FLUSH`; the original HTML has the same duplication. The items above and errors below are given once.

**streamio.7-13** [DEC] `I_SETSIG` tells the stream head that the user wants the kernel to send `SIGPOLL` when particular events occur on the stream associated with `fildes`; it supports asynchronous processing. `arg` is a bitmask, the bitwise OR of any combination of `S_INPUT`, `S_HIPRI`, `S_OUTPUT`, `S_MSG`.
  Test: `I_SETSIG` with `S_INPUT`, install a `SIGPOLL` handler, write to the peer end of a stream pipe; the handler runs.

**streamio.7-14** [DEC] `S_INPUT`: a non-priority message has arrived on a stream head read queue and no other messages were on that queue before it; this is set even if the message is of zero length.
  Test: register `S_INPUT`, send a zero-length non-priority message to an empty queue; `SIGPOLL` is delivered; send a second message while the first is queued; no second `SIGPOLL`.

**streamio.7-15** [DEC] `S_HIPRI`: a priority message is present on the stream head read queue; set even if the message is of zero length.
  Test: register `S_HIPRI`, `putmsg` a zero-length priority message from the peer; `SIGPOLL` is delivered.

**streamio.7-16** [DEC] `S_OUTPUT`: the write queue just below the stream head is no longer full, meaning there is room on the queue to send (write) data downstream.
  Test: fill a stream's write queue with `O_NDELAY` writes until `EAGAIN`, register `S_OUTPUT`, drain the peer; `SIGPOLL` is delivered.

**streamio.7-17** [DEC] `S_MSG`: a STREAMS signal message containing the `SIGPOLL` signal has reached the front of the stream head read queue.
  Test: have a test driver send a signal message carrying `SIGPOLL`; with `S_MSG` registered, `SIGPOLL` is delivered.

**streamio.7-18** [DEC] A process may ask to be signalled only of priority messages by setting `arg` to `S_HIPRI`.
  Test: register only `S_HIPRI`; a normal message produces no `SIGPOLL`, a priority message does.

**streamio.7-19** [DEC] Processes that wish to receive `SIGPOLL` must explicitly register using `I_SETSIG`.
  Test: without `I_SETSIG`, data arriving on the stream produces no `SIGPOLL`.

**streamio.7-20** [DEC] If several processes register for the same event on the same stream, each of them is signalled when the event occurs.
  Test: parent and child both `I_SETSIG` `S_INPUT` on a shared stream; one message arriving signals both.

**streamio.7-21** [DEC] If `arg` is zero, the calling process is unregistered and receives no further `SIGPOLL` signals.
  Test: register, then `I_SETSIG` with 0; data arrival no longer raises `SIGPOLL`, and `I_GETSIG` fails with `EINVAL`.

**streamio.7-22** [DEC] `I_GETSIG` returns, as a bitmask in the location pointed to by `arg`, the events for which the calling process is currently registered for `SIGPOLL` (the same event bits as `I_SETSIG`).
  Test: `I_SETSIG` with `S_INPUT|S_HIPRI`, then `I_GETSIG` stores `S_INPUT|S_HIPRI`.

**streamio.7-23** [DEC] `I_FIND` compares the names of all modules present in the stream with the name pointed to by `arg`; it returns 1 if the named module is present and 0 if it is not.
  Test: `I_FIND` of a pushed module returns 1; after `I_POP`, returns 0.

**streamio.7-24** [DEC] `I_PEEK` retrieves the information in the first message on the stream head read queue without removing the message. `arg` points to a `strpeek` structure with members `struct strbuf ctlbuf`, `struct strbuf databuf`, `long flags`.
  Test: write "abc" from the peer, `I_PEEK` returns 1 with "abc" in `databuf`, then `read` still returns "abc".

**streamio.7-25** [DEC] For `I_PEEK`, the `maxlen` field of `ctlbuf` and `databuf` must be set to the number of bytes of control and/or data information to retrieve.
  Test: set `databuf.maxlen` to 2 with a 3-byte message queued; at most 2 data bytes are returned.

**streamio.7-26** [DEC] If `flags` is set to `RS_HIPRI`, `I_PEEK` looks only for a priority message on the stream head read queue.
  Test: with only a normal message queued, `I_PEEK` with `flags = RS_HIPRI` returns 0.

**streamio.7-27** [DEC] `I_PEEK` returns 1 if a message was retrieved, and 0 if no message was on the read queue or if `RS_HIPRI` was set and no priority message was present. It does not wait for a message to arrive.
  Test: `I_PEEK` on an empty stream returns 0 immediately without blocking.

**streamio.7-28** [DEC] On return from `I_PEEK`, `ctlbuf` describes the control buffer contents, `databuf` describes the data buffer contents, and `flags` holds 0 or `RS_HIPRI`.
  Test: peek a priority message and check `flags == RS_HIPRI`; peek a normal message and check `flags == 0`.

**streamio.7-29** [DEC] `I_SRDOPT` sets the read mode from `arg`. Legal values: `RNORM` (byte-stream mode, the default), `RMSGD` (message-discard mode), `RMSGN` (message-nondiscard mode). Read modes are described in `read(2)`.
  Test: on a new stream `I_GRDOPT` gives `RNORM`; `I_SRDOPT` `RMSGD` then `I_GRDOPT` gives `RMSGD`.

**streamio.7-30** [DEC] `I_GRDOPT` returns the current read mode in an `int` pointed to by `arg`.
  Test: as in streamio.7-29.

**streamio.7-31** [DEC] `I_NREAD` stores in the location pointed to by `arg` the number of data bytes in data blocks of the first message on the stream head read queue; the ioctl's return value is the number of messages on the read queue. A zero in `arg` with a return value greater than zero means a zero-length message is next.
  Test: send two messages of 5 and 3 bytes; `I_NREAD` returns 2 and stores 5. Send one zero-length message to an empty stream; returns 1 and stores 0.

**streamio.7-32** [DEC] `I_FDINSERT` creates a message from user buffer(s), adds information about another stream, and sends it downstream. The message has a control part and an optional data part, given in separate buffers. `arg` points to a `strfdinsert` structure with members `struct strbuf ctlbuf`, `struct strbuf databuf`, `long flags`, `int fildes`, `int offset`.
  Test: with a test driver, `I_FDINSERT` a control part and data part; the driver receives one message with both parts.

**streamio.7-33** [DEC] For `I_FDINSERT`, `ctlbuf.len` must be set to the size of a pointer plus the number of bytes of control information to send.
  Test: set `ctlbuf.len` smaller than `sizeof(void *) + offset`; expect `EINVAL` (see the errors).

**streamio.7-34** [DEC] `strfdinsert.fildes` gives the file descriptor of the other stream. `offset`, which must be word-aligned, gives the number of bytes from the start of the control buffer at which `I_FDINSERT` stores a pointer; that pointer is the address of the read queue structure of the driver for the stream given by `strfdinsert.fildes`.
  Test: a test driver checks that the pointer at `offset` in the received control part is the read queue of the other stream's driver.

**streamio.7-35** [DEC] For `I_FDINSERT`, `databuf.len` must be set to the number of data bytes to send, or zero if no data part is to be sent.
  Test: `I_FDINSERT` with `databuf.len = 0`; the driver receives a message with no data part.

**streamio.7-36** [DEC] `I_FDINSERT` `flags` selects the message type: 0 creates a non-priority message; `RS_HIPRI` creates a priority message.
  Test: send with `RS_HIPRI`; a test driver sees a priority message.

**streamio.7-37** [DEC] For non-priority messages, `I_FDINSERT` blocks if the stream write queue is full due to internal flow control; for priority messages it does not block on this condition. For non-priority messages with `O_NDELAY` set and the write queue full, it does not block but fails with `EAGAIN`.
  Test: fill the write queue; a non-priority `I_FDINSERT` on an `O_NDELAY` fd fails with `EAGAIN`; a priority one does not block.

**streamio.7-38** [DEC] `I_FDINSERT` also blocks, unless prevented by lack of internal resources, waiting for message blocks to become available in the stream, regardless of priority or of `O_NDELAY`. No partial message is sent.
  Test: Not testable from user space in a portable way (needs control over STREAMS buffer exhaustion).

**streamio.7-39** [DEC] `I_STR` builds an internal STREAMS ioctl message from the data pointed to by `arg` and sends it downstream; it sends user ioctl requests to downstream modules and drivers, allows data to be sent with the ioctl, and returns to the user any information sent upstream by the recipient.
  Test: `I_STR` to a test driver that echoes data back; the returned data appears in the `ic_dp` buffer.

**streamio.7-40** [DEC] `I_STR` blocks until a positive or negative acknowledgement arrives, or until the request times out; on timeout it fails with `errno` `ETIME`.
  Test: `I_STR` with `ic_timout = 1` to a driver that never acknowledges; returns −1 with `ETIME` after about 1 second.

**streamio.7-41** [DEC] At most one `I_STR` can be active on a stream; further `I_STR` calls block until the active one completes at the stream head.
  Test: two threads/processes issue `I_STR` to a slow driver; the second does not reach the driver until the first is acknowledged.

**streamio.7-42** [DEC] The default timeout interval for `I_STR` requests is 15 seconds.
  Test: `I_STR` with `ic_timout = 0` to a driver that never answers; fails with `ETIME` after about 15 seconds.

**streamio.7-43** [DEC] The `O_NDELAY` flag has no effect on `I_STR`.
  Test: on an `O_NDELAY` fd, `I_STR` to a slow-acknowledging driver still blocks until the acknowledgement.

**streamio.7-44** [DEC] For `I_STR`, `arg` points to a `strioctl` structure with members `int ic_cmd` (downstream command), `int ic_timout` (ACK/NAK timeout), `int ic_len` (length of data argument), `char *ic_dp` (pointer to data argument).
  Test: compile code that sets all four fields.

**streamio.7-45** [DEC] `ic_cmd` is the internal ioctl command for a downstream module or driver.
  Test: a test driver receives the `ic_cmd` value sent.

**streamio.7-46** [DEC] `ic_timout` is the number of seconds an `I_STR` waits for acknowledgement: −1 means infinite, 0 means use the default, greater than 0 means as specified.
  Test: `ic_timout = -1` with a non-answering driver blocks beyond 15 seconds; `ic_timout = 2` times out after about 2 seconds.

**streamio.7-47** [DEC] `ic_len` is the number of bytes in the data argument on input; on return it holds the number of bytes being returned to the user. `ic_dp` points to the data argument; that buffer should be large enough for the maximum data any module or driver in the stream can return.
  Test: driver returns 7 bytes to a request sending 3; after the call `ic_len == 7`.

**streamio.7-48** [DEC] The stream head converts the `strioctl` information into an internal ioctl command message and sends it downstream.
  Test: as in streamio.7-39.

**streamio.7-49** [DEC] `I_SENDFD` asks the stream associated with `fildes` to send a message containing a file pointer to the stream head at the other end of a stream pipe; the file pointer corresponds to `arg`, which must be an integer file descriptor.
  Test: on a stream pipe, `I_SENDFD` an open file's fd; the other end's `I_RECVFD` gets a working descriptor for the same file.

**streamio.7-50** [DEC] `I_SENDFD` converts `arg` to the system file pointer, allocates a message block holding it, and also inserts the sending process's user id and group id; the message is placed directly on the read queue of the stream head at the other end of the stream pipe.
  Test: receiver's `strrecvfd.uid`/`gid` equal the sender's user and group ids.

**streamio.7-51** [DEC] `I_RECVFD` retrieves the file descriptor carried by a message sent with `I_SENDFD` over a stream pipe. `arg` points to a buffer large enough for a `strrecvfd` structure with members `int fd`, `unsigned short uid`, `unsigned short gid`, `char fill[8]`; `fd` is an integer file descriptor and `uid`/`gid` are the user and group id of the sending stream.
  Test: as in streamio.7-49 and streamio.7-50.

**streamio.7-52** [DEC] If `O_NDELAY` is not set, `I_RECVFD` blocks until a message is present at the stream head; if `O_NDELAY` is set and no message is present, it fails with `EAGAIN`.
  Test: `I_RECVFD` on an empty `O_NDELAY` stream pipe end returns −1 with `EAGAIN`; without `O_NDELAY` it blocks until a sender acts.

**streamio.7-53** [DEC] If the message at the stream head was sent by `I_SENDFD`, a new user file descriptor is allocated for its file pointer, placed in the `fd` field of `strrecvfd`, and the structure is copied into the buffer pointed to by `arg`.
  Test: received `fd` is a new descriptor (not equal to any previously open one) and `fstat` on it matches the sent file.

**streamio.7-54** [DEC] `I_LINK` and `I_UNLINK` connect and disconnect multiplexed STREAMS configurations.
  Test: covered by streamio.7-55 to streamio.7-58.

**streamio.7-55** [DEC] `I_LINK` connects two streams: `fildes` is the stream connected to the multiplexing driver, `arg` is the fd of a stream connected to another driver; the stream designated by `arg` is connected below the multiplexing driver.
  Test: with a multiplexing test driver, `I_LINK` a second stream; afterwards ioctls on the linked stream's fd fail with `EINVAL` (streamio.7-E1).

**streamio.7-56** [DEC] `I_LINK` requires the multiplexing driver to send an acknowledgement message to the stream head. On success it returns a multiplexor ID number (used to disconnect with `I_UNLINK`); on failure it returns −1.
  Test: `I_LINK` on a multiplexing test driver returns a value other than −1, and `I_UNLINK` with that value succeeds.

**streamio.7-57** [DEC] `I_UNLINK` disconnects the two streams given by `fildes` and `arg`; `fildes` is the stream connected to the multiplexing driver and must be the stream on which the `I_LINK` was issued; `arg` is the multiplexor ID returned by `I_LINK`. Like `I_LINK`, it requires the multiplexing driver to acknowledge.
  Test: `I_UNLINK` with the ID from `I_LINK` returns 0; the lower stream can then be used again.

**streamio.7-58** [DEC] If `arg` to `I_UNLINK` is −1, all streams linked to `fildes` are disconnected.
  Test: link two lower streams, `I_UNLINK` with −1; both lower streams become usable.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**streamio.7-E1** `EINVAL`: (any command) the stream referred to by `fildes` is linked below a multiplexor, or `command` is not a valid value for a stream; no control function is processed.

**streamio.7-E2** (any command) the errors described in `ioctl(2)`.

**streamio.7-E3** (any command) the value carried in an error message sent to the stream head by a module or driver causes subsequent calls to fail with that value.

**streamio.7-E4** `EINVAL` (`I_PUSH`): invalid module name.

**streamio.7-E5** `EFAULT` (`I_PUSH`): `arg` points outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E6** `ENXIO` (`I_PUSH`): the open routine of the new module failed.

**streamio.7-E7** `ENXIO` (`I_PUSH`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E8** `EINVAL` (`I_POP`): no module present in the stream.

**streamio.7-E9** `ENXIO` (`I_POP`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E10** `EFAULT` (`I_LOOK`): `arg` points outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E11** `EINVAL` (`I_LOOK`): no module present in the stream.

**streamio.7-E12** `ENOSR` (`I_FLUSH`): unable to allocate buffers for the flush message due to insufficient STREAMS memory resources.

**streamio.7-E13** `EINVAL` (`I_FLUSH`): invalid `arg` value.

**streamio.7-E14** `ENXIO` (`I_FLUSH`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E15** `EINVAL` (`I_SETSIG`): `arg` value is invalid, or `arg` is zero and the process is not registered to receive `SIGPOLL`.

**streamio.7-E16** `EAGAIN` (`I_SETSIG`): allocation of a data structure to store the signal request failed.

**streamio.7-E17** `EINVAL` (`I_GETSIG`): process not registered to receive `SIGPOLL`.

**streamio.7-E18** `EFAULT` (`I_GETSIG`): `arg` points outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E19** `EFAULT` (`I_FIND`): `arg` points outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E20** `EINVAL` (`I_FIND`): `arg` does not contain a valid module name.

**streamio.7-E21** `EFAULT` (`I_PEEK`): `arg` points, or the buffer area given in `ctlbuf` or `databuf` is, outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E22** `EBADMSG` (`I_PEEK`): the queued message to be read is not valid for `I_PEEK`.
Note: The page introduces the `I_PEEK` errors with "errno is set to the following value" (singular) but lists two values.

**streamio.7-E23** `EINVAL` (`I_SRDOPT`): `arg` is not one of `RNORM`, `RMSGD`, `RMSGN`.

**streamio.7-E24** `EFAULT` (`I_GRDOPT`): `arg` points outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E25** `EFAULT` (`I_NREAD`): `arg` points outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E26** `EAGAIN` (`I_FDINSERT`): a non-priority message was specified, `O_NDELAY` is set, and the stream write queue is full due to internal flow control.

**streamio.7-E27** `ENOSR` (`I_FDINSERT`): buffers could not be allocated for the message due to insufficient STREAMS memory resources.

**streamio.7-E28** `EFAULT` (`I_FDINSERT`): `arg` points, or the buffer area given in `ctlbuf` or `databuf` is, outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E29** `EINVAL` (`I_FDINSERT`): one of: `fildes` in the `strfdinsert` structure is not a valid, open stream file descriptor; the size of a pointer plus `offset` is greater than the `len` field of the buffer given through `ctlptr`; `offset` does not specify a properly aligned location in the data buffer; an undefined value is stored in `flags`.
Note: The page says "ctlptr" (no such member is defined; the structure member is `ctlbuf`) and "properly-aligned location in the data buffer" although `offset` is described as an offset into the control buffer.

**streamio.7-E30** `ENXIO` (`I_FDINSERT`): hangup received on the ioctl's `fildes` or on `fildes` in the `strfdinsert` structure.

**streamio.7-E31** `ERANGE` (`I_FDINSERT`): `databuf.len` is outside the range given by the maximum and minimum packet sizes of the topmost stream module; or `databuf.len` is larger than the maximum configured size of the data part of a message; or `ctlbuf.len` is larger than the maximum configured size of the control part of a message.

**streamio.7-E32** (`I_FDINSERT`) if an error message was received by the stream head of the stream given by `fildes` in the `strfdinsert` structure, `errno` is set to the value in that message.

**streamio.7-E33** `ETIME` (`I_STR`): the request timed out (a downstream ioctl timed out before acknowledgement was received).

**streamio.7-E34** `ENOSR` (`I_STR`): unable to allocate buffers for the ioctl message due to insufficient STREAMS memory resources.

**streamio.7-E35** `EFAULT` (`I_STR`): `arg` points, or the buffer area given by `ic_dp` and `ic_len` (separately for data sent and data returned) is, outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E36** `EINVAL` (`I_STR`): `ic_len` is less than 0, or `ic_len` is larger than the maximum configured size of the data part of a message, or `ic_timout` is less than −1.

**streamio.7-E37** `ENXIO` (`I_STR`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E38** (`I_STR`) if, while waiting for an acknowledgement, a message indicating an error or a hangup is received at the stream head, or an error code is returned in the positive or negative acknowledgement because the downstream ioctl failed, `errno` is set to the value in the message.

**streamio.7-E39** `EAGAIN` (`I_SENDFD`): the sending stream cannot allocate a message block to hold the file pointer.

**streamio.7-E40** `EAGAIN` (`I_SENDFD`): the read queue of the receiving stream head is full and cannot accept the message.

**streamio.7-E41** `EBADF` (`I_SENDFD`): `arg` is not a valid, open file descriptor.

**streamio.7-E42** `EINVAL` (`I_SENDFD`): `fildes` is not connected to a stream pipe.

**streamio.7-E43** `ENXIO` (`I_SENDFD`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E44** `EAGAIN` (`I_RECVFD`): no message was present at the stream head read queue and `O_NDELAY` is set.

**streamio.7-E45** `EBADMSG` (`I_RECVFD`): the message at the stream head read queue was not a message containing a passed file descriptor.

**streamio.7-E46** `EFAULT` (`I_RECVFD`): `arg` points outside the allocated address space.

**streamio.7-E47** `EMFILE` (`I_RECVFD`): `NOFILES` file descriptors are currently open.

**streamio.7-E48** `ENXIO` (`I_RECVFD`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E49** `ENXIO` (`I_LINK`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E50** `ETIME` (`I_LINK`): timed out before the acknowledgement message was received at the stream head.

**streamio.7-E51** `EAGAIN` (`I_LINK`): temporarily unable to allocate storage to perform the `I_LINK`.

**streamio.7-E52** `ENOSR` (`I_LINK`): unable to allocate storage to perform the `I_LINK` due to insufficient STREAMS memory resources.

**streamio.7-E53** `EBADF` (`I_LINK`): `arg` is not a valid, open file descriptor.

**streamio.7-E54** `EINVAL` (`I_LINK`): the `fildes` stream does not support multiplexing.

**streamio.7-E55** `EINVAL` (`I_LINK`): `arg` is not a stream, or is already linked under a multiplexor.

**streamio.7-E56** `EINVAL` (`I_LINK`): the link would cause a "cycle" in the resulting configuration, that is, a given stream head would be linked into a multiplexing configuration in more than one place.

**streamio.7-E57** (`I_LINK`) if, while waiting for the multiplexing driver to acknowledge, a message indicating an error or a hangup is received at the stream head of `fildes`, or an error code is returned in the positive or negative acknowledgement, `errno` is set to the value in the message.

**streamio.7-E58** `ENXIO` (`I_UNLINK`): hangup received on `fildes`.

**streamio.7-E59** `ETIME` (`I_UNLINK`): timed out before the acknowledgement message was received at the stream head.

**streamio.7-E60** `ENOSR` (`I_UNLINK`): unable to allocate storage to perform the `I_UNLINK` due to insufficient STREAMS memory resources.

**streamio.7-E61** `EINVAL` (`I_UNLINK`): `arg` is an invalid multiplexor ID number, or `fildes` is not the stream on which the `I_LINK` that returned `arg` was performed.

**streamio.7-E62** (`I_UNLINK`) if, while waiting for the multiplexing driver to acknowledge, a message indicating an error or a hangup is received at the stream head of `fildes`, or an error code is returned in the positive or negative acknowledgement, `errno` is set to the value in the message.
Note: The page says `I_UNLINK` can fail "while waiting for the multiplexing driver to acknowledge the link request"; it presumably means the unlink request.

Related: close(2), fcntl(2), getmsg(2), ioctl(2), open(2), poll(2), putmsg(2), read(2), signal(2), write(2)

### tty(7)

Page: `man7/tty.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**tty.7-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `#include <sys/termios.h>`. The page describes the special file `/dev/tty` and the terminal drivers; terminal behaviour is governed largely by the terminal's `termios` structure (defined in `termios.h`), which holds input and output processing, control and local modes.
  Test: compile a program including `<sys/termios.h>` that declares a `struct termios`.

**tty.7-2** [OSF/1] Two line disciplines are available for terminals: Standard (POSIX-compliant, with job control, sessions, `termios.h` support) and Kanji-support (POSIX-compliant with support for the Japanese character set Kanji and multibyte characters).
  Test: `TIOCSETD` with `TTYDISC` and with `KJIDISC` on a pty both succeed.

**tty.7-3** [OSF/1] The line discipline is switched with `ioctl(f, TIOCSETD, &ldisc)` where `ldisc` is an `int`; `TTYDISC` selects the standard POSIX driver and `KJIDISC` the Kanji driver. By convention the standard driver is discipline 0 and the Kanji driver is discipline 8.
  Test: check `TTYDISC == 0` and `KJIDISC == 8`; set `KJIDISC` and read back with `TIOCGETD`.

**tty.7-4** [OSF/1] Other disciplines exist for special purposes, such as using communications lines for network connections.
  Test: Not testable from user space as stated (no disciplines are named).

**tty.7-5** [OSF/1] `TIOCGETD` obtains the current line discipline.
  Test: `TIOCSETD` with `TTYDISC`, then `TIOCGETD` stores `TTYDISC`.

**tty.7-6** [OSF/1] Pending input is discarded when the line discipline is changed.
  Test: write input into a pty master, `TIOCSETD` on the slave, then `FIONREAD` on the slave gives 0.

**tty.7-7** [OSF/1] All low-speed asynchronous communications ports can use any available line discipline, whatever the hardware.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware.

**tty.7-8** [OSF/1] Any process can have a controlling terminal. Keyboard-generated signals (for example interrupt, quit, suspend) affect all processes in the process group associated with the controlling terminal.
  Test: two processes in the pty's foreground group both receive `SIGINT` when `^C` is written to the master.

**tty.7-9** [OSF/1] The controlling terminal determines the physical device accessed when `/dev/tty` is opened.
  Test: with pty slave as controlling terminal, write via `/dev/tty`; the data appears on that pty's master.

**tty.7-10** [OSF/1] In OSF/1 (per POSIX 1003.1) a process must be a session leader to allocate a controlling terminal, and allocation is done explicitly with `ioctl()` (`TIOCSCTTY`); a terminal is not implicitly assigned on `open`. The page says this implies the `O_NOCTTY` flag to `open()` is ignored.
  Test: after `setsid()`, open a pty slave without `O_NOCTTY`; `open("/dev/tty")` still fails until `ioctl(fd, TIOCSCTTY, 0)` is called, after which it succeeds.

**tty.7-11** [OSF/1] The page's example sequence for obtaining a controlling tty is: `setsid()` (become group and session leader and remove any controlling tty), `open("/dev/console", O_RDWR)`, then `ioctl(fd, TIOCSCTTY, 0)`, which attaches the console to the current session as its controlling terminal. The process must not already be a session or process group leader, and the console must not already be the controlling tty of any other session.
  Test: a forked child (not a group leader) runs the sequence, using a pty slave in place of the console; afterwards `open("/dev/tty")` succeeds and refers to that slave.

**tty.7-12** [OSF/1] A process removes its association with its controlling terminal by opening `/dev/tty` and calling `ioctl(fd, TIOCNOTTY, 0)`.
  Test: after `TIOCNOTTY`, `open("/dev/tty")` fails.

**tty.7-13** [OSF/1] When a control terminal file is closed, pending input is removed and pending output is sent to the receiving device.
  Test: write output to a pty slave, close the last slave fd; the master can still read the output.

**tty.7-14** [OSF/1] Opening a terminal file blocks until carrier is detected. With `O_NONBLOCK`, `open()` does not wait; instead the first `read()` or `write()` waits for carrier. If `CLOCAL` is set, the driver assumes no modem control, and `open()`, `read()` and `write()` proceed without waiting for carrier.
  Test: Not testable from user space without modem-controlled hardware (ptys have no carrier line).

**tty.7-15** [OSF/1] Each process belongs to a process group with a process group ID, the process group of its creating process.
  Test: a forked child's `getpgrp()` equals the parent's.

**tty.7-16** [OSF/1] Process group IDs are unique and cannot be reused for other process groups until the original group is disbanded.
  Test: while a group exists, no new process gets a PID equal to that group ID (stress fork and compare).

**tty.7-17** [OSF/1] A process group leader has the same process ID as its process group.
  Test: after `setsid()`, `getpid() == getpgrp()`.

**tty.7-18** [OSF/1] Each process group belongs to a session, and each process in it belongs to that session.
  Test: child of a session member has the same session (via `TIOCGPGRP`/`getpgrp` checks within one session).

**tty.7-19** [OSF/1] A process that is not a process group leader can create a new session and process group with `setsid()`; it becomes session leader of the new session and of the new process group, its process ID is assigned to the new process group, and the new session has no controlling terminal until the session leader assigns one.
  Test: forked child calls `setsid()`; `getpgrp() == getpid()` and `open("/dev/tty")` fails.

**tty.7-20** [OSF/1] Other processes can be added to a process group with `setpgid()`.
  Test: parent `setpgid(child, parent_pgrp_of_choice)` and child's `getpgrp()` reflects it.

**tty.7-21** [OSF/1] A controlling terminal can have a foreground process group, which receives signals generated by the `INTR`, `QUIT` and `SUSP` characters; certain terminal operations are restricted to processes in it.
  Test: put a child in a background group; writing `^C` to the pty master signals only the foreground group.
