**tty.7-22** [OSF/1] The foreground process group is changed with `tcsetpgrp()` and obtained with `tcgetpgrp()`.
  Test: `tcsetpgrp(fd, pg)` then `tcgetpgrp(fd) == pg`.

**tty.7-23** [OSF/1] Canonical mode: input is collected and processed one line at a time; lines end with newline (`\n`), EOF or EOL. A read does not return until the line is terminated or a signal is received.
  Test: write "ab" to the master; a blocking slave read does not return; write "\n"; read returns "ab\n".

**tty.7-24** [OSF/1] The maximum number of unread input bytes allowed on a terminal is 255 (`MAX_INPUT`, "Currently this limit is 255 characters"). Beyond that, behaviour depends on `IMAXBEL`.
  Test: write 300 bytes without newline to the master in canonical mode; the slave never holds more than 255 unread bytes.

**tty.7-25** [OSF/1] In canonical mode, erase and kill processing are performed on input not yet terminated by a line terminator; erase removes the last character in the line and kill removes the whole line.
  Test: write "abc", `VERASE`, "\n"; read returns "ab\n". Write "abc", `VKILL`, "x\n"; read returns "x\n".

**tty.7-26** [OSF/1] Noncanonical mode: no erase or kill processing; input characters are available as typed, not processed into lines; received bytes are handled according to `MIN` and `TIME` in `c_cc`. `MIN` is the minimum number of bytes received before a read is considered successful; `TIME` is in units of 0.1 second and times out sporadic input.
  Test: clear `ICANON`, write `VERASE` byte; it is read as data.

**tty.7-27** [OSF/1] `MIN>0, TIME>0`: `TIME` is an interbyte timer, started after the first byte and reset after each byte. The read succeeds if `MIN` bytes arrive before `TIME` runs out; if `TIME` runs out first, the bytes received are returned.
  Test: `MIN=5, TIME=2`; write 2 bytes; read returns 2 bytes about 0.2 s after the last byte.

**tty.7-28** [OSF/1] `MIN>0, TIME=0`: only `MIN` is used; a queued `read()` waits until `MIN` bytes are received or a signal is received.
  Test: `MIN=3, TIME=0`; write 2 bytes; read stays blocked; write a third; read returns 3.

**tty.7-29** [OSF/1] `MIN=0, TIME>0`: `TIME` is a read timer started when `read()` is called; the read finishes when one byte is read or `TIME` runs out.
  Test: `MIN=0, TIME=5`, no input; read returns with no data after about 0.5 s; with a byte written before the timeout, read returns that 1 byte.

**tty.7-30** [OSF/1] `MIN=0, TIME=0`: the lesser of the number of requested bytes and the number of available bytes is returned; `read()` returns zero if no data was read.
  Test: no input; read returns 0 immediately. With 3 bytes queued, read of 2 returns 2.

**tty.7-31** [OSF/1] Canonical mode is entered by setting `ICANON` in `c_lflag`; other input processing follows the other `c_iflag` and `c_lflag` flags.
  Test: toggle `ICANON` and observe line vs byte delivery.

**tty.7-32** [OSF/1] A terminal normally operates full-duplex; characters may be typed at any time, even during output.
  Test: write to master while slave is writing output; input is not lost.

**tty.7-33** [OSF/1] Characters are lost only when the system's character input buffers become completely choked ("which is rare"), or when the unread input reaches `MAX_INPUT` (currently 255): the driver then refuses further input and rings the bell if `IMAXBEL` is set in `c_iflag`, or, if `IMAXBEL` is not set, throws away all input and output without notice.
  Test: with `IMAXBEL` set, overflow input; master reads a BEL (`\007`). With it clear, overflow; queued input is discarded.

**tty.7-34** [OSF/1] Input characters are normally accepted with even or odd parity and the parity bit is stripped before the program sees them; `ISTRIP` in `c_iflag` controls stripping (set: stripped; not set: not stripped).
  Test: with `ISTRIP` set write byte 0xC1; slave reads 0x41; with it clear, reads 0xC1.

**tty.7-35** [OSF/1] By setting `PARENB` in `c_cflag` and setting (or not setting) `PARODD`, input characters with EVEN (or ODD) parity can be discarded or marked.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware producing parity errors.

**tty.7-36** [OSF/1] In all line disciplines, `TIOCSTI` simulates terminal input: its third argument is the address of a character, which the system pretends was typed on the terminal. The terminal must be the process's control terminal unless the process has superuser privileges.
  Test: as non-root, `TIOCSTI` 'x' on the controlling pty slave; a read returns 'x'. On a non-controlling tty, as non-root, the call fails.

**tty.7-37** [OSF/1] Input is normally echoed by placing characters in the output queue as they arrive; echo is disabled by clearing `ECHO` in `c_lflag` via `tcsetattr()` or the `TIOCSETA`, `TIOCSETAW` or `TIOCSETAF` ioctls.
  Test: with `ECHO` set, input "a" written to master is read back from master; with `ECHO` clear, it is not.

**tty.7-38** [OSF/1] In canonical mode, a read normally suspends until a whole line is received (but see `SIGTTIN`). At most one line is returned per read regardless of the count requested; any number of characters, even one, may be requested without losing information.
  Test: write "ab\ncd\n"; read(100) returns "ab\n"; read(1) then returns "c".

**tty.7-39** [OSF/1] If `O_NONBLOCK` is not set, `read()` blocks until data or a signal arrives. If it is set, `read()` does not block: if some data is available, it returns the data available and the byte count (whether or not that satisfies the request).
  Test: noncanonical, `O_NONBLOCK`, 2 bytes queued; read(10) returns 2.

**tty.7-40** [OSF/1] Line editing: the erase character (`VERASE`) erases the last character typed and the kill character (`VKILL`) erases the current input line; neither erases beyond the start of the current input line or an EOF.
  Test: write "a\n" then `VERASE`; the next line read is not shortened; first read returns "a\n".

**tty.7-41** [OSF/1] Special control characters can be entered literally by preceding them with the literal-next character `VLNEXT` (default `^V`).
  Test: write `^V` `VERASE` "\n"; read returns the erase byte followed by "\n".

**tty.7-42** [OSF/1] The drivers normally treat newline, EOF, or EOL as terminating an input line, echoing a return and line feed.
  Test: with `ECHO`, write "a\n"; master reads back "a\r\n".

**tty.7-43** [OSF/1] If `ICRNL` is set in `c_iflag`, carriage returns are translated to newlines on input and normally echoed as CR-LF. If `ICRNL` is not set, CR is echoed simply as a return and does not terminate canonical ("cooked") input.
  Test: `ICRNL` set: write "a\r", read "a\n". Clear: write "a\r"; a read stays blocked.

**tty.7-44** [OSF/1] The POSIX driver provides a word-erase character `VWERASE` (normally `<Ctrl-W>`), which erases the preceding word but not spaces before it. A word is a sequence of nonblank characters, tabs counting as blanks; if `ALTWERASE` is set in `c_lflag`, a word is any sequence of alphanumerics or underscores bounded by other characters.
  Test: write "ab cd" `^W` "\n"; read returns "ab \n". With `ALTWERASE`, "ab.cd" `^W` "\n" returns "ab.\n".

**tty.7-45** [OSF/1] The reprint character `VREPRINT` (normally `<Ctrl-R>`) retypes the pending input starting on a new line. Retyping happens automatically in canonical mode if characters that would be erased from the screen have been fouled by program output.
  Test: with `ECHO`, write "ab" then `^R`; master reads the echo of "ab" again after a newline.

**tty.7-46** [OSF/1] `c_iflag` masks (bitwise inclusive-OR-able): `BRKINT` (interrupt signalled on break), `ICRNL` (map CR to NL on input), `IGNBRK` (ignore break), `IGNCR` (ignore CR), `IGNPAR` (ignore characters with parity errors), `INLCR` (map NL to CR on input), `INPCK` (enable input parity check), `ISTRIP` (strip eighth bit), `IXOFF` (send stop/start for input flow control), `IXON` (recognise stop/start for output flow control), `IXANY` (any character restarts output after stop), `IUCLC` (map upper case to lower case on input), `PARMRK` (mark parity errors with a three-character sequence), `IMAXBEL` (ring the bell when the input queue fills).
  Test: compile a program referencing each constant; the values are distinct and can be ORed together.

**tty.7-47** [OSF/1] `IGNBRK` set: break conditions are ignored. Not set but `BRKINT` set: a break acts as if `VINTR` had been typed. Neither set: break is input as the single character `'\0'`, or, if `PARMRK` is set, as three characters `'\377'`, `'\0'`, `'\0'`.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a line that can deliver a break (ptys cannot).

**tty.7-48** [OSF/1] `IGNPAR` set: a byte with a parity or framing error (except breaks) is discarded. Not set but `PARMRK` set: such a byte is passed as `'\377'`, `'\0'`, X (X being the received data). If `ISTRIP` is not set, a valid `'\377'` is passed as two bytes `'\377'`, `'\377'`. Neither `PARMRK` nor `IGNPAR` set: framing or parity errors, including breaks, are passed as the single character `'\0'`.
  Note: The page text prints the doubled character as "’\377’, ’377’"; the backslash on the second is missing (damage or typo).
  Test: with `PARMRK` set and `IGNPAR` and `ISTRIP` clear, write byte 0377 to the pty master; the slave reads 0377 0377 (the error cases need real hardware).

**tty.7-49** [OSF/1] `INPCK` enables input parity checking; if not set, characters with parity errors pass through as is. Input parity checking is independent of output parity generation.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware.

**tty.7-50** [OSF/1] `ISTRIP` strips the eighth bit of the eight valid input bits before processing; if not set, all eight bits are processed.
  Test: see tty.7-34.

**tty.7-51** [OSF/1] `INLCR` causes a newline to be read as a carriage return; if `IGNCR` is also set, the (resulting) carriage return is ignored.
  Test: `INLCR` alone (noncanonical): write "\n", read "\r". With `IGNCR` too, nothing is read.

**tty.7-52** [OSF/1] The STOP character (normally `<Ctrl-S>`) suspends output and START (normally `<Ctrl-Q>`) restarts it. With `IXON` set, START and STOP are not read but perform flow control; extra STOPs while stopped have no effect, unless START and STOP are the same character, in which case output resumes. With `IXON` clear, START and STOP are read as data.
  Test: `IXON` set: write `^S` to master, slave output does not appear at master until `^Q`. Clear: `^S` is read by the slave.

**tty.7-53** [OSF/1] `IXOFF` enables stop/start input control: the driver sends STOP to the device when the input queue is in danger of overflowing (exceeding `MAX_INPUT`), and sends START once enough characters have been read to bring the queue to an acceptable level.
  Test: `IXOFF` set, write near 255 unread bytes to master; master reads a `^S`; drain the slave; master reads `^Q`.

**tty.7-54** [OSF/1] Echo modes are controlled by bits in `c_lflag`. `ECHOPRT` (normally set for hardcopy terminals): logically erased characters are printed backwards, preceded by `\` and followed by `/`.
  Test: `ECHOPRT` set, write "ab" then two `VERASE`; master reads echo containing "\ba/".

**tty.7-55** [OSF/1] `ECHOE` may be set to erase input from the screen with backspace-space-backspace for character or word deletion; `ECHOKE` additionally erases this way on line kill.
  Test: `ECHOE` set, write "a" `VERASE`; master reads "a\b \b".

**tty.7-56** [OSF/1] If `ECHOCTL` is set, nonprinting control characters are normally echoed as `^X` rather than unmodified; DELETE is echoed as `^?`.
  Test: `ECHOCTL` set, write byte 0x01 (noncanonical); master echo is "^A"; byte 0x7f echoes "^?".

**tty.7-57** [OSF/1] Written characters are transmitted as soon as previously written characters have finished. A process producing output faster than the terminal accepts it is suspended when its output queue exceeds some limit and resumed when the queue drains to some threshold.
  Test: write a large buffer to the slave without reading the master; the writer blocks; reading the master unblocks it.

**tty.7-58** [OSF/1] Even parity is normally generated on output.
  Test: Not testable from user space without serial hardware.

**tty.7-59** [OSF/1] If `NOEOT` is set in `c_oflag`, the EOT character (`<Ctrl-D>`) is not transmitted.
  Test: set `NOEOT`, write 0x04 to the slave; master does not receive it.

**tty.7-60** [OSF/1] The drivers provide output processing for canonical and noncanonical modes, including delays after backspace (`BSDLY`), formfeed (`FFDLY`), carriage return (`CRDLY`), tab (`TABDLY`) and newline (`NLDLY`), and parity generation; optionally tabs are expanded to spaces with stops every eight columns, and newlines optionally converted to CR followed by NL. Output processing is controlled by `c_oflag`.
  Test: set tab expansion in `c_oflag`, write "a\tb"; master reads "a" followed by 7 spaces and "b".
  Note: The page does not name the `c_oflag` bits for tab expansion and NL-to-CR-NL conversion.

**tty.7-61** [OSF/1] `OLCUC` maps lowercase to uppercase on output, for terminals lacking lower case.
  Test: set `OLCUC`, write "ab"; master reads "AB".

**tty.7-62** [OSF/1] The output flush character (normally `<Ctrl-O>`) sets `FLUSHO` in the local mode word, flushing subsequent output until `FLUSHO` is cleared by a program or more input is typed; it works in canonical and noncanonical modes and causes pending input to be retyped.
  Test: write `^O` to master; `tcgetattr` shows `FLUSHO`; subsequent slave output does not reach master.

**tty.7-63** [OSF/1] `TIOCFLUSH` flushes characters in the input or output queues (see tty.7-79).
  Test: see tty.7-79.

**tty.7-64** [OSF/1] If `IUCLC` is set in `c_iflag`, all uppercase letters are mapped to lowercase on input; an uppercase letter can be produced by preceding it with `\`. Uppercase letters are preceded by `\` on output.
  Test: `IUCLC` set, write "A\\B\n" (A, backslash, B); read returns "aB\n".
  Note: The page attaches the backslash-output behaviour to `IUCLC` without naming a separate output flag.

**tty.7-65** [OSF/1] If `XCASE` is set in `c_lflag`, these escapes are generated on output and accepted on input: `` ` `` as `\´`, `|` as `\!`, `~` as `\^`, `{` as `\(`, `}` as `\)`.
  Test: `XCASE` set, write "\\(\n" to master; slave reads "{\n".

**tty.7-66** [OSF/1] `TIOCSBRK` sets the break bit in the hardware interface, causing a break condition; `TIOCCBRK` clears it (usually after a delay with `sleep(3)`). `tcsendbreak()` can also cause a break for a specified time. Breaks in input are handled per `c_iflag`.
  Test: `ioctl(fd, TIOCSBRK)` then `TIOCCBRK` on a tty both return 0 (effect requires hardware).

**tty.7-67** [OSF/1] `TIOCCDTR` clears data terminal ready; `TIOCSDTR` sets it again.
  Test: Not testable from user space without modem hardware; calls should return 0 on a serial line.

**tty.7-68** [OSF/1] When carrier drops, `SIGHUP` is sent to the processes in the terminal's distinguished process group (usually terminating them), unless `CLOCAL` is set in `c_cflag`. Access to the terminal by other processes is then normally revoked, so further reads fail and programs testing for end-of-file terminate.
  Test: close the pty master (simulated hangup); the foreground group of the slave receives `SIGHUP` and later reads return EOF or fail.

**tty.7-69** [OSF/1] When `ISIG` is set in `c_lflag`, the signal characters work in canonical and noncanonical modes and their signals go to the terminal's foreground process group. If `NOFLSH` is not set, typing them also flushes pending input and output. The characters may be changed.
  Test: `ISIG` set, queue "abc" then write `^C`; foreground gets `SIGINT` and pending "abc" is discarded; with `NOFLSH` it is kept.

**tty.7-70** [OSF/1] Defaults: `^C` is `VINTR` and generates `SIGINT`; `^\` is `VQUIT` and generates `SIGQUIT` (used to terminate with a core image, if possible, in file `core` in the current directory); `^Z` is `VSUSP` and generates `SIGTSTP` (suspends the current process group); `^Y` is `VDSUSP` and generates `SIGTSTP` when a program attempts to read the `^Y`, rather than when it is typed.
  Test: write each character to the master and check the corresponding signal; for `^Y`, no signal until the slave reads.

**tty.7-71** [OSF/1] A process reading its controlling terminal while not in the foreground process group causes `SIGTTIN` to be sent to its (background) process group, which normally stops it. If the process ignores or blocks `SIGTTIN`, or its process group is orphaned, the read returns −1 with `EIO` and no signal is sent.
  Test: background child reads the pty slave; it is stopped by `SIGTTIN`. With `SIGTTIN` ignored, read fails with `EIO`.

**tty.7-72** [OSF/1] A process writing its controlling terminal while not in the foreground group, with `TOSTOP` set in `c_lflag`, causes `SIGTTOU` to be sent to its process group and the write is prohibited. If `TOSTOP` is not set, or it is set and the process blocks or ignores `SIGTTOU`, the write is allowed and no signal is sent. If `TOSTOP` is set, the process group is orphaned, and `SIGTTOU` is not blocked, the write returns −1 with `EIO` and no signal is sent.
  Test: background child writes with `TOSTOP` set; it receives `SIGTTOU`; with `SIGTTOU` ignored, the write succeeds.
  Note: The page says writes are allowed if the process is "blocking or ignoring" `SIGTTOU`, but the orphaned-group case only requires `SIGTTOU` "not blocked", leaving an orphaned group that ignores `SIGTTOU` covered by both rules.

**tty.7-73** [OSF/1] The driver stores, but does not use internally, the current terminal/window size, and provides a uniform access mechanism to get and set it. When the size is changed, `SIGWINCH` is sent to the terminal's process group.
  Test: `TIOCSWINSZ` with a new size; the foreground group receives `SIGWINCH`.

**tty.7-74** [OSF/1] The POSIX terminal parameters are contained in a single `termios` structure defined in `sys/termios.h`.
  Test: compile check, as tty.7-1.

**tty.7-75** [OSF/1] `ioctl(fildes, code, arg)` with `struct termios *arg`: `TIOCGETA` gets the `termios` structure; the page says "The interface delays until output is quiescent, then throws away any unread characters."
  Note: The page attaches the drain-and-discard behaviour to `TIOCGETA` (a get); recorded as stated.
  Test: `TIOCGETA` returns 0 and fills a `termios` matching `tcgetattr`.

**tty.7-76** [OSF/1] `TIOCSETA` sets the parameters from the `termios` structure; `TIOCSETAW` drains output first, then sets like `TIOCSETA`; `TIOCSETAF` drains output and flushes input first, then sets like `TIOCSETA`.
  Test: queue input, `TIOCSETAF`; `FIONREAD` gives 0. `TIOCSETA` and `TIOCSETAW` change the settings, read back with `TIOCGETA`.

**tty.7-77** [OSF/1] `TIOCEXCL` (arg ignored) sets exclusive-use mode: no further opens are permitted until the file has been closed.
  Test: `TIOCEXCL` on a pty slave; a second non-root `open` of the slave fails.

**tty.7-78** [OSF/1] `TIOCNXCL` (arg ignored) turns off exclusive-use mode.
  Test: after `TIOCNXCL`, a second `open` succeeds.

**tty.7-79** [OSF/1] `TIOCFLUSH` with `arg` pointing to an `int`: if the value is zero, all characters waiting in input and output queues are flushed; otherwise the value holds `FREAD`/`FWRITE` bits from `sys/file.h`: `FREAD` flushes input queues, `FWRITE` flushes output queues.
  Test: queue input, `TIOCFLUSH` with `FWRITE`; input remains; with `FREAD`, input is gone.

**tty.7-80** [OSF/1] `TIOCSCTTY` sets the terminal as the controlling terminal of the calling process; `TIOCNOTTY` voids the terminal as a controlling terminal.
  Test: see tty.7-11 and tty.7-12.

**tty.7-81** [OSF/1] For the miscellaneous ioctls below, arguments are described where required; otherwise `arg` should be 0.
  Test: covered by the following items.

**tty.7-82** [OSF/1] `TIOCSTI`: argument points to a character the system pretends was typed on the terminal.
  Test: see tty.7-36.

**tty.7-83** [OSF/1] `TIOCSBRK` sets and `TIOCCBRK` clears the break bit; `TIOCSDTR` sets and `TIOCCDTR` clears data terminal ready.
  Test: see tty.7-66, tty.7-67.

**tty.7-84** [OSF/1] `TIOCSTOP` stops output as if the stop character had been typed; `TIOCSTART` restarts output as if the start character had been typed.
  Test: `TIOCSTOP` on slave; slave writes do not appear at master until `TIOCSTART`.
  Note: The page prints "Putput" for "Output" under `TIOCSTART`.

**tty.7-85** [OSF/1] `TIOCGPGRP`: `arg` points to an `int` that receives the process group ID of the process group for which this terminal is the control terminal.
  Test: `TIOCGPGRP` equals `tcgetpgrp(fd)`.

**tty.7-86** [OSF/1] `TIOCSPGRP`: `arg` points to an `int` giving the value to which the terminal's process group ID is set.
  Test: `TIOCSPGRP` to own group, then `TIOCGPGRP` returns it.

**tty.7-87** [OSF/1] `TIOCOUTQ` returns, in the `int` pointed to by `arg`, the number of characters queued for output to the terminal.
  Test: stop output with `TIOCSTOP`, write 5 bytes; `TIOCOUTQ` gives 5.

**tty.7-88** [OSF/1] `TIOCREMOTE` sets the terminal for remote input editing.
  Test: Not testable as stated (the page gives no argument or observable effect).
  Note: The page does not describe `TIOCREMOTE`'s argument or effect further.

**tty.7-89** [OSF/1] `FIONREAD` returns, in the `int` pointed to by `arg`, the number of characters immediately readable from the descriptor; it works for files, pipes and terminals.
  Test: write 4 bytes to a pipe; `FIONREAD` gives 4. Same for a regular file at offset 0 of a 10-byte file (expect 10) and a noncanonical tty.

**tty.7-90** [OSF/1] Modem ioctls: `TIOCMODG` (`arg` points to an `int` with the modem control state), `TIOCMODS` (`arg` points to an `int` with the state to set), `TIOCMSET` (sets all modem bits), `TIOCMBIS` (`arg` points to an `int` of bits to set), `TIOCMBIC` (`arg` points to an `int` of bits to clear), `TIOCMGET` (gets all modem bits into the `int` pointed to by `arg`).
  Test: on a serial line, `TIOCMBIS` then `TIOCMGET` shows the bits set; otherwise Not testable from user space without modem hardware.

**tty.7-91** [OSF/1] Each terminal stores its window size in `struct winsize`: `ws_row` (rows, in characters), `ws_col` (columns, in characters), `ws_xpixel` (horizontal size, pixels), `ws_ypixel` (vertical size, pixels), all `unsigned short`.
  Test: compile check of the four fields and their types.

**tty.7-92** [OSF/1] A value of 0 in any `winsize` field means "undefined"; the whole structure is zeroed on final close.
  Test: set a size, close all fds of a pty slave, reopen; `TIOCGWINSZ` gives all zeros.

**tty.7-93** [OSF/1] `TIOCGWINSZ`: `arg` points to a `struct winsize` that receives the current size.
  Test: after `TIOCSWINSZ` {24,80,0,0}, `TIOCGWINSZ` returns the same.

**tty.7-94** [OSF/1] `TIOCSWINSZ`: `arg` points to a `struct winsize` used to set the size; if the new information differs from the old, `SIGWINCH` is sent to the terminal's process group.
  Test: setting the same size twice sends `SIGWINCH` only the first time.

**tty.7-95** [OSF/1] Files: `/dev/tty` is the special file for tty; `/dev/tty*` are special files for ttys where `*` is the tty number; `/dev/console` is the console device special file.
  Test: `stat("/dev/tty")` and `stat("/dev/console")` show device special files.

Errors (the call returns −1 and sets `errno`, unless the page says otherwise):

**tty.7-E1** `EAGAIN`: `read()` with `O_NONBLOCK` set and no data available.

**tty.7-E2** `EIO`: `read()` from the controlling terminal by a process not in the foreground process group that ignores or blocks `SIGTTIN`, or whose process group is orphaned; no signal is sent.

**tty.7-E3** `EIO`: `write()` to the controlling terminal by a process not in the foreground process group when `TOSTOP` is set, the process group is orphaned, and `SIGTTOU` is not blocked; no signal is sent.

Related: Functions: ioctl(2), sigvec(2), tcsetattr(3), tcgetattr(3), tcdrain(3), tcflush(3), tcsendbreak(3), tcgetpgrp(3), tcsetpgrp(3); Commands: csh(1), tset(1), getty(8); IEEE Std POSIX 1003.1-1988; Application Environment Specification - Operating System/Programming Interfaces Volume


## Section 8 — system administration

### cfgmgr(8)

Page: `man8/cfgmgr.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**cfgmgr.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `cfgmgr [-c database] [-d -f -v]`.
  Test: `cfgmgr -f -c /tmp/test.tab` starts without detaching.

**cfgmgr.8-2** [OSF/1] `-c database` uses the given configuration database instead of the default `/etc/sysconfigtab`.
  Test: start with `-c` pointing at a test file marking a subsystem automatic; that subsystem is configured.

**cfgmgr.8-3** [OSF/1] `-d` produces debugging information during operation.
  Test: start with `-d -f`; syslog shows debug messages absent without `-d`.

**cfgmgr.8-4** [OSF/1] `-f` makes `cfgmgr` not detach from the current controlling tty (session).
  Test: run `cfgmgr -f` in the foreground; the shell does not get control back and the process keeps the tty's session.

**cfgmgr.8-5** [OSF/1] `-v` produces more verbose information during operation.
  Test: compare syslog volume with and without `-v`.

**cfgmgr.8-6** [OSF/1] `cfgmgr` manages dynamically configurable subsystems and is usually started at system startup.
  Test: Not testable from user space as a requirement (startup scripts); check it is running after boot.

**cfgmgr.8-7** [OSF/1] On start, `cfgmgr` configures all subsystems marked automatic in the configuration database.
  Test: see cfgmgr.8-2.

**cfgmgr.8-8** [OSF/1] `cfgmgr` then listens on a communications socket for command requests from `sysconfig`.
  Test: with `cfgmgr` running, `sysconfig` command requests are answered.

**cfgmgr.8-9** [OSF/1] On `SIGHUP`, `cfgmgr` rereads the configuration database.
  Test: edit the database, send `SIGHUP`, then `sysconfig` reflects the change.

**cfgmgr.8-10** [OSF/1] `cfgmgr` logs operational output and error messages to `syslogd`; the amount of operational information is controlled by `-d` and `-v`.
  Test: see cfgmgr.8-3 and cfgmgr.8-5.

**cfgmgr.8-11** [OSF/1] Files: command path `/sbin/cfgmgr`; configuration database `/etc/sysconfigtab`.
  Test: `test -x /sbin/cfgmgr`.

Related: Commands: sysconfig(8), sysconfigdb(8), syslogd(8); Files: sysconfigtab(4)

### getty(8)

Page: `man8/getty.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**getty.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `getty [-h] [-t time] line speed_label terminal line_discipline` and `getty -c file`.
  Test: `getty -c /etc/gettydefs` runs and prints to standard output.

**getty.8-2** [OSF/1] `-h` holds carrier during initialisation and does not hang up.
  Test: Not testable from user space without modem-controlled hardware.

**getty.8-3** [OSF/1] `-t time` sets a time period in seconds; the line is dropped after that time if nothing is typed.
  Test: run `getty -t 2` on a pty slave, type nothing; it exits/drops the line after about 2 seconds.

**getty.8-4** [OSF/1] `-c` checks the specified gettydefs file: it scans the file the same way it scans gettydefs for terminal information and prints the results to standard output.
  Test: `getty -c` on a test file with one entry prints results to standard output.

**getty.8-5** [OSF/1] `getty` sets and manages terminals by setting speed, terminal flags and line discipline, adapting the system to any command flags given.
  Test: run getty on a pty slave with a known speed_label; `stty` on the slave shows the gettydefs flags.

**getty.8-6** [OSF/1] `getty` prints the login prompt, waits for a username, and invokes `login`.
  Test: run getty on a pty; master sees the prompt; write a name; `login` is executed (process image changes).

**getty.8-7** [OSF/1] `getty` uses `/etc/gettydefs` for terminal information. `line` is the device name in `/dev`; `speed_label` points into `/etc/gettydefs` where speed and associated flags are defined; `terminal` is the terminal type name; `line_discipline` is the line discipline name.
  Test: as getty.8-5.

**getty.8-8** [OSF/1] Files: command path `/usr/sbin/getty`; terminal line database `/etc/gettydefs`.
  Test: `test -x /usr/sbin/getty`.

Related: Commands: init(8), login(1), stty(1)

### halt(8)

Page: `man8/halt.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**halt.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `halt -l`, `halt -n`, `halt -q`, `halt -y`.
  Test: Not testable from user space without stopping the machine (run only in a disposable VM).

**halt.8-2** [OSF/1] `halt` writes data to the disks and then stops the processor(s), without rebooting the machine.
  Test: in a disposable VM, write a file, run `halt`; after manual restart the file is intact and the VM did not reboot by itself.

**halt.8-3** [OSF/1] Only root can run `halt`.
  Test: run `halt` as a non-root user; it fails and the system keeps running.

**halt.8-4** [OSF/1] `-l` does not log the halt using syslog.
  Test: in a VM, `halt -l`; after restart, no halt entry in syslog.

**halt.8-5** [OSF/1] `-n` prevents the sync before stopping and does not log via syslog.
  Test: Not testable from user space in a reliable way (absence of sync).

**halt.8-6** [OSF/1] `-q` causes a quick halt, does not log via syslog, and makes no attempt to kill all processes.
  Test: in a VM, `halt -q`; no syslog entry.

**halt.8-7** [OSF/1] `-y` halts the system from a dial-up operation.
  Test: Not testable from user space without a dial-up line.
  Note: The page does not say how `-y` changes behaviour.

**halt.8-8** [OSF/1] Use `halt` when not restarting immediately; when the message `....Halt completed....` is displayed, power can be turned off.
  Test: in a VM, console output contains "....Halt completed....".

**halt.8-9** [OSF/1] Without `-l`, `-n` or `-q`, `halt` logs the shutdown via `syslogd` and records it in the login accounting file `/var/adm/wtmp`. `-q` and `-n` imply `-l`.
  Test: in a VM, plain `halt`; after restart, syslog and `/var/adm/wtmp` contain a shutdown record; with `-n`, no syslog entry appears.
  Note: The page does not say whether `-l` also suppresses the `/var/adm/wtmp` record.

**halt.8-10** [OSF/1] Caution: do not use `halt` if other users are logged in or if the system is at a multiuser run level.
  Test: Not testable (advice to administrators).

**halt.8-11** [OSF/1] Files: command path `/usr/sbin/halt`; syslog daemon `/usr/sbin/syslogd`; login accounting file `/var/adm/wtmp`.
  Test: `test -x /usr/sbin/halt`.

Related: Commands: fasthalt(8), reboot(8), shutdown(8), syslogd(8); Functions: halt(2), reboot(2), sync(2), syslog(3)

### init(8)

Page: `man8/init.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**init.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `init [0s23]`.
  Test: as root in a disposable VM, `init 2` changes to run level 2.

**init.8-2** [OSF/1] `init` initialises the system by creating and controlling processes; the processes run at each run level are defined in `inittab`, whose entries `init` reads and acts on.
  Test: add an inittab entry for level 2 that runs a marker command; after entering level 2 the marker exists.

**init.8-3** [OSF/1] The system is always in a run level, each with its own group of processes. `init` operates in one of four run levels: 0, s, 2, 3.
  Test: covered by init.8-8 (the page does not say what happens with an unlisted run level).
  Note: The page does not say what happens with an unlisted run level.

**init.8-4** [OSF/1] The run level changes when a privileged user invokes `init`; the new `init` sends appropriate signals to the original `init` telling it which run level to change to.
  Test: non-root `init 2` fails; root `init 2` works.

**init.8-5** [OSF/1] `init` runs as the last step of boot after the root file system is mounted.
  Test: Not testable from user space (boot sequence).

**init.8-6** [OSF/1] `init` looks in `inittab` for an entry with the `initdefault` keyword and, if present, enters that run level initially. If the entry or the file is absent, it asks the user for a run level on `/dev/console`.
  Test: in a VM, remove `initdefault` and reboot; the console prompts for a run level.

**init.8-7** [OSF/1] If the user enters `s`, `init` enters single-user state, assigns the virtual console terminal to the user's terminal and opens it for reading and writing; `su` is invoked and a message on the console states where the virtual console is.
  Test: in a VM, answer `s` at the prompt; `su` is run on the console and the virtual-console location message is displayed.

**init.8-8** [OSF/1] Run level values: 0 shuts down and halts the system; `s` is single-user with only essential kernel services; 2 is multiuser with local processes and daemons; 3 is multiuser with remote processes and daemons.
  Test: in a VM, `init 3` starts remote daemons (e.g. network services) not running at level 2.

**init.8-9** [OSF/1] On the first post-boot entry to a run level other than single-user, `init` searches `inittab` for entries at the new level with the `boot` or `bootwait` keywords and acts on them before other entries if the level matches. Special initialisation (for example checking and mounting file systems) happens before users are allowed on. `init` then scans `inittab` for all entries for that level.
  Test: in a VM, a `bootwait` entry's marker is written before a `respawn` entry's marker at level 2.

**init.8-10** [OSF/1] For each entry that should be respawned, `init` forks a child process. After spawning, `init` waits for a descendant to stop, a power-fail signal, or a signal to change run level; on any of these it re-examines `inittab`.
  Test: kill a respawned process; `init` starts a new one.

**init.8-11** [OSF/1] Edits to `inittab` are not noticed until one of those three conditions occurs; `init -q` forces immediate re-examination.
  Test: add an entry, check it is not started, run `init -q`, it starts.
  Note: The page's synopsis does not list `-q`.

**init.8-12** [OSF/1] Files: command path `/sbin/init`; control file `/tcb/files/inittab`; boot-time script for systems that do not support inittab `tcb/files/sysinitrc`; permanent login accounting file `/var/adm/wtmp`.
  Note: The page gives `tcb/files/sysinitrc` without a leading slash.
  Test: `test -x /sbin/init && test -f /tcb/files/inittab`.

Related: Commands: getty(8), rc0(8), rc2(8), rc3(8), shutdown(8); Calls: kill(2), reboot(2); Files: inittab(4)

### killall(8)

Page: `man8/killall.html`. The page header is marked "Environment_Note_Added".
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**killall.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `killall [- | -signal_name | -signal_number]` and `killall -l`.
  Test: `killall -l` exits 0 and prints signal names.

**killall.8-2** [OSF/1] `killall` terminates all processes started by the user, except the calling process; it kills all processes created by the shell you control.
  Test: start two `sleep` processes, run `killall`; both are gone and the invoking shell survives.

**killall.8-3** [OSF/1] `-` alone sends `SIGTERM`, then sends `SIGKILL` to all processes that survive for 30 seconds after the first signal, giving processes that catch `SIGTERM` a chance to clean up.
  Test: start a process that ignores `SIGTERM`; `killall -`; it survives about 30 seconds and then dies by `SIGKILL`.

**killall.8-4** [OSF/1] `-signal_name` sends the named signal; names are given without the `SIG` prefix (such as `KILL`).
  Test: `killall -INT` against a process with a `SIGINT` handler; the handler runs.

**killall.8-5** [OSF/1] `-signal_number` sends the given signal, either a name stripped of `SIG` or a number (such as 9); signal names and numbers are as in the `signal()` system call.
  Test: `killall -2` delivers `SIGINT`.

**killall.8-6** [OSF/1] `-l` lists signal names in numerical order (as in `/usr/include/signal.h`), stripped of the `SIG` prefix; the list "may vary from system to system".
  Test: `killall -l` prints signal names without the `SIG` prefix, in increasing signal-number order.

**killall.8-7** [OSF/1] When started by the superuser, `killall` kills all processes that can be terminated except those that started it, kernel processes, and processes 0 and 1 (`init`).
  Test: in a VM, root `killall -TERM`; process 1 still exists.

**killall.8-8** [OSF/1] With no arguments, `killall` sends all background processes signal 9 (`SIGKILL`).
  Test: background process with handlers for all catchable signals dies after plain `killall`.

**killall.8-9** [OSF/1] Files: command path `/usr/sbin/killall`.
  Test: `test -x /usr/sbin/killall`.

**killall.8-10** [DEC] The root of the directory tree containing commands modified for SVID-2 compliance is specified in `/etc/svid2_path`; `/etc/svid2_profile` can be used as or included in `.profile`, and it reads `/etc/svid2_path` and puts those entries first in `PATH` so the SVID-2 commands are found first.
  Test: source `/etc/svid2_profile`; `PATH` begins with the contents of `/etc/svid2_path`.

**killall.8-11** [DEC] In the SVID-2 habitat, the hyphen before the `signal_number` parameter is optional.
  Test: with the SVID-2 `PATH`, `killall 2` delivers `SIGINT`.

Related: Calls: kill(2), sigaction(2), signal(2)

### kloadsrv(8)

Page: `man8/kloadsrv.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**kloadsrv.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `kloadsrv [-f] [-d debug-level] [-p kernel-package-name] [kernel-object-filename]`.
  Test: as root, `kloadsrv -f -d 1` runs in the foreground and logs messages.

**kloadsrv.8-2** [OSF/1] `-p kernel-package-name` overrides the default kernel package name, `kernel`.
  Test: Not testable from user space without inspecting the kernel export list; check that later loads resolve symbols under the given package name.

**kloadsrv.8-3** [OSF/1] `-f` keeps `kloadsrv` in the foreground.
  Test: `kloadsrv -f` does not return to the shell.

**kloadsrv.8-4** [OSF/1] `-d debug-level` sets the debug level, a small integer; 0 disables debugging; non-zero values cause various log messages.
  Test: compare output of `-d 0` and `-d 2`.

**kloadsrv.8-5** [OSF/1] `kloadsrv` is the kernel load server, responsible for loading kernel modules into the kernel, and is typically started during system startup.
  Test: after boot, a `kloadsrv` process exists.

**kloadsrv.8-6** [OSF/1] During initialisation it builds the kernel's initial export list by reading the kernel object file, by default `/vmunix`. Each exported symbol belongs to some package; any symbol not in a package goes in the default kernel package, named `kernel` by default.
  Test: Not testable from user space directly; `ldr_xlookup_package` for "kernel" succeeds after startup.

**kloadsrv.8-7** [OSF/1] After successful initialisation, `kloadsrv` puts itself in the background and enters its server loop, waiting for and responding to kernel load requests.
  Test: `kloadsrv` without `-f` returns to the shell while the server keeps running.

**kloadsrv.8-8** [OSF/1] An optional `kernel-object-filename` overrides the default `/vmunix`.
  Test: run with a copy of the kernel file path; it initialises successfully.

**kloadsrv.8-9** [OSF/1] Files: command path `/sbin/kloadsrv`; default kernel object file `/vmunix`; `/var/run/kloadsrv.pid` holds the process ID of the current kernel load server.
  Test: `/var/run/kloadsrv.pid` contains the PID of the running `kloadsrv`.

Related: Commands: cfgmgr(8), sysconfig(8), sysconfigdb(8); Functions: ldr_kernel_process(2), ldr_xattach(2), ldr_xdetach(2), ldr_xload(2), ldr_xunload(2), ldr_xentry(2), ldr_xlookup_package(2), ldr_inq_module(2), ldr_inq_region(2), ldr_next_module(2)

### MAKEDEV(8)

Page: `man8/MAKEDEV.html`.
Origin: Written by Digital, not OSF (the page is headed "Digital"): its items are tagged [DEC] and are a guide, not a requirement.

Note: The page's header line reads "Digital". Items the page ties to particular DEC machines are tagged `[DEC]`; the rest are tagged `[DEC]`.

**MAKEDEV.8-1** [DEC] Synopsis: `/dev/MAKEDEV [ argument ] [ device-name? ...]`.
  Test: as root, in a scratch copy of `/dev`, run `MAKEDEV std`; it completes.

**MAKEDEV.8-2** [DEC] `MAKEDEV` is a shell script normally used to install special files; it resides in `/dev`, the normal location of special files.
  Test: `test -f /dev/MAKEDEV` and `sh -n /dev/MAKEDEV` accepts it as a shell script.

**MAKEDEV.8-3** [DEC] Arguments are usually of the form `device-name?`, where `device-name` is a device listed in Section 4 of the Reference Pages and `?` is a logical unit number.
  Test: in a scratch directory copy, `sh MAKEDEV` with a Section 4 device name and unit number creates the matching node.

**MAKEDEV.8-4** [DEC] `DS_3100` creates the standard special device files for the DECstation 3100; `DS_5000_100` for the DECstation 5000 Model 100; `DS_5000_200` for the DECstation 5000 Model 200; `DS_5100` for the DECsystem 5100.
  Test: run each argument in a scratch copy of `/dev` and check the nodes listed in MAKEDEV.8-6 for that machine exist.

**MAKEDEV.8-5** [DEC] `std` creates all standard device files for all systems: `klog`, `kmem`, `mem`, `null`, `console`, `tty`, `pty0`, and `ty1`.
  Note: The page text is damaged here: the last name reads "ty1" (in the HTML as well), probably a broken name; recorded as read.
  Test: `MAKEDEV std` in a scratch copy creates each listed node.

**MAKEDEV.8-6** [DEC] Machine-specific standard devices: DECstation 3100: `pm0`, `xcons`, `dc0`; DECstation 5000 Model 200: `pm0`, `xcons`, `dc0`; DECstation 5000 Model 100: `pm0`, `xcons`, `scc0`; DECsystem 5100: `mdc0`.
  Test: as MAKEDEV.8-4.

**MAKEDEV.8-7** [DEC] `local` creates site-specific devices by executing the shell file `/dev/MAKEDEV.local`, which must exist before `local` is used; site-specific commands (for example dialup lines as `ttyd?`, and special files for non-Digital devices) belong in that file.
  Test: create `/dev/MAKEDEV.local` that touches a marker file; `MAKEDEV local` creates the marker.

**MAKEDEV.8-8** [DEC] All devices are created with `mknod(8)`, so the script is useful only to the superuser.
  Test: run `MAKEDEV null` as non-root in a scratch dir; node creation fails.

**MAKEDEV.8-9** [DEC] Errors are either self-explanatory or produced by programs the script calls; `sh -x MAKEDEV` is suggested for troubleshooting.
  Test: `sh -x /dev/MAKEDEV std` prints a trace of commands.

Related: intro(7), config(8), mknod(8)

### mknod(8)

Page: `man8/mknod.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mknod.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `mknod special_file [ b major_device# minor_device# | c major_device# minor_device#]` and `mknod filename p`.
  Test: `mknod /tmp/p p` succeeds as any user.

**mknod.8-2** [OSF/1] `b` makes a special file for a block-oriented device (disk or tape); `c` for a character-oriented device; `p` creates a named pipe (FIFO).
  Test: as root, `mknod /tmp/b b 1 2` and `mknod /tmp/c c 1 2`; `ls -l` shows types `b` and `c`; `mknod /tmp/f p` shows type `p`.

**mknod.8-3** [OSF/1] `mknod` makes a directory entry; the first argument is the name of the special file.
  Test: after mknod, the named entry exists.

**mknod.8-4** [OSF/1] In the first form, the second argument is `b` or `c` and the last two are the major device number (which helps the operating system find the driver code) and the minor device number ("the unit drive, or line number"); the page says "which may be either decimal or octal".
  Test: as root, `mknod /tmp/x c 1 010`; `stat` shows major 1 and minor 8.
  Note: The page places "which may be either decimal or octal" after the minor-device description, so it is unclear whether it also covers the major number.
  Note: The page does not say how octal is distinguished (e.g. a leading 0).

**mknod.8-5** [OSF/1] Major device number assignment is specific to each system; numbers can be found in the `conf.c` system source file; adding a driver to `conf.c` requires rebuilding the kernel.
  Test: Not testable from user space (documentation of system configuration).

**mknod.8-6** [OSF/1] Only the superuser can create a character or device special file.
  Test: as non-root, `mknod /tmp/c c 1 2` fails; `mknod /tmp/f p` succeeds.
  Note: The page says "character or device special file"; presumably block is meant for the second.

**mknod.8-7** [OSF/1] Example: `mknod /dev/ra2 b 1 2` creates block special file `/dev/ra2` with major 1, minor 2; `mknod pipe p` creates a FIFO named `pipe` in the current directory.
  Test: run the FIFO example in a temp directory; `test -p pipe`.

**mknod.8-8** [OSF/1] Files: command path `/usr/sbin/mknod`; `conf.c` is the system device numbers specification file.
  Test: `test -x /usr/sbin/mknod`.

### mount(8), umount(8)

Page: `man8/mount.html`; same text as `umount(8)`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**mount.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis (mount): `mount`; `mount -a [-v] [-t type]`; `mount [-rv] [-o option, ...] [-t type] file_system directory`; `mount [-v] file_system`; `mount [-v] directory`.
  Test: run each form and check it is accepted (forms that change mounts require root).

**mount.8-2** [OSF/1] Synopsis (umount): `umount [-h host]`; `umount -a [-v] [-t type]`; `umount [-v] file_system | directory ...`.
  Test: run each form as root and check it is accepted.
Note: The page gives no meaning for `mount` with no arguments.

**mount.8-3** [OSF/1] `mount -a` attempts to mount all file systems described in `/etc/fstab`; `file_system` and `directory` are then taken from `/etc/fstab`.
  Test: as root, with unmounted entries in `/etc/fstab`, run `mount -a` and check they become mounted.

**mount.8-4** [OSF/1] With `mount -a` and a type given, all file systems in `/etc/fstab` with that type are mounted.
  Test: as root, run `mount -a -t ufs` and check only `ufs` entries are mounted.

**mount.8-5** [OSF/1] With `mount -a`, file systems are "not necessarily mounted in the order listed" in `/etc/fstab`.
  Test: none required; a test must not depend on mount order.

**mount.8-6** [OSF/1] `-o` takes a comma-separated list of options; some options are valid for all file system types, others only for a specific type.
  Test: as root, `mount -o ro,nosuid dev dir` and check both options take effect.

**mount.8-7** [OSF/1] The default options on all file systems are `rw,noquota`.
  Test: mount without `-o` and check the file system is writable and quotas are not enforced.

**mount.8-8** [OSF/1] Option `quota`: usage limits are enforced.
  Test: mount with `-o quota` on a file system with quotas and exceed a limit; expect failure.

**mount.8-9** [OSF/1] Option `noquota`: usage limits are not enforced.
  Test: mount with `-o noquota` and exceed a quota limit; expect success.

**mount.8-10** [OSF/1] Option `rw`: read/write.
  Test: mount with `-o rw` and create a file; expect success.

**mount.8-11** [OSF/1] Option `ro`: read-only.
  Test: mount with `-o ro` and try to create a file; expect failure.

**mount.8-12** [OSF/1] Option `suid`: set-user-ID execution is allowed.
  Test: mount with `-o suid`, run a setuid program from it as another user, check effective UID changes.

**mount.8-13** [OSF/1] Option `nosuid`: set-user-ID execution is not allowed.
  Test: mount with `-o nosuid`, run a setuid program from it, check effective UID does not change.

**mount.8-14** [OSF/1] NFS option `bg`: if the first mount attempt fails, retries in the background.
  Test: mount an unreachable NFS server with `-o bg`; check `mount` returns and retries continue in background.

**mount.8-15** [OSF/1] NFS option `fg`: retries in the foreground.
  Test: mount an unreachable NFS server with `-o fg,retry=1`; check `mount` does not return until retries end.

**mount.8-16** [OSF/1] NFS option `retry=n`: sets the number of mount failure retries to n.
  Test: mount an unreachable server with `retry=2` and count attempts.

**mount.8-17** [OSF/1] NFS option `rsize=n`: sets the read buffer size to n bytes.
  Test: mount with `rsize=1024` and observe read request size on the wire.

**mount.8-18** [OSF/1] NFS option `wsize=n`: sets the write buffer size to n bytes.
  Test: mount with `wsize=1024` and observe write request size on the wire.

**mount.8-19** [OSF/1] NFS option `timeo=n`: sets the NFS time-out to n tenths of a second.
  Test: mount with `timeo=5`, stop the server, measure the first retransmission delay (~0.5 s).

**mount.8-20** [OSF/1] NFS option `retrans=n`: sets the number of NFS retransmissions to n.
  Test: mount `soft,retrans=2`, stop the server, count retransmissions before the error.

**mount.8-21** [OSF/1] NFS option `port=n`: sets the server IP port number to n.
  Test: run the server on a nonstandard port and mount with `port=` that port; expect success.

**mount.8-22** [OSF/1] NFS option `soft`: returns an error if the server does not respond.
  Test: mount `soft`, stop the server, read a file; expect an error after retransmissions.

**mount.8-23** [OSF/1] NFS option `hard`: retries the request until the server responds.
  Test: mount `hard`, stop the server, read a file; check it blocks and completes after the server restarts.

**mount.8-24** [OSF/1] NFS defaults are `fg,retry=10000,timeo=10,retrans=10,port=NFS_PORT,hard`.
  Test: mount NFS without options and check (e.g. with `mount -l` on this system) the reported values.

**mount.8-25** [OSF/1] Defaults for `rsize` and `wsize` are set by the kernel.
  Test: none beyond observing the values; no fixed number is required.

**mount.8-26** [OSF/1] `bg` causes `mount` to run in the background if the server's `mountd` does not respond.
  Test: as for mount.8-14.

**mount.8-27** [OSF/1] `mount` attempts each request `retry=n` times before giving up.
  Test: as for mount.8-16.

**mount.8-28** [OSF/1] Once mounted, each NFS request made in the kernel waits `timeo=n` tenths of a second for a response; if none arrives, the time-out is multiplied by 2 and the request is retransmitted.
  Test: stop the server and measure intervals between retransmissions; each should double.

**mount.8-29** [OSF/1] When `retrans=n` retransmissions have been sent with no reply, a soft-mounted file system returns an error on the request and a hard-mounted one retries the request.
  Test: as for mount.8-22 and mount.8-23.

**mount.8-30** [OSF/1] File systems mounted `rw` "should use the hard option" (advice).
  Test: Not testable; advice only.

**mount.8-31** [OSF/1] The number of bytes in a read or write request can be set with `rsize` and `wsize`.
  Test: as for mount.8-17 and mount.8-18.

**mount.8-32** [OSF/1] `-r` mounts the file system read-only; it is shorthand for `mount -o ro file_system directory`.
  Test: `mount -r dev dir`, then try to create a file; expect failure.

**mount.8-33** [OSF/1] Physically write-protected and magnetic tape file systems must be mounted read-only, or errors occur when access times are updated, whether or not an explicit write is attempted.
  Test: mount a write-protected medium read/write and read a file; expect errors.

**mount.8-34** [OSF/1] `-t type` specifies the file system type; accepted types are `ufs`, `s5fs`, `nfs`, `mfs`. See fstab(4) for the legal types.
  Test: `mount -t ufs dev dir` succeeds for a `ufs` file system; likewise for each listed type.

**mount.8-35** [OSF/1] `mount -v` displays a message saying which file system is being mounted.
  Test: `mount -v dev dir` and check a message naming the file system is printed.

**mount.8-36** [OSF/1] `umount -a` attempts to unmount all currently mounted file systems (listed in `/etc/fstab`); `file_system` is then taken from `/etc/fstab`.
  Test: as root, `umount -a` and check `/etc/fstab` file systems are unmounted.

**mount.8-37** [OSF/1] `umount -h host` unmounts all file systems listed in `/etc/fstab` that are remotely mounted from `host`.
  Test: mount two NFS file systems from different hosts; `umount -h hostA` removes only hostA's.

**mount.8-38** [OSF/1] `umount -t type` unmounts all file systems listed in `/etc/fstab` of that type.
  Test: `umount -a -t nfs` and check only NFS file systems are unmounted.

**mount.8-39** [OSF/1] `umount -v` displays a message saying which file system is being unmounted.
  Test: `umount -v dir` and check a message is printed.

**mount.8-40** [OSF/1] `mount` attaches `file_system` to the file tree at `directory`, which must already exist.
  Test: mount on a nonexistent directory; expect failure.

**mount.8-41** [OSF/1] `directory` becomes the name of the newly mounted root, and its previous contents are hidden until the file system is unmounted.
  Test: put a file in `dir`, mount on it, check the file is not visible; unmount, check it is visible again.

**mount.8-42** [OSF/1] If `file_system` has the form `host:path`, the type is assumed to be NFS.
  Test: `mount serv:/x /mnt` without `-t`; check it is mounted as NFS.

**mount.8-43** [OSF/1] `umount` removes the file system previously mounted on `directory`; either the file system name or the mounted-on directory may be given.
  Test: unmount once by device name and once by directory; both succeed.

**mount.8-44** [OSF/1] Given only one of `file_system` or `directory`, `mount` searches `/etc/fstab` for an entry whose directory or file_system field matches, and uses that entry (e.g. `mount /usr` or `mount /dev/xy0g` for the line `/dev/xy0g /usr ufs rw 1 1`).
  Test: add an fstab line and run `mount dir`, then (after unmount) `mount dev`; both mount the entry.

**mount.8-45** [OSF/1] Command paths: `/usr/sbin/mount` and `/usr/sbin/umount`; file used: `/etc/fstab`.
  Test: check both files exist and are executable.

**mount.8-46** [OSF/1] NOTES: no more than one user should mount a disk partition read/write, or the file system may become corrupted.
  Test: Not testable; advice only.

**mount.8-47** [OSF/1] NOTES: if the mount directory is a symbolic link, the file system is mounted on the directory the link refers to, not on top of the link itself.
  Test: create symlink `l -> d`, `mount dev l`; check the mount point is `d` and `l` is still a symlink.

**mount.8-48** [DEC] (ULTRIX Compatibility) `cdfs` option `defperm`: ignores permission bits if present and defaults all file and directory permissions to 0666, with a zero UID (owned by root).
  Test: mount a CD-ROM with `-o defperm`; `stat` files and expect mode 0666, UID 0.

**mount.8-49** [DEC] Files and directories on an ISO 9660 file system "may or may not have permission bits"; `defperm` is a default option because most CD-ROM permissions do not map to the UID scheme used.
  Test: mount a CD-ROM without options and expect `defperm` behaviour.

**mount.8-50** [DEC] `cdfs` option `nodefperm`: uses the on-disk permission bits if present; a file or directory recorded without permission bits gets the 0666 default.
  Test: mount with `-o nodefperm` and compare `stat` modes with recorded bits.

**mount.8-51** [DEC] `cdfs` option `noversion`: strips the `;#` version extension from file names that have one; use it for CD-ROMs containing MS-DOS applications.
  Test: mount with `-o noversion` and check names lack `;1`.

**mount.8-52** [DEC] `cdfs` defaults are `ro, defperm`.
  Test: mount a CD-ROM without options; check it is read-only and uses `defperm`.

**mount.8-53** [DEC] Attribute-cache options affect how quickly updates made by another host are seen; increasing them gives slightly better performance, decreasing them shortens the time to see remote changes. If you are the only person modifying files under the mount point, the page advises increasing them.
  Test: as for mount.8-54 to mount.8-60.
Note: The page does not say which file system types these options apply to; by context (another host) they appear to be NFS options.

**mount.8-54** [DEC] `acdirmin=n`: hold cached directory attributes for at least n seconds.
  Test: set `acdirmin=10`, change a directory on the server, check the change is not seen within 10 s.
Note: The page text shows `acdirmin=Vn` (and likewise for the other four options); the "V" appears in the original HTML and seems to be damage; the value is n.

**mount.8-55** [DEC] `acdirmax=n`: hold cached directory attributes for no more than n seconds; maximum value 3600.
  Test: set `acdirmax=5`, change a directory on the server, check it is seen within 5 s.

**mount.8-56** [DEC] `acregmin=n`: hold cached file attributes for at least n seconds.
  Test: as mount.8-54 for a regular file.

**mount.8-57** [DEC] `acregmax=n`: hold cached file attributes for no more than n seconds; maximum value 3600.
  Test: as mount.8-55 for a regular file.

**mount.8-58** [DEC] `actimeo=n`: sets all four attribute cache timeouts to n.
  Test: set `actimeo=2`; check file and directory changes are seen within 2 s.

**mount.8-59** [DEC] `noac`: no attribute caching; equivalent to `actimeo=0`.
  Test: with `noac`, a change on the server is seen immediately.

**mount.8-60** [DEC] `nocto`: do not get a fresh attribute when opening a file.
  Test: with `nocto`, change a file on the server and open it at once; old attributes may be seen.

**mount.8-61** [DEC] Attribute cache defaults are `acdirmin=30, acdirmax=60, acregmin=3, acregmax=60`.
  Test: check reported values with `mount -l`.

**mount.8-62** [DEC] `-t` additionally accepts type `cdfs`.
  Test: `mount -t cdfs -o noversion /dev/rz3c /cdfs` succeeds with a CD-ROM present.

**mount.8-63** [DEC] `mount` can mount an ISO 9660 or High Sierra (HSG) formatted file system onto a directory.
  Test: mount an HSG disc with `-t cdfs`; expect success.

**mount.8-64** [DEC] NOTES: if an ISO 9660 or HSG mount fails with `cdfs_mount: Operation Not Supported`, see cdfs(4) for the configuration options needed before using CDFS.
  Test: Not testable as a requirement; the page only says where to look if this message appears.

**mount.8-65** [DEC] (Digital Extensions) Synopsis: `mount [-l] [-d] [-f] [-u]`.
  Test: run each flag and check it is accepted.

**mount.8-66** [DEC] `mount -l` displays the value of all file system options.
  Test: `mount -l` lists options for each mounted file system.

**mount.8-67** [DEC] `mount -d` mounts a CDrom UFS file system.
  Test: mount a UFS CD-ROM with `-d`; expect success.

**mount.8-68** [DEC] `mount -f` performs a "fake" mount and does not actually mount the file system.
  Test: `mount -f dev dir`; check `dir` contents unchanged.

**mount.8-69** [DEC] `mount -u` mounts the specified file system read-write.
  Test: `mount -u` on a read-only mount; check it becomes writable.

**mount.8-70** [DEC] Synopsis: `umount [-f]`; `-f` performs a fast unmount: only remote file systems are unmounted, without notifying the server.
  Test: `umount -f` with local and NFS mounts; only NFS ones are removed and the server gets no unmount request.

Related: Commands: mountd(8), nfsd(8). Functions: mount(3), umount(3). Files: fstab(4).

### rc0(8)

Page: `man8/rc0.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**rc0.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `rc0`.
  Test: check `/sbin/rc0` exists and is executable.

**rc0.8-2** [OSF/1] `rc0` contains run commands for a smooth shutdown, bringing the system to a single-user state (run levels 0 and s).
  Test: Not testable from user space; it shuts the system down.

**rc0.8-3** [OSF/1] Besides its own commands, `rc0` runs commands found in `/sbin/rc0.d`.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a shutdown.

**rc0.8-4** [OSF/1] The script defines conditions under which commands run: some run if the system is being shut down, others if it is shut down and rebooted to single user.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a shutdown.

**rc0.8-5** [OSF/1] By convention, files in `/sbin/rc0.d` begin with `K` or `S`, followed by a two-digit number and a file name (e.g. `K00enlogin`, `K05lpd`, `K60cron`, `K30nfs`).
  Test: list `/sbin/rc0.d` and check names match `[KS][0-9][0-9]name`.

**rc0.8-6** [OSF/1] In general, `S` commands are started and `K` commands are stopped.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a shutdown.

**rc0.8-7** [OSF/1] The numbers are sorted and the commands run in ascending order.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a shutdown.

**rc0.8-8** [OSF/1] Files in `/sbin/rc0.d` are normally links to files in `/etc/init.d`.
  Test: none required; "normally" only, so a test must not require links.

**rc0.8-9** [OSF/1] An `inittab` entry causes `rc0` to run, for example `ss:Ss:wait:/sbin/rc0 shutdown ...` and `s0:0:wait:/sbin/rc0 off ...` with stdin/stdout/stderr on `/dev/console`.
  Test: check `/etc/inittab` has entries invoking `/sbin/rc0`.

**rc0.8-10** [OSF/1] Typical operations: notify users of the shutdown; sync the disks; stop system services and daemons; stop processes; kill processes; unmount file systems; invoke `init` if shutting down to single user.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a shutdown.

**rc0.8-11** [OSF/1] `killall` sends `SIGTERM` to stop running processes, followed by `SIGKILL` to kill all processes except the one that initiated the call.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a shutdown.

**rc0.8-12** [OSF/1] `umount -a` unmounts all file systems except the root file system.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a shutdown.

**rc0.8-13** [OSF/1] Files: `/sbin/rc0` is the command path; `/sbin/rc0.d` is the directory of commands for the run level.
  Test: check both exist.

Related: Commands: init(8), killall(8), rc2(8), rc3(8), shutdown(8)

### rc2(8)

Page: `man8/rc2.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**rc2.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `rc2`.
  Test: check `/sbin/rc2` exists and is executable.

**rc2.8-2** [OSF/1] `rc2` contains run commands that initialize the system to a multiuser state, run level 2.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a run-level change.

**rc2.8-3** [OSF/1] Besides its own commands, `rc2` runs certain commands found in `/sbin/rc2.d`.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a run-level change.

**rc2.8-4** [OSF/1] The script defines conditions: some commands run if the system is booting, others if it is changing run levels.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires boot or run-level change.

**rc2.8-5** [OSF/1] By convention, files in `/sbin/rc2.d` begin with `K` or `S`, followed by a two-digit number and a file name (e.g. `K00lpd`, `S00savecore`, `S25uucp`).
  Test: list `/sbin/rc2.d` and check the naming.

**rc2.8-6** [OSF/1] In general, `S` commands are started and `K` commands stopped; `K` commands run only when changing from a higher to a lower run level; `S` commands run in all cases.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires run-level changes.

**rc2.8-7** [OSF/1] The numbers are sorted and the commands run in ascending order.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a run-level change.

**rc2.8-8** [OSF/1] Files in `/sbin/rc2.d` are normally links to files in `/etc/init.d`.
  Test: none required; "normally" only, so a test must not require links.

**rc2.8-9** [OSF/1] An `inittab` entry runs `rc2`, for example `s2:23:wait:/sbin/rc2 < /dev/console > /dev/console 2>&1`.
  Test: check `/etc/inittab` has an entry invoking `/sbin/rc2`.

**rc2.8-10** [OSF/1] Typical operations, depending on the state entered or left: setting the time zone; checking the current run level; stopping network services and daemons; starting (or stopping) system services and daemons; starting the cron daemon; setting up paging and dump facilities; setting up uucp files.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a run-level change.

**rc2.8-11** [OSF/1] Setting the `TIMEZONE` variable is one of the first operations of `rc2`, giving the default time zone for later commands.
  Test: inspect `/sbin/rc2` and check `TIMEZONE` is set near the start.

**rc2.8-12** [OSF/1] Files: `/sbin/rc2` is the command path; `/sbin/rc2.d` is the directory of commands for the run level.
  Test: check both exist.

Related: Commands: init(8), rc0(8), rc3(8)
