### reboot(8)

Page: `man8/reboot.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**reboot.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `reboot [-lnq]`.
  Test: check `/usr/sbin/reboot` exists; running it is not testable from user space (restarts the machine).

**reboot.8-2** [OSF/1] By default `reboot` stops all running processes, syncs the disks, logs the reboot, and writes a shutdown entry in `/var/adm/wtmp`.
  Test: after `reboot` on a test machine, check `/var/adm/wtmp` has a shutdown entry and syslog has a reboot message.

**reboot.8-3** [OSF/1] `-l`: does not log the reboot using syslog.
  Test: after `reboot -l`, check no reboot message was logged.

**reboot.8-4** [OSF/1] `-n`: does not sync the disks or log the reboot using syslog.
  Test: after `reboot -n`, check no reboot message was logged.

**reboot.8-5** [OSF/1] `-q`: quick reboot without first shutting down running processes; does not log the reboot using syslog.
  Test: after `reboot -q`, check no reboot message and processes received no termination signal.

**reboot.8-6** [OSF/1] Advice: with multiple users logged in, use `shutdown -r`; if no users are logged in, use `reboot`.
  Test: Not testable; advice only.

**reboot.8-7** [OSF/1] `reboot` uses the `sync` call to synchronize the disks and performs other shutdown activities such as resynchronizing the hardware time-of-day clock; then the system reboots.
  Test: write a file, `reboot`, check the file's data survived.

**reboot.8-8** [OSF/1] By default the system starts and file systems are automatically checked; if start-up succeeds, the system comes up in the default run level.
  Test: after reboot, check `fsck` ran and the run level is the default.

**reboot.8-9** [OSF/1] Root privileges are required to use `reboot`.
  Test: run `reboot` as a non-root user; expect refusal and no reboot.

**reboot.8-10** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/sbin/reboot` (command path), `/var/adm/wtmp` (login accounting file), `/usr/sbin/syslogd` (syslog daemon).
  Test: check the files exist.

**reboot.8-11** [OSF/1] CAUTIONS: using `-n` can result in file system damage.
  Test: Not testable; warning only.

Related: Commands: fsck(8), halt(8), init(8), shutdown(8), syslogd(8). Functions: sync(2), syslog(3)

### savecore(8)

Page: `man8/savecore.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**savecore.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `savecore [-cfv] directory [system]`.
  Test: run `savecore -v /tmp/crash` as root and check it is accepted.

**savecore.8-2** [OSF/1] `savecore` saves the most recent core dump of the system and writes a reboot message in the shutdown log.
  Test: after a crash dump, run `savecore dir`; check dump files and a log message.
Note: The page text runs this sentence into the SYNOPSIS line.

**savecore.8-3** [OSF/1] `-c`: does not copy the dump, only marks it invalid.
  Test: `savecore -c dir`; no `vmcore.n` written, and a later `savecore dir` finds no valid dump.

**savecore.8-4** [OSF/1] `-f`: copies the dump even if it appears invalid; if both `-c` and `-f` are given, `-f` is ignored.
  Test: `savecore -cf dir` behaves as `-c`.

**savecore.8-5** [OSF/1] `-v`: prints more verbose information.
  Test: compare output of `savecore -v dir` and `savecore dir`.

**savecore.8-6** [OSF/1] `savecore` is usually invoked during system startup, before the dump partition is accessed.
  Test: none required; "usually" only.

**savecore.8-7** [OSF/1] `savecore` checks that a dump was made recently (during the last 3 days) and that there is enough space to save it; `-f` overrides these conditions.
  Test: with a dump older than 3 days, `savecore dir` does not save it; `savecore -f dir` does.

**savecore.8-8** [OSF/1] The dump and the system (default `/vmunix`) are saved in `directory` as `vmcore.n` and `vmunix.n`.
  Test: after `savecore dir`, check `dir/vmcore.n` and `dir/vmunix.n` exist.

**savecore.8-9** [OSF/1] n is the number in `directory/bounds`, incremented by `savecore`; if the file does not exist it is created and initialized with 0.
  Test: with no `bounds` file, run `savecore`; check files `.0` are written and `bounds` now holds the next number.

**savecore.8-10** [OSF/1] `directory/minfree` gives the minimum number of kilobytes to leave free on the file system containing `directory` after the dump is taken; default 0.
  Test: set `minfree` above free space; `savecore dir` does not save the dump.

**savecore.8-11** [OSF/1] `savecore` logs a reboot message using facility `LOG_CRIT`; if the crash was a panic, it also logs the panic string.
  Test: after a panic, run `savecore` and check syslog for the reboot message and panic string.
Note: The page says "facility LOG_CRIT"; `LOG_CRIT` is normally a priority level, not a facility.

**savecore.8-12** [OSF/1] If the dump was from a system other than `/vmunix`, its name must be supplied as the `system` argument.
  Test: boot `/vmunix.alt`, crash, run `savecore dir /vmunix.alt`; check `vmunix.n` is a copy of it.

**savecore.8-13** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/sbin/savecore` (command path); `/vmunix` (current system); `directory/bounds` (number of next dump files); `directory/minfree` (minimum kilobytes left after a dump).
  Test: check `/usr/sbin/savecore` exists.

**savecore.8-14** [DEC] (ULTRIX Compatibility) `-e`: saves only the kernel syslog message buffer from the dump; core and namelist images are not saved.
  Test: `savecore -e dir`; check no `vmcore.n`/`vmunix.n` is written but the msgbuf file is.

**savecore.8-15** [DEC] `savecore` attempts to save the kernel syslog message buffer from the dump; the `msgbuf.err` entry in `/etc/syslog.conf` gives the file name and location.
  Test: set the `msgbuf.err` entry to a path, run `savecore` after a crash; check the file appears there.

**savecore.8-16** [DEC] The default `/etc/syslog.conf` specification is `msgbuf.err /var/adm/crash/msgbuf.savecore`.
  Test: check the default `/etc/syslog.conf` contains that line.

**savecore.8-17** [DEC] If no `msgbuf.err` entry is in `/etc/syslog.conf`, the msgbuf dump file is not saved.
  Test: remove the entry, run `savecore` after a crash; no msgbuf file is written.

**savecore.8-18** [DEC] The msgbuf dump file can not be forwarded to any system.
  Test: set `msgbuf.err` to `@host`; check no file is sent.

**savecore.8-19** [DEC] Syslog messages left unprocessed by a crash are recovered on the next reboot: `savecore` runs during reboot, checks for a core dump, and saves the message buffer.
  Test: Not testable from user space; requires a crash.

**savecore.8-20** [DEC] When `syslogd` initializes it checks for the msgbuf dump file; if found, it processes the file and then deletes it.
  Test: place a msgbuf file at the configured path, start `syslogd`; check messages logged and the file removed.

Related: Functions: syslog(3)

### startup(8)

Page: `man8/startup.html`. The page's NAME line covers acct, chargefee, ckpacct, dodisk, lastlogin, monacct, nulladm, prctmp, prdaily, prtacct, remove, shutacct, startup, turnacct.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**startup.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `chargefee User Number`; `ckpacct [BlockSize]`; `dodisk [-o] [File ....]`; `lastlogin`; `monacct [Number]`; `nulladm [File ....]`; `prctmp File ....`; `prdaily [[-l] [mmdd]] | [-c]`; `prtacct [-f Specification] [-v] File ['Heading']`; `remove`; `shutacct ['Reason']`; `startup`; `turnacct on | off | switch`.
  Test: check each exists under `/usr/sbin/acct/` and accepts its forms.

**startup.8-2** [OSF/1] There are 13 commands in the `/usr/sbin/acct/*` group; with other accounting commands they produce system accounting records and files.
  Test: list `/usr/sbin/acct/` and check the 13 named commands are present.
Note: The page's NAME line lists 14 names (including `acct`); the SYNOPSIS gives 13 commands.

**startup.8-3** [OSF/1] Many `acct/*` commands produce daily accounting records when called by `runacct`; some are called when activity is interrupted and must restart or when active files grow too large; others are for occasional administrator use.
  Test: Not testable as a single behaviour; descriptive.

**startup.8-4** [OSF/1] Periodic accounting files are usually produced by `acct/*` commands in a crontabs file processed by `cron`; they are records produced at the end of any process and on a daily and monthly basis.
  Test: check `/usr/spool/cron/crontabs/adm` can run them.

**startup.8-5** [OSF/1] A prime-time period may be specified for any 24-hour weekday: the contiguous hours for which premium fees might be charged; non-prime time is the other contiguous hours, plus weekends and holidays listed in `/usr/sbin/acct/holidays`.
  Test: list a holiday in `/usr/sbin/acct/holidays`; check usage on that day is counted as non-prime.

**startup.8-6** [OSF/1] Recommended setup: entries in `/usr/spool/cron/crontabs/adm` to run `dodisk` (disk-usage accounting) and `ckpacct` (check `/var/adm/pacct` size), usually daily in non-prime time, and `monacct` to produce monthly summaries in `/var/adm/acct/fiscal` from the daily files.
  Test: Not testable; setup advice.

**startup.8-7** [OSF/1] `chargefee User Number` charges Number units to login name User; Number may be an integer or a decimal value.
  Test: `chargefee smith 10` and `chargefee smith 2.5`; both succeed.

**startup.8-8** [OSF/1] `chargefee` writes a record to `/var/adm/fee`; this is then merged with other accounting records by `acctmerg` to create a daily `/var/adm/fee` report.
  Test: after `chargefee smith 10`, check a new record for smith in `/var/adm/fee`.

**startup.8-9** [OSF/1] `chargefee` uses `printpw` to get the list of all users in the password database.
  Test: Not testable directly; the page states only that `printpw` is used.
Note: The page does not say what happens for an unknown user.

**startup.8-10** [OSF/1] `ckpacct [BlockSize]` checks the size of `/var/adm/pacct`; normally run by `cron`.
  Test: run `ckpacct` with a small `pacct`; nothing changes.

**startup.8-11** [OSF/1] When the active data files exceed BlockSize blocks, `ckpacct` invokes `turnacct switch`; default BlockSize is 500.
  Test: make `pacct` larger than 10 blocks, run `ckpacct 10`; check a new `pacctn` exists and a fresh `pacct` was started.
Note: The page says `turnacct switch` is invoked "to turn off process accounting", but `switch` is described elsewhere as starting a new file and restarting accounting.

**startup.8-12** [OSF/1] When free disk blocks in the `var` file system fall below 500, `ckpacct` inhibits accounting via `turnacct off`; when at least 500 free blocks are available again, accounting is reactivated. This is sensitive to how often `ckpacct` runs.
  Test: fill `/var` to under 500 free blocks, run `ckpacct`; check accounting off; free space, run again; check it is on.

**startup.8-13** [OSF/1] If `MAILCOM` is set to `mail root adm`, a mail message is sent to root and adm on error.
  Test: set `MAILCOM`, provoke an error in `ckpacct`; check mail for root and adm.

**startup.8-14** [OSF/1] `dodisk` starts disk-usage accounting by calling `diskusg` and `acctdisk`; normally run by `cron`.
  Test: run `dodisk` and check disk accounting output is produced.

**startup.8-15** [OSF/1] `dodisk -o` calls `acctdusg` instead of `diskusg`, for slower, more thorough accounting by login directory.
  Test: run `dodisk -o` and check `acctdusg` is invoked.

**startup.8-16** [OSF/1] By default `dodisk` accounts on special files recorded in `/etc/fstab`; with File arguments, only those files are accounted.
  Test: `dodisk /dev/rz0a` and check only that file system is reported.

**startup.8-17** [OSF/1] Without `-o`, File should be special file names of mountable file systems; with `-o` and Files, File should be mount points of mounted file systems.
  Test: `dodisk -o /usr` reports for `/usr`.

**startup.8-18** [OSF/1] `lastlogin` updates `/var/adm/acct/sum/loginlog` to show the last date each user logged in; normally called by `runacct` under `cron`, which adds the information to the daily report, but may be run by the administrator. It uses `printpw` to get users from the password database.
  Test: log in as a user, run `lastlogin`; check the user's date in `loginlog`.

**startup.8-19** [OSF/1] `monacct` collects daily or periodic records into summary files in `/var/adm/acct/fiscal`; after that it removes the old files from `/var/adm/acct/sum`, replaces them with the new summary files, and restarts new summary files in `/var/adm/acct/sum`.
  Test: run `monacct`; check new files in `fiscal` and `sum` reset.

**startup.8-20** [OSF/1] `cron` should run `monacct` once a month, on the first day of the following month or another day after all dailies are produced.
  Test: Not testable; advice only.

**startup.8-21** [OSF/1] `monacct` Number is the month whose daily files are processed, in the range "1 < n < 12"; default is the current month.
  Test: `monacct 3` processes March files; `monacct` with no argument uses the current month.
Note: The page states the range as 1 < n < 12, which would exclude months 1 and 12; probably 1 to 12 is meant.

**startup.8-22** [OSF/1] `nulladm File` creates the file, gives read and write permission to owner and group and read permission to others (mode 0664), and makes owner and group `adm`. Used by accounting procedures and to set up files such as `/var/adm/wtmp`.
  Test: `nulladm /tmp/x`; `stat` shows mode 0664, owner and group `adm`.

**startup.8-23** [OSF/1] `prctmp File` outputs the session record file created by `acctcon1` (normally `/var/adm/acct/nite/ctmp`).
  Test: `prctmp /var/adm/acct/nite/ctmp` prints its records.

**startup.8-24** [OSF/1] `prdaily` is invoked from `runacct` to format an ASCII file of the previous day's accounting data, from `/var/adm/acct/sum/rprtmmdd`; mmdd selects a date other than the current day.
  Test: `prdaily 0102` prints the contents for January 2.

**startup.8-25** [OSF/1] `prdaily -c` reports exceptional resource usage by command; only for the current day's records.
  Test: `prdaily -c` prints a by-command exception report.

**startup.8-26** [OSF/1] `prdaily -l [mmdd]` reports exceptional usage by login ID for the date.
  Test: `prdaily -l 0102` prints a by-login exception report.

**startup.8-27** [OSF/1] `prtacct` formats and displays any total accounting (`tacct`) file named by File, to the default output device; Heading (in single or double quotes) gives a report title.
  Test: `prtacct /var/adm/acct/sum/tacct 'Daily'` prints a report headed "Daily".

**startup.8-28** [OSF/1] `prtacct -f Specification` selects `tacct` members to output, using the member selection mechanism of `acctmerg`.
  Test: `prtacct -f 1,2 file` prints only the selected fields.

**startup.8-29** [OSF/1] `prtacct -v` gives verbose output with more precise floating-point notation.
  Test: compare `prtacct -v` and `prtacct` output precision.

**startup.8-30** [OSF/1] The `tacct` structure (in `tacct.h`) defines a total accounting record; members declared as an array of two doubles hold prime-time and non-prime values.
  Test: compile a program using `struct tacct` and check the arrays have 2 elements.

**startup.8-31** [OSF/1] `uid_t ta_uid`: user ID.
  Test: check the member type with a compile test.

**startup.8-32** [OSF/1] `char ta_name[NSZ]`: login name, with the same number of characters `NSZ` as `ut_user` in `utmp`.
  Test: check `sizeof(ta_name) == sizeof(((struct utmp*)0)->ut_user)`.

**startup.8-33** [OSF/1] `double ta_cpu[2]`: cumulative CPU time in minutes.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-34** [OSF/1] `double ta_kcore[2]`: cumulative k-core time in minutes.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-35** [OSF/1] `double ta_io[2]`: cumulative number of characters transferred in blocks of 512 bytes.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-36** [OSF/1] `double ta_rw[2]`: cumulative number of blocks read and written.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-37** [OSF/1] `double ta_con[2]`: cumulative connect time in minutes.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-38** [OSF/1] `double ta_du`: cumulative disk-usage time in minutes.
  Test: compile test of type.
Note: The page calls disk usage a "time in minutes"; this seems odd for disk usage.

**startup.8-39** [OSF/1] `long ta_qsys`: queueing system (printer) fee in number of pages.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-40** [OSF/1] `double ta_fee`: special services fee in units.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-41** [OSF/1] `long ta_pc`: count of processes.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-42** [OSF/1] `unsigned short ta_sc`: count of login sessions.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-43** [OSF/1] `unsigned short ta_dc`: count of disk samples.
  Test: compile test of type.

**startup.8-44** [OSF/1] `remove` deletes all `/var/adm/acct/sum/wtmp*`, `/var/adm/acct/sum/pacct*`, and `/var/adm/acct/nite/lock*` files, as part of the daily cleanup called by `runacct`.
  Test: create such files, run `remove`; check they are gone.

**startup.8-45** [OSF/1] `shutacct ['Reason']` turns process accounting off and adds a Reason record to `/var/adm/wtmp`; usually invoked during shutdown.
  Test: `shutacct test`; check accounting is off and `wtmp` has a record with "test".

**startup.8-46** [OSF/1] `startup` turns on the accounting functions and adds a reason record to `/var/adm/wtmp`; usually called from `/etc/rc` at system start-up (e.g. `/bin/su - adm -c /usr/sbin/acct/startup`).
  Test: run `startup` as adm; check accounting is on and `wtmp` has a new record.

**startup.8-47** [OSF/1] The `startup` procedure records the time and cleans up the records produced the previous day.
  Test: create previous-day records, run `startup`, check they are cleaned up.

**startup.8-48** [OSF/1] `turnacct` is an interface to `accton` to turn process accounting on or off, or to create a new `/var/adm/pacctn` file; only a superuser or the `adm` login may run it; only one of `on`, `off`, `switch` may be given.
  Test: run `turnacct on` as an ordinary (non-adm) user; expect failure.

**startup.8-49** [OSF/1] `turnacct on` turns process accounting on; `turnacct off` turns it off.
  Test: `turnacct on`, run a command, check `/var/adm/pacct` grows; `turnacct off`, check it does not.

**startup.8-50** [OSF/1] `turnacct switch` creates a new `/var/adm/pacctn` when the current one is too large; n (a positive integer) marks the previous active file; after renaming, a new active `/var/adm/pacct` is created and accounting restarts.
  Test: `turnacct switch`; check `/var/adm/pacctN` exists with old data and a new empty `pacct` is in use.

**startup.8-51** [OSF/1] `turnacct` is usually called by `ckpacct` under `cron` to keep `pacct` a manageable size.
  Test: as for startup.8-11.

**startup.8-52** [OSF/1] NOTES: accounting files should not be shared among nodes in a distributed environment; each node should have its own copy.
  Test: Not testable; advice only.

**startup.8-53** [OSF/1] NOTES: when also using `sa`, `sa` does not know whether information is in the incremental `/var/adm/pacctn` file or in another `/var/adm/pacctn` summary file made by the `acct/*` commands.
  Test: Not testable; informational.

**startup.8-54** [OSF/1] Examples: crontab lines `5 * * * * /usr/sbin/acct/ckpacct` (5 minutes past every hour), `0 2 * * 4 /usr/sbin/acct/dodisk` (2 AM each Thursday), `15 5 1 * * /usr/sbin/acct/monacct` (5:15 on the first of each month).
  Test: install these lines in `/usr/spool/cron/crontabs/adm` and check `cron` runs the commands at those times.

**startup.8-55** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/sbin/acct/*` (command path); `/usr/include/sys/acct.h` (accounting structures); `/var/adm/fee` (fees per login); `/var/adm/pacct` (current process accounting file); `/var/adm/pacctn` (another process accounting file produced when `pacct` is too large); `/var/adm/wtmp` (login/logout database); `/usr/sbin/acct/ptelus.awk` (limits for exceptional usage by login ID); `/usr/sbin/acct/ptecms.awk` (limits for exceptional usage by command name); `/var/adm/acct/nite` (daily working directory); `/etc/fstab` (file systems); `/var/adm/acct/sum` (summary subdirectory).
  Test: check each file or directory exists on an installed system.

Related: Commands: acctcms(8), acctcom(8), acctcon(8), acctmerg(8), acctprc(8), fwtmp(8), printpw(8), runacct(8). Daemons: cron(8). Functions: acct(2). Guide to System Administration

### swapon(8)

Page: `man8/swapon.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**swapon.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `swapon [-avp] [-l lowsize] [-h highsize] filename`.
  Test: as root, run `swapon /paging/swapon`; expect success.

**swapon.8-2** [OSF/1] `swapon` specifies additional paging files; calls normally occur during multiuser initialization.
  Test: after `swapon file`, check the paging space increased.

**swapon.8-3** [OSF/1] `-a` activates all devices marked `sw` (swap) in `/etc/fstab`; normally this option is used.
  Test: add an `sw` entry to `/etc/fstab`, run `swapon -a`; check the device is in use for paging.

**swapon.8-4** [OSF/1] `-v` generates verbose output.
  Test: `swapon -v file` prints output.

**swapon.8-5** [OSF/1] `-p` marks the file as preferred; the system pages to a preferred file before a non-preferred one.
  Test: add one preferred and one plain file, cause paging; check the preferred file is used first.

**swapon.8-6** [OSF/1] `-l lowsize` sets the low water mark: once the paging file has grown above it and then shrinks, the system does not make the file smaller than the low water mark. Default 20 Mbytes.
  Test: grow the paging file past `-l`, release memory, check its size does not drop below the mark.

**swapon.8-7** [OSF/1] `-h highsize` sets the high water mark: the system will not expand the paging file beyond it. Default unlimited.
  Test: `swapon -h 64M file`, cause heavy paging, check the file never exceeds 64 MB.

**swapon.8-8** [OSF/1] Sizes may be given with an `M` suffix, e.g. `swapon -l 16M -h 64M /paging/swapon2`.
  Test: run the example and check it is accepted.

**swapon.8-9** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/sbin/swapon` is the command path.
  Test: check it exists.

**swapon.8-10** [OSF/1] NOTES: there is no way to stop paging and swapping on a device, so devices that may be dismounted during operation cannot be used.
  Test: after `swapon` on a device, check no command removes it from paging.

Related: Functions: swapon(2)

### sync(8)

Page: `man8/sync.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sync.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `sync`.
  Test: run `sync`; expect it to complete without error.

**sync.8-2** [OSF/1] `sync` runs the sync system primitive, which writes all unwritten system buffers to disk, including modified inodes and delayed block I/O.
  Test: write a file, run `sync`, then check (e.g. by reading the raw device) that the data is on disk.

**sync.8-3** [OSF/1] Commands that bring the system down, such as `shutdown`, issue their own sync calls; use `sync` when the system must be stopped under unusual circumstances, to ensure file system integrity.
  Test: Not testable; advice only.

**sync.8-4** [OSF/1] Writing of unwritten buffers, although scheduled, is not necessarily complete on return from `sync`; in some circumstances consecutive `sync` commands may be appropriate.
  Test: none required; a test must not assume the write is complete when `sync` returns.

**sync.8-5** [OSF/1] Files: `/usr/sbin/sync` is the command path.
  Test: check it exists.

Related: Functions: sync(2)

### sysconfig(8)

Page: `man8/sysconfig.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**sysconfig.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `sysconfig [-vs] [-c | -u | -q] name`.
  Test: `sysconfig -q name` for a configured subsystem; expect output.

**sysconfig.8-2** [OSF/1] `-c` configures the named subsystem into the running system: it asks the `cfgmgr` daemon to load and configure `name` into the kernel.
  Test: as root, `sysconfig -c name`; check the subsystem is loaded.

**sysconfig.8-3** [OSF/1] `-u` unconfigures the subsystem: it asks `cfgmgr` to deconfigure and unload `name` from the kernel.
  Test: as root, `sysconfig -u name`; check it is unloaded.

**sysconfig.8-4** [OSF/1] `-q` asks `cfgmgr` to query information about the configured subsystem `name`.
  Test: `sysconfig -q name` prints information.

**sysconfig.8-5** [OSF/1] `-v` requests verbose output from `cfgmgr`.
  Test: compare output with and without `-v`.

**sysconfig.8-6** [OSF/1] `-s` requests that output from `cfgmgr` be suppressed.
  Test: `sysconfig -s -q name` prints nothing.

**sysconfig.8-7** [OSF/1] `sysconfig` opens a communications socket to `cfgmgr`, sends the request and receives output back through the socket.
  Test: run `sysconfig -q name` with `cfgmgr` running and check output is returned from it.

**sysconfig.8-8** [OSF/1] `name` is the subsystem name as given in `/etc/sysconfigtab`; `/sbin/sysconfigdb` lists the current names.
  Test: take a name from `sysconfigdb` output and query it with `sysconfig -q`.

**sysconfig.8-9** [OSF/1] Files: `/sbin/sysconfig` (command path), `/sbin/cfgmgr` (configuration daemon), `/etc/sysconfigtab` (configuration database).
  Test: check the files exist.

Related: Commands: cfgmgr(8), sysconfigdb(8). Files: sysconfigtab(4)

### update(8)

Page: `man8/update.html`.
Origin: An OSF reference page (headed "OSF").

**update.8-1** [OSF/1] Synopsis: `update`.
  Test: run `update`; check it is accepted.

**update.8-2** [OSF/1] `update` executes a `sync` system call every 30 seconds, so the file system is up to date if the system crashes.
  Test: run `update` and trace the background process; check `sync` runs about every 30 s.

**update.8-3** [OSF/1] `update` is provided as a script in `/sbin`.
  Test: check `/sbin/update` is a shell script.
Note: The page FILES section gives the path as `/usrsbin/update`, which disagrees with "a script in /sbin"; the text is probably damaged.

**update.8-4** [OSF/1] `cron` also provides the functionality of `update`.
  Test: Not testable; informational.

**update.8-5** [OSF/1] The script typically runs, in the background, a loop of `sync` then `sleep 30`, and then exits with status 0.
  Test: run `update`; check exit status 0 and a background shell remains running.

Related: Commands: cron(8), init(8), sync(8). Functions: sync(2)


## Appendix A — errors DEC changed by DEC OSF/1 3.0 [DEC]

For each section 2 page whose list of errors differs between OSF/1 1.0
and DEC OSF/1 3.0 for Alpha AXP (`typewritten.org/Manual/DEC/OSF:1/3.0/`),
the error numbers only in 1.0 and those 3.0 added. Most additions are
NFS's (`ESTALE`, `EREMOTE`) and DEC's. They are DEC's changes and not
requirements; they show where a test written from 1.0 may meet a later
system's answer. Made by comparing the bracketed error names in each
page's ERRORS section; the conditions were not compared.
